title: Physically Based Rendering in the Latent Space
comment: 15 pages, 12 figures. Pacific Graphics 2026, Journal Track (Computer Graphics Forum). Code: https://github.com/trinity-graphics/latent-rendering
summary: Image diffusion models have shown impressive image generation capabilities but are often hard to control, in contrast to classical computer graphics pipelines such as physically based rendering. However, we observe that there is a bridge between light transport phenomena and the distribution of latent space values produced by such models. Thus, we introduce physically based rendering in the feature space learned by the variational autoencoders in generative models, enabling light transport simulation in the latent space. This allows us to leverage physically based rendering techniques to output latent maps for physically guided content generation. We propose modifications to the rendering equation, which, when paired with a differentiable renderer, can yield an optimal set of scene parameters that require only minimal refinement to accurately render into the pretrained latent space. We train our method on a single rendered image, and then demonstrate the generalization of the method to scene geometry changes, lighting changes, and camera view changes.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces physically based rendering (PBR) into the latent space of generative models (specifically VAEs in diffusion models), enabling light transport simulation for controlled image generation. The method modifies the rendering equation and uses a differentiable renderer to find optimal scene parameters that can be directly mapped to the pretrained latent space.
AI.motivation: Image diffusion models have impressive generation capabilities but lack control compared to classical computer graphics pipelines like physically based rendering. The authors observe a connection between light transport phenomena and latent space values in generative models, which provides an opportunity to bridge these two approaches.
AI.method:
1. Introduce PBR in the feature space learned by VAEs in generative models
2. Enable light transport simulation in latent space
3. Modify the rendering equation for latent space application
4. Use differentiable renderer to find optimal scene parameters
5. Train on a single rendered image
AI.result: The method can output latent maps for physically guided content generation. The approach requires only minimal refinement to accurately render into the pretrained latent space. It demonstrates generalization to scene geometry changes, lighting changes, and camera view changes.
AI.conclusion: This work successfully bridges the gap between diffusion models and physically based rendering by operating in latent space, enabling better control over image generation while maintaining the generative capabilities of diffusion models.

title: GestureFAR: Streaming Co-Speech Gesture Generation with Flow Autoregression
summary: Generating natural co-speech gestures from streaming speech is essential for embodied conversational agents, where motion must be produced while a user is still speaking. Recent streaming gesture systems make online generation possible by autoregressing over discrete motion tokens, but this design compresses high-dimensional continuous motion into finite codebooks and can limit the realism and diversity of generated gestures. To preserve both causality and continuous expressiveness, we propose \textbf{GestureFAR}, a flow-autoregressive framework for streaming co-speech gesture generation. First, GestureFAR autoregresses over causal continuous motion latents, using a transformer to model streaming audio-motion context and a per-token flow-matching head to sample the next latent from a continuous distribution. Second, we introduce a head-only flow distillation strategy that freezes the causal backbone and distills the multi-step per-token flow head into a single network evaluation using consistency and distribution-matching objectives. This keeps the model token-causal while removing the main latency bottleneck for live interaction. Experiments on BEAT2 show that GestureFAR significantly improves the quality--latency trade-off among streaming-capable methods, preserving strong gesture quality while enabling real-time token-causal generation. Project Page: https://andypinxinliu.github.io/GestureFAR

AI.tldr: GestureFAR is a flow-autoregressive framework for real-time co-speech gesture generation that preserves continuous motion expressiveness while maintaining token causality. It uses a transformer with per-token flow-matching head for continuous motion latent sampling, and employs head-only flow distillation to reduce latency for live interaction.
AI.motivation: Existing streaming gesture systems use discrete motion tokens that compress high-dimensional continuous motion into finite codebooks, limiting realism and diversity. The need to preserve both causality and continuous expressiveness in real-time gesture generation for embodied conversational agents motivates this work.
AI.method: 1) Autoregressive framework over causal continuous motion latents using a transformer to model streaming audio-motion context. 2) Per-token flow-matching head to sample next latent from continuous distribution. 3) Head-only flow distillation strategy that freezes causal backbone and distills multi-step per-token flow head into single network evaluation using consistency and distribution-matching objectives.
AI.result: GestureFAR significantly improves quality-latency trade-off among streaming-capable methods on BEAT2 dataset, preserving strong gesture quality while enabling real-time token-causal generation.
AI.conclusion: The flow-autoregressive approach successfully bridges the gap between continuous motion expressiveness and real-time streaming generation, with the distillation strategy effectively removing the latency bottleneck for live interaction.

title: Helpful but Fallible: Developer Experiences of AI Tools Under a Coordinated Industrial Roll-out
summary: AI-enabled software development tools (AI-devtools) are being industrially adopted under strong expectations of productivity gains, yet developers' experiences of such roll-outs are underexplored. Organizations commit budgets, evaluate staff, and revise practice on a partial picture, since the evidence base is mainly tool evaluations, productivity metrics, and surveys, with few qualitative in-situ accounts of ongoing, coordinated roll-outs. We report a case study of a coordinated roll-out of AI-devtools at a large Swedish telecommunications company, investigating how developers experience the roll-out and how they anticipate their profession will change. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 12 software professionals across three sites, analyzed with process coding and thematic analysis, and interpreted through the extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM2) as a post-hoc analytical lens. Our findings on use cases, productivity, frustrations, and tool limitations corroborate prior survey work. Beyond corroboration, the interviews surface a management-developer expectation gap that maps onto the TAM2 constructs of subjective norm and voluntariness, and show that participants weigh perceived risk heavily, a factor that TAM2 and similar acceptance models do not represent. AI-devtools emerge as helpful but fallible assistants whose value is shaped by organizational expectations, system scale, and developers' skills.

title: The Internet Archive Music Dataset
summary: We introduce the Internet Archive Music Dataset (IAMD), a large-scale collection of captioned music segments derived from the Internet Archive. To the best of our knowledge, IAMD constitutes the largest publicly available music-caption dataset to date with over 34,000 hours of audio, providing a valuable benchmark for training and evaluating music understanding and generative models. The dataset is built from content declared to be distributed under Creative Commons licenses, and cross-referencing with MusicBrainz is done to improve license information reliability. To annotate IAMD, we present an automatic captioning pipeline that augments base captions produced by an audio-language model (ALM) with textual metadata sourced from the Internet Archive and imputed metadata obtained using audio classification models. Caption quality is assessed objectively and subjectively, and results indicate that the annotation pipeline is reliable and does not degrade caption quality with scaling.

AI.tldr: IAMD is the largest publicly available music-caption dataset with over 34,000 hours of audio from Internet Archive under Creative Commons licenses. It uses an automatic captioning pipeline combining audio-language model outputs, textual metadata, and imputed metadata from audio classifiers, with quality assessment showing reliable scaling.
AI.motivation: There is a need for large-scale music-caption datasets to train and evaluate music understanding and generative models. Existing datasets are limited in size, and this work aims to provide the largest publicly available benchmark to date.
AI.method: The dataset was constructed by collecting audio from Internet Archive under Creative Commons licenses, with license verification via MusicBrainz cross-referencing. An automatic captioning pipeline was developed combining: (1) base captions from an audio-language model (ALM), (2) textual metadata from Internet Archive, and (3) imputed metadata from audio classification models. Caption quality was evaluated through both objective and subjective assessments.
AI.result: IAMD contains over 34,000 hours of captioned music segments, making it the largest publicly available music-caption dataset. The annotation pipeline demonstrated reliability and maintained caption quality without degradation as the dataset scaled.
AI.conclusion: IAMD provides a valuable benchmark dataset for training and evaluating music understanding and generative models, with a scalable and reliable automatic annotation pipeline.

title: TAPe+ML: A Compact Structured Representation for Multi-Task Computer Vision
comment: 39 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables. Project page: https://ml.comexp.net
summary:
We present TAPe+ML v3, a compact computer vision system based on TAPe (Theory of Active Perception), a structured representation that encodes relations among perceptual elements before recognition. Instead of operating directly on pixel tensors, the system uses a shared TAPe representation and a modular recognition architecture for image classification, object detection, and instance segmentation.
  TAPe+ML v3 combines background and contour processing, local object localization, prototype-based classification, and a coordinator for specialized submodels. Across the reported experiments, it uses fewer than 100,000 parameters. On COCO object detection, it obtains 84.7 mAP50 and 65.3 mAP50-95. On COCO instance segmentation, it obtains 80.7 mask mAP50 and 58.4 mask mAP50-95. In classification experiments, it reaches 92 percent validation accuracy on Imagenette under an identical-training comparison with a raw-pixel baseline, and 89.9 percent Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-Real. We also evaluate compactness in video scene detection and adaptation under distribution shift in an industrial pilot. The results suggest that shifting part of the modeling burden from network parameters to a structured input representation can support compact multi-task vision systems with reduced data, memory, and compute requirements.

AI.tldr: TAPe+ML v3 is a compact computer vision system (<100K parameters) that uses TAPe (Theory of Active Perception) - a structured representation encoding relations among perceptual elements - instead of raw pixel tensors. It performs image classification, object detection, and instance segmentation with state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the inefficiency of traditional deep learning vision systems that operate directly on pixel tensors, requiring large models with massive data, memory, and compute requirements. The authors propose shifting part of the modeling burden from network parameters to a structured input representation.
AI.method: TAPe+ML v3 uses a shared TAPe representation and modular recognition architecture combining: (1) background and contour processing, (2) local object localization, (3) prototype-based classification, and (4) a coordinator for specialized submodels.
AI.result: COCO object detection: 84.7 mAP50 / 65.3 mAP50-95; COCO instance segmentation: 80.7 mask mAP50 / 58.4 mask mAP50-95; Imagenette: 92% validation accuracy; ImageNet-Real: 89.9% Top-1 accuracy. All achieved with fewer than 100,000 parameters.
AI.conclusion: Shifting modeling burden from network parameters to structured input representation (TAPe) can support compact multi-task vision systems with significantly reduced data, memory, and compute requirements while maintaining competitive performance.

title: RBS-Attention: Radius-Bounded Sparse Prefill for Long-Context Large Language Models
summary: Long-context large language model inference is increasingly limited by prefill, where dense self-attention processes the entire prompt before generation begins. Sparse block selection can reduce this cost, but a block centroid may hide a highly relevant token among many irrelevant ones. We call this failure mode mean dilution and propose RBS-Attention, a training-free sparse-prefill method with two complementary selection branches. A centroid base branch captures average relevance, while a rescue branch uses the maximum key-block radius and its prompt-, layer-, and head-dependent distribution to identify blocks at risk of underestimation. Independently thresholding the two branches and combining their masks controls the contribution of rescue blocks while preserving regular block-sparse FlashAttention execution. On H100 GPUs, RBS-Attention achieves 20.65$\times$ standalone prefill-attention speedup, 11.92$\times$ vLLM prefill-attention speedup, and 5.97$\times$ end-to-end time-to-first-token speedup at 128K on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-FP8. On the dense Qwen3-32B model, it obtains 88.65 overall RULER accuracy versus 89.52 for dense attention; LongBench-v2, InfiniteBench, and Video-MME provide additional quality evaluation. Supporting experiments measure actual retention, compare selectors at matched density, and characterize block-size, threshold, and memory behavior. Together, these results support radius-adaptive dual-branch selection as an effective approach to long-context prefill.

AI.tldr: RBS-Attention is a training-free sparse-prefill method that addresses "mean dilution" in long-context LLM inference by using dual-branch selection: a centroid base branch for average relevance and a rescue branch for identifying blocks at risk of underestimation using maximum key-block radius. It achieves up to 20.65× prefill speedup while maintaining quality comparable to dense attention.
AI.motivation: Long-context LLM inference is increasingly limited by the prefill phase, where dense self-attention processes the entire prompt before generation begins. Sparse block selection can reduce this cost, but a block centroid may hide highly relevant tokens among many irrelevant ones - a failure mode called "mean dilution."
AI.method: RBS-Attention uses two complementary selection branches: (1) Centroid base branch captures average relevance; (2) Rescue branch uses maximum key-block radius with its prompt-, layer-, and head-dependent distribution to identify blocks at risk of underestimation. The two branches are independently thresholded and combined to control rescue block contribution while preserving regular block-sparse FlashAttention execution.
AI.result: On H100 GPUs: 20.65× standalone prefill-attention speedup, 11.92× vLLM prefill-attention speedup, and 5.97× end-to-end time-to-first-token speedup at 128K on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-FP8. On dense Qwen3-32B: 88.65 overall RULER accuracy vs 89.52 for dense attention. Quality evaluated on LongBench-v2, InfiniteBench, and Video-MME.
AI.conclusion: Radius-adaptive dual-branch selection (RBS-Attention) is an effective approach to long-context prefill, achieving significant speedups while maintaining quality comparable to dense attention. The rescue branch successfully addresses mean dilution by identifying blocks that would otherwise be underestimated due to centroid averaging.

title: Sparse Priors for Efficient Distribution Learning
summary: Despite the widespread use and success of generative AI techniques today, theoretical guarantees on learning a distribution supported in $d$ dimensions from $n$ samples degrade as $O(n^{-1/Θ(d)})$, though shown to be minimax optimal. We hypothesize that present bounds are too pessimistic because smoothness assumptions are not enough to capture the structure of distributions that often appear in real applications. Consequently, we introduce the class of sparse priors and define the "Sparse Dimension" as a measure of sparsity of a prior over the space of all distributions. We show that distribution learning under a $k$-sparse prior achieves a Bayesian risk lower bound of $Ω(\sqrt{k/n})$ under common distance metrics, and show a matching (up to logarithmic terms asymptotically in $n,k$) upper bound for the TV distance under mild additional assumptions. We show the statistical equivalence of distribution learning and learning to sample in the Bayesian setting so that our results apply to learning to sample as well. While $k$ can still depend on the dimension $d$, or a notion of intrinsic dimension, our results show that learning under an appropriate prior overcomes the curse of dimensionality with respect to the dependence on $n$.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the curse of dimensionality in distribution learning for generative AI. The authors argue that standard smoothness assumptions lead to pessimistic bounds (O(n^{-1/Θ(d)})) and propose "sparse priors" with a "Sparse Dimension" measure to capture structure in real-world distributions. They prove a lower bound of Ω(√(k/n)) and matching upper bound for TV distance, showing that appropriate priors can overcome the curse of dimensionality.
AI.motivation: The authors hypothesize that current minimax optimal bounds for learning distributions supported in d dimensions from n samples are too pessimistic because smoothness assumptions fail to capture the structure of real-world distributions. They seek to develop a framework that better reflects practical distribution learning scenarios.
AI.method: The authors introduce the class of sparse priors and define "Sparse Dimension" as a measure of sparsity over the space of all distributions. They use information-theoretic and statistical learning techniques to derive lower bounds and upper bounds on the Bayesian risk, establishing equivalence between distribution learning and learning to sample in the Bayesian setting.
AI.result: The key results are: (1) A Bayesian risk lower bound of Ω(√(k/n)) under k-sparse priors for common distance metrics; (2) A matching upper bound (up to logarithmic terms asymptotically in n and k) for TV distance under mild assumptions; (3) Statistical equivalence between distribution learning and learning to sample in the Bayesian setting.
AI.conclusion: Learning under an appropriate sparse prior can overcome the curse of dimensionality with respect to sample complexity dependence. While k may still depend on dimension d or intrinsic dimension, the results demonstrate that the pessimistic O(n^{-1/Θ(d)}) dependence can be improved when the underlying distribution has sparse structure.

title: Embedding Drift in Code Vulnerability Models Under Intended Behaviour-Preserving Transformations
summary: Code edits that preserve program behaviour can shift frozen code embeddings across classifier decision boundaries, causing correctly detected vulnerabilities to be predicted as benign. Such instability is problematic because semantically neutral changes, including comment removal, insertion of unreachable code, variable renaming, and loop rewriting, should not alter a model's security judgment. We investigate this issue using 15,000 C/C++ functions organized as 7,500 vulnerable-patched pairs from the Big-Vul dataset. Four mutation tracks are applied to both vulnerable and benign samples: comment removal, unreachable code insertion, variable renaming, loop rewriting, and a combined setting that applies all transformations. Using frozen microsoft/codebert-base embeddings with six downstream classifiers, we evaluate the robustness of vulnerability predictions and introduce a train-only defence that projects clean and mutated representations closer together while preserving vulnerability-class information. Under combined mutations, the baseline Vulnerable Flip Rate (VFR) ranges from 35.55% to 42.15%. The proposed defence reduces the mean common-set VFR from 22.60% to 11.32% and improves mean mutated accuracy from 55.33% to 57.10%. For Logistic Regression, VFR decreases by 17.29 percentage points, although benign-to-vulnerable flips increase by 11.95 percentage points. These results indicate that the defence improves robustness to semantics-preserving code transformations but introduces a false-positive trade-off and does not fully eliminate prediction instability.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how semantically neutral code transformations (comment removal, unreachable code insertion, variable renaming, loop rewriting) can cause vulnerability detection models to incorrectly flip their predictions. Using 15,000 C/C++ functions from Big-Vul dataset with CodeBERT embeddings, the study shows baseline Vulnerable Flip Rates (VFR) of 35.55-42.15% under combined mutations. A proposed defence reduces mean VFR from 22.60% to 11.32% but introduces a false-positive trade-off.
AI.motivation: Code transformations that preserve semantics (like comment removal or variable renaming) should not alter security judgments, but they can shift frozen code embeddings across classifier decision boundaries, causing correctly detected vulnerabilities to be misclassified as benign. This instability is a significant robustness concern for vulnerability detection models.
AI.method: The study uses 15,000 C/C++ functions organized as 7,500 vulnerable-patched pairs from Big-Vul dataset. Four mutation tracks are applied: comment removal, unreachable code insertion, variable renaming, loop rewriting, and a combined setting. Frozen microsoft/codebert-base embeddings are extracted and fed to six downstream classifiers. A train-only defence is proposed that projects clean and mutated representations closer together while preserving vulnerability-class information.
AI.result: Under combined mutations, baseline VFR ranges from 35.55% to 42.15%. The defence reduces mean common-set VFR from 22.60% to 11.32% and improves mean mutated accuracy from 55.33% to 57.10%. For Logistic Regression specifically, VFR decreases by 17.29 percentage points, though benign-to-vulnerable flips increase by 11.95 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: The proposed defence improves robustness to semantics-preserving code transformations but introduces a false-positive trade-off and does not fully eliminate prediction instability. The approach reduces vulnerability flip rates significantly but at the cost of increased false positives.

title: Composer2Vec: A Continuous Embedding Space of Composer Style Learned from Symbolic Melody Generation
summary: We analyze the composer embeddings learned by a composer-conditioned Transformer as a continuous latent space of compositional style, rather than merely as an internal representation for generation. A model that recursively predicts melody continuations was trained on melodic sequences extracted from MIDI data, conditioned on composer identity (124 composers). Principal component analysis of the learned composer embedding matrix (124x128) shows that the first principal component correlates strongly with composer birth year (r = -0.884, p < 0.001, n = 123), a stronger correlation than we obtain by applying the same PC1-birth-year analysis to existing general-purpose audio-text embeddings (CLAP, MuQ-MuLan) trained on unrelated audio-text corpora, not on symbolic melody generation. A shuffle test (2,000 permutations) confirms that the Silhouette score for stylistic-period labels is statistically significant (0.0110, p < 0.001). We further show that vector arithmetic in the embedding space captures meaningful stylistic relationships between composers. These results suggest that composer embeddings, learned without supervision beyond composer identity, form an interpretable latent space that captures musical-historical structure.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether composer embeddings learned by a composer-conditioned Transformer model (trained on melodic sequences from 124 composers) can serve as an interpretable latent space for compositional style analysis, rather than just being an internal representation for melody generation.
AI.motivation: The researchers aimed to explore whether composer embeddings, learned without supervision beyond composer identity during symbolic melody generation, can capture meaningful musical-historical structure and serve as an interpretable latent space for analyzing compositional style.
AI.method: A Transformer model that recursively predicts melody continuations was trained on melodic sequences extracted from MIDI data, conditioned on 124 composers. Principal component analysis was applied to the learned composer embedding matrix (124×128). The first principal component was correlated with composer birth year and compared with correlations from general-purpose audio-text embeddings (CLAP, MuQ-MuLan). A shuffle test with 2,000 permutations was used to assess the statistical significance of the Silhouette score for stylistic-period labels.
AI.result: The first principal component (PC1) correlates strongly with composer birth year (r = -0.884, p < 0.001, n = 123), which is a stronger correlation than obtained from general-purpose audio-text embeddings (CLAP, MuQ-MuLan). The shuffle test confirms that the Silhouette score for stylistic-period labels (0.0110) is statistically significant (p < 0.001). Additionally, vector arithmetic in the embedding space captures meaningful stylistic relationships between composers.
AI.conclusion: Composer embeddings learned without supervision beyond composer identity form an interpretable latent space that captures musical-historical structure, suggesting that symbolic melody generation models can learn meaningful stylistic representations.

title: MemeTAG: Keyword-Driven Meme Classification through Tag Embedding Reconstruction
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures; published in the Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV), 2026
summary: The proliferation of harmful internet memes poses a significant societal threat, yet their automated classification remains a formidable algorithmic challenge due to the nuanced, multimodal nature of their content. To address this, we introduce MemeTAG, a novel dual-objective framework that pioneers a keyword-aware approach to meme classification. Our core innovation is a two-part semantic guidance mechanism: first, we leverage a pretrained Vision-Language Model to generate a set of descriptive keywords, that capture the high-level semantics. Second, we introduce the Aggregated Tag Inference Network (ATIN), an attention-based module that distills these keywords into a single, rich semantic embedding. This embedding serves as a target for a novel auxiliary reconstruction loss, which compels the model to learn deeply aligned visual and textual features. This approach, combined with an efficient three-stage training strategy, establishes a new state-of-the-art on the HarMeme, Hateful Memes Challenge (HMC), and PrideMM datasets, decisively outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: MemeTAG is a novel dual-objective framework for harmful internet meme classification that uses a Vision-Language Model to generate descriptive keywords and an attention-based module (ATIN) to distill these into semantic embeddings, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of harmful internet memes poses a significant societal threat, yet their automated classification remains challenging due to the nuanced, multimodal nature of their content.
AI.method: The framework employs a two-part semantic guidance mechanism: (1) a pretrained Vision-Language Model generates descriptive keywords capturing high-level semantics; (2) the Aggregated Tag Inference Network (ATIN), an attention-based module, distills these keywords into a single rich semantic embedding. This embedding serves as a target for a novel auxiliary reconstruction loss that enforces deep alignment between visual and textual features. The approach uses an efficient three-stage training strategy.
AI.result: MemeTAG establishes a new state-of-the-art on the HarMeme, Hateful Memes Challenge (HMC), and PrideMM datasets, decisively outperforming existing methods.
AI.conclusion: The keyword-aware dual-objective approach with ATIN and auxiliary reconstruction loss effectively addresses the multimodal challenge in harmful meme classification, demonstrating superior performance across multiple benchmark datasets.

title: Attention-Aware Routing: Coupling Routing and Attention in MoEs
summary: In Mixture-of-Experts language models, the router typically selects and weights experts based on the token's hidden state, utilizing limited contextual information. We propose Attention-Aware Routing (AAR), which augments the router with temporal and spectral features extracted from a sliding window of attention weights that represent a summary of the model's contextual state, disentangled from the hidden state. Keeping the base transformer entirely frozen, we train only the routing parameters, isolating routing as the sole variable. AAR improves GSM8K by +3.37 pp over a routing-only SFT baseline on OLMoE. Beyond performance, we show that routing and attention form a coupled circuit: routing changes at layer l propagate through the residual stream to amplify attention sinks at layer l+1, reshaping attention without any direct update to the attention mechanism itself. Further, AAR reduces long diverging generation, with incorrect answers getting shorter, while correct answers remain unchanged in length. Finally, AAR is strongly depth-sensitive: applying it indiscriminately across layers can degrade factual retrieval, whereas mathematical reasoning gains persist when it is introduced deeper in the network. This sensitivity exposes a retrieval--reasoning tension across depth and makes layer-selective AAR a controlled probe of the routing-relevant information carried by attention at different layers.

AI.tldr: AAR augments MoE routers with temporal and spectral features from attention weights, improving math reasoning by +3.37 pp on GSM8K while revealing depth-sensitive trade-offs between factual retrieval and reasoning.
AI.motivation: Current MoE routers rely on limited contextual information from token hidden states. This work proposes enriching routing decisions with attention-derived features that capture broader contextual state without modifying the base transformer.
AI.method: Extract temporal and spectral features from a sliding window of attention weights to augment the router. Keep the base transformer entirely frozen; train only routing parameters, isolating routing as the sole variable.
AI.result: AAR improves GSM8K by +3.37 pp over routing-only SFT baseline on OLMoE. It reduces long diverging generation (incorrect answers become shorter while correct answers remain unchanged). The method is strongly depth-sensitive: mathematical reasoning gains persist when applied deeper, while factual retrieval degrades with indiscriminate application across layers.
AI.conclusion: Attention-Aware Routing effectively enhances MoE routing by leveraging attention-derived features. Routing and attention form a coupled circuit where routing changes propagate through the residual stream to reshape attention. Layer-selective application exposes a retrieval-reasoning tension across depth, making AAR a controlled probe of routing-relevant information in attention at different layers.

title: BI-Agent and BI-Bench: Towards Automating End-to-End Business Intelligence
comment: code and data are available at \url{https://github.com/Hu-Chuxuan/bi-agent}
summary:
Business intelligence (BI) is a cornerstone of enterprise decision-making and is widely used by enterprise users in software such as Power BI and Tableau. In traditional BI workflows, users need to prepare data by (1) identifying relevant tables, (2) performing data transformations, and (3) building join relationships, before they can (4) answer their business questions. These steps can be complex and time-consuming, making BI challenging.
  Given the strong capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in working with data, we study their ability to answer BI questions end-to-end, without requiring users to manually perform the tedious preparation steps. To do this, we harvest a large collection of real-world BI projects from public sources, and manually extract pairs of (questions, ground-truth answers) from real user dashboards. The resulting benchmark, BI-Bench, is the first benchmark to systematically study LLMs' ability on end-to-end BI.
  We find that even frontier LLMs perform poorly on BI-Bench, with less than 50% accuracy. To address their limitations, we design a tool-augmented BI-Agent that decomposes BI workflows into subtasks on structured data, such as search, join, and transform, and orchestrates specialized data management methods across BI stages. Furthermore, we develop a post-training framework that synthesizes training trajectories from real BI projects, enabling BI-Agent to be further post-trained using both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). BI-Agent achieves substantial accuracy gains of up to 40 percentage points with vanilla LLMs, and post-trained BI-Agent yields gains of up to 30 points. Our results highlight the importance of combining tool-augmented reasoning with domain-specific post-training in complex BI workflows, and point to promising directions for future research.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BI-Bench, the first benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to answer Business Intelligence questions end-to-end without manual data preparation. It also proposes BI-Agent, a tool-augmented system that decomposes BI workflows into specialized subtasks, which can be further improved through post-training with SFT and RL. The method achieves up to 40 percentage points accuracy improvement over vanilla LLMs.
AI.motivation: Traditional BI workflows require users to manually perform complex and time-consuming data preparation steps (identifying tables, data transformations, building join relationships) before answering business questions. This complexity makes BI challenging for enterprise users. The motivation is to leverage LLMs' capabilities to automate this entire process end-to-end.
AI.method: 1) Collected real-world BI projects from public sources and extracted (question, ground-truth answer) pairs from user dashboards to create BI-Bench benchmark; 2) Designed BI-Agent that decomposes BI workflows into subtasks (search, join, transform) and orchestrates specialized data management methods across BI stages; 3) Developed post-training framework using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) on training trajectories synthesized from real BI projects.
AI.result: Even frontier LLMs perform poorly on BI-Bench with less than 50% accuracy. BI-Agent achieves substantial accuracy gains of up to 40 percentage points compared to vanilla LLMs. The post-trained BI-Agent yields additional gains of up to 30 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: The study highlights the importance of combining tool-augmented reasoning with domain-specific post-training for complex BI workflows. The results point to promising directions for future research in automating BI tasks using LLMs.

title: License Compliance in Open Source Cybersecurity Projects
summary: Developers of cybersecurity software often include and rely upon open source software packages in their commercial software products. Before open source code is absorbed into a proprietary product, developers must check the package license to see if the project is permissively licensed, thereby allowing for commercial-friendly inheritance and redistribution. However, there is a risk that the open source package license could be inaccurate due to being silently contaminated with restrictively licensed open source code that may prohibit the sale or confidentiality of commercial derivative work. Contamination of commercial products could lead to expensive remediation costs, damage to the company's reputation, and costly legal fees. In this article, we report on our preliminary analysis of more than 200 open source cybersecurity projects to identify the most frequently used license types and languages and to look for evidence of permissively licensed open source projects that are likely contaminated by restrictive licensed material (i.e., containing commercial-unfriendly code). Our analysis identified restrictive license contamination cases occurring in permissively licensed open source projects. Furthermore, we found a high proportion of code that lacked copyright attribution. We expect that the results of this study will: i) provide managers and developers with an understanding of how contamination can occur, ii) provide open source communities with an understanding on how they can better protect their intellectual property by including licenses and copyright information in their code, and iii) provide entrepreneurs with an understanding of the open source cybersecurity domain in terms of licensing and contamination and how they affect decisions about cybersecurity software architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes over 200 open source cybersecurity projects to identify license types, programming languages, and evidence of permissively licensed projects contaminated with restrictive code. The study found actual contamination cases and a high proportion of code lacking copyright attribution.
AI.motivation: The research addresses the risk of license contamination in open source software, where restrictively licensed code silently infiltrates permissively licensed projects, potentially causing legal issues, remediation costs, and reputation damage for commercial software developers.
AI.method: Preliminary analysis of more than 200 open source cybersecurity projects to identify frequently used license types, programming languages, and evidence of permissive projects contaminated with restrictive licensed material.
AI.result: The analysis identified restrictive license contamination cases occurring in permissively licensed open source projects, along with a high proportion of code lacking copyright attribution.
AI.conclusion: The study aims to provide managers and developers with understanding of contamination mechanisms, help open source communities protect their IP better through proper licensing, and equip entrepreneurs with knowledge about licensing risks in cybersecurity software architecture decisions.

title: Voice-Light: A Full-Duplex Cascaded Voice Agent with Causal Turn-Taking and Speculative Generation
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Code, datasets, and model artifacts: https://github.com/BertilBraun/Voice-Light ; live demo: https://voice.bertil-braun.de
summary: Natural spoken interaction requires more than streaming ASR, language generation, and speech synthesis: a system must react to overlap without canceling on every acknowledgment, prepare a response before a turn is certain, and ensure canceled audio cannot enter conversation history. We present Voice-Light, a full-duplex cascaded voice agent that combines immediate acoustic onset, a causal adapter sharing a streaming ASR encoder, reversible playback control, and private speculative response generation. Structured tool calls execute concurrently with audible bridge speech, while browser acknowledgments make rendered audio authoritative for durable history. Locked evaluation on 1,673 real-conversation silence candidates found that an earlier learned completion checkpoint preserved a 2.70% false-cutoff rate but reached only 12.53% end-of-turn recall, compared with 95.60% for a Silero timing policy. The deployed system therefore retains a hybrid controller rather than claiming a learned-policy replacement. Across three unscripted operator-run microphone sessions, 36 measured response turns had a 758 ms median from final VAD endpoint to first server audio; 21 turns were below 800 ms. These sessions are an instrumented case study, not a controlled user evaluation. We release the synthetic data, model artifacts, evaluation code and summaries, source code, and deployment configuration supporting the result.

AI.tldr: Voice-Light is a full-duplex cascaded voice agent that handles natural spoken interaction by combining immediate acoustic onset, causal adapter with streaming ASR encoder, reversible playback control, and private speculative response generation. Evaluation on 1,673 silence candidates shows a hybrid controller outperforms learned policies, with 758ms median response latency across 36 measured turns.
AI.motivation: Natural spoken interaction requires more than streaming ASR, language generation, and speech synthesis: systems must react to overlap without canceling on every acknowledgment, prepare responses before turn certainty, and ensure canceled audio cannot enter conversation history.
AI.method: Voice-Light combines: (1) immediate acoustic onset detection, (2) causal adapter sharing a streaming ASR encoder, (3) reversible playback control, (4) private speculative response generation. Structured tool calls execute concurrently with audible bridge speech while browser acknowledgments make rendered audio authoritative for durable history.
AI.result: Locked evaluation on 1,673 real-conversation silence candidates: learned completion checkpoint achieved 2.70% false-cutoff rate but only 12.53% end-of-turn recall, while Silero timing policy achieved 95.60% end-of-turn recall. Across three unscripted operator sessions (36 response turns), median latency was 758ms from final VAD endpoint to first server audio; 21 turns were below 800ms.
AI.conclusion: The deployed system retains a hybrid controller rather than claiming a learned-policy replacement. The system releases synthetic data, model artifacts, evaluation code and summaries, source code, and deployment configuration.

title: Image-Derived PM10 Estimation in Cattle Feedlot Using Machine Learning: Addressing Concentration Ranges Beyond Existing Digital Imaging Methods
summary: Affordable dust monitoring remains a pressing need for the cattle feedlot industry, yet camera-based PM estimation, despite its growing body of research in urban air quality settings, has not been evaluated under the extended concentration ranges characteristic of intensive livestock operations. This study developed an image-based approach using contrast panel features and machine learning to estimate PM10 concentrations in a commercial cattle feedlot, where hourly average PM10 ranged from 250 to 1,000 ug/m^-3 and instantaneous concentrations reached 5,000 to 20,000 ug/m^-3. Grayscale images were captured during the evening dust peak period, and features including panel contrast, black and white panel pixel values, and overall image brightness were extracted. The model also incorporated recent past values from preceding images and solar zenith angle as predictors. Among the candidate models evaluated, XGBoost achieved the highest predictive performance, with an R^2 of 0.792 and a median absolute error of 103 ug/m^-3. Feature importance analysis revealed that (a) panels positioned farthest from the camera contributed most strongly to predictions and (b) that black panel pixel values were more sensitive than white panel values to changes in PM10 concentration. Prediction accuracy during the sunset transition, which coincides with the onset of the feedlot evening dust peak, remains an area for further refinement. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of image-based PM10 estimation across PM concentration ranges substantially exceeding those reported in prior urban studies and provide practical guidelines for future deployment in feedlot environments.

AI.tldr: This study developed an image-based machine learning approach using contrast panel features to estimate PM10 concentrations in commercial cattle feedlots, achieving an R² of 0.792 and median absolute error of 103 ug/m³ across concentration ranges (250-1,000 ug/m³ hourly average, 5,000-20,000 ug/m³ instantaneous) that substantially exceed prior urban air quality studies.
AI.motivation: Affordable dust monitoring remains a pressing need for the cattle feedlot industry. While camera-based PM estimation has been studied in urban air quality settings, it has not been evaluated under the extended concentration ranges characteristic of intensive livestock operations, creating a gap in practical monitoring solutions for feedlots.
AI.method: The study developed an image-based approach using contrast panel features and machine learning. Grayscale images were captured during evening dust peak periods. Features extracted included panel contrast, black and white panel pixel values, and overall image brightness. The model also incorporated recent past values from preceding images and solar zenith angle as predictors. Among candidate models, XGBoost was evaluated for predictive performance.
AI.result: XGBoost achieved the highest predictive performance with an R² of 0.792 and median absolute error of 103 ug/m³. Feature importance analysis revealed that panels positioned farthest from the camera contributed most strongly to predictions, and black panel pixel values were more sensitive than white panel values to changes in PM10 concentration. Accuracy during the sunset transition (coinciding with evening dust peak onset) remains an area for further refinement.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate the feasibility of image-based PM10 estimation across PM concentration ranges substantially exceeding those reported in prior urban studies. The study provides practical guidelines for future deployment in feedlot environments, though prediction accuracy during sunset transition requires further improvement.

title: CaLR: Causal Latent Revision for Robust Diffusion Reasoning
summary: Autoregressive (AR) models suffer from local greediness, while diffusion language models (DLMs) often lack the strict causal structure required for reasoning. To combine the advantages and overcome the drawbacks of the dual, we propose Causal Latent Revision (CaLR), a framework that reformulates reasoning as constrained latent optimization. By adopting a causal topology matrix (CTM) from an expert model and implicit differentiation, CaLR performs gradient-guided ``thought revision" to enforce logical consistency, enabling dynamic self-correction of intermediate steps during parallel generation. Empirically, CaLR achieves SOTA DLM performance on complex benchmarks, surpassing strong AR baselines and demonstrating superior robustness in constrained tasks like Sudoku.

AI.tldr: CaLR is a framework that combines autoregressive and diffusion language models by reformulating reasoning as constrained latent optimization, using causal topology matrices and implicit differentiation to enable dynamic self-correction during parallel generation.
AI.motivation: Address the limitations of two major language model paradigms: autoregressive (AR) models suffer from local greediness, while diffusion language models (DLMs) lack strict causal structure required for reasoning. The goal is to combine their advantages while overcoming their individual drawbacks.
AI.method: The framework adopts a causal topology matrix (CTM) from an expert model and uses implicit differentiation to perform gradient-guided "thought revision" that enforces logical consistency, enabling dynamic self-correction of intermediate steps during parallel generation.
AI.result: CaLR achieves state-of-the-art DLM performance on complex benchmarks, surpassing strong autoregressive baselines and demonstrating superior robustness in constrained tasks like Sudoku.
AI.conclusion: CaLR successfully combines the benefits of AR and DLM approaches through constrained latent optimization, providing a promising direction for improving reasoning capabilities in language models through causal structure enforcement and dynamic self-correction.

title: Elastic Threshold Attention: Learned Contextual Sparsity for Long-Context Decoding
summary: Massive KV caches can cause severe memory-bandwidth bottlenecks during long-context decoding. Sparse attention methods mitigate this via selective loading, but that comes at a cost: rigid heuristics drop necessary context, leading to quality degradation. We introduce \textbf{Elastic Threshold Attention (ETA)}, an end-to-end trainable architecture that achieves hardware-accelerated decoding speed without sacrificing dense model quality. ETA predicts dynamic, contextual thresholds directly from query representations, allowing the model to allocate dense-like context to difficult retrieval or reasoning steps while pruning routine tokens. To learn this policy from scratch without representation collapse, ETA \emph{multiplicatively suppresses} sub-threshold logits toward zero during training rather than deleting them. Training against this smooth uniform attention floor provides a distributed probability reservoir that \textbf{causes localized attention sinks on initial tokens to disappear}. It also enables the model to hard-prune uninformative KV blocks at inference time and absorb incidental tokens co-admitted by coarse GPU block selection. As a result, a 1.45B pretrained ETA model rivals dense attention across language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and long-context needle retrieval at $\approx 85\%$ training sparsity and $\approx 38\%$ active decode density. At inference time, we implement a custom decode kernel in Triton that screens KV blocks in $O(1)$ time using cached geometric-probabilistic bounds, delivering up to $2.5\times$ wall-clock decode speedups over FlashAttention-2 on sequences up to 512K tokens. Finally, we introduce an offline calibration algorithm for domain-specific deployments that freezes per-head constant thresholds to eliminate predictor overhead, cutting attention compute by an additional $27\%$.

AI.tldr: Elastic Threshold Attention (ETA) is an end-to-end trainable sparse attention architecture that achieves hardware-accelerated decoding speed without sacrificing dense model quality. It uses dynamic, query-driven thresholds to allocate context selectively, with a multiplicative suppression training mechanism that eliminates attention sinks and enables efficient hard-pruning at inference time.
AI.motivation: Massive KV caches cause severe memory-bandwidth bottlenecks during long-context decoding. Existing sparse attention methods use rigid heuristics that drop necessary context, leading to quality degradation. The authors sought a solution that achieves hardware-accelerated decoding speed while maintaining dense model quality.
AI.method: ETA predicts dynamic, contextual thresholds directly from query representations. During training, it multiplicatively suppresses sub-threshold logits toward zero (rather than deleting them) to create a distributed probability reservoir that eliminates attention sinks. At inference time, it enables hard-pruning of uninformative KV blocks and absorption of incidental tokens. The implementation includes a custom Triton decode kernel that screens KV blocks in O(1) time using cached geometric-probabilistic bounds, plus an offline calibration algorithm for domain-specific deployments.
AI.result: A 1.45B pretrained ETA model rivals dense attention across language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and long-context needle retrieval at ~85% training sparsity and ~38% active decode density. It delivers up to 2.5× wall-clock decode speedups over FlashAttention-2 on sequences up to 512K tokens. The offline calibration algorithm cuts attention compute by an additional 27%.
AI.conclusion: ETA demonstrates that end-to-end trainable sparse attention can achieve hardware-accelerated decoding speeds while maintaining dense model quality. The multiplicative suppression training mechanism effectively eliminates attention sinks and enables efficient inference-time pruning, making it a promising approach for long-context decoding applications.

title: What Stops a Small Language Model From Driving a Database Agent
comment: 16 pages, 8 tables. Dataset, scorer and a verifier that regenerates every figure: https://doi.org/10.57967/hf/10485
summary: Small open-weight language models are assumed to fail at agentic database work because they lack the reasoning capacity for it. We test that against a production system. Over eleven days we drove the agent mode of an open-source SQL client with 39 open-weight models served locally and one hosted control, across six task surfaces: 8,199 runs, 110,711 ledger events, 14,008 refused tool calls. Of the 2,100 model-attributed agent-mode losses, 1,590, or 75.7%, came from runs that had invoked at least one tool. That majority is what survives resampling models rather than runs: it holds in 99.7% of clustered resamples and in 15 of the 22 models with at least twenty losses. Within it, transport, a run that used the tools and never got a deliverable through, is the largest class at 36.2% and capability, a run that invoked no tool at all, the smallest at 17.3%; we report that ordering as a property of this corpus rather than a general finding, since clustered by model it holds in only 74.5% of resamples. Transport failures decompose into a few mechanical argument shapes. Production ledgers record refusal codes and never the model's arguments, so these were invisible for ten days; capturing them exposed five server defects, one of which demanded a field on one tool, forbade it on the sibling that composed it, then failed the run for its absence. Five server changes, touching no model, prompt or sampling setting, moved six models by 6 to 21 cells out of 30. We also report a confound we believe affects published local-model benchmarks, ours included: with no context cap, one 7.1 GB model was admitted at its full 262,144-token window and held 51 GB on a 64 GB machine, producing runs indistinguishable in any ordinary log from a model timing out. The corpus, the scorer and a verifier that regenerates every figure are released.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the assumption that small open-weight language models fail at agentic database work due to lack of reasoning capacity. Through 8,199 runs across 40 models, the authors find that 75.7% of losses occur in runs that invoked at least one tool (transport failures), not in runs that failed to invoke tools (capability failures). They also discovered that server-side defects and resource constraints (not model capacity) significantly impact performance.
AI.motivation: The researchers sought to test the common assumption that small open-weight language models cannot handle agentic database tasks because they lack sufficient reasoning capacity. They wanted to determine whether the actual bottleneck is model capability or other factors like server defects and system configuration.
AI.method: Over eleven days, the researchers drove an open-source SQL client's agent mode with 39 open-weight models served locally and one hosted control, across six task surfaces. They analyzed 8,199 runs, 110,711 ledger events, and 14,008 refused tool calls. They used clustered resampling by model and captured previously invisible model arguments by recording refusal codes.
AI.result: 75.7% of losses (1,590 out of 2,100) came from runs that had invoked at least one tool. Transport failures (used tools but never got deliverable) account for 36.2%, while capability failures (invoked no tool) are only 17.3%. Five server defects were exposed by capturing refusal codes, and five server changes (touching no model/prompt/sampling) moved six models by 6-21 cells out of 30. A confound was found: a 7.1GB model with 262k-token window held 51GB on a 64GB machine, causing runs indistinguishable from timeouts.
AI.conclusion: The assumption that small open-weight models fail at agentic database work due to lack of reasoning is challenged. The majority of failures come from transport issues (tool invocation but no deliverable), not capability issues (no tool invocation). Server defects and resource constraints are significant confounders in local-model benchmarks. The authors released the corpus, scorer, and verifier.

title: Online Algorithms for Independent Low-Rank Matrix Analysis and Rank-Constrained Spatial Covariance Matrix Estimation Based on Maximum Weighted Likelihood Estimation
summary: Real-time multichannel speech extraction (MSE) under diffuse noise conditions is an important task with a wide range of applications, such as speech recognition and hearing aids. In this paper, we propose online algorithms for independent low-rank matrix analysis (ILRMA) and rank-constrained spatial covariance matrix estimation (RCSCME). Previously, we proposed a real-time extension of the RCSCME-based method: an MSE method based on ILRMA and RCSCME using the blockwise batch algorithm. However, it assumes that the spatial characteristics are stationary within a single batch, and thus, in dynamic situations where the target speaker moves, its performance may degrade. To address this problem, we derive the online algorithms for ILRMA and RCSCME in the following three steps. First, we formulate framewise cost functions for ILRMA and RCSCME on the basis of maximum weighted likelihood estimation. Second, we derive the update rules for the framewise cost functions on the basis of auxiliary-function techniques. These naive update rules are computationally costly for real-time execution on a practical machine. Thus, we finally derive the online algorithms by approximating some intermediate parameters with their estimates. Furthermore, we propose stabilization and further acceleration techniques for these online algorithms. In experiments, we simulate situations where a target speaker is stationary or moves and show that the proposed method achieves superior speech extraction performance compared with conventional methods. In addition, using real-world recorded signals, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in practical scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes online algorithms for independent low-rank matrix analysis (ILRMA) and rank-constrained spatial covariance matrix estimation (RCSCME) to address dynamic speech extraction when the target speaker moves. The approach derives framewise cost functions using maximum weighted likelihood estimation and approximates intermediate parameters to achieve real-time computational feasibility.
AI.motivation: Previous real-time MSE methods based on ILRMA and RCSCME use blockwise batch algorithms that assume spatial characteristics are stationary within a single batch. This assumption causes performance degradation in dynamic situations where the target speaker moves, which is common in practical applications like speech recognition and hearing aids.
AI.method: The proposed method consists of three main steps: (1) Formulating framewise cost functions for ILRMA and RCSCME based on maximum weighted likelihood estimation, (2) Deriving update rules using auxiliary-function techniques, and (3) Approximating intermediate parameters to reduce computational cost. Additionally, stabilization and acceleration techniques are proposed for the online algorithms.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves superior speech extraction performance compared with conventional methods in both stationary and moving target speaker scenarios. Effectiveness is also demonstrated using real-world recorded signals in practical scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The online algorithms for ILRMA and RCSCME successfully address the limitation of stationary spatial characteristics assumption in previous batch methods, enabling effective real-time speech extraction even when the target speaker moves. The method shows promise for practical applications in speech recognition and hearing aids.

title: Fragment-Aware Vision Transformers for Fresco-Fragment Style Classification
summary: Artistic style classification is usually studied on complete artworks, where models can exploit global composition, spatial organisation, and iconographic structure. In archaeological settings, however, artworks often survive only as fragmented remains, forcing recognition from incomplete, irregular, and context-limited visual evidence. We study fresco-fragment style classification using a progressive transformer-based framework. Starting from a ViT-B/16 baseline, we introduce foreground-guided masking to suppress background-only tokens, inpainting-based geometric regularisation to align irregular fragment supports with the ViT patch grid, and a supervised contrastive objective that operates on predictive distributions through a Kullback-Leibler similarity and consistently improves every branch. We combine the branches with a deliberately simple learnable logit ensemble. Experiments on CLEOPATRA and POMPAAF show that fragment-aware modelling improves over the standard ViT baseline, with the ensemble increasing accuracy from 0.604 to 0.656 and macro-F1 from 0.596 to 0.648 on CLEOPATRA, and outperforming the best single branch in four of six fragmentation settings on POMPAAF. We additionally evaluate a more complex graph-fusion variant and find that it matches the simple ensemble on POMPAAF while offering only a small, dataset-specific gain on CLEOPATRA, which does not justify its added complexity. Beyond these empirical gains, our contribution is twofold: a distribution-level contrastive objective that consistently sharpens single-branch recognition, and an interpretability analysis that verifies the models exploit genuine painted evidence, while quantifying that the inpainting-based branch draws part of its attribution from the synthesised surround.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses fresco-fragment style classification in archaeological settings, where artworks survive only as incomplete fragments. The authors propose a progressive transformer-based framework combining foreground-guided masking, inpainting-based geometric regularization, and a supervised contrastive objective using KL divergence. The simple learnable logit ensemble achieves 0.656 accuracy and 0.648 macro-F1 on CLEOPATRA, outperforming the 0.604 baseline.
AI.motivation: Artistic style classification is typically studied on complete artworks, but archaeological settings often present only fragmented remains with incomplete, irregular, and context-limited visual evidence. Existing methods designed for complete artworks fail in this scenario, necessitating fragment-aware modeling approaches.
AI.method: The authors propose a progressive transformer-based framework with three main components: (1) Foreground-guided masking to suppress background-only tokens; (2) Inpainting-based geometric regularization to align irregular fragment supports with the ViT patch grid; (3) A supervised contrastive objective operating on predictive distributions through Kullback-Leibler similarity. These branches are combined using a simple learnable logit ensemble. A graph-fusion variant is also evaluated for comparison.
AI.result: On CLEOPATRA, the ensemble increases accuracy from 0.604 to 0.656 and macro-F1 from 0.596 to 0.648. On POMPAAF, the ensemble outperforms the best single branch in four of six fragmentation settings. The graph-fusion variant matches the simple ensemble on POMPAAF but offers only marginal gains on CLEOPATRA. Interpretability analysis confirms models exploit genuine painted evidence while quantifying that the inpainting-based branch draws attribution from synthesized surroundings.
AI.conclusion: Fragment-aware modeling improves over standard ViT baselines for archaeological fresco-fragment style classification. The distribution-level contrastive objective consistently sharpens single-branch recognition. The simple learnable logit ensemble is preferred over complex graph-fusion due to comparable performance with lower complexity. The interpretability analysis validates that models use genuine painted evidence rather than spurious features.

title: LoRA Enhanced Contrastive Learning with SAS Vision Transformers
summary: Automatic target recognition (ATR) with synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) supports advanced naval capabilities, but deep learning is constrained by scarce target imagery, background clutter, and human-in-the-loop assessment. We adapt DINOv3 Vision Transformer (ViT) models to underwater SAS ATR using a three-stage parameter-efficient framework. Stage 1 uses Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) while freezing the ViT backbone, bridging the gap between natural-image pretraining and underwater acoustic propagation. Stage 2 uses hard-negative mining to strengthen the decision boundary against acoustic mimics, including rocks and sediment formations resembling man-made targets. Stage 3 uses Supervised Contrastive Learning (SupCon) to separate target and clutter representations. We evaluate at-sea SAS data using a mission-level geographic split, compare all arms at 85 percent test recall, and repeat each comparison over three random seeds. LoRA accounts for the primary effect, increasing area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) from 0.300 to 0.679 +/- 0.027 using the same frozen backbone. Rank 4 achieves this result while training only 0.26 percent of weights. Neither refinement stage exceeds its matched control: hard-negative mining changes AUPRC by -0.0045 +/- 0.0119 versus an equal-size random curriculum, and SupCon changes AUPRC by +0.0002 +/- 0.0096 versus the preceding stage. These null results indicate that mining occurred on data the encoder had already fit and that supervised stages had already imposed most target-clutter geometry. One efficient adaptation stage is sufficient; stacked refinement is not.

AI.tldr: This paper adapts DINOv3 Vision Transformers to underwater synthetic aperture sonar automatic target recognition using a three-stage parameter-efficient framework. Only the first stage (LoRA) shows significant improvement, increasing AUPRC from 0.300 to 0.679, while subsequent refinement stages (hard-negative mining and supervised contrastive learning) provide no additional benefit.
AI.motivation: Deep learning for underwater ATR is constrained by scarce target imagery, background clutter, and human-in-the-loop assessment. The gap between natural-image pretraining and underwater acoustic imaging needs to be bridged efficiently.
AI.method: Three-stage parameter-efficient framework: (1) LoRA adaptation while freezing ViT backbone, (2) hard-negative mining against acoustic mimics (rocks, sediment), (3) Supervised Contrastive Learning for target-clutter separation. Evaluation uses at-sea SAS data with mission-level geographic split, testing at 85% recall across three random seeds.
AI.result: LoRA significantly improves AUPRC from 0.300 to 0.679 ± 0.027 while training only 0.26% of weights (Rank 4). Neither hard-negative mining (-0.0045 ± 0.0119) nor SupCon (+0.0002 ± 0.0096) shows improvement over matched controls.
AI.conclusion: One efficient adaptation stage (LoRA) is sufficient for SAS ATR; stacked refinement stages are unnecessary. The null results indicate the encoder had already fit the data from hard-negative mining, and supervised stages had already imposed most target-clutter geometry.

title: Bio-MF: Low-Latency and High-Fidelity EEG-to-fNIRS Cross-Modal Generation for Hybrid Motor-Imagery Brain--Computer Interfaces
summary: Hybrid motor-imagery brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) combining EEG and fNIRS can outperform EEG-only systems by exploiting complementary electrophysiological and hemodynamic information. To obtain such hybrid information when paired EEG-fNIRS acquisition is unavailable or inconvenient, recent studies have focused on EEG-to-fNIRS cross-modal generation. However, existing methods still suffer from slow generation and often require pretraining, limiting their use in real-time MI-BCI scenarios. Although one-step generative models offer an attractive route to low-latency synthesis, removing the iterative refinement process can reduce generation fidelity and introduce non-physiological artifacts. To address these problems, this paper proposes Bio-MF, a latent-free one-step MeanFlow framework for EEG-conditioned fNIRS generation. Bio-MF performs direct signal-space x-prediction, converts this signal-space output into MeanFlow velocity supervision, and completes inference with one network evaluation. To preserve task-relevant hemodynamic structure under heterogeneous sensor layouts, Bio-MF integrates Spatial-Temporal Interactive 4D Encoding, cross-modal classifier-free guidance, and noise-level-gated FFT regularization. On Dataset 1, EEG + synthetic fNIRS improves ACC over EEG-only by 3.37 and 4.15 percentage points for HbR and HbO, respectively. On Dataset 2, the corresponding gains remain 2.98 and 2.50 percentage points under the unseen 64-channel EEG montage. On an RTX PRO 6000 GPU, Bio-MF generates one fNIRS trial in 7.0 ms, corresponding to an 857x speedup over the 1000-step SCDM latency. These results show that Bio-MF enables fast EEG-to-fNIRS synthesis while preserving task-relevant generation quality for downstream hybrid MI decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/psychosiwa/Bio-MF.

AI.tldr: Bio-MF is a latent-free one-step MeanFlow framework for EEG-to-fNIRS cross-modal generation in hybrid MI-BCIs. It achieves 857x speedup (7.0ms per trial) over iterative methods while improving classification accuracy by 2.50-4.15 percentage points over EEG-only systems.
AI.motivation: Hybrid EEG-fNIRS BCI systems outperform EEG-only systems, but paired acquisition is often unavailable. Existing EEG-to-fNIRS methods suffer from slow generation and require pretraining, limiting real-time MI-BCI applications. One-step generative models offer low-latency synthesis but risk reduced fidelity and artifacts.
AI.method: Bio-MF performs direct signal-space prediction, converts output to MeanFlow velocity supervision, and completes inference with one network evaluation. Key innovations include: Spatial-Temporal Interactive 4D Encoding for heterogeneous sensor layouts, cross-modal classifier-free guidance, and noise-level-gated FFT regularization to preserve task-relevant hemodynamic structure.
AI.result: On Dataset 1, EEG + synthetic fNIRS improves accuracy over EEG-only by 3.37% (HbR) and 4.15% (HbO). On Dataset 2 with unseen 64-channel EEG montage, gains are 2.98% (HbR) and 2.50% (HbO). Generation latency is 7.0ms per trial on RTX Pro 6000 GPU, representing 857x speedup over 1000-step SCDM.
AI.conclusion: Bio-MF enables fast EEG-to-fNIRS synthesis while preserving task-relevant generation quality for downstream hybrid MI decoding. The method successfully generalizes to unseen EEG montages and achieves real-time performance suitable for practical BCI applications.

title: Cross-Platform vs Native Mobile Development: An Empirical Study of Software Quality Trade-offs
summary:
Cross-platform mobile frameworks promise code reuse, shorter delivery cycles, and lower implementation effort, but their trade-offs relative to native development remain difficult to assess objectively. Many comparisons rely on simplified applications, inconsistent feature sets, or a narrow set of metrics. This paper compares five implementations of the same plant-management application: native iOS, native Android, Flutter, React Native, and Kotlin Multiplatform. The shared approaches target both Android and iOS, yielding eight executable variants. Guided by ISO/IEC 25010, the study examines time behavior, implementation footprint, source-code organization, and observable rendering responsiveness.
  All implementations share the same domain, backend services, functional requirements, and benchmark contract. The supplied dataset contains 2,000 completed runs per variant and covers authenticated and cached retrieval, image transfer and decoding, list rendering and scrolling, local synchronization, and media upload. Backend preparation and framework-specific UI drivers are analyzed separately from the primary client workflow.
  Native records the lowest non-UI client subtotal on both operating systems, with Kotlin Multiplatform the closest cross-platform implementation, while operation and UI-wrapper rankings vary by task. The shared approaches contain less authored mobile source than the native applications combined, and the source inventory shows different patterns of file size, organization, and dependency use. Rather than identifying a universally superior technology, the study shows that each approach's advantages and costs depend on the quality attribute, workload, platform, and measurement boundary.

AI.tldr: This paper compares five implementations of the same plant-management application across native iOS, native Android, Flutter, React Native, and Kotlin Multiplatform, evaluating eight executable variants using ISO/IEC 25010 standards. The study analyzes time behavior, implementation footprint, source-code organization, and rendering responsiveness across 2,000 runs per variant covering authenticated retrieval, image processing, list rendering, local synchronization, and media upload.
AI.motivation: Cross-platform mobile frameworks promise code reuse and lower implementation effort, but their trade-offs relative to native development are difficult to assess objectively due to reliance on simplified applications, inconsistent feature sets, or narrow metrics in existing comparisons.
AI.method: The study implements the same plant-management application across all five frameworks targeting both Android and iOS (eight variants total). All implementations share identical domain, backend services, functional requirements, and benchmark contract. Evaluation follows ISO/IEC 25010, examining time behavior, implementation footprint, source-code organization, and observable rendering responsiveness. Each variant ran 2,000 completed tests covering authenticated/cached retrieval, image transfer/decoding, list rendering/scrolling, local synchronization, and media upload.
AI.result: Native implementations recorded the lowest non-UI client subtotal on both operating systems, with Kotlin Multiplatform being the closest cross-platform implementation. Rankings varied by task for operation and UI-wrapper performance. Shared approaches contained less authored mobile source than combined native applications, with different patterns in file size, organization, and dependency use.
AI.conclusion: No universally superior technology exists; each approach's advantages and costs depend on quality attribute, workload, platform, and measurement boundary. The study provides a more rigorous and comprehensive comparison than prior work by using identical application functionality, consistent metrics, and extensive benchmarking.

title: I'll Keep an Ear Out: Teaching AudioLLMs Proactive Audio Assistance
summary: Audio large language models (AudioLLMs) operate reactively, responding only when queried. We introduce proactive audio assistance, where an AudioLLM monitors an audio stream and autonomously decides when to alert the user from a single natural-language intent, motivated by wearable applications for Deaf and Hard of Hearing users. We propose Interrupt and Silent Modeling (ISM), a model-agnostic paradigm that embeds proactive decisions into LLM decoding via two special tokens: \texttt{<interrupt>} and \texttt{<silent>}, capturing four states: onset detection, sustained-relevance triggering, irrelevance suppression, and de-duplication. Applied to Qwen2-Audio-7B, ISM achieves 99.6\% interrupt F1 and perfect de-duplication recall on ESC-50. On noisy Epic-Sounds kitchen audio, ISM achieves the highest interrupt F1 without domain-specific training, the only method maintaining strong onset detection without over-triggering or over-suppression. Streaming evaluation confirms real-time viability with 3.5-second average latency.

AI.tldr: ISM introduces proactive audio assistance to AudioLLMs by embedding interrupt and silent decision tokens into LLM decoding, enabling autonomous monitoring and alerting for Deaf/Hard of Hearing users. Achieves 99.6% interrupt F1 on ESC-50 and real-time performance with 3.5s latency.
AI.motivation: Current AudioLLMs are reactive, only responding when explicitly queried. This is insufficient for wearable applications for Deaf and Hard of Hearing users who need continuous monitoring of their audio environment to be proactively alerted to relevant sounds (alarms, doorbells, conversations) without manual prompting.
AI.method: Proposes Interrupt and Silent Modeling (ISM), a model-agnostic paradigm that embeds proactive decisions into LLM decoding via two special tokens: <interrupt> and <silent>. The system captures four states: (1) onset detection, (2) sustained-relevance triggering, (3) irrelevance suppression, and (4) de-duplication. Applied to Qwen2-Audio-7B.
AI.result: On ESC-50: achieves 99.6% interrupt F1 and perfect de-duplication recall. On noisy Epic-Sounds kitchen audio: achieves highest interrupt F1 without domain-specific training; the only method maintaining strong onset detection without over-triggering or over-suppression. Streaming evaluation confirms real-time viability with 3.5-second average latency.
AI.conclusion: ISM successfully enables proactive audio assistance in AudioLLMs through a model-agnostic approach using special decision tokens. The method demonstrates strong performance across datasets, maintains real-time capability, and addresses the critical need for continuous audio monitoring for deaf/hard of hearing users without requiring domain-specific training.

title: MAGIC: Marginal-Guided Compression with Optimal Transport for Efficient Visual Document Retrieval
summary: Recent visual document retrieval (VDR) systems such as ColPali use multi-vector page embeddings, in which patch-level vectors enable fine-grained evidence matching but incur substantial index storage and MaxSim scoring overhead. Post-hoc merging offers a practical route to efficient VDR by reducing this cost without retraining the retriever, but its uniform reconstruction objectives are poorly aligned with the sparse, non-uniform patch usage induced by late-interaction retrieval. Under aggressive compression, this misalignment can preserve rarely used patches while concentrating retrieval activity on too few retained representatives. To address this misalignment, we propose Marginal-Guided Compression with Optimal Transport (MAGIC), a training-free post-hoc compressor for efficient retrieval with frozen multi-vector embeddings.
