MAGIC derives a MaxSim-induced compression surrogate and optimizes it through a two-marginal entropic optimal-transport formulation, where a retrieval-demand source marginal prioritizes high-use patches and a balanced target marginal regularizes retained-facet usage. Across ViDoRe benchmarks, keep ratios, and retrieval backbones, MAGIC consistently outperforms strong post-hoc compressors, with particularly large gains in the aggressive-compression regime; component ablations verify the complementary effects of its two marginals. We release the code at: https://github.com/xandery-geek/MAGIC.

AI.tldr: MAGIC is a training-free post-hoc compressor for multi-vector embeddings in visual document retrieval. It uses a MaxSim-induced compression surrogate optimized through two-marginal entropic optimal transport to address the misalignment between uniform reconstruction objectives and the sparse, non-uniform patch usage in late-interaction retrieval.
AI.motivation: Multi-vector page embeddings in VDR systems (like ColPali) enable fine-grained evidence matching but incur substantial index storage and MaxSim scoring overhead. Post-hoc merging offers efficiency without retraining, but existing approaches use uniform reconstruction objectives poorly aligned with sparse, non-uniform patch usage induced by late-interaction retrieval. This misalignment causes problems under aggressive compression: rarely used patches are preserved while retrieval activity concentrates on too few retained representatives.
AI.method: MAGIC derives a MaxSim-induced compression surrogate and optimizes it through a two-marginal entropic optimal-transport formulation. The method uses: (1) a retrieval-demand source marginal that prioritizes high-use patches, and (2) a balanced target marginal that regularizes retained-facet usage. This is a training-free approach that works with frozen multi-vector embeddings.
AI.result: Across ViDoRe benchmarks, various keep ratios, and retrieval backbones, MAGIC consistently outperforms strong post-hoc compressors. Particularly large gains are observed in the aggressive-compression regime. Component ablations verify the complementary effects of its two marginals.
AI.conclusion: MAGIC provides an effective solution for compressing multi-vector embeddings in VDR systems without retraining. By addressing the misalignment between compression objectives and actual patch usage patterns through optimal transport, it achieves superior performance especially under aggressive compression, making it practical for efficient visual document retrieval.

title: Detecting Hallucination in LLMs: Tracing the Topological Signatures of Impaired Context Sharing
summary: In this work, we examine the topology of information flow patterns within attention graphs to effectively distinguish hallucinated from non-hallucinated responses. We analyze the Forman-Ricci curvature to identify structural patterns indicating information bottlenecks in attention graphs. We then introduce a method that captures both semi-local and global information-flow characteristics of attention heads associated with hallucinated responses. We evaluate our approach extensively across several LLMs and established benchmarks. Empirical results demonstrate that our proposed single-pass approach provides consistent improvements over existing attention-based and multi-response baselines across two hallucination-detection benchmarks, while achieving competitive performance across diverse LLM architectures. Further analysis reveals that impaired context sharing among tokens during causal generation is strongly associated with hallucination occurrences in LLMs. In particular, hallucinated responses are consistently characterized by an over-reliance on self-attention, diffused context retrieval from earlier tokens, or information over-squashing, especially in the final transformer layer.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel method for detecting hallucinations in LLM responses by analyzing the topological structure of attention graphs using Forman-Ricci curvature. The approach captures both semi-local and global information-flow characteristics across attention heads, identifying that impaired context sharing, over-reliance on self-attention, and information over-squashing in the final transformer layer are strongly associated with hallucination occurrences.
AI.motivation: Current hallucination detection methods either rely on attention-based features that lack global perspective or require multiple responses, which is computationally expensive. This work aims to address these limitations by introducing a single-pass approach that analyzes the topology of information flow in attention graphs to effectively distinguish hallucinated from non-hallucinated responses.
AI.method: The method uses Forman-Ricci curvature to identify structural patterns indicating information bottlenecks in attention graphs. It captures both semi-local and global information-flow characteristics of attention heads associated with hallucinated responses. The approach is evaluated across several LLMs and established benchmarks.
AI.result: The proposed single-pass approach provides consistent improvements over existing attention-based and multi-response baselines across two hallucination-detection benchmarks, while achieving competitive performance across diverse LLM architectures. The analysis reveals that impaired context sharing among tokens during causal generation is strongly associated with hallucination occurrences.
AI.conclusion: Hallucinated responses are characterized by over-reliance on self-attention, diffused context retrieval from earlier tokens, or information over-squashing, especially in the final transformer layer. This topological analysis provides a promising single-pass solution for hallucination detection with broad applicability across different LLM architectures.

title: Continuous Delayed-Memory Stochastic Gradient Descent and Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning from History of Astrophysical Time Series Studies
comment: Keywords: Stochastic process, Stochastic gradient descent, Continuous-Delayed-Memory Stochastic Gradient Descent, Stochastic Delay Differential Equation, Reinforcement Learning, Adjoint method
summary: Quasars are luminous objects in the universe that exhibit stochastic brightness variations encoding information about the supermassive black holes powering them, and modeling these variations from ground-based survey data time series, known as light curves, is a statistical challenge. This paper reviews how stochastic differential equations (SDEs) have been adapted with neural network parameterizations to overcome this challenge in history. We create the Continuous-Delayed-Memory Stochastic Gradient Descent which depend on the past state of the discrete iteration process. We performed the simulation on some 2-dimensional landscape and observed some wider-exploration and more precise convergent behavior compared to Vanilla SGD by adjusting hyperparameters. Besides, we proposed a reinforcement learning structure with continuous time policy gradients for exploratory policies without solving HJB PDE, and we show that its optimality conditions recover the Gibbs policy of previous works.

AI.tldr: This paper presents two main contributions: (1) a new optimization method called Continuous-Delayed-Memory Stochastic Gradient Descent (CDMSGD) for training neural networks, and (2) a reinforcement learning framework with continuous time policy gradients. The methods are motivated by the challenge of modeling quasar brightness variations from light curve data using stochastic differential equations (SDEs).
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from the statistical challenge of modeling stochastic brightness variations in quasars from ground-based survey data time series (light curves). These variations encode information about supermassive black holes, and traditional methods struggle to capture the complexity of these stochastic processes.
AI.method: The paper proposes: (1) Continuous-Delayed-Memory Stochastic Gradient Descent (CDMSGD), which depends on the past state of the discrete iteration process; (2) A reinforcement learning structure with continuous time policy gradients for exploratory policies without solving Hamilton-Jacob-Bellman (HJB) partial differential equations.
AI.result: For CDMSGD: Simulation on 2-dimensional landscape shows wider-exploration and more precise convergent behavior compared to Vanilla SGD by adjusting hyperparameters. For the RL framework: The optimality conditions recover the Gibbs policy from previous works, demonstrating theoretical consistency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CDMSGD method offers improved exploration and convergence properties over standard gradient descent for certain optimization landscapes. The RL framework with continuous time policy gradients provides a tractable approach to exploratory policies without requiring PDE solutions, with theoretical guarantees linking to prior Gibbs policy formulations.

title: GameLogicBench: Evaluating Coding Agents on Runtime Game Logic with Tick-Level State Assertions
comment: 36 pages, 9 figures, 13 tables. Xinyu Che, Yunfei Ge, Shihao Li, Yanchen Liu, Hang Yan, and Xinping Lei contributed equally. Jiaheng Liu is the corresponding author. Code and benchmark: https://github.com/NJU-LINK/GameLogicBench
summary: Coding agents can modify and test code across large software projects. Game development is a domain where agents must implement gameplay rules. A game can end in a valid state even after violating its rules during the run. Current game-development benchmarks replay fixed examples, score videos, or ask another model to judge the result. However, no existing benchmark checks game rules throughout execution across varied evaluator-selected scenarios while ensuring exactly reproducible verdicts. We introduce GameLogicBench, a benchmark of 72 gameplay-logic tasks in Godot projects. An automated evaluator checks each game's rules at every simulation tick. Across 403 hand-designed scenarios, seeded parameter variations produce 1,451 test cases. To ensure that the evaluator measures behavior rather than implementation choice, it must accept different correct implementations for each task while rejecting mutants, implementations with one required capability removed. The tasks span isolated mechanics, multi-system interactions, and repository-scale features. Across 20 combinations of language models and scaffolds, the best observed run solves 52.78% of tasks. Under Claude Code, all twelve models solve fewer tasks as task scope expands from isolated mechanics, through interacting systems, to repository-scale features. Agents inspect code more often and make more tool calls on repository-scale tasks than on isolated-mechanic tasks. Most unsuccessful submissions are runnable, but implement some required game behavior incorrectly. We compared versions of our benchmark evaluator built with and without validation using mutants. Without this validation, incorrect agent submissions passed. A separate analysis finds agents copying code from public repositories when network access is open. Reliable evaluation thus depends both on what the tests reject and on what external code agents can access.

AI.tldr: GameLogicBench is a benchmark of 72 gameplay-logic tasks in Godot projects that checks game rules at every simulation tick. Testing 20 model/scaffold combinations, the best run solves 52.78% of tasks, with performance declining as task scope expands from isolated mechanics to repository-scale features. Validation using mutants is critical to prevent false positives, and network access enables agents to copy code rather than solve problems.
AI.motivation: Current game-development benchmarks have critical limitations: they replay fixed examples, score videos, or ask another model to judge results. No existing benchmark checks game rules throughout execution across varied evaluator-selected scenarios while ensuring exactly reproducible verdicts. Additionally, a game can end in a valid state even after violating its rules during runtime, creating evaluation challenges.
AI.method: Introduced GameLogicBench, a benchmark of 72 gameplay-logic tasks in Godot projects. An automated evaluator checks each game's rules at every simulation tick. Across 403 hand-designed scenarios with seeded parameter variations, this produces 1,451 test cases. The evaluator accepts different correct implementations while rejecting mutants (implementations with one required capability removed). Tasks span isolated mechanics, multi-system interactions, and repository-scale features. Tested 20 combinations of language models and scaffolds.
AI.result: Best observed run solves 52.78% of tasks. Under Claude Code, all twelve models solve fewer tasks as task scope expands from isolated mechanics, through interacting systems, to repository-scale features. Agents inspect code more often and make more tool calls on repository-scale tasks than on isolated-mechanic tasks. Most unsuccessful submissions are runnable but implement some required game behavior incorrectly. Without validation using mutants, incorrect agent submissions passed. When network access is open, agents copy code from public repositories.
AI.conclusion: Reliable evaluation in coding agent benchmarks depends both on test design (what tests reject) and on controlling external code access. The benchmark reveals that current agents struggle with multi-system interactions and repository-scale features, with task complexity significantly impacting performance.

title: GenTraceBench: A Benchmark for Tracing Audio Deepfakes Across Pre- and Post-training Stages
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Accepted to the 15th International Symposium on Chinese Spoken Language Processing (ISCSLP 2026)
summary: Modern text-to-speech (TTS) systems are rarely deployed as unchanged pre-trained models. They are often adapted through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or preference optimization such as DPO and GRPO. This raises a practical question for audio deepfake forensics: do fingerprints learned from a foundation generator remain valid after adaptation? We present GenTraceBench, a controlled benchmark spanning five TTS architectures, 16 pre-/post-training variants, and 49,728 utterances generated with fixed texts and speaker prompts. Under a train-on-foundation, test-on-adapted protocol, we evaluate binary detection, closed-set attribution, and open-set verification. DPO and GRPO generally preserve fingerprints, whereas some SFT and pre-training-data changes cause substantial drift; effect sizes vary across three forensic backbones. Repeated training runs confirm the largest W2V-BERT attribution drop, while a data-mixture control with comparable speech quality shows that composition change need not cause drift. In W2V-BERT verification, multi-shot enrollment reduces EER for the SFT condition from 44.4% to 11.0%, whereas the SingNet-only condition remains at or above 45% EER.

AI.tldr: GenTraceBench is a benchmark evaluating whether audio fingerprints from foundation TTS models remain detectable after model adaptation (SFT, DPO, GRPO). The study tests 5 TTS architectures, 16 variants, and ~50K utterances under train-on-foundation, test-on-adapted protocol. DPO and GRPO generally preserve fingerprints, while some SFT and pre-training data changes cause significant drift. Multi-shot enrollment improves verification significantly for SFT conditions.
AI.motivation: The practical problem addressed is whether forensic detection fingerprints learned from foundation TTS models remain valid after the models are adapted through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or preference optimization (DPO, GRPO). This is crucial for audio deepfake forensics in real-world deployment scenarios.
AI.method: Controlled benchmark with 5 TTS architectures, 16 pre-/post-training variants, 49,728 utterances using fixed texts and speaker prompts. Evaluation under train-on-foundation, test-on-adapted protocol across three forensic backbones (W2V-BERT, SingNet). Tasks include binary detection, closed-set attribution, and open-set verification. Includes repeated training runs and data-mixture control experiments.
AI.result: DPO and GRPO generally preserve fingerprints; some SFT and pre-training-data changes cause substantial drift. W2V-BERT shows largest attribution drop across repeated runs. Data-mixture control shows comparable speech quality doesn't necessarily cause drift. In W2V-BERT verification, multi-shot enrollment reduces EER from 44.4% to 11.0% for SFT condition, while SingNet-only remains at 45%+ EER.
AI.conclusion: Fingerprint preservation varies by adaptation method: preference optimization (DPO/GRPO) preserves fingerprints well, while some SFT and pre-training data changes cause significant drift. Multi-shot enrollment can significantly improve verification performance for SFT conditions. The forensic effectiveness depends on both the adaptation method and the detection backbone used.

title: MarsFM: Shading-Regularized Flow Matching for Martian Relief Estimation
summary: We present MarsFM, an image-conditioned latent flow-matching model for local Martian relief estimation from single-band HiRISE RED orthoimagery. The method combines a pretrained generative prior with stereo-derived geometric supervision and a differentiable Lunar--Lambert shading objective. Relief, normal, gradient, curvature, and ordinal terms constrain complementary aspects of terrain structure, while a positive-affine-invariant image comparison constrains rendered appearance. An evaluation comprising 2024 gathered patch records per integration-step count yields mean affine-aligned RMSE between 0.0935 and 0.0957 in normalized signed-log relief space for one to twenty Euler steps. These scores measure agreement with VAE-reconstructed references on positive-reference support. Their narrow range supports low-step inference under this protocol. Spatial, differential, and spectral diagnostics show broad terrain correspondence alongside smoothing, amplitude compression, and boundary mismatch. MarsFM provides a framework for combining learned terrain priors with image-based constraints; establishing improved physical terrain resolution requires matched baselines and independent high-resolution reference data. Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/SuperComputer/mars_hirise_dtm_processed-6aa9b66ba461e07f; code: https://github.com/Marius-Juston/MarsRecon.

AI.tldr: MarsFM is an image-conditioned latent flow-matching model that estimates local Martian relief from single-band HiRISE RED orthoimagery by combining pretrained generative priors with stereo-derived geometric supervision and differentiable Lunar-Lambert shading objective.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to improve Martian terrain relief estimation from single images by combining learned terrain priors with multi-modal physical constraints, as current methods lack the ability to integrate geometric and photometric cues effectively.
AI.method: MarsFM combines: (1) a pretrained generative prior, (2) stereo-derived geometric supervision, (3) a differentiable Lunar-Lambert shading objective, and (4) multiple terrain structure constraints including relief, normal, gradient, curvature, and ordinal terms. A positive-affine-invariant image comparison constrains rendered appearance. Evaluation used 2024 patch records per integration-step count (1-20 Euler steps).
AI.result: Mean affine-aligned RMSE of 0.0935-0.0957 in normalized signed-log relief space for 1-20 Euler steps. The narrow range supports low-step inference. Spatial, differential, and spectral diagnostics show broad terrain correspondence but also reveal smoothing, amplitude compression, and boundary mismatch issues.
AI.conclusion: MarsFM provides a framework for combining learned terrain priors with image-based constraints. Establishing improved physical terrain resolution requires matched baselines and independent high-resolution reference data.

title: Decoupling Internal Representational Changes and Causal Importance in Fine-Tuned Large Language Models
summary: Fine-tuning has emerged as a widely adopted approach for adapting LLMs to a variety of downstream tasks. However, how it reshapes their internal mechanisms remains poorly understood. To address this, we investigate how fine-tuning alters internal representations in LLMs, including attention patterns and layer-wise activations, and examine whether these changes are linked to task-relevant components identified by EAP (e.g., attention heads and logit-level activations) that drive task performance. We find that EAP-identified components are concentrated within specific layers, indicating a degree of functional localisation in how models internalise task-specific behavior. Notably, the distribution of these components across layers is largely uncorrelated with the layers undergoing the most substantial representational changes during fine-tuning. Furthermore, we observe that overlap in EAP-identified components across tasks does not translate into cross-task performance transfer if the tasks are different in nature (e.g. classification vs. generative tasks). More specifically, fine-tuning on one task can lead to a degradation of performance on another when the two tasks exhibit a high degree of overlap in their EAP-identified components.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning reshapes LLM internal representations (attention patterns and activations), but these changes are largely uncorrelated with task-relevant components identified by EAP. Overlap in EAP components across tasks doesn't guarantee cross-task transfer and can cause performance degradation.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning is widely used to adapt LLMs to downstream tasks, but how it reshapes internal mechanisms remains poorly understood. This study investigates the relationship between fine-tuning-induced changes and task-relevant components.
AI.method: Investigated how fine-tuning alters internal representations in LLMs, including attention patterns and layer-wise activations, and examined whether these changes correlate with task-relevant components identified by EAP (attention heads and logit-level activations).
AI.result: 1) EAP-identified components are concentrated within specific layers, indicating functional localization. 2) Distribution of these components is largely uncorrelated with layers undergoing substantial representational changes. 3) Overlap in EAP components across tasks doesn't translate into cross-task performance transfer if tasks differ in nature (e.g., classification vs. generative). 4) Fine-tuning on one task can degrade performance on another when tasks share high overlap in EAP components.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning-induced representational changes are not well-aligned with task-relevant components. Overlap in task-relevant components does not guarantee positive transfer and can even cause negative transfer, challenging the assumption that shared components enable knowledge transfer.

title: Do Quantum Models Scale Like LLMs?
summary: In this work, we study the neural scaling laws of RydbergGPT, an autoregressive transformer model trained on qubit projective measurement data gathered from interacting Rydberg atom arrays. The quantum system is known to exhibit a finite-size remnant of a critical point as the laser detuning parameter is varied. We find that near the critical point the transformer loss as a function of training dataset size is well described by a power-law with a loss floor correction. However, away from criticality the quality of the power-law description is substantially reduced. We then compare the statistical structure of both Rydberg measurements and natural-language corpora using an entropy-normalised, finite sample corrected mutual information "two-point" function. We find that near-critical statistics of the two point functions are closest to those observed in natural-language, whilst other qubit configurations far from the critical point have two-point functions that decay more rapidly. This supports the hypothesis that multi-scale dependence contributes to stable neural scaling, and that scaling behaviour should be viewed as a property of the model-data pair.

AI.tldr: This paper studies neural scaling laws for RydbergGPT, an autoregressive transformer trained on quantum measurement data from Rydberg atom arrays. The key finding is that scaling behavior depends critically on proximity to a quantum critical point—power-law scaling works well near criticality but fails away from it. The statistical structure of near-critical quantum data resembles natural language corpora, suggesting multi-scale dependence is essential for stable neural scaling.
AI.motivation: The authors investigate whether neural scaling laws—a cornerstone of large language model development—are intrinsic to the data or depend on the model-data combination. They use a quantum physics system (Rydberg atom arrays) as a testbed to understand how statistical structure of data affects scaling behavior.
AI.method: 1) Train RydbergGPT (autoregressive transformer) on qubit projective measurement data from interacting Rydberg atom arrays. 2) Analyze loss vs. training dataset size using power-law with loss floor correction. 3) Compare statistical structure of Rydberg measurements to natural language corpora using entropy-normalized, finite sample-corrected mutual information ("two-point" function).
AI.result: Near the critical point: transformer loss follows power-law scaling with loss floor correction. Away from criticality: power-law description substantially degrades. Near-critical two-point functions most closely match natural language statistics; non-critical configurations show faster decay.
AI.conclusion: Neural scaling behavior is NOT universal—it depends on the statistical structure of the data. Multi-scale dependence (present in both near-critical quantum data and natural language) contributes to stable, predictable scaling. This challenges the view that scaling laws are inherent properties of models alone and suggests they emerge from specific model-data combinations.

title: Labelling Bug-Fixing Commits with Local Open-Weight Language Models
summary: Defect prediction depends on knowing which commits fix bugs, yet the labels that encode this are produced by routes that each introduce noise. Reused benchmarks carry documented data-quality problems, issue-tracker links are biased and the underlying reports are frequently mistyped, and matching keywords in commit messages is a coarse heuristic. This paper examines whether commits can be labelled as bug fixes from their content alone, using open-weight language models that run locally and therefore keep the process reproducible, inexpensive at corpus scale, usable on proprietary code, and independent of any issue tracker. Against datasets of manually validated and curated bug fixes spanning Java, Python, and JavaScript, we compare a keyword baseline with a set of open-weight models of varying size, prompting each with the commit message and the code diff. On the manually validated corpus the keyword baseline recovers fewer than half of the fixes, whereas the open-weight models recover the large majority and outperform it repository by repository with statistical significance, and larger models do not consistently outperform smaller ones. We further show that evaluation corpora without negative examples cannot support a precision-aware comparison of such classifiers. We release the labelling pipeline together with a labelled, multi-language corpus produced by the recommended configuration, as a reproducible silver-standard resource for building current, project-specific datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of noisy bug-fix labels in defect prediction by using open-weight language models to automatically label commits as bug fixes based on commit messages and code diffs, outperforming traditional keyword-based approaches.
AI.motivation: Defect prediction models depend on correctly labeled bug-fix commits, but existing labeling methods (reused benchmarks, issue-tracker links, keyword matching) each introduce significant noise. The authors propose using content-based classification with open-weight language models to create a reproducible, inexpensive, and privacy-preserving labeling approach.
AI.method: The authors compared a keyword baseline against multiple open-weight language models of varying sizes on manually validated datasets spanning Java, Python, and JavaScript. Each model was prompted with commit messages and code diffs to classify commits as bug fixes. Evaluation was performed on a manually curated corpus with both positive and negative examples.
AI.result: The keyword baseline recovered fewer than 50% of bug fixes, while open-weight models recovered the majority and outperformed the baseline repository-by-repository with statistical significance. Larger models did not consistently outperform smaller ones. The study also found that evaluation corpora without negative examples cannot support precision-aware comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight language models effectively label bug-fix commits from content alone, outperforming keyword baselines. The authors release their labeling pipeline and a labeled multi-language corpus as a reproducible silver-standard resource for building project-specific defect prediction datasets. Key insight: model size is not the primary factor—proper prompting with commit content matters more.

title: Training Music Sample Identification Models on Real Sample Pairs
summary: Sample identification (SI) is the task of matching pairs of tracks, where one track is created by musically transforming an element of the other. In the absence of sample annotations at scale, the dominant training paradigm has depended on artificially creating sample pairs. Although a recently released dataset provides annotations of real sample pairs at scale, an effective training recipe is missing. In this work, we present SI Embeddings (SIE), an SI model that achieves state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks, including a large-scale test set. We show that the previous state of the art trained on artificial pairs generalizes only partially to real pairs, and that its training data limits its performance. We also show that real pairs do not fully account for SIE's performance: its architecture and training recipe contribute substantially. We provide the first fully supervised training recipe for real-world SI, establishing a strong foundation for future research in the field.

AI.tldr: This paper presents SIE (SI Embeddings), a state-of-the-art model for Sample Identification - the task of matching pairs of tracks where one track is a musical transformation of another. The work addresses the gap between training on artificial sample pairs and real-world sample identification.
AI.motivation: Previous sample identification models were trained on artificially created sample pairs, but a new dataset provides real sample pair annotations. The research aims to develop an effective training recipe using real-world data and establish a strong foundation for future SI research.
AI.method: The paper proposes SIE (SI Embeddings), a model architecture with a supervised training recipe designed specifically for real-world sample identification. The approach combines real sample pairs with careful architectural design and training methodology.
AI.result: SIE achieves state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks, including a large-scale test set. Key findings show that: (1) previous SOTA trained on artificial pairs only generalizes partially to real pairs, (2) training data limits performance, and (3) both the architecture and training recipe contribute substantially to SIE's performance beyond just using real pairs.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first fully supervised training recipe for real-world sample identification, establishing a strong foundation for future research in the field. The study demonstrates that combining real sample pairs with appropriate architecture and training methodology is essential for achieving optimal SI performance.

title: 4DGS-Fixer: Generative Sparse-View 4D Gaussian Splatting with Iterative Refinement Guided by Video Diffusion Priors
summary: This paper addresses the challenges of dynamic scene synthesis from sparse-view videos. Existing methods employ geometric priors, adaptive optimization, or density-control strategies to improve 4D Gaussian modeling under sparse observations. However, they cannot fundamentally resolve the ill-posed problem caused by insufficient observations and missing scene information. Moreover, sparse-view 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) often suffers from poor geometric initialization: with only a few input views, COLMAP typically reconstructs sparse and incomplete point clouds, leaving large scene regions without sufficient Gaussian support and making them difficult to recover through subsequent optimization. To address these limitations, we propose a novel iterative refinement framework based on a video diffusion model to improve the completeness and consistency of dynamic 4D scenes. Specifically, we first estimate multi-view depth maps and fuse them into dense point clouds to provide more complete geometric initialization for a dynamic 4DGS representation. We then employ a pretrained video restoration model to refine sequences rendered along novel camera trajectories at different time steps. The restored sequences serve as pseudo-supervision to regularize and iteratively refine the 4DGS representation. Experiments on a widely used benchmark dataset demonstrate that our method substantially outperforms existing baselines, achieving nearly a 2 dB PSNR improvement over the previous best-performing method.

title: TinyCeNN-LM: Quality-Gated Conversion of Pretrained Attention with CeNN-Inspired Cellular-Recurrent Layers
summary: Replacing attention in a pretrained language model is a compatibility problem: a plausible substitute may alter representations expected by later layers. TinyCeNN-LM introduces a \emph{quality-gated post-training conversion} framework using CeNN-inspired cellular-recurrent layers with bounded local processing, compact recurrent memory, routing, fusion, and accept-or-rollback validation. Three implementations are studied: Integrated Memory, MemoryFusion, and PDelta3-GDN2-CLVR+Local32. Strict PDelta3 conversion accepts a layer only when representation and NLL criteria pass fixed thresholds. On SmolLM2-135M, layers 0-2 are accepted with cumulative $Δ\mathrm{NLL}=+0.01209$, while layer 3 is rejected despite acceptable NLL because representation fidelity fails. On Qwen3.5-0.8B, full-attention layers 3, 7, and 11 are accepted with final $Δ\mathrm{NLL}=+0.02073$. Integrated Memory keeps perplexity within $-0.07\%$ to $+0.93\%$ while reducing total cache by up to $6.01\%$. A sampled 200-item downstream sanity check gives $28.5\%$--$32.0\%$ overall accuracy for converted Qwen releases. The results support conservative, quality-gated structural conversion rather than universal attention replacement or speedup.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces TinyCeNN-LM, a quality-gated post-training conversion framework that replaces attention mechanisms in pretrained language models with CeNN-inspired cellular-recurrent layers. The framework uses bounded local processing, compact recurrent memory, and accept-or-rollback validation to ensure representation fidelity. Experiments on SmolLM2-135M and Qwen3.5-0.8B show that layers can be selectively converted while maintaining perplexity within ±0.93%, though downstream performance shows modest accuracy (28.5-32%). The authors advocate for conservative, quality-gated structural conversion over universal attention replacement.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that replacing attention mechanisms in pretrained language models creates compatibility issues - the substitute layers may alter representations that downstream layers expect, leading to degraded performance. The motivation is to develop a framework that can safely replace attention while preserving the model's original representations and behavior.
AI.method: The paper proposes a quality-gated post-training conversion framework with several key components: (1) CeNN-inspired cellular-recurrent layers with bounded local processing, (2) compact recurrent memory, (3) routing and fusion mechanisms, and (4) accept-or-rollback validation. Three implementations are studied: Integrated Memory, MemoryFusion, and PDelta3-GDN2-CLVR+Local32. The strict PDelta3 conversion only accepts a layer when both representation fidelity and NLL (negative log-likelihood) criteria pass fixed thresholds. Layers that fail representation fidelity checks are rejected even if NLL is acceptable.
AI.result: On SmolLM2-135M, layers 0-2 were accepted with cumulative ΔNLL=+0.01209, while layer 3 was rejected despite acceptable NLL due to representation fidelity failure. On Qwen3.5-0.8B, full-attention layers 3, 7, and 11 were accepted with final ΔNLL=+0.02073. Integrated Memory maintained perplexity within -0.07% to +0.93% while reducing total cache by up to 6.01%. A 200-item downstream sanity check showed 28.5%-32.0% overall accuracy for converted Qwen releases.
AI.conclusion: The results support a conservative, quality-gated approach to structural conversion rather than universal attention replacement or speedup. The key insight is that not all layers can be safely converted - representation fidelity is a critical constraint that must be validated. The approach shows promise for selective layer replacement with minimal performance degradation, but significant work remains to improve downstream task performance.

title: When AI Reviews Train AI Reviewers: Scientific-Judgment Collapse and Mitigation
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly participate in scientific evaluation, both as automated reviewers and as assistants to human reviewers. As model-generated reviews enter public data and future training corpora, AI peer review can become recursive: later reviewers learn from judgments produced by earlier models. We study one step of this feedback loop in a controlled setting. Starting from Llama 3.1 8B, we first fine-tune a reviewer on official ICLR reviews from 2018--2023 and then train four successor models on ICLR 2024 data with systematically varied mixtures of official and model-generated reviews. Our study shows that introducing synthetic reviews compresses rating distributions and reduces both same-paper and corpus-level semantic diversity. We call this pattern $\textbf{scientific-judgment collapse}$.
  To mitigate this failure mode, we introduce $\textbf{TrustReviewer}$, an open-source LLM-based system for generating peer reviews of AI and machine learning papers. TrustReviewer intervenes at two complementary stages. For training-time prevention, we train the core reviewer in a single stage on a curated corpus designed to reduce low-quality and semantically degenerate supervision. For test-time correction, paired activation steering aims to further mitigate residual tendencies toward collapsed judgments without further training or additional expert annotation. Together, these results characterize a concrete risk of recursive reviewer training and provide practical interventions for preserving judgment diversity and improving recommendation alignment in AI-assisted scientific evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates recursive AI peer review, where LLM-generated reviews enter training corpora for future reviewers. Using Llama 3.1 8B fine-tuned on ICLR reviews, the study demonstrates that model-generated reviews cause "scientific-judgment collapse" - compressing rating distributions and reducing semantic diversity. TrustReviewer is proposed as an open-source mitigation system with training-time curation and test-time activation steering.
AI.motivation: As LLMs increasingly participate in scientific evaluation (as automated reviewers or assistants), model-generated reviews enter public data and future training corpora, creating a recursive feedback loop where later reviewers learn from earlier model judgments. This study aims to characterize and mitigate this risk.
AI.method: Starting from Llama 3.1 8B, the authors first fine-tuned a reviewer on official ICLR reviews from 2018-2023, then trained four successor models on ICLR 2024 data with systematically varied mixtures of official and model-generated reviews. They introduced TrustReviewer with two interventions: (1) training-time prevention using a curated corpus to reduce low-quality supervision, and (2) test-time correction via paired activation steering to mitigate collapsed judgments without further training.
AI.result: Introducing synthetic reviews compresses rating distributions and reduces both same-paper and corpus-level semantic diversity. This pattern is characterized as "scientific-judgment collapse."
AI.conclusion: TrustReviewer provides practical interventions for preserving judgment diversity and improving recommendation alignment in AI-assisted scientific evaluation. The study characterizes a concrete risk of recursive reviewer training and offers viable solutions at both training and test time.

title: From Smarter to Hungrier: the Role of Energy Efficiency in Software-defined Vehicles
comment: Accepted in the 9th Annual Conference on Technology Ethics (TETHICS 2026), Lahti, Finland, November 11-12, 2026
summary: Automated features and advanced driving support systems have enabled a range of life-saving and comfort applications in modern personal vehicles. Development from mostly mechanical entities towards truly software-defined devices also means that added sensor complexity, processing power, and networking capabilities provide a platform for running even more complex algorithms and applications. As vehicles become smarter, they require even more energy to enable advanced machine learning- and artificial intelligence-based functionalities. This paper discusses the implications for sustainability and the threats to environmental ethics posed by the development of software-defined vehicles. We discuss the balance between introducing more resource-hungry software and hardware components and their effect on society and sustainability. We underscore the need for novel tools to measure, manage, and optimise energy consumption and other sustainability indicators, with design guidance and actionable recommendations.

title: Investigating the Performance and Energy Costs of Replicating Band-Split RNN for Music Source Separation
summary: Band-split recurrent neural network (BSRNN) is a popular music source separation model that yields close to state-of-the-art results using reasonable computational resources and public datasets. It is therefore interesting from a reproducible research perspective, but achieving its performance is not straightforward since its full code is not available. In this paper, we conduct a replication of BSRNN via implementing the full pipeline. We extend the original paper's analysis by experimentally studying various design choices about data preprocessing, the optimization protocol, and architectural parameters. We report and discuss this project's energy cost, and we underline how its footprint could have been substantial lower upon availability of the full pipeline, which advocates for more reproducible research practices. To comply with this objective, we publicly release our code and pre-trained models.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a replication study of Band-split recurrent neural network (BSRNN), a popular music source separation model, since the original paper did not release full code. The authors implement the full pipeline and publicly release their code and pre-trained models.
AI.motivation: The original BSRNN paper yields close to state-of-the-art results using reasonable computational resources but does not provide full code, making replication difficult. The authors aim to address reproducibility issues in MIR research and study various design choices that affect performance.
AI.method: The authors implement the complete BSRNN pipeline from scratch. They conduct experiments examining data preprocessing, optimization protocol, and architectural parameters. They also analyze the energy cost and environmental footprint of their experiments.
AI.result: The authors successfully replicate BSRNN and provide code and pre-trained models. They analyze the energy cost of their experiments and discuss how the footprint could have been substantially lower with access to the original pipeline.
AI.conclusion: The study highlights the importance of reproducible research practices. The authors advocate for more open science in the MIR community by publicly releasing their implementation, which enables better reproducibility and reduces redundant research effort.

title: OnomatoBridge: Onomatopoeia Translation and Rendering Pipeline in Manga
summary: Manga is a comic drawn by black and white paints gaining popularity around the world. Onomatopoeia in Manga specifically appeals to the audience with its unique visual styles, which convey sound, motion, and emotion. Visual onomatopoeia translation requires the clean replacement of Japanese onomatopoeia with onomatopoeia in the other language while preserving their visual style. Existing approaches often produce residual artifacts or style inconsistency when removing the Japanese onomatopoeia and rendering stylized English onomatopoeia. To approach these problems, we present OnomatoBridge, a filtering pipeline for visual onomatopoeia translation. We evaluate OnomatoBridge from Japanese to English on the Manga109 onomatopoeia dataset and compare it with baseline image editing models. Experimental results show that the filtered outputs by the proposed method outperform those of conventional methods. OnomatoBridge improves English text correctness by roughly 10 to 25 points and reduces residual Japanese text by about 20 to 50% in relative terms.

AI.tldr: OnomatoBridge is a filtering pipeline for visual onomatopoeia translation in Manga, addressing artifacts and style inconsistency issues when replacing Japanese onomatopoeia with English while preserving visual style.
AI.motivation: Visual onomatopoeia in Manga conveys sound, motion, and emotion through unique visual styles. Existing translation approaches produce residual artifacts or style inconsistency when removing Japanese onomatopoeia and rendering stylized English text.
AI.method: The paper proposes OnomatoBridge, a filtering pipeline for visual onomatopoeia translation evaluated from Japanese to English on the Manga109 onomatopoeia dataset, comparing with baseline image editing models.
AI.result: OnomatoBridge improves English text correctness by roughly 10 to 25 points and reduces residual Japanese text by about 20 to 50% in relative terms compared to conventional methods.
AI.conclusion: The filtered outputs by the proposed method outperform those of conventional methods on the Manga109 onomatopoeia dataset.

title: Clinician-Grounded Quality Assurance for AI-Assisted Psychiatric Intake
summary: Before patients can use AI-assisted psychiatric intake systems, health systems need practical ways to routinely evaluate these tools against their clinical standards for quality assurance. Because clinicians may use different intake styles, evaluation for this task must (1) support comparison across interviewing approaches, (2) minimize clinician burden, and (3) measure clinically relevant performance for health systems deploying these technologies. We present a clinician-grounded evaluation platform built around a memory-augmented patient simulator for open-ended AI interviewing, InterviewPlayground. We created interactive patients using InterviewPlayground with our expert-authored vignettes, constructed a simulated intake platform for the interviews, and designed evaluation modalities relevant to intake. In a pilot of 6 clinicians in a 25-minute assessment compared to a GPT-based LLM intake interviewer, the LLM recovered more of the clinically relevant items embedded in the patient vignettes (88.0% vs. 38.9%), but made more clinical inferences not based on the interview (56.8% vs. 27.8%), and characterized identified safety concerns less often (33.3% vs. 66.7%), setting the stage for deployed quality assurance for this task.

AI.tldr: InterviewPlayground is a clinician-grounded evaluation platform with memory-augmented patient simulators for assessing AI-assisted psychiatric intake systems. In a pilot study of 6 clinicians compared to a GPT-based LLM, the LLM recovered more clinical items (88% vs 38.9%) but made more unsupported inferences (56.8% vs 27.8%) and characterized safety concerns less often (33.3% vs 66.7%).
AI.motivation: Health systems need practical methods to routinely evaluate AI-assisted psychiatric intake tools against clinical quality standards, while supporting different intake styles, minimizing clinician burden, and measuring clinically relevant performance.
AI.method: Built InterviewPlayground platform using expert-authored patient vignettes with memory-augmented interactive patient simulators, created a simulated intake platform, and designed evaluation modalities relevant to psychiatric intake assessment.
AI.result: The LLM intake interviewer recovered more clinically relevant items (88.0% vs 38.9%) but made more clinical inferences not based on interview content (56.8% vs 27.8%), and characterized identified safety concerns less often (33.3% vs 66.7%).
AI.conclusion: The platform establishes a foundation for deployed quality assurance of AI psychiatric intake systems, highlighting that while LLMs gather more information, they require monitoring for unsupported inferences and safety concern documentation.

title: Efficient Bayes-Adaptive Reinforcement Learning with Temporal Logic Specifications
comment: ©~2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media, including reprinting/republishing this material for advertising or promotional purposes, creating new collective works, for resale or redistribution to servers or lists, or reuse of any copyrighted component of this work in other works
summary: We present a novel end-to-end model-based Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithm for efficient policy synthesis under given Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specifications (e.g., safety or reachability) in unknown environments. To do so, a Limit-Deterministic B{ü}chi Automaton (LDBA) representation of the LTL task is synchronised with a Bayes-Adaptive Markov Decision Process (BAMDP) representation of the environment, which allows us to leverage an enhanced exploration-exploitation trade-off that is achieved via Bayesian RL, as opposed to traditional non-Bayesian approaches. We further propose a novel Bayes-Adaptive Monte-Carlo Planning (BAMCP) algorithm to allow for approximate Bayes-optimal strategy synthesis in the synchronised BAMDP construct. A range of finite- and infinite-horizon task experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in terms of both property satisfaction and sample efficiency, when compared to traditional model-free approaches. Additional ablation studies also successfully highlight the value of the novel BAMCP algorithm in comparison to classical BAMCP for LTL task satisfaction. Finally, we also showcase a successful application of our approach for \textit{cautious} RL, namely to reduce the number of task violations incurred during policy training.

AI.tldr: A novel end-to-end model-based RL algorithm that combines Limit-Deterministic Büchi Automaton (LDBA) with Bayes-Adaptive MDP (BAMDP) for synthesizing policies that satisfy Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specifications in unknown environments. Uses a new Bayes-Adaptive Monte-Carlo Planning (BAMCP) algorithm for approximate Bayes-optimal planning.
AI.motivation: Traditional RL approaches for LTL specifications either fail to leverage exploration-exploitation trade-offs effectively or require extensive sampling in unknown environments. The need is to develop a more efficient approach that can synthesize policies satisfying LTL specifications while maintaining good sample efficiency.
AI.method: 1) Represent LTL task as LDBA; 2) Synchronize LDBA with BAMDP to create a combined model; 3) Apply novel BAMCP algorithm for approximate Bayes-optimal strategy synthesis in the synchronized construct; 4) Use Bayesian RL for enhanced exploration-exploitation balance.
AI.result: Demonstrated effectiveness in finite- and infinite-horizon tasks: (1) Achieves property satisfaction and improved sample efficiency compared to model-free approaches; (2) Ablation studies confirm the novel BAMCP outperforms classical BAMCP for LTL tasks; (3) Successfully applicable to cautious RL, reducing task violations during training.
AI.conclusion: The proposed end-to-end model-based RL algorithm with LDBA-BAMDP synchronization and novel BAMCP provides an effective solution for LTL-specified tasks in unknown environments, offering better sample efficiency and task compliance than traditional approaches, with potential for safe/ cautious RL applications.

title: Supporting Industrial Test-Failure Analysis with LLM-Based Systems: An Experience Report
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, accepted to PROFES 2026, 30 Nov to 2 Dec 2026, Karlskrona, Sweden
summary: This study examines tool-augmented Large Language Model (LLM) systems for supporting Root Cause Analysis (RCA) of nightly test failures at Westermo Network Technologies AB. Nightly test executions produce heterogeneous test data and logs that practitioners currently inspect manually across multiple sources. We implemented an RCA workflow in single-agent and orchestrated multi-agent configurations, both with access to test metadata and logs. An exploratory industrial case study used two real failure scenarios. Six practitioners evaluated the scenario reports through a survey and focus group, and operational measurements were collected from 120 repeated executions. The evaluation covered practitioner-perceived correctness, reasoning quality, fix realism, clarity, usefulness, and trust, as well as cost, duration, and consistency. Neither configuration showed a consistent practitioner-perceived quality advantage across the two scenarios. The single agent system generated reports faster and at lower cost, making it the more practical baseline in this context. The potential benefits of agent architectures require further evaluation in more complex scenarios.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates tool-augmented LLM systems for Root Cause Analysis of nightly test failures at an industrial company. Both single-agent and multi-agent configurations were tested, with the single-agent system proving more practical due to faster execution and lower cost.
AI.motivation: Nightly test executions produce heterogeneous test data and logs that require manual inspection across multiple sources, which is time-consuming and inefficient. This study aims to automate RCA using tool-augmented LLM agents.
AI.method: An RCA workflow was implemented in single-agent and orchestrated multi-agent configurations, both with access to test metadata and logs. An exploratory industrial case study used two real failure scenarios. Six practitioners evaluated scenario reports through a survey and focus group, and operational measurements were collected from 120 repeated executions.
AI.result: Neither configuration showed a consistent practitioner-perceived quality advantage across the two scenarios. The single-agent system generated reports faster and at lower cost, making it the more practical baseline.
AI.conclusion: The potential benefits of agent architectures require further evaluation in more complex scenarios. The single-agent approach serves as a practical baseline for RCA in this context.

title: Spherical Harmonic Sliced Wasserstein Displacement Interpolation for Acoustic Source and Reflection Density Modeling
summary: Spatial room impulse responses (SRIRs) capture directional distributions of acoustic sound-sources and their reflections. However, collecting SRIRs of moving sound-sources remains a challenge, requiring complex interpolations across measurements that account for multi-path spatial-temporal dynamics. This paper investigates the Wasserstein metric and displacement for evaluating interpolated SRIR echo densities in the spherical harmonic domain. We present novel sum-of-magnitude square expansions for efficiently fitting probability density functions, maximizing likelihood, inverse sampling, and computing spherical sliced Wasserstein interpolations. Experiments compare the Wasserstein displacements and metric to linear and geometric interpolations of SRIR image-source densities on a line-path, and demonstrate model-order reduction.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the use of Wasserstein metric and displacement for evaluating interpolated spatial room impulse responses (SRIRs) of moving sound-sources in the spherical harmonic domain. Novel computational methods including sum-of-magnitude square expansions, likelihood maximization, inverse sampling, and spherical sliced Wasserstein interpolations are proposed.
AI.motivation: Collecting SRIRs of moving sound-sources is challenging due to the complexity of interpolating across measurements while accounting for multi-path spatial-temporal dynamics. Existing methods may not adequately capture the directional distributions and echo densities of acoustic reflections.
AI.method: The paper proposes using the Wasserstein metric and displacement in the spherical harmonic domain. Novel sum-of-magnitude square expansions are presented for fitting probability density functions, maximizing likelihood, inverse sampling, and computing spherical sliced Wasserstein interpolations. Experiments compare Wasserstein-based methods to linear and geometric interpolations of SRIR image-source densities on a line-path.
AI.result: The Wasserstein displacement and metric are compared to linear and geometric interpolations, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach for evaluating SRIR echo densities. Model-order reduction is also demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: The Wasserstein metric provides a valuable framework for evaluating interpolated SRIRs for moving sound-sources, offering advantages in capturing spatial-temporal dynamics and echo density distributions. The proposed computational methods enable efficient processing in the spherical harmonic domain.

title: Hand-Aware Transition Modeling for Bimanual Procedural Anomaly Detection
summary: Procedural anomaly detection in bimanual assembly requires judging each hand action against the execution so far. A corrective action may look unusual in isolation, while a visually plausible action can violate the order of the procedure. We present HACT, a transition model over predicted per-hand events. A role-preserving history keeps the concurrent responsibilities of both hands, and a marked temporal point process assigns each observed transition a semantic and temporal surprisal. A supervised evidence head and a two-state filter convert these surprisals into per-hand anomaly posteriors. A recovery-aware protocol on predicted events and participant-disjoint folds reports the recovery false-positive rate at an operating point selected on validation participants. On two bimanual power-tool procedures HACT has the highest AUPRC and F1 among the compared methods and the fewest recovery alarms. Applied without retraining to a different assembly order of the same product, it retains the highest AUPRC and F1. The source code is available at https://github.com/Kratos-Wen/HACT.

AI.tldr: HACT is a transition model-based approach for detecting procedural anomalies in bimanual assembly tasks. It uses role-preserving history to track concurrent hand responsibilities and marked temporal point process to compute semantic and temporal surprisal. The method converts surprisals into per-hand anomaly posteriors via a supervised evidence head and two-state filter, achieving state-of-the-art performance on two bimanual power-tool procedures.
AI.motivation: Procedural anomaly detection in bimanual assembly is challenging because: (1) a corrective action may look unusual in isolation but be correct in context, and (2) a visually plausible action can violate the order of the procedure. Existing methods fail to adequately capture the temporal and semantic dependencies between both hands' actions.
AI.method: HACT combines: (1) A transition model over predicted per-hand events, (2) Role-preserving history that maintains concurrent responsibilities of both hands, (3) Marked temporal point process assigning semantic and temporal surprisal to observed transitions, (4) Supervised evidence head and two-state filter converting surprisals into per-hand anomaly posteriors, (5) Recovery-aware protocol on predicted events with participant-disjoint folds for evaluation.
AI.result: HACT achieves the highest AUPRC and F1 among compared methods on two bimanual power-tool procedures, with the fewest recovery alarms. It also generalizes well - when applied without retraining to a different assembly order of the same product, it retains the highest AUPRC and F1.
AI.conclusion: The proposed HACT method effectively addresses the challenge of procedural anomaly detection in bimanual assembly by modeling temporal dependencies and hand interactions. Its success on cross-domain generalization (different assembly order) demonstrates strong practical applicability for real-world manufacturing scenarios.

title: Can Agents Design Better Chips with a Higher Level Abstraction?
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly being explored for chip design, but most existing approaches operate directly at RTL. We ask whether agents can design better chips by leveraging higher-level abstractions. We compare Direct RTL Design, Agent-based HLS Design, Post-Compiler HLS Refinement, and Post-HLS RTL Refinement, and combine Agent-based HLS Design with Post-HLS RTL Refinement as Agent-based HLS with RTL Refinement (AHRR). We use FPGAs as a practical, easy-to-deploy platform for end-to-end evaluation, but note that the design-flow tradeoffs we study are largely independent of the target technology. Across a diverse 11-tasks benchmark suite, AHRR achieves a 2.6$\times$ geometric-mean speedup over Direct RTL Design across our benchmark suite. Case studies show that HLS distills design knowledge into abstractions that agents can leverage, while RTL refinement recovers lower-level optimization opportunities. Together, these results make AHRR a promising workflow for agentic chip design. The code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/ZijD/AHRR.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes AHRR (Agent-based HLS with RTL Refinement), a novel LLM agent-based chip design workflow that combines High-Level Synthesis (HLS) with RTL refinement. It achieves 2.6x geometric-mean speedup over Direct RTL Design across 11 benchmark tasks, using FPGAs as the evaluation platform.
AI.motivation: Most existing LLM agent approaches for chip design operate directly at RTL (Register Transfer Level). This paper investigates whether agents can design better chips by leveraging higher-level abstractions instead of working directly at RTL.
AI.method: The study compares four design approaches: (1) Direct RTL Design, (2) Agent-based HLS Design, (3) Post-Compiler HLS Refinement, and (4) Post-HLS RTL Refinement. The researchers combined Agent-based HLS Design with Post-HLS RTL Refinement to create AHRR. Evaluation was conducted across a diverse 11-task benchmark suite using FPGAs as the deployment platform.
AI.result: AHRR achieves a 2.6× geometric-mean speedup over Direct RTL Design across the benchmark suite. Case studies reveal that HLS distills design knowledge into abstractions that agents can leverage, while RTL refinement recovers lower-level optimization opportunities.
AI.conclusion: AHRR represents a promising workflow for agentic chip design. The combination of HLS abstraction for design knowledge capture and RTL refinement for lower-level optimizations provides an effective approach for LLM-based chip design.

title: From Switching to Dynamic Regret: A Simple Reduction via Unbiased Random Sequences
summary: In non-stationary online learning, dynamic regret has attracted increasing attention as a measure of how well an online learner performs against a time-varying comparator sequence. Despite considerable advances, attaining optimal bounds for strongly convex and exp-concave losses often involves intricate analysis. In this paper, we present a \textit{simple} framework that reduces dynamic regret minimization to switching regret minimization. As a result, we can derive dynamic regret bounds by using off-the-shelf algorithms with switching regret guarantees. The key idea of our reduction is to construct, for \textit{any} comparator sequence, an auxiliary random sequence that is unbiased at each round, with the controlled variance and a manageable number of switches. Combining this construction with suitable surrogate losses, we can decompose dynamic regret into the expected switching regret against the random sequence and its controlled variance. Theoretically, for strongly convex and exp-concave losses, we establish the $\widetilde{O}(T^{1/3}P_T^{2/3})$ dynamic regret bounds, where $T$ denotes the time horizon and $P_T$ denotes the path-length of the comparator sequence. Moreover, for general convex losses, the same reduction also recovers the $O(\sqrt{T(1+P_T)})$ dynamic regret bound. Notably, all our findings match the minimax optimal results for these three types of losses, highlighting the versatility of our proposed framework.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a simple framework that reduces dynamic regret minimization to switching regret minimization in non-stationary online learning. By constructing an auxiliary random sequence that is unbiased at each round, the authors derive optimal dynamic regret bounds for strongly convex, exp-concave, and general convex losses.
AI.motivation: Dynamic regret is a crucial measure in non-stationary online learning, but achieving optimal bounds for strongly convex and exp-concave losses involves complex analysis. The authors aim to simplify this by developing a framework that reduces dynamic regret minimization to the well-studied switching regret problem.
AI.method: The key approach involves: (1) constructing an auxiliary random sequence that is unbiased at each round with controlled variance and manageable number of switches, (2) combining this construction with suitable surrogate losses to decompose dynamic regret into expected switching regret against the random sequence and its controlled variance, (3) using off-the-shelf algorithms with switching regret guarantees.
AI.result: For strongly convex and exp-concave losses: Õ(T^{1/3}P_T^{2/3}) dynamic regret bounds. For general convex losses: O(√(T(1+P_T))) dynamic regret bound. Both match minimax optimal results.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully reduces dynamic regret minimization to switching regret minimization, providing a simple yet versatile approach that achieves minimax optimal bounds across different loss function types.

title: How Researchers Use and Verify AI Coding Assistants: Tasks and Validation Practices in Scientific Programming
summary: Generative AI has entered research programming, yet there is little evidence about which tasks researchers hand to it or how they decide whether its code is correct. We draw on 527 free-text responses to a 2025 survey of researchers who write code, most of them at U.S. universities. In each response, a researcher recounts a single task from their own work, the way they used an AI tool for it, and what they did to assess the result. We coded the task and the evaluation strategies reported, and related both to programming experience, research area, and confidence ratings. Use was concentrated in five tasks: data handling, visualization, debugging, mathematical/scientific computing, and statistical analysis. Evaluation was informal and individual. Over half of accounts described running the generated code, while automated tests and review by another person were rare. Use cases and evaluation strategies varied little with programming experience, but confidence did: Less experienced programmers trusted the AI more than themselves, and experienced programmers the reverse. Evaluation confidence was not associated with the strategies reported. Its strongest correlates were confidence in the tool and in oneself. Validating AI contributions to scientific code rested largely on individual judgment, outside shared infrastructure for testing or review. Interfaces could support task-appropriate evaluation rather than leave it to the user.

AI.tldr: Survey of 527 researchers reveals that generative AI use in research programming is concentrated in five tasks (data handling, visualization, debugging, mathematical/scientific computing, statistical analysis), with evaluation being informal and individual. Over half simply run the code; automated tests and peer review are rare. Confidence in AI outputs correlates more with trust in the tool or oneself than evaluation strategies used.
AI.motivation: To understand how researchers are using generative AI in their programming work, what specific tasks they delegate to AI, and how they assess whether AI-generated code is correct—areas with little existing evidence.
AI.method: 2025 survey of 527 researchers who write code (mostly at U.S. universities). Each respondent provided a free-text account describing a single task, how they used an AI tool for it, and how they evaluated the result. Responses were coded for task type and evaluation strategies, then related to programming experience, research area, and confidence ratings.
AI.result: AI use concentrated in five task categories: data handling, visualization, debugging, mathematical/scientific computing, and statistical analysis. Evaluation was informal and individual—over half simply ran the code, while automated tests and peer review were rare. Use cases and evaluation strategies varied little with programming experience. However, confidence showed the opposite pattern: less experienced programmers trusted AI more than themselves, while experienced programmers trusted themselves more. Evaluation confidence was not associated with reported strategies; its strongest predictors were confidence in the tool and in oneself.
AI.conclusion: Validating AI-generated scientific code relies heavily on individual judgment, operating outside shared infrastructure for testing or review. Current interfaces do not support task-appropriate evaluation, leaving users to develop their own strategies. Interface design could better support appropriate evaluation methods based on the specific task.

title: Listen Before You Speak: Response Planning from Listener Facial Reactions for Conversational Speech Generation
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 2026 ECCV Workshop (11th ABAW) Best Student Paper Award
summary: Conversational speech depends on dialogue context and the listener's immediately preceding behavior. We propose ReACT-TTS, a two-stage framework that uses a one-second pre-response listener facial sequence to plan the next utterance's emotion and prosody before speech realization. On a strict dyadic MELD protocol, Temporal conditioning yields higher mean macro-F1 and VAD concordance than Text-only across ten seeds, while accuracy remains essentially unchanged. Ablations show that temporal modeling performs best among the visual variants and that an explicit early-to-late difference is unnecessary; correct listener reactions also outperform cyclic mismatches on average. In a contextual-appropriateness study with 20 speech researchers, 76% of judgments prefer Temporal, 9% Text-only, and 15% report no preference. We further connect the predicted response style to a Grad-TTS backbone for end-to-end speech realization. Overall, the results support pre-response listener dynamics as complementary cues for conversational response planning. The source code is available at https://github.com/CYJ1/ReACT-TTS_public.

AI.tldr: ReACT-TTS is a two-stage framework for conversational speech synthesis that uses one-second pre-response listener facial sequences to plan emotion and prosody before speech realization. It connects predicted response styles to a Grad-TTS backbone for end-to-end speech synthesis.
AI.motivation: Conversational speech depends on dialogue context and the listener's immediately preceding behavior. Existing text-to-speech systems lack mechanisms to incorporate listener feedback into response planning, which is crucial for natural conversation.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: (1) Temporal conditioning using one-second pre-response listener facial sequences to predict emotion and prosody; (2) End-to-end speech realization using Grad-TTS backbone. Compared Text-only vs Temporal conditioning across ten seeds on MELD protocol.
AI.result: Temporal conditioning yields higher mean macro-F1 and VAD concordance than Text-only, while accuracy remains unchanged. Ablations show temporal modeling outperforms other visual variants, explicit early-to-late difference is unnecessary, and correct listener reactions outperform cyclic mismatches. Human evaluation: 76% prefer Temporal, 9% Text-only, 15% no preference.
AI.conclusion: Pre-response listener dynamics serve as complementary cues for conversational response planning. The approach successfully integrates listener facial behavior into speech synthesis, improving emotional and prosodic appropriateness of generated speech.

title: Multi-viewpoint Geo-localization with Event Cameras
summary: Robot localization is an ongoing challenge that demands mapping and positioning systems that are tolerant to viewpoint change. Event cameras are attracting increasing interest and adoption in robotics; however, dealing with viewpoint variance is an under-investigated problem in existing event-based localizers. In addition, event-based datasets that emphasize viewpoint variance for challenging localization situations are scarce. Here, we introduce an event-based visual place recognition (VPR) system that performs robustly under viewpoint changes. We converted five large-scale geo-tagged datasets, conventionally used to train frame-based localization systems, into synthetic event streams using Image-to-Event (I2E) conversion, and used them to fine-tune a pre-trained event-based vision transformer backbone with a multi-loss function, yielding a system we call MegaEvent that learns viewpoint-robust features for place recognition. We achieved an average Recall@1 of 82% across three existing event-based localization datasets, leading the next best event-based method by 20 recall points, and frame-based VPR models applied directly to event frames by 8 to 26 recall points. We introduce a new, challenging dataset - Springfield-Event-VPR - which features a 3.7km walking route recorded in three camera orientations for a total of 11.1km, which MegaEvent outperforms the strongest baseline by 9 recall points. The code for MegaEvent is available at https://github.com/AdamDHines/megaevent.

AI.tldr: MegaEvent is an event-based visual place recognition (VPR) system that achieves robust localization under viewpoint changes. It uses synthetic event streams converted from 5 large-scale geo-tagged datasets via Image-to-Event (I2E) conversion to fine-tune a pre-trained event-based vision transformer with a multi-loss function, learning viewpoint-robust features.
AI.motivation: Robot localization requires mapping and positioning systems tolerant to viewpoint changes. While event cameras are increasingly adopted in robotics, handling viewpoint variance remains under-investigated in event-based localizers. Additionally, event-based datasets emphasizing viewpoint variance are scarce.
AI.method: Converting five large-scale geo-tagged datasets (conventionally used for frame-based localization) into synthetic event streams using Image-to-Event (I2E) conversion, then fine-tuning a pre-trained event-based vision transformer backbone with a multi-loss function to learn viewpoint-robust features for place recognition.
AI.result: Achieved an average Recall@1 of 82% across three existing event-based localization datasets, outperforming the next best event-based method by 20 recall points and frame-based VPR models by 8 to 26 recall points. On the new Springfield-Event-VPR dataset (3.7km route, 3 orientations, 11.1km total), MegaEvent outperformed the strongest baseline by 9 recall points.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MegaEvent system demonstrates that synthetic event data converted from conventional datasets combined with a multi-loss fine-tuned vision transformer can effectively learn viewpoint-robust features, achieving state-of-the-art performance in event-based visual place recognition under significant viewpoint changes.

title: SpecOpt: Contact-Diff Reasoning for Agentic Molecule Optimization Toward Binding Specificity
summary: Off-target protein binding is a major source of adverse effects for small-molecule drugs, yet most structure-based molecular design methods focus on generating selective compounds de novo rather than improving the selectivity of existing, well- characterized drugs. We introduce specificity optimization (SpecOpt), a molecular design task that seeks constrained structural modifications to an existing compound that increase its binding preference for an intended target over known off-targets while preserving its structural identity and drug-like properties. To enable systematic evaluation, we construct a ChEMBL-derived benchmark from compound-target interaction data, identifying intended targets through curated drug-mechanism annotations and off- targets through measured activities. We then develop an agentic framework that docks each compound against its intended target and off-targets, compares the resulting poses through residue-aware atom-protein contacts, and provides these differential interactions to a large language model to propose targeted structural modifications. Candidates are retained only if they satisfy molecular similarity, ADMET, and target-off-target docking selectivity criteria. On 915 compounds, the agent improves the target- off-target binding gap for 84.8% of compounds, shifting the mean gap from -0.72 to +0.47 kcal/mol while maintaining a mean Tanimoto similarity of 0.72 to the starting compounds. Ablation studies identify residue-specific contact information as the critical optimization signal: replacing residue identities with binary contact indicators eliminates improvement on all 29 ablation compounds. These results establish SpecOpt as a distinct molecular design problem and demonstrate residue-aware differential interactions as an effective signal for improving the specificity of existing compounds.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SpecOpt, a novel molecular design task that optimizes existing drugs for better target specificity by modifying their structure while preserving drug-like properties. They develop an agentic framework using residue-aware atom-protein contacts and LLM to propose modifications, achieving improved selectivity for 84.8% of 915 compounds tested.
