AI.motivation: Off-target binding is a major cause of adverse drug effects, but current structure-based design focuses on generating new selective compounds rather than improving existing drugs. There was a need for a systematic approach to optimize the specificity of well-characterized drugs.
AI.method: The authors constructed a ChEMBL-derived benchmark identifying intended targets through drug-mechanism annotations and off-targets through measured activities. They developed an agentic framework that: 1) docks compounds against target and off-targets, 2) compares poses via residue-aware atom-protein contacts, 3) uses LLM to propose structural modifications, and 4) filters candidates by molecular similarity, ADMET, and docking selectivity criteria.
AI.result: On 915 compounds, the agent improved target-off-target binding gap for 84.8% of compounds, shifting mean gap from -0.72 to +0.47 kcal/mol while maintaining mean Tanimoto similarity of 0.72. Ablation studies showed residue-specific contact information was critical - replacing residue identities with binary contact indicators eliminated improvement on all 29 ablation compounds.
AI.conclusion: SpecOpt represents a distinct molecular design problem distinct from de novo drug generation. Residue-aware differential interactions serve as an effective signal for improving compound specificity, offering a promising approach for optimizing existing drugs to reduce adverse effects.

title: Generative inversion for early ranking of competing geologic interpretations
summary: High-consequence subsurface decisions are often made under severe data scarcity. Experts may arrive at competing interpretations of the same subsurface system, yet early in a project there is rarely a practical way to determine which one is most realistic. This uncertainty can persist until several wells are drilled, often costing millions of dollars. Existing approaches for evaluating geologic interpretations rely either on subjective judgment or on dense data that are rarely available in early-stage investigations. We present a workflow that addresses this challenge by translating competing geologic interpretations into alternative spatial priors and ranking them according to their consistency with hydraulic-head observations. For each interpretation, a text-to-image foundation model generates an ensemble of 1600 geologic images, and a separately trained variational autoencoder provides an interpretation-specific latent representation. A supervised inverse network maps the head observations into this latent space, and the frozen decoder produces an image that is mapped to a log-conductivity field. Steady-state flow simulation then provides predicted heads, and the resulting mismatch is converted into a Gaussian-form compatibility score. We evaluate the framework using a synthetic benchmark based on the Johansen Formation and three interpretations of decreasing consistency with the reference representation. Across 925 test cases, the mean head RMSE increases from 0.197 for the Precise \& Accurate interpretation to 0.227 for the Accurate interpretation and 0.280 for the Mismatched interpretation. We subsequently apply the workflow to two published conceptual models of the Culebra Dolomite Member at the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant. The revised model receives a compatibility weight of 0.991, compared with 0.009 for the original model, consistent with the independent evidence.

AI.tldr: A workflow that ranks competing geologic interpretations by translating them into spatial priors and evaluating consistency with hydraulic-head observations using text-to-image models, variational autoencoders, and inverse modeling.
AI.motivation: High-consequence subsurface decisions are made under severe data scarcity, with experts often having competing interpretations that cannot be practically validated until wells are drilled, costing millions of dollars. Existing evaluation approaches rely on subjective judgment or dense data rarely available early.
AI.method: The workflow: (1) Translates geologic interpretations into alternative spatial priors; (2) Uses text-to-image foundation model to generate 1600 geologic images per interpretation; (3) Employs variational autoencoder for interpretation-specific latent representation; (4) Uses supervised inverse network to map head observations into latent space; (5) Frozen decoder produces images mapped to log-conductivity fields; (6) Steady-state flow simulation provides predicted heads; (7) Mismatch converted to Gaussian-form compatibility score.
AI.result: Synthetic benchmark (Johansen Formation): Mean head RMSE increases from 0.197 (Precise & Accurate) to 0.227 (Accurate) to 0.280 (Mismatched) across 925 test cases. Real application (Culebra Dolomite at WIPP): Revised model gets compatibility weight of 0.991 vs 0.009 for original model, consistent with independent evidence.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully evaluates and ranks competing geologic interpretations using limited data, demonstrating value for early-stage decision-making in subsurface characterization. The method can help avoid costly drilling of wells in poorly characterized formations.

title: SWE-Proof: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World Issues with Machine-Checked Proofs?
summary: Ensuring the correctness of LLM-generated code is a core challenge for modern software engineering. Benchmarks for agentic code generation check correctness with held-out test suites, which are inherently incomplete and increasingly susceptible to memorization. Formal verification avoids both problems, but existing work covers only standalone tasks whose specifications are given as input, not real issues, which touch large repositories and state intent in vague natural language. We present Benchproofer, a pipeline that turns a coding task with a known correct patch into a formally verified one: it writes a specification for the new code, summarizes the existing functions that code calls with axioms, and admits an instance only after mechanical and adversarial gates agree. Applying it to SWE-bench Verified yields SWE-Proof, 500 real issues whose correctness is formally verified rather than tested, and it extends to SWE-bench Pro. Across two frontier models, verification catches what tests miss: a quarter to a half of test-passing patches admit counterexamples, which a structured natural-language specification does not fix, while a correct formal one lifts resolution from 85% to 95% for Opus 4.8. Writing that specification is the hard part: models that must write their own gain nothing over an unaided baseline, and only 62% of their specifications pass our audit. The usual failure is faithfulness, a specification that constrains part of the required behavior and leaves the rest free. Specification quality still tracks the outcome, failing on 89% of unresolved instances against 47% of resolved ones, making faithful specification synthesis a concrete open problem.

AI.tldr: Benchproofer is a pipeline that transforms coding tasks with known correct patches into formally verified ones by writing specifications, summarizing existing functions with axioms, and using mechanical/adversarial gates. Applied to SWE-bench, it creates SWE-Proof (500 formally verified real issues) and reveals that 25-50% of test-passing patches have counterexamples, while faithful specification synthesis remains an open problem.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks for agentic code generation use held-out test suites that are incomplete and prone to memorization. Formal verification avoids these problems but existing work only covers standalone tasks with explicit specifications, not real issues in large repositories with vague natural language intent.
AI.method: Benchproofer pipeline: (1) writes formal specifications for new code, (2) summarizes existing functions that code calls with axioms, (3) admits instances only after mechanical and adversarial gates agree on correctness. Applied to SWE-bench Verified to create SWE-Proof dataset.
AI.result: Verification catches what tests miss: 25-50% of test-passing patches admit counterexamples. A correct formal specification improves resolution from 85% to 95% for Opus 4.8. However, models writing their own specifications gain nothing over baseline, with only 62% passing audit. The main failure mode is faithfulness (specifying only partial behavior). Specification quality correlates with outcomes: 89% of unresolved vs 47% of resolved instances have specification failures.
AI.conclusion: Formal verification significantly outperforms testing for evaluating LLM-generated code patches. However, faithful specification synthesis is a critical bottleneck - current models cannot reliably write specifications that capture full required behavior. This represents a concrete open problem: achieving faithful automatic specification writing would substantially improve LLM code generation capabilities.

title: VGGT-CAD: Reconstructing Parametric CAD 3D Model with Geometric Grounding
summary: Parametric CAD reconstruction requires recovering both precise geometry and editable modeling operations from visual observations, making it challenging under limited and ambiguous views. Existing methods mainly rely on 2D appearance cues and lack strong multi-view geometric priors. In this work, we present VGGT-CAD, a geometry-aware framework for parametric CAD reconstruction from single- and multi-view observations. We transfer pretrained 3D geometric priors into CAD reconstruction by encoding camera parameters as condition tokens and jointly modeling them with image tokens. To handle varying numbers of viewpoints, we introduce a variable-view cross-view context aggregation module that adaptively fuses multi-view features. We further develop a training-free geometry-aware view selection strategy to select complementary and reliable frames during inference. The resulting representation is decoded into CAD command sequences using a non-autoregressive decoder. We also develop VideoCAD, a large-scale multi-view video benchmark derived from existing CAD data through multi-view re-rendering. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of VGGT-CAD for visual CAD reconstruction under different observation configurations.

AI.tldr: VGGT-CAD is a geometry-aware framework for parametric CAD reconstruction from single- and multi-view observations. It transfers pretrained 3D geometric priors into CAD reconstruction by encoding camera parameters as condition tokens, uses a variable-view cross-view context aggregation module for multi-view feature fusion, and employs a training-free geometry-aware view selection strategy. The method decodes outputs into CAD command sequences using a non-autoregressive decoder. A new benchmark called VideoCAD is also introduced.
AI.motivation: Parametric CAD reconstruction requires recovering both precise geometry and editable modeling operations from visual observations. This is challenging under limited and ambiguous views because existing methods mainly rely on 2D appearance cues and lack strong multi-view geometric priors.
AI.method: VGGT-CAD transfers pretrained 3D geometric priors into CAD reconstruction by encoding camera parameters as condition tokens and jointly modeling them with image tokens. It introduces a variable-view cross-view context aggregation module that adaptively fuses multi-view features to handle varying numbers of viewpoints. A training-free geometry-aware view selection strategy is developed to select complementary and reliable frames during inference. The resulting representation is decoded into CAD command sequences using a non-autoregressive decoder.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of VGGT-CAD for visual CAD reconstruction under different observation configurations. The method performs well on both single-view and multi-view scenarios.
AI.conclusion: VGGT-CAD successfully integrates 3D geometric priors into parametric CAD reconstruction, showing improved performance across various observation configurations. The proposed VideoCAD benchmark provides a large-scale multi-view video dataset for further research in this domain.

title: Implicit Rule Induction with Test-Time Task Embeddings in ARC-like Tasks
summary: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus and related benchmarks evaluate whether AI models can solve novel reasoning tasks, but often leave unclear whether success reflects inference of the intended underlying rule or reliance on shortcuts. We address this gap by studying test-time task embeddings in Vision ARC (VARC), a model in which a pre-trained backbone is complemented by a trainable embedding representing the transformation rule. In the original VARC, test-time training (TTT) is jointly applied to the backbone and task embedding. Here we introduce a novel two-step TTT protocol: first finetune only the task embedding (Embed-TTT), then freeze it and finetune the backbone. Across ARC-AGI-1, ConceptARC, and two controlled datasets with known rules, Embed-TTT consistently yields improved task embeddings, ones that align better with underlying task rules, improve embedding-based retrieval, and enable accurate linear probing of known rules. Qualitatively, Embed-TTT identifies more semantically meaningful relations between test and train tasks on ARC-AGI-1. We also show that optimizing only task embeddings (less than 0.01% of model parameters) already solves a non-trivial fraction of ARC-AGI-1, ConceptARC, and Mini-ARC tasks, while the full two-step pipeline improves final performance. Finally, we show that Embed-TTT recovers the underlying geometric structure of parametric rules and learns compositional capabilities that enable rule-wise interpolation, but not extrapolation. These findings support a clearer separation between rule induction and rule execution in ARC-like evaluations, motivating benchmarks that better distinguish in-distribution from out-of-distribution rules.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel two-step test-time training (TTT) protocol for Vision ARC (VARC) that first finetunes only the task embedding (Embed-TTT), then freezes it and finetunes the backbone. This approach separates rule induction from rule execution, achieving improved task embeddings that better align with underlying rules while using less than 0.01% of model parameters.
AI.motivation: ARC benchmarks evaluate AI reasoning but leave unclear whether success reflects understanding underlying rules or using shortcuts. The authors address this gap by studying test-time task embeddings to distinguish rule induction from rule execution.
AI.method: Novel two-step TTT protocol: (1) finetune only task embedding (Embed-TTT), then (2) freeze it and finetune the backbone. Tested on ARC-AGI-1, ConceptARC, and two controlled datasets with known rules. Evaluated through embedding retrieval, linear probing, and qualitative analysis.
AI.result: Embed-TTT consistently yields improved task embeddings that align better with underlying rules, improve embedding-based retrieval, and enable accurate linear probing. Optimizing only task embeddings (<0.01% of parameters) solves a non-trivial fraction of tasks. The method recovers geometric structure of parametric rules and learns compositional capabilities for interpolation but not extrapolation.
AI.conclusion: The findings support clearer separation between rule induction and rule execution in ARC-like evaluations, motivating benchmarks that better distinguish in-distribution from out-of-distribution rules.

title: ASGARD: Action-Space Guard for UAV Resilience via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) controllers have been recently adopted for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV) navigation and control. However, they are susceptible to action-space attacks that overwrite the action commands after the policy generates them and before the actuators execute them. While most existing defenses target attacks on the policy's inputs, those addressing action-space attacks retrain the policy at training time and are not resilient to corrupted actions at runtime. We propose ASGARD, a two-phase teacher-student pipeline for making RL-based UAV control resilient to action-space attacks. In the teacher phase, an encoder combines the UAV's physical state with action-attack-related privileged information to produce an action-attack-aware latent that trains the RL control policy and a monitor that outputs corrected action commands to the actuators. In the student phase, both the encoder and the monitor are trained via supervised learning from their teacher counterparts to run on-board using only the UAV's physical state history. We evaluate ASGARD across attack scenarios targeting different action commands on UAV. We find that ASGARD is resilient to action-space attacks and completes the missions despite the attack. We further find that ASGARD generalizes to unseen attacks and remains resilient against stealthy attacks.

AI.tldr: ASGARD is a two-phase teacher-student defense pipeline that makes reinforcement learning-based UAV control resilient to action-space attacks, where attackers modify action commands after they are generated by the policy but before actuators execute them. The system uses a teacher phase with privileged attack information to train an encoder, RL policy, and monitor, followed by a student phase that learns to run on-board using only physical state history.
AI.motivation: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) reinforcement learning controllers are vulnerable to action-space attacks that overwrite action commands between policy generation and actuator execution. Existing defenses either target input-space attacks or require policy retraining at training time, making them ineffective against runtime action-space attacks. There is a need for a defense mechanism that can detect and correct corrupted actions in real-time without requiring policy retraining.
AI.method: ASGARD employs a two-phase teacher-student architecture: (1) Teacher Phase - An encoder combines the UAV's physical state with action-attack-related privileged information to produce an action-attack-aware latent representation. This latent trains both the RL control policy and a monitor that outputs corrected action commands. (2) Student Phase - Both the encoder and monitor are trained via supervised learning from their teacher counterparts to run on-board using only the UAV's physical state history, eliminating the need for privileged information at runtime.
AI.result: ASGARD demonstrates resilience to action-space attacks across various attack scenarios targeting different action commands, successfully completing missions despite attacks. The system generalizes to unseen attacks and remains resilient against stealthy attacks.
AI.conclusion: ASGARD provides an effective defense mechanism against action-space attacks on RL-based UAV control systems. The teacher-student pipeline architecture enables the system to learn attack detection and correction capabilities from privileged information during training, then deploys lightweight on-board components that operate using only physical state history, achieving runtime resilience without requiring policy retraining.

title: Efficient Benchmarking in Production: A Study of an Evolving LLM Agent
comment: A study of efficient recurring evaluation of a production LLM agent based on real-world historical data
summary: Production LLM agents are evaluated repeatedly as they evolve, but full agent benchmarks are costly to rerun. We study efficient recurring evaluation for a production analytics agent serving tens of thousands of monthly active users and report first-hand deployment experience. Using 574 historical runs of the production benchmark, split chronologically into calibration and held-out periods, we compare random sampling, historical caching, fixed representative subsets, and IRT-based adaptive testing. The results show that multidimensional 2PL adaptive testing achieves the best overall score fidelity: executing 200 questions, 38.5% of a full run, yields 1.03 pp of MAE. We nevertheless deployed difficulty-stratified fixed subsets because of their operational simplicity, and show they transfer without recalibration to five other agent families and remain stable across calibration windows as short as one day. Drawing on this deployment experience, we report practical recommendations for recurring production-agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses efficient recurring evaluation for production LLM agents by comparing four methods: random sampling, historical caching, fixed representative subsets, and IRT-based adaptive testing. The study uses 574 historical runs of a production analytics agent benchmark and finds that 2PL adaptive testing achieves highest accuracy (1.03 MAE with 38.5% of questions), but difficulty-stratified fixed subsets are deployed due to operational simplicity and transferability across agent families.
AI.motivation: Full agent benchmarks are costly to rerun repeatedly as production LLM agents evolve. There is a need for efficient evaluation methods that maintain score fidelity while reducing computational and time costs.
AI.method: Using 574 historical runs of a production analytics agent benchmark (tens of thousands of monthly active users), split chronologically into calibration and held-out periods, the researchers compared four evaluation approaches: random sampling, historical caching, fixed representative subsets, and Item Response Theory (IRT)-based multidimensional 2PL adaptive testing.
AI.result: Multidimensional 2PL adaptive testing achieved the best score fidelity: executing 200 questions (38.5% of full run) yields 1.03 percentage points of Mean Absolute Error (MAE). However, difficulty-stratified fixed subsets were deployed due to operational simplicity. These subsets transfer without recalibration to five other agent families and remain stable across calibration windows as short as one day.
AI.conclusion: Difficulty-stratified fixed subsets offer a practical balance between efficiency and accuracy for production-agent evaluation, with strong transferability across agent families and stability with minimal calibration data. The paper provides practical recommendations for recurring production-agent evaluation.

title: Multiclass Semantic Segmentation of Wildland Fire Images Using Context-Aware Centralized Copy-Paste Data Augmentation
summary: Producing accurate annotations for deep learning based image segmentation is both costly and labor intensive. This challenge is especially evident in wildland fire applications, where accurately labeled datasets are scarce due to the difficulty of collecting and annotating dynamic fire scenes. To address this problem, our previous work introduced the Centralized Copy-Paste Data Augmentation (CCPDA) method for semantic segmentation of wildland fire imagery, which generates artificial training samples by randomly pasting fire clusters from source images onto target images. However, random placement can produce contextually unrealistic scenes, such as fire burning on asphalt. In this paper, we present a context-aware strategy designed specifically to improve data quality and realism in small multiclass wildland fire datasets, ensuring that augmented samples remain contextually meaningful. The proposed method restricts fire placement to semantically valid target regions and selects the location whose Ash-Vegetation composition most closely matches the source context. This approach preserves existing fire regions in the target image, prevents unrealistic placements, and maintains contextual accuracy by generating images that resemble real wildland fire scenes. We evaluate the Context-Aware CCPDA strategy through numerical analysis and comparisons with other augmentation methods by a weighted sum-based multi-objective optimization (MOO) approach. The results confirm that the context-aware data augmentation strategy leads to improved segmentation performance and contextual realism, outperforming other augmentation procedures.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a context-aware data augmentation strategy (Context-Aware CCPDA) for improving semantic segmentation of wildland fire imagery. The method addresses limitations of random fire placement in previous work by restricting fire clusters to semantically valid regions that match the Ash-Vegetation composition of source images, creating more realistic augmented training samples.
AI.motivation: Producing accurate annotations for deep learning image segmentation is costly and labor-intensive. In wildland fire applications, labeled datasets are scarce due to the difficulty of collecting and annotating dynamic fire scenes. Previous work (CCPDA) used random copy-paste augmentation but could produce unrealistic scenes like fire on asphalt. This paper aims to improve data quality and realism by ensuring augmented samples remain contextually meaningful.
AI.method: The proposed context-aware strategy restricts fire placement to semantically valid target regions and selects locations whose Ash-Vegetation composition most closely matches the source context. This preserves existing fire regions, prevents unrealistic placements, and maintains contextual accuracy. Evaluation uses numerical analysis and weighted sum-based multi-objective optimization (MOO) approach to compare with other augmentation methods.
AI.result: The context-aware data augmentation strategy leads to improved segmentation performance and contextual realism, outperforming other augmentation procedures.
AI.conclusion: The context-aware approach successfully addresses the limitation of random fire placement in CCPDA by ensuring semantic validity and contextual matching between source and target images, resulting in better segmentation performance and more realistic augmented samples for wildland fire imagery.

title: AI-GRACE: A Use-Case Operationalization Framework for Agentic AI: From Organizational Objectives and Obligations to Deployment Capabilities and Architecture
summary: Organizations deploying agentic artificial intelligence must determine more than whether a model is trustworthy; they must establish what to validate, control, and observe for a use case to deliver its intended outcome while meeting applicable obligations. This paper proposes AI-GRACE (Agentic Intelligence-Governance, Risk, Assurance, Controls, and Evidence) as a use-case operationalization framework connecting organizational governance with technical implementation. The proposal draws on professional observations and a purposive synthesis of standards and literature, using design science to frame the method contribution and situational method engineering to guide contextual tailoring and reuse. The framework establishes objectives and obligations and then assesses risks in seven proposed domains, including mission and value realization. It derives requirements for assurance before deployment, runtime controls, and evidence, which guide capability qualification, gap assessment, and a logical architecture. An Agent Operating Envelope specifies permitted actions and escalation conditions, while Risk-Aligned Independence Levels (RAIL) summarize the authorized independence. A fictional retail banking application illustrates the method. The contribution is a traceable basis for deciding what an organization must implement, what it already supports, and what remains unresolved. Empirical evaluation must establish whether it improves deployment decisions, efficiency, and reuse.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes AI-GRACE, a use-case operationalization framework for agentic AI that bridges organizational governance with technical implementation, providing methods for risk assessment, assurance requirements, runtime controls, and evidence gathering.
AI.motivation: Organizations deploying agentic AI face the challenge of determining not just whether a model is trustworthy, but what to validate, control, and observe to ensure use cases deliver intended outcomes while meeting regulatory and ethical obligations.
AI.method: The framework is developed through design science (for method contribution) and situational method engineering (for contextual tailoring and reuse), drawing on professional observations and a purposive synthesis of existing standards and literature.
AI.result: AI-GRACE establishes objectives and obligations, assesses risks across seven domains (including mission and value realization), derives requirements for pre-deployment assurance, runtime controls, and evidence. It provides capability qualification, gap assessment, logical architecture, an Agent Operating Envelope (specifying permitted actions and escalation conditions), and Risk-Aligned Independence Levels (RAIL) summarizing authorized independence.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a traceable basis for organizations to decide what must be implemented, what is already supported, and what remains unresolved. Empirical evaluation is needed to determine whether it improves deployment decisions, efficiency, and reuse.

title: From Stress to Affect: Multimodal Deep Learning for Physiological Emotion Recognition Across Wearable Sensor Modalities
summary: Physiological emotion recognition using wearable sensors has important applications in mental health monitoring, affective computing, and human-computer interaction. However, existing studies typically evaluate a single model, sensing configuration, or dataset, limiting our understanding of how these factors influence recognition performance. We present a comparative study of temporal deep learning architectures for physiological emotion recognition using two multimodal wearable datasets: WESAD and EmoWear. Bidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM), temporal convolutional network (TCN), and Transformer models are evaluated under wrist-only, chest-only, and multimodal sensing configurations using participant-independent leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSO-CV). We also investigate soft-voting ensembles, sensor ablation, sampling frequency, and gradient-based saliency. The Transformer achieved the highest multimodal accuracy on WESAD (99.02% +/- 0.51%), whereas the LSTM achieved the best multimodal accuracy on EmoWear for both arousal (91.80% +/- 1.06%) and valence (89.96% +/- 0.36%). These results show that relative architecture performance depends on dataset characteristics rather than one architecture being uniformly superior. Multimodal sensing consistently outperformed wrist-only and chest-only configurations across both datasets. Sampling-frequency analysis showed that 4 Hz provides a practical operating point, with performance comparable to higher frequencies at substantially lower training cost. These findings provide guidance for selecting architectures, sensing modalities, and sampling frequencies for wearable physiological emotion recognition.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comparative study of temporal deep learning architectures (BiLSTM, TCN, Transformer) for physiological emotion recognition using wearable sensors, evaluated on WESAD and EmoWear datasets across different sensing configurations.
AI.motivation: Existing studies typically evaluate a single model, sensing configuration, or dataset, limiting understanding of how these factors influence recognition performance in wearable physiological emotion recognition.
AI.method: The study evaluated three temporal deep learning architectures (BiLSTM, TCN, Transformer) under three sensing configurations (wrist-only, chest-only, multimodal) using participant-independent leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSO-CV). Additional analyses included soft-voting ensembles, sensor ablation, sampling frequency, and gradient-based saliency.
AI.result: Transformer achieved the highest multimodal accuracy on WESAD (99.02% ± 0.51%), while LSTM achieved the best multimodal accuracy on EmoWear for both arousal (91.80% ± 1.06%) and valence (89.96% ± 0.36%). Multimodal sensing consistently outperformed single-modality configurations. Sampling frequency analysis showed that 4 Hz provides a practical operating point with performance comparable to higher frequencies.
AI.conclusion: Relative architecture performance depends on dataset characteristics rather than one architecture being universally superior. Multimodal sensing consistently outperforms single-modality approaches. The findings provide guidance for selecting architectures, sensing modalities, and sampling frequencies for wearable physiological emotion recognition.

title: GameASG-Bench: Benchmarking Autonomous Software Generation for Game Development
summary: Autonomous software generation (ASG) aims to turn human requirements into executable applications, but delivering these applications does not necessarily establish that their interacting components satisfy the specified behavioral requirements. We introduce GameASG-Bench, a benchmark that makes behavioral testability part of the generation task for game development. Our design declares an evaluation interface specification before generation, fixing legal starting scenarios, player-level actions, stable snapshots, rejection behavior, and invariants while leaving private implementations open. Concretely, we include: (i) static L1 checks that assess source-level compliance; and (ii) browser-executed L2 checks that combine semantic observations with real input and runtime evidence. We implement this protocol as 47 browser-native game-generation tasks spanning 12 primary genres and both 2D and 3D interaction, each with executable checks and an independently verified reference implementation. Our experiments answer four key questions about end-to-end agent performance, tool access and nominal turn budget, reasoning effort, and harness choice. Across nine agent stacks, the highest observed mean L2 check pass rate is 93.2%, yet the highest observed strict task success rate, requiring all L1 and applicable L2 prerequisite and core requirement checks, is only 55.3% (26/47 tasks). For DeepSeek-V4-Flash, full tool access and larger nominal turn budgets yield more strict task successes, while the strict task success rate is not monotonic in reasoning effort. Both tested harnesses achieve 18 strict task successes, but only ten tasks succeed under both. These results expose task-level compliance gaps that high average check pass rates actually obscure.

AI.tldr: GameASG-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating autonomous software generation (ASG) in game development, focusing on behavioral testability. It uses 47 browser-native game tasks with two-level checks (static L1 and runtime L2) to assess if generated applications meet specified behavioral requirements. Across nine agent stacks, maximum L2 pass rate is 93.2% but strict task success rate is only 55.3%, revealing significant compliance gaps.
AI.motivation: Current ASG systems can generate executable applications from human requirements, but this doesn't guarantee that the generated applications' interacting components satisfy the specified behavioral requirements. The authors argue that behavioral testability should be part of the generation task itself.
AI.method: The benchmark declares an evaluation interface specification before generation, fixing legal starting scenarios, player-level actions, stable snapshots, rejection behavior, and invariants while leaving private implementations open. It implements: (i) static L1 checks for source-level compliance; and (ii) browser-executed L2 checks combining semantic observations with real input and runtime evidence. 47 browser-native game-generation tasks span 12 primary genres with both 2D and 3D interaction.
AI.result: Highest mean L2 check pass rate is 93.2%, but highest strict task success rate (requiring all L1 and applicable L2 checks) is only 55.3% (26/47 tasks). For DeepSeek-V4-Flash: full tool access and larger nominal turn budgets yield more strict task successes; strict task success rate is not monotonic in reasoning effort. Both tested harnesses achieve 18 strict task successes, but only ten tasks succeed under both.
AI.conclusion: Results expose task-level compliance gaps that high average check pass rates actually obscure. The gap between high L2 pass rates (93.2%) and low strict success rates (55.3%) reveals that individual check pass rates are poor proxies for overall task success, highlighting the need for comprehensive behavioral testing in ASG evaluation.

title: SafeStyle: Calibrated Style Residual Injection for Controllable Style-Leakage Trade-off in Diffusion Stylization
summary: Reference-guided diffusion stylization aims to transfer visual style from a reference image while preserving the semantics specified by a text prompt. However, image conditioning often entangles transferable style cues with reference-specific content, leading to an inherent trade-off: stronger conditioning improves style fidelity but increases content leakage, whereas aggressive suppression reduces leakage at the cost of style expression. This challenge is further complicated by the distinct spatial organization of texture- and geometry-dominant styles. To address these issues, we propose SafeStyle, a training-free framework for calibrated style residual injection in frozen diffusion models. SafeStyle first estimates style-supported and content-associated subspaces from compact calibration sets, preserving their informative overlap while suppressing useless content variations. It then transports the purified style evidence over adaptive spatial granularity and constrains its effective influence through an explicit residual-norm budget. Experiments across texture- and geometry-dominant styles show that SafeStyle achieves a DINO style similarity of 0.432 while maintaining competitive text alignment. On a semantically disjoint leakage-stress benchmark, it further achieves a DINO style similarity of 0.474 with only 0.8\% semantic leakage, demonstrating an effective balance between style fidelity and reference-content suppression.

AI.tldr: SafeStyle is a training-free framework for reference-guided diffusion stylization that addresses the trade-off between style fidelity and content leakage by estimating style-supported and content-associated subspaces from calibration sets, then transporting purified style evidence over adaptive spatial granularity with explicit residual-norm budget constraints.
AI.motivation: Reference-guided diffusion stylization suffers from an inherent trade-off: stronger image conditioning improves style fidelity but increases content leakage, while aggressive suppression reduces leakage at the cost of style expression. This is complicated by different spatial organizations of texture- and geometry-dominant styles.
AI.method: SafeStyle uses a training-free approach with three key components: 1) Estimates style-supported and content-associated subspaces from compact calibration sets, preserving informative overlap while suppressing useless content variations; 2) Transports purified style evidence over adaptive spatial granularity; 3) Constrains effective influence through an explicit residual-norm budget.
AI.result: SafeStyle achieves DINO style similarity of 0.432 while maintaining competitive text alignment. On a semantically disjoint leakage-stress benchmark, it achieves DINO style similarity of 0.474 with only 0.8% semantic leakage, demonstrating effective balance between style fidelity and reference-content suppression.
AI.conclusion: SafeStyle successfully balances style fidelity and reference-content suppression in reference-guided diffusion stylization, working effectively for both texture- and geometry-dominant styles without requiring training.

title: Information-Gain Rewards over Diversity-Pruned Tests: GT-Anchored Verifier Co-Training for Reliable Code Generation
summary: Self-play methods that co-train a single language model as both coder and test author promise to move code-generation RL beyond fixed test suites, but they suffer from two coupled pathologies: permissiveness collapse, where pass-rate rewards are maximised by trivial, non-discriminative tests, and concentration bias, where i.i.d. sampled tests cluster on modal inputs and inflate estimator variance. We introduce CoVer (Co-trained Coder and Verifier), a single-policy GRPO framework that addresses both failure modes. First, an information-gain (IG) reward scores each self-generated test by the mutual information between its pass/fail vector and a graded, ground-truth-anchored correctness signal y [0, 1] m, gated by the sign of their covariance so that only positively discriminative tests receive reward. Second, a three-stage diversity-aware selection step prunes a candidate pool to a behaviourally non-redundant suite (invalidity, input-string, execution-profile filtering), raising the effective sample size of the IG estimator at fixed execution budget. On five benchmarks (LiveBench, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, CodeContests, Code-Forces), CoVer raises one-shot pass@1 by +5.8 points at 7B and +7.1 points at 14B over the Qwen2.5-Instruct backbone, and achieves the highest macro-average among all compared methods at both scales. As a drop-in backbone inside the CodeT ranking pipeline, CoVer-7B adds +3.5 points, demonstrating the dual benefit of co-training for both generation and selection.

AI.tldr: CoVer addresses two failure modes in self-play code generation RL (permissiveness collapse and concentration bias) using an information-gain reward with covariance gating and a three-stage diversity-aware test selection, achieving significant improvements on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Self-play RL methods for code generation suffer from two coupled pathologies: (1) permissiveness collapse - where pass-rate rewards are maximized by trivial, non-discriminative tests, and (2) concentration bias - where i.i.d. sampled tests cluster on modal inputs and inflate estimator variance. Existing methods fail to address both issues simultaneously.
AI.method: CoVer uses a single-policy GRPO framework with two key components: (1) Information-Gain (IG) reward that scores self-generated tests by mutual information between pass/fail vector and graded ground-truth correctness signal, gated by covariance sign to reward only positively discriminative tests; (2) Three-stage diversity-aware selection (invalidity, input-string, execution-profile filtering) to prune candidate pool to behaviorally non-redundant suite, raising effective sample size at fixed execution budget.
AI.result: CoVer raises one-shot pass@1 by +5.8 points at 7B and +7.1 points at 14B over Qwen2.5-Instruct backbone, achieving highest macro-average among all compared methods at both scales. As a drop-in backbone in CodeT ranking pipeline, CoVer-7B adds +3.5 points.
AI.conclusion: CoVer successfully addresses both permissiveness collapse and concentration bias through IG reward with covariance gating and diversity-aware selection, demonstrating dual benefits for both code generation and test selection across five benchmarks (LiveBench, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, CodeContests, Code-Forces).

title: MOSAIC-SR: Transformer-Guided Symbolic Regression for Scientific Equation Recovery
summary: Symbolic regression aims to recover closed-form equations from observations, providing interpretable models for scientific discovery. Existing approaches struggle to combine flexible structural search with efficient inference. Search-based methods can refine expression structure but often rely on costly combinatorial optimization with random initialization. Pretrained neural models generate formulas almost instantly, but their predictions often contain symbolic errors. We introduce MOSAIC-SR, which uses a pretrained Transformer to propose multiple initial sketches. These sketches initialize searches in several promising regions, avoiding random starts in the vast expression space. Each search jointly recovers structure and constants through scale-aware constant optimization and local symbolic repair. We evaluate MOSAIC-SR on the SRSD-Feynman dataset with and without dummy variables and on six additional benchmarks. MOSAIC-SR obtains the highest symbolic solution rate on every dataset while ranking among the top two methods in predictive accuracy. This advantage persists in the presence of irrelevant dummy inputs. The results show that learned priors can focus search on promising equation structures, and that numerical optimization and symbolic repair are important for recovery.

AI.tldr: MOSAIC-SR is a symbolic regression method that combines pretrained Transformers for initial equation sketch proposal with multi-start search for structure and constant optimization. It achieves state-of-the-art symbolic solution rates across multiple benchmarks while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy, even with irrelevant dummy variables.
AI.motivation: Existing symbolic regression methods have a key limitation: search-based approaches are computationally expensive due to combinatorial optimization with random initialization, while pretrained neural models generate formulas quickly but contain symbolic errors. There was a need for a method that combines the strengths of both approaches.
AI.method: MOSAIC-SR uses three key components: (1) A pretrained Transformer that proposes multiple initial equation sketches, providing learned priors to initialize searches in promising regions; (2) Scale-aware constant optimization for joint recovery of structure and constants; (3) Local symbolic repair to fix symbolic errors in generated formulas. The method performs multi-start searches from these proposed sketches rather than random initialization.
AI.result: MOSAIC-SR achieves the highest symbolic solution rate on every dataset tested, including the SRSD-Feynman benchmark (with and without dummy variables) and six additional benchmarks. It also ranks among the top two methods in predictive accuracy. The method maintains its advantage even when irrelevant dummy inputs are present.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that learned priors from pretrained neural models can effectively focus search on promising equation structures, and that combining numerical optimization with symbolic repair is crucial for accurate equation recovery. This hybrid approach successfully bridges the gap between fast neural generation and accurate search-based methods.

title: Geometry-Aware Diffusion Guidance via Curvature-Adaptive Tubular Correction
summary: Gradient-guided diffusion samplers provide flexible priors for inverse problems and conditional generation, but strong guidance can move the sampling trajectory into regions where the learned score is poorly supported. Existing tangent-projection strategies limit first-order departure from an iso-density surface, yet discard potentially useful normal motion and overlook the second-order departure induced by tangent motion on a curved surface. We introduce curvature-adaptive tubular correction (CAT), a training-free plugin that regulates both effects within a shared, noise-dependent geometric budget. CAT decomposes the guidance gradient into normal and tangent components, charges normal displacement at first order and tangent displacement according to directional curvature, and obtains their jointly optimal magnitudes from a one-dimensional dual equation. Armijo backtracking calibrates the resulting finite step against the actual guidance objective, while matrix-free directional derivatives avoid constructing the full score Jacobian. We establish local guarantees for the tubular approximation, uniqueness of the correction, and sufficient objective decrease. Across seven inverse problems on FFHQ and ImageNet, CAT improves the evaluated pixel- and latent-space host samplers, with particularly consistent gains in perceptual metrics. It also improves black hole reconstruction on InverseBench and yields the lowest FID among the compared methods at every tested classifier-free guidance scale, while maintaining stable saturation and contrast. These results support curvature-aware tubular control as a reusable mechanism for stabilizing diffusion guidance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CAT (Curvature-adaptive tubular correction), a training-free plugin for gradient-guided diffusion samplers that regulates both normal and tangent displacement effects within a noise-dependent geometric budget. It addresses the problem where strong guidance moves sampling trajectories into regions where the learned score is poorly supported.
AI.motivation: Gradient-guided diffusion samplers can move sampling trajectories into regions where the learned score is poorly supported when strong guidance is applied. Existing tangent-projection strategies only limit first-order departure from iso-density surfaces but discard useful normal motion and overlook second-order departure from curved surfaces.
AI.method: CAT decomposes the guidance gradient into normal and tangent components, charges normal displacement at first order and tangent displacement according to directional curvature, and obtains jointly optimal magnitudes from a one-dimensional dual equation. It uses Armijo backtracking for step calibration and matrix-free directional derivatives to avoid constructing the full score Jacobian.
AI.result: Across seven inverse problems on FFHQ and ImageNet, CAT improves both pixel and latent-space host samplers with particularly consistent gains in perceptual metrics. It also improves black hole reconstruction on InverseBench and achieves the lowest FID among compared methods at every tested classifier-free guidance scale while maintaining stable saturation and contrast.
AI.conclusion: Curvature-aware tubular control serves as a reusable mechanism for stabilizing diffusion guidance, providing theoretical guarantees (local guarantees for tubular approximation, uniqueness of correction, sufficient objective decrease) and strong empirical results across various inverse problems and benchmarks.

title: Ability-Residual Decoupled Modeling for Affective Cognitive Diagnosis
summary: Cognitive diagnosis infers students' concept mastery from response logs. However, students' responses are not determined by mastery alone: non-cognitive factors such as emotion, engagement, and fatigue can also affect performance. Affective cognitive diagnosis therefore extends conventional cognitive diagnosis by incorporating affective states. Existing methods often assume that the cognitive diagnosis backbone has already explained ability, item, and concept effects, so the remaining errors can be attributed mainly to affect. We argue that this assumption can be insufficient in real educational data: item calibration bias, systematic concept bias, personalized student-concept deviations, and latent student-item matching can form stable cognitive residuals. Without an explicit modeling pathway, these residuals may leak into affective representations, producing affect contamination. To address this problem, we propose an ability-residual decoupled framework for affective cognitive diagnosis. The model first captures unmodeled cognitive residuals through student, item, concept, student-concept, and low-rank student-item components, and then uses an affective module to modulate guess/slip effects. A Q-matrix-constrained concept residual attention mechanism adaptively aggregates only item-relevant concept residuals. Experiments on ASSIST2017, ASSIST2012, ASSIST2009, and Junyi with six cognitive diagnosis backbones show response-prediction gains across the reported comparisons and generally improved affect alignment when affect labels are available. Ablation studies, leakage probes, principal component analysis visualization, long-tail analysis, and case studies further indicate that ability residuals absorb stable cognitive bias, reduce cognitive contamination in the affective branch, and enhance the robustness and predictive accuracy of cognitive diagnosis models.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses "affect contamination" in affective cognitive diagnosis, where unmodeled cognitive residuals (item bias, concept bias, student-concept deviations, student-item matching) leak into affective representations. The proposed ability-residual decoupled framework explicitly models these residuals before applying affective modulation, improving both response prediction and affect alignment across four datasets and six cognitive diagnosis backbones.
AI.motivation: Existing affective cognitive diagnosis methods assume that after cognitive diagnosis captures ability, item, and concept effects, the remaining errors are primarily due to affect. However, this assumption is insufficient in real educational data where item calibration bias, systematic concept bias, personalized student-concept deviations, and latent student-item matching form stable cognitive residuals that can contaminate affective representations.
AI.method: The proposed ability-residual decoupled framework has two stages: (1) Capture unmodeled cognitive residuals through student, item, concept, student-concept, and low-rank student-item components; (2) Use an affective module to modulate guess/slip effects. A Q-matrix-constrained concept residual attention mechanism adaptively aggregates only item-relevant concept residuals.
AI.result: Experiments on ASSIST2017, ASSIST2012, ASSIST2009, and Junyi datasets with six cognitive diagnosis backbones show response-prediction gains across all comparisons and generally improved affect alignment when affect labels are available. Ablation studies, leakage probes, PCA visualization, long-tail analysis, and case studies confirm that ability residuals absorb stable cognitive bias and reduce cognitive contamination in the affective branch.
AI.conclusion: The ability-residual decoupled framework successfully addresses affect contamination by explicitly modeling cognitive residuals before affective analysis. This approach enhances robustness and predictive accuracy of cognitive diagnosis models, providing a more accurate separation of cognitive ability and affective states in educational data.

title: On the Limits of Maximal Coding Rate Reduction for Out-of-Distribution Generalisation
summary: Substantial efforts have been devoted to making deep learning objectives, representations, and architectures interpretable, with the goal of improving the safety, robustness, and generalisation of learning systems in diverse real-world applications. The recently proposed maximal coding rate reduction ($\mathrm{MCR}^{2}$) offers a promising information-theoretic framework for learning structured, discriminative representations of class-wise submanifolds and has inspired interpretable white-box architectures. However, we observe that $\mathrm{MCR}^{2}$ can completely fail under distribution shift, motivating our study of its out-of-distribution (OOD) generalisation limits. We establish two limitations of $\mathrm{MCR}^{2}$ for OOD generalisation. First, the $\mathrm{MCR}^{2}$ objective alone can admit complete prediction failure: a representation based entirely on unstable environmental features can achieve the global coding optimum yet fail completely after correlation reversal, despite an available perfectly stable feature. This exact-optimum example includes test inputs that cannot occur during training. Even when every possible test input can also occur during training, coding quality can be arbitrarily close to optimal while prediction error is arbitrarily close to 100%. Second, directly incorporating the invariance principle underlying widely successful invariant risk minimisation (IRM) and risk extrapolation (REx) does not eliminate this failure. The failing representation admits the same optimal coding operator across training environments, showing that shared coding optimality does not ensure stable prediction. Reliable OOD guarantees for $\mathrm{MCR}^{2}$ therefore require additional new assumptions or learning principles that establish stable predictive relationships across environments.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization limits of Maximal Coding Rate Reduction (MCR²), a popular information-theoretic framework for learning structured representations. The authors demonstrate that MCR² can completely fail under distribution shift through two key limitations: (1) the objective can achieve optimal coding yet fail completely after correlation reversal, even with stable features available; and (2) incorporating invariance principles from IRM or REx does not resolve this failure. The findings indicate that additional assumptions or learning principles are needed for reliable OOD guarantees.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from the observation that while MCR² offers a promising framework for learning structured, discriminative representations and has inspired interpretable white-box architectures, it can completely fail under distribution shift. This motivates the authors to systematically study the OOD generalization limits of MCR² to understand when and why it fails.
AI.method: The authors use theoretical analysis to establish two limitations of MCR² for OOD generalization. They construct exact-optimum examples showing how representations based on unstable environmental features can achieve global coding optimum yet fail after correlation reversal. They also analyze whether incorporating invariance principles from IRM (Invariant Risk Minimisation) and REx (Risk Extrapolation) can resolve these failures.
AI.result: The authors establish two key results: (1) MCR² alone can admit complete prediction failure - a representation based entirely on unstable environmental features can achieve global coding optimum yet fail completely after correlation reversal, despite available perfectly stable features. This failure can occur even when every test input can occur during training, with coding quality arbitrarily close to optimal while prediction error is arbitrarily close to 100%. (2) Incorporating invariance principles from IRM or REx does not eliminate the failure - the failing representation admits the same optimal coding operator across training environments, showing that shared coding optimality does not ensure stable prediction.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion states that reliable OOD guarantees for MCR² require additional new assumptions or learning principles that establish stable predictive relationships across environments. The current framework is insufficient for ensuring robustness to distribution shift.

title: Edit-VAR: Taming Visual Autoregressive Model for Precise Video Editing
summary: Text-guided video editing modifies target content while preserving the appearance and temporal coherence of unedited regions. Training-based approaches provide strong control but demand substantial data and computation. Training-free methods fall into inversion-free and inversion-based paradigms. Inversion-free approaches avoid trajectory recovery, but their source-preserving guidance can limit editing strength and leave semantic changes incomplete. Inversion-based approaches recover a latent trajectory before regeneration, where approximation errors can accumulate and cause source-content drift and temporal inconsistency. We introduce Edit-VAR, the first training-free and inversion-free framework for text-guided video editing with a pretrained visual autoregressive video model. Edit-VAR directly encodes the source video into multi-scale discrete tokens and performs probability-guided conditional token replacement for source preservation. Attention-guided token-wise and scale-aware modulation selectively relaxes source constraints over edit-relevant positions and generation stages. Scale-Decoupled Generation, implemented as late-scale constraint release, regenerates motion-consistent details and reduces texture fragmentation. Residual-guided token pruning further exploits redundancy at the final two high-resolution scales to reduce inference cost. Extensive experiments and a blind user study demonstrate that Edit-VAR outperforms existing training-free video editing methods overall in editing fidelity, source preservation, temporal coherence, and inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: Edit-VAR is the first training-free and inversion-free framework for text-guided video editing using a pretrained visual autoregressive video model. It encodes source video into multi-scale discrete tokens and performs probability-guided conditional token replacement for source preservation.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free video editing methods have limitations: inversion-free approaches limit editing strength due to source-preserving guidance, while inversion-based approaches suffer from approximation errors causing source-content drift and temporal inconsistency. Training-based methods require substantial data and computation.
AI.method: Edit-VAR uses multi-scale discrete token encoding from source video, probability-guided conditional token replacement for source preservation, attention-guided token-wise and scale-aware modulation to selectively relax source constraints, Scale-Decoupled Generation with late-scale constraint release for motion-consistent details, and residual-guided token pruning for efficiency.
AI.result: Edit-VAR outperforms existing training-free video editing methods in editing fidelity, source preservation, temporal coherence, and inference efficiency, as demonstrated by extensive experiments and a blind user study.
AI.conclusion: This work introduces a novel training-free and inversion-free paradigm for text-guided video editing that achieves superior performance across multiple metrics while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: A Fully Differentiable Neuro-Soft-Symbolic Framework for Perceptual Task Planning
summary: Perceptual planning tasks require two key capabilities: accurately perceiving uncertain scenes and planning valid action sequences following logical rules. Conventional methods convert perception into discrete symbolic facts and then plan, discarding perceptual uncertainty and severing task-level feedback to perception. We introduce a generic, fully differentiable neuro-soft-symbolic framework that connects visual perception and task planning within a single computational graph. The framework maintains a continuous soft symbolic state, lifts domain rules into a differentiable soft-$T_P$ transition operator, and optimizes action logits over a short planning horizon. Gradients from the planning objective can also update the perception parameters, allowing task-relevant perceptual representations to be refined during planning. On Blocksworld, our method solves 40/40 LatPlan-40 tasks and 596/600 PlanBench-600 tasks, compared with 33/40 for LatPlan and 587/600 for the reasoning-model baseline, while requiring substantially less computation and time. In the perceptual-uncertainty ablation, our method improves the success rate from 59\% with frozen perception to 83\%. We further conduct task-and-motion simulations on Blocksworld scenes, providing an execution-level validation of the compatibility between decoded task plans and downstream robotic motion execution.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a differentiable neuro-soft-symbolic framework that integrates visual perception and task planning within a single computational graph, addressing the limitation of conventional methods that discard perceptual uncertainty and sever task-level feedback to perception.
AI.motivation: Conventional perceptual planning methods convert perception into discrete symbolic facts before planning, which discards perceptual uncertainty and severs task-level feedback to perception. This separation prevents the planning objective from refining perception parameters, limiting performance in uncertain scenes.
AI.method: The framework maintains a continuous soft symbolic state, lifts domain rules into a differentiable soft-T_P transition operator, and optimizes action logits over a short planning horizon. Gradients from the planning objective can update perception parameters, allowing task-relevant perceptual representations to be refined during planning.
AI.result: On Blocksworld, the method solves 40/40 LatPlan-40 tasks (vs 33/40 for LatPlan) and 596/600 PlanBench-600 tasks (vs 587/600 for reasoning-model baseline), while requiring substantially less computation and time. In perceptual-uncertainty ablation, success rate improved from 59% with frozen perception to 83%. Task-and-motion simulations provide execution-level validation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed neuro-soft-symbolic framework successfully bridges visual perception and task planning, achieving superior performance over baseline methods while enabling bidirectional feedback between perception and planning. The approach demonstrates the value of maintaining perceptual uncertainty and using task-level gradients to refine perception.

title: Scaling Discovery through Test-Time Communication
summary: Science advances not in isolation but through collaboration, yet existing agentic systems capture little of this. Whether communicating agents help remains an open question with mixed prior results. We show that test-time communication can substantially outperform independent parallel attempts on challenging tasks, where sharing a breakthrough can push the whole group forward. We first study the effect of scaling multi-agent test-time communication, where agents have no predefined roles and communicate via a shared directory, on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark requiring novel problem solving. We find that a team of $k$ communicating agents, team@$k$, matches the success rate of $4k$ independent agents, and this advantage grows with $k$, suggesting gains compound with scale. The effect is not merely efficiency: a task that no single agent can solve, a team of agents can solve reliably. Furthermore, these gains transfer to research-oriented tasks, given sufficient compute. On polyomino packing, communicating agents outperform best@$k$ and exceed the prior best-known score. On MNIST classifier compression, communication surpasses the best-known human solution. A team of four agents produced a 1,957-byte classifier submission achieving 99.4% test accuracy, smaller than both the best-known human solution and the best single-agent result. These gains are not unconditional. Independent agents may outperform communication when compute is limited or when a clear measure of progress is absent. However, under sufficient compute and clear feedback, multi-agent communication consistently yields stronger results.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that test-time communication between AI agents substantially outperforms independent parallel attempts on challenging tasks. A team of k communicating agents (team@k) matches the success rate of 4k independent agents, with advantages compounding at scale. The approach achieves state-of-the-art results on polyomino packing and MNIST classifier compression (1,957 bytes at 99.4% accuracy), though gains require sufficient compute and clear feedback signals.
AI.motivation: Science advances through collaboration, but existing agentic systems capture little of this. Whether communicating agents help remains an open question with mixed prior results. This work investigates whether test-time communication between agents can improve problem-solving compared to independent attempts.
AI.method: The study examines scaling multi-agent test-time communication where agents have no predefined roles and communicate via a shared directory. Experiments span three domains: ARC-AGI-3 (novel problem solving benchmark), polyomino packing, and MNIST classifier compression. The team@k approach is compared against independent agents (best@k) and human solutions.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) team@k matches the success rate of 4k independent agents, with advantage growing with k; (2) a team can solve tasks that no single agent can solve; (3) on polyomino packing, communication outperforms best@k and exceeds prior best-known score; (4) on MNIST classifier compression, a team of 4 agents produced a 1,957-byte classifier with 99.4% test accuracy, beating both the best human solution and best single-agent result.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent communication consistently yields stronger results under sufficient compute and clear feedback signals. However, independent agents may outperform communication when compute is limited or when a clear measure of progress is absent. The effect is not merely efficiency—communication enables emergent capabilities that no single agent possesses.

title: Beyond Exact Match: Task-Aware GRPO for Cross-Domain PCBA Visual Question Answering
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Accepted to the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026)
summary: In automated Printed Circuit Board Assembly (PCBA) inspection, standards-guided decisions require systems to jointly reason over fine-grained visual cues, component semantics, and manufacturing knowledge. Although large vision-language models (VLMs) provide a promising foundation, their deployment is hindered by the domain shift between standards-derived samples and real-world production-line imagery, together with heterogeneous output spaces spanning choice-based and numerical counting tasks. To address these challenges, we propose a multimodal reasoning framework for cross-domain PCBA visual question answering. The framework converts standards-derived, real-world, and auxiliary PCB-domain data into a unified instruction format and constructs verified reasoning traces aligned with visual evidence, question semantics, candidate options, and ground-truth answers. We further introduce Task-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which moves beyond exact-match supervision by integrating multi-component semantic rewards for choice-based questions, distance-aware rewards for counting questions, and an auxiliary format reward for valid outputs. During inference, answer-option semantic consistency correction, self-consistency voting, and multi-model arbitration are combined to improve prediction robustness. The proposed system achieves an Overall Score of 83.24 on the official PCBA Standard-to-Real Grand Challenge leaderboard, demonstrating the effectiveness of task-aware reward design and robust inference for cross-domain PCBA visual question answering.

AI.tldr: A multimodal reasoning framework for cross-domain PCBA visual question answering that addresses domain shift between standards-derived and real-world production imagery, using Task-Aware GRPO with multi-component semantic rewards, distance-aware rewards, and auxiliary format rewards, combined with inference-time correction mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Automated PCBA inspection requires systems to jointly reason over fine-grained visual cues, component semantics, and manufacturing knowledge. However, deployment is hindered by domain shift between standards-derived samples and real-world production-line imagery, along with heterogeneous output spaces spanning choice-based and numerical counting tasks.
AI.method: 1) Convert standards-derived, real-world, and auxiliary PCB-domain data into unified instruction format; 2) Construct verified reasoning traces aligned with visual evidence, question semantics, candidate options, and ground-truth answers; 3) Introduce Task-Aware GRPO with multi-component semantic rewards for choice-based questions, distance-aware rewards for counting questions, and auxiliary format reward for valid outputs; 4) Inference: answer-option semantic consistency correction, self-consistency voting, and multi-model arbitration.
AI.result: The proposed system achieves an Overall Score of 83.24 on the official PCBA Standard-to-Real Grand Challenge leaderboard.
AI.conclusion: Task-aware reward design and robust inference mechanisms effectively address cross-domain PCBA visual question answering challenges, demonstrating the framework's effectiveness for standards-guided inspection decisions in automated PCBA assembly.

title: CogGym: Towards Large-Scale Comparative Evaluation of Human and Machine Cognition
summary: Understanding and modeling human intelligence are parallel goals shared by artificial intelligence (AI) and cognitive science. As AI systems grow increasingly capable, in what ways do model responses resemble human responses, and where do they systematically diverge? The sheer breadth and diversity of the tasks humans can perform and think about pose a challenge for scalable and rigorous comparison between humans and models. We introduce CogGym, a scalable, unified framework grounded in cognitive science for systematically comparing model and human behavior on matched experimental trials. CogGym uses a semi-automated, human-in-the-loop pipeline to standardize diverse experimental paradigms into a task-agnostic Experiment Markup Language (EML), enabling reproducible and faithful comparison at scale. For initial release, we curate and standardize 258 cognitive experiments from 100 papers that focuses on human commonsense reasoning, and evaluate 50 large language models against human responses. We find a clear scaling trend where larger and more recent AI models better reproduce human judgments. Yet AI models' improvement on such common reasoning tasks is considerably slower than the gains observed on formal-reasoning benchmarks like math and coding, and model--human fit remains well below human splithalf reliability ($R^2 = 0.93$ on text, $0.95$ on image, and $0.92$ on video) with the best models achieving $R^2 = 0.59$ on text, $0.58$ on image, and $0.43$ on video experiments. We intend for CogGym to provide a living evaluation framework that continually incorporates new cognitive science experiments to characterize where model behavior resembles human behavior, where it systematically diverges, and how those patterns change as models and experiments evolve.

AI.tldr: CogGym is a unified framework for systematically comparing AI model and human behavior by standardizing 258 cognitive experiments into a task-agnostic Experiment Markup Language (EML). Evaluation of 50 LLMs against human responses reveals that while larger models better reproduce human judgments, model-human fit remains significantly below human split-half reliability (best R² = 0.59 on text, 0.58 on image, 0.43 on video vs. human R² ~0.93).
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the challenge of scalable and rigorous comparison between AI systems and human behavior, as AI capabilities grow. The breadth and diversity of human cognitive tasks make such comparison difficult. The authors aim to understand where model responses resemble human responses and where they systematically diverge.
AI.method: The authors developed a semi-automated, human-in-the-loop pipeline to standardize diverse experimental paradigms into a task-agnostic Experiment Markup Language (EML). They curated and standardized 258 cognitive experiments from 100 papers focusing on human commonsense reasoning, and evaluated 50 large language models against human responses.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) A clear scaling trend exists where larger and more recent AI models better reproduce human judgments. (2) AI models' improvement on commonsense reasoning tasks is considerably slower than gains on formal-reasoning benchmarks (math and coding). (3) Model-human fit remains well below human split-half reliability, with best models achieving R² = 0.59 (text), 0.58 (image), and 0.43 (video), compared to human split-half reliability of R² = 0.93 (text), 0.95 (image), and 0.92 (video).
AI.conclusion: CogGym serves as a living evaluation framework that continually incorporates new cognitive science experiments to characterize where model behavior resembles human behavior, where it systematically diverges, and how those patterns change as models and experiments evolve. The significant gap between model-human fit and human split-half reliability indicates substantial room for improvement in AI models' ability to replicate human cognition.

title: Stiefel-AdamW: Geometry-Aware AdamW for Linear Factorization Blocks
summary: A pervasive structural pattern in modern deep learning is the linear factorization block: a submodule of the form $W = BA$ in which two parameter matrices are multiplied directly, with no intervening nonlinearity. Such blocks appear in LoRA adapters, low-rank compressed layers, query-key products of self-attention, and share a common pathology: the factorization is non-unique, which can destabilize training and limit usable learning rates. Despite this, factorization blocks are typically optimized with standard Euclidean methods that ignore the underlying geometry. We introduce Stiefel-AdamW, a near drop-in replacement for AdamW for use wherever such blocks appear. By constraining one factor on the Stiefel manifold while leaving the other Euclidean, Stiefel-AdamW relaxes the full $\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{R}^r)$ gauge symmetry to a compact orthogonal symmetry, ruling out factor blow-up while retaining the coordinate-wise diagonal preconditioning that gives AdamW its practical strength. Moment estimation is performed in the ambient Euclidean space, with geometry entering only through a tangent-space projection and a manifold retraction. The implementation overhead over AdamW is minimal, and we show that the resulting optimizer inherits both the stability benefits of Riemannian methods and standard convergence guarantees. We validate Stiefel-AdamW on LoRA-style fine-tuning of GPT2, ViT, and Mistral 7B and on full pretraining of GPT2 on OpenWebText, showing consistent improvements over strong baselines at essentially no additional cost over AdamW.

AI.tldr: Stiefel-AdamW is an optimizer that constrains one factor of linear factorization blocks (W=BA) to the Stiefel manifold, addressing the non-unique factorization problem that destabilizes training in deep learning models. It preserves AdamW's diagonal preconditioning while adding Riemannian geometry, showing consistent improvements across LoRA fine-tuning and full pretraining tasks.
AI.motivation: Linear factorization blocks (W=BA) appear in many deep learning architectures (LoRA adapters, low-rank layers, attention mechanisms). These blocks suffer from non-unique factorization, which can destabilize training and limit usable learning rates. Standard optimizers like AdamW ignore this underlying geometry, leading to potential issues.
AI.method: Stiefel-AdamW constrains one factor to the Stiefel manifold while leaving the other in Euclidean space. This relaxes the full GL(R^r) gauge symmetry to a compact orthogonal symmetry. The method performs moment estimation in ambient Euclidean space, with geometry entering only through tangent-space projection and manifold retraction. Implementation overhead over AdamW is minimal.
AI.result: Stiefel-AdamW shows consistent improvements over strong baselines across multiple tasks: LoRA-style fine-tuning of GPT2, ViT, and Mistral 7B, and full pretraining of GPT2 on OpenWebText, at essentially no additional computational cost over AdamW.
AI.conclusion: Stiefel-AdamW successfully combines the stability benefits of Riemannian optimization with standard convergence guarantees, providing a near drop-in replacement for AdamW wherever linear factorization blocks appear in neural networks.

title: Combining Object Detection with Geometry-Aware Clustering to Distinguish Overlapping Plants in UAV Imagery
summary:
Reliable plant-level information from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery is important for automated crop monitoring.
