While recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in video understanding, existing benchmarks remain confined to simple scene-level queries or global summaries that require only single-step inference. Real-world video understanding involves more challenging tasks that require multi-hop multimodal reasoning, and there is a critical absence of video benchmarks equipped to rigorously evaluate these agentic capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce AgentVidBench, a multi-hop video question answering benchmark focused on evaluating the spatial, temporal, and causal reasoning capabilities of MLLM agents. Beyond standard question-answer pairs, AgentVidBench provides step-by-step solution traces to support trajectory evaluation that assesses whether agents explicitly acquire the evidence needed to justify their answers. Experiments with 12 proprietary and open-source MLLMs show that single-turn performance remains limited on AgentVidBench, while integrating these models into state-of-the-art agentic workflows generally improves performance with respect to both accuracy and trajectory scores. We further present a simple yet effective agentic strategy that serves as a competitive baseline on AgentVidBench, establishing our benchmark as a holistic testbed for future research on agentic video understanding. Code and datasets are available at https://github.com/krafton-ai/agentvidbench and https://huggingface.co/datasets/agentvidbench/agentvidbench.

AI.tldr: AgentVidBench is a new benchmark for evaluating multi-hop multimodal reasoning capabilities of MLLM agents in video understanding, focusing on spatial, temporal, and causal reasoning with trajectory evaluation support.
AI.motivation: Existing video understanding benchmarks are limited to simple scene-level queries requiring only single-step inference, lacking the ability to evaluate complex agentic capabilities like multi-hop reasoning that are essential for real-world video understanding.
AI.method: The benchmark provides multi-hop video QA pairs with step-by-step solution traces for trajectory evaluation. Experiments tested 12 proprietary and open-source MLLMs, comparing single-turn performance against agentic workflows.
AI.result: Single-turn performance remains limited on AgentVidBench. Integrating models into agentic workflows improves both accuracy and trajectory scores. A simple yet effective agentic strategy serves as a competitive baseline.
AI.conclusion: AgentVidBench establishes a holistic testbed for future research on agentic video understanding, demonstrating that agentic approaches outperform traditional single-turn methods for complex video reasoning tasks.

title: LogicTrack: Auditing Reasoning Trajectories of Large Language Models with Formal Logic Solvers
summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has been shown to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs), yet existing optimization methods largely rely on outcome-based feedback, leaving the logical validity of intermediate reasoning steps largely unverified. To address the gap whereby LLMs arrive at correct final answers through logically flawed intermediate reasoning chains, we propose LogicTrack, a neuro-symbolic framework that audits reasoning trajectories by auto-formalizing each reasoning step into symbolic representations and verifying it with automated theorem provers. LogicTrack introduces Solver-Based Backtracking Reward (SBR), a step-wise scoring mechanism that quantifies logical soundness and guides backtracking tree search at inference time. We further extend LogicTrack to construct supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data with backtracking traces from its trajectories, enabling fine-tuned models to internalize step-wise auditing as an intrinsic capability. Extensive experiments across 8 reasoning benchmarks and 7 LLMs demonstrate that LogicTrack effectively improves both the verifiability of reasoning chains and final answer pass rate, thereby enhancing overall CoT quality and trustworthiness in high-stakes domains.

AI.tldr: LogicTrack is a neuro-symbolic framework that improves Chain-of-Thought reasoning in LLMs by auditing reasoning trajectories through auto-formalization and automated theorem proving, addressing the problem of correct answers being derived from logically flawed intermediate steps.
AI.motivation: Existing CoT optimization methods rely on outcome-based feedback and fail to verify logical validity of intermediate reasoning steps, allowing LLMs to arrive at correct answers through flawed reasoning chains, which is problematic for high-stakes applications.
AI.method: LogicTrack uses: (1) Auto-formalization of each reasoning step into symbolic representations, (2) Automated theorem provers for verification, (3) Solver-Based Backtracking Reward (SBR) for step-wise logical soundness scoring, (4) Backtracking tree search at inference time, (5) Construction of SFT data with backtracking traces for fine-tuning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across 8 reasoning benchmarks and 7 LLMs demonstrate that LogicTrack improves both reasoning chain verifiability and final answer pass rate.
AI.conclusion: LogicTrack effectively enhances CoT quality and trustworthiness in high-stakes domains by enabling LLMs to internalize step-wise auditing as an intrinsic capability through fine-tuning.

title: M2G-LLM: Enhancing Clinical Prediction via Multimodal Graph Reasoning and LLM Context Injection
summary: Integrating diverse data modalities --- such as clinical notes, laboratory results, and medical imaging --- is essential for advancing clinical decision-making. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performance in processing unstructured clinical text, their limited capacity to incorporate non-text modalities hinders their broader utility in healthcare applications. Here, we introduce M2G-LLM (Multimodal MedGraph-LLM), a novel framework that enhances LLMs with multimodal integration and alignment via Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Our approach models temporal relationships between patient visits, propagates information across clinically similar patients, and aligns heterogeneous data sources to construct enriched multimodal context vectors. These vectors are injected into the intermediate layers of the LLM, enabling joint reasoning over textual and non-textual modalities. We evaluate M2G-LLM on the MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-CXR datasets, demonstrating improvements in clinical prediction tasks over strong baseline models. Our results highlight the promise of combining the language understanding of LLMs with the relational reasoning capabilities of GNNs for comprehensive, multimodal healthcare analysis.

AI.tldr: M2G-LLM is a novel framework that combines Large Language Models with Graph Neural Networks to enable multimodal clinical decision-making by integrating clinical notes, laboratory results, and medical imaging through temporal patient visit modeling and cross-patient information propagation.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs excel at processing unstructured clinical text but struggle to incorporate non-text modalities (lab results, medical imaging), limiting their utility in comprehensive healthcare applications that require reasoning across heterogeneous data sources.
AI.method: M2G-LLM uses Graph Neural Networks to: (1) model temporal relationships between patient visits, (2) propagate information across clinically similar patients, and (3) align heterogeneous data sources into enriched multimodal context vectors. These vectors are injected into intermediate layers of the LLM for joint reasoning over textual and non-textual modalities.
AI.result: Evaluated on MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-CXR datasets, M2G-LLM demonstrates improvements in clinical prediction tasks compared to strong baseline models.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLMs' language understanding with GNNs' relational reasoning capabilities enables comprehensive multimodal healthcare analysis, representing a promising direction for clinical AI systems.

title: A Scene Language Model for Open-Vocabulary Scene Mapping
summary: Open-vocabulary 3D scene mapping aims to build a persistent representation of the objects in an environment. Existing systems typically rely on engineered mapping pipelines to associate observations, merge information across views, and maintain a consistent scene representation over time. Many additionally store feature-rich object representations, such as embeddings or image crops, increasing the size and complexity of the persistent memory. We introduce SceneLM, a Scene-Language Model that directly maintains a textual scene map. The full scene is represented as a structured text list of objects, which serves as the model's only persistent memory. For each input image, the model reads the current scene state and updates the map by adding, editing, and removing objects. To learn this behavior, we introduce supervision tasks for iterative scene map maintenance together with an automatic annotation pipeline that generates training data from images without human labels. We evaluate SceneLM on both a language-grounded retrieval benchmark and a localization benchmark. Across both benchmarks, the model produces a scene map that achieves competitive performance with complete mapping systems built from dedicated perception and geometric modules while producing a scene representation that is 6-12x more compact. We further show that SceneLM can be run online on an edge device through experiments on a quadruped. These results show that a persistent open-vocabulary 3D scene map can be maintained directly by a single vision-language model using only a lightweight text representation. Training and inference code is available on https://goldengait.github.io/scenelm/.

AI.tldr: SceneLM is a vision-language model that maintains a persistent open-vocabulary 3D scene map using only a lightweight textual representation. Instead of complex feature embeddings, it represents the scene as a structured text list of objects, which it updates by adding, editing, or removing objects based on incoming images.
AI.motivation: Existing open-vocabulary 3D scene mapping systems rely on engineered pipelines with feature-rich representations (embeddings, image crops), which increase memory size and complexity. This paper aims to simplify this by using a single vision-language model with only text-based persistent memory.
AI.method: SceneLM uses a vision-language model that maintains a textual scene map as its only persistent memory. For each input image, it reads the current scene state and updates the map through add/edit/remove operations. The model is trained using supervised tasks for iterative scene map maintenance, with training data generated via an automatic annotation pipeline (no human labels required).
AI.result: SceneLM achieves competitive performance with complete mapping systems (built from dedicated perception and geometric modules) on both language-grounded retrieval and localization benchmarks. The text-based scene representation is 6-12x more compact. The model can run online on edge devices, demonstrated on a quadruped robot.
AI.conclusion: A persistent open-vocabulary 3D scene map can be maintained directly by a single vision-language model using only a lightweight text representation, eliminating the need for complex feature-based memory systems.

title: PolyBridgeBench: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Physics-Grounded Bridge Design
summary: Multimodal large language models, or MLLMs, perform well at visual understanding and structured generation, yet these capabilities do not establish whether an engineering design will work when executed. Existing benchmarks assess spatial reasoning, structural validity, or physics-grounded construction, but they do not determine whether MLLMs can synthesize complete load-bearing structures and repair them after simulator execution exposes a failure. We introduce PolyBridgeBench, an executable benchmark for multimodal bridge design. A model receives a visual scene and structured engineering constraints and generates a complete node--member--material topology. Deterministic legality checks gate execution in a native dynamic physics simulation. Following an execution failure, the benchmark returns temporal visual evidence from the failed rollout and evaluates repair under a fixed interaction budget. Separate measurements of deterministic validity, dynamic functional success, and post-failure recovery identify the stage at which design fails. Experiments with six representative MLLMs across 189 levels expose a substantial gap between deterministic validity and dynamic success, pronounced sensitivity to material budgets, and limited post-failure recovery under the primary strict-budget setting.

AI.tldr: PolyBridgeBench is an executable benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on bridge design tasks, assessing their ability to synthesize complete load-bearing structures and repair them after physics simulation failures.
AI.motivation: Current MLLM benchmarks assess spatial reasoning, structural validity, or physics-grounded construction, but fail to determine whether MLLMs can synthesize complete load-bearing structures and repair them after execution failures are exposed.
AI.method: The benchmark provides models with visual scenes and structured engineering constraints to generate complete node--member--material topologies. Deterministic legality checks gate execution in a native dynamic physics simulation. Following execution failure, temporal visual evidence from the failed rollout is returned, and repair is evaluated under a fixed interaction budget. Three separate measurements are taken: deterministic validity, dynamic functional success, and post-failure recovery.
AI.result: Experiments with six representative MLLMs across 189 levels reveal: (1) a substantial gap between deterministic validity and dynamic success, (2) pronounced sensitivity to material budgets, and (3) limited post-failure recovery under the primary strict-budget setting.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark exposes significant limitations in current MLLMs for engineering design tasks, particularly in translating structurally valid designs into functionally successful ones and recovering from failures within constrained budgets.

title: TierKV: Long-Context On-Device LLMs via Predictive Multi-Tier KV Caching
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are moving onto mobile devices for increasingly diverse workloads over text, images, video, and audio. These applications often require long contexts, making the Key-Value (KV) cache a dominant memory bottleneck because it grows linearly with sequence length and is accessed at every decoding step. Prior work reduces KV-cache footprint through low-rank compression, token eviction, or flash offloading, but the resulting reconstruction overhead, irreversible token loss, or I/O stalls can offset the benefit of saving memory. We present TierKV, a mobile LLM inference framework built on Predictive Multi-Tier Cache Optimization (PMCO). Before decoding starts, PMCO predicts future cache demand from prefill hidden states and jointly assigns tokens to exact, low-rank, and flash-offloaded tiers under the device memory and accuracy budgets. This formulation retains access to the full context, removes the circular dependency of reactive eviction, and admits a closed-form solver that selects tier boundaries and per-layer ranks at runtime. Across eight text, vision, and audio models on three mobile SoCs, TierKV improves prefill throughput by up to 17.6x over existing mobile LLM frameworks, reduces RAM-resident KV cache by 12.5-34%, thereby enabling substantially longer contexts under the same memory budget, while incurring only minor accuracy degradation.

AI.tldr: TierKV is a mobile LLM inference framework that uses Predictive Multi-Tier Cache Optimization (PMCO) to manage KV cache memory efficiently. It predicts future cache demand from prefill hidden states and assigns tokens to three tiers (exact, low-rank, and flash-offloaded) under memory and accuracy budgets, achieving up to 17.6x prefill throughput improvement and 12.5-34% RAM reduction.
AI.motivation: Mobile LLM applications require long contexts, but the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length and is accessed at every decoding step, becoming a dominant memory bottleneck. Existing solutions (low-rank compression, token eviction, flash offloading) suffer from reconstruction overhead, irreversible token loss, or I/O stalls.
AI.method: PMCO predicts future cache demand from prefill hidden states before decoding starts. It jointly assigns tokens to three tiers: exact (full precision), low-rank (compressed), and flash-offloaded (storage). The formulation uses device memory and accuracy budgets as constraints and admits a closed-form solver to select tier boundaries and per-layer ranks at runtime.
AI.result: Across eight text, vision, and audio models on three mobile SoCs, TierKV improves prefill throughput by up to 17.6x over existing mobile LLM frameworks, reduces RAM-resident KV cache by 12.5-34%, enabling substantially longer contexts under the same memory budget, while incurring only minor accuracy degradation.
AI.conclusion: TierKV effectively addresses the KV cache memory bottleneck in mobile LLM inference by using predictive multi-tier caching with runtime optimization, providing significant performance gains with minimal accuracy loss.

title: SIRA: Reasoning-Aware Surgical Instrument Segmentation via Query-Anchored Alignment
summary: Surgical instrument segmentation (SIS) plays a critical role in robotic assistance and surgical workflow analysis. However, most existing SIS methods formulate segmentation as a category-driven localization problem, limiting their ability to capture procedural context and task-dependent semantics in surgical workflows. We introduce Reasoning-Aware Surgical Instrument Segmentation (RA-SIS), a task formulation that frames segmentation as query-conditioned inference under surgical context. To benchmark this setting, we construct SurgRS, a surgical reasoning segmentation dataset consisting of 41,000 image-text pairs, which aligns instance-level masks with structured query-answer supervision to enable semantic grounding at the pixel level. Based on SurgRS, we propose Surgical Instrument Reasoning and Segmentation Assistant (SIRA), a multimodal framework that disentangles target-level and query-level semantics and integrates them with visual features through query-anchored dual alignment. By aligning query semantics with spatial features and segmentation prompts, SIRA enhances semantic-visual consistency in mask prediction. Extensive experiments on SurgRS demonstrate improvements over existing reasoning-aware baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/linxir226/SIRA.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Reasoning-Aware Surgical Instrument Segmentation (RA-SIS), a new task formulation that frames surgical instrument segmentation as query-conditioned inference under surgical context. The authors propose SurgRS dataset (41,000 image-text pairs) and SIRA framework with query-anchored dual alignment to enhance semantic-visual consistency in mask prediction.
AI.motivation: Existing SIS methods treat segmentation as category-driven localization, limiting their ability to capture procedural context and task-dependent semantics in surgical workflows. There is a need for a framework that can reason about surgical instruments based on contextual queries.
AI.method: 1) Construct SurgRS dataset with 41,000 image-text pairs aligning instance-level masks with structured query-answer supervision; 2) Propose SIRA framework that disentangles target-level and query-level semantics and integrates them with visual features through query-anchored dual alignment (aligning query semantics with spatial features and segmentation prompts).
AI.result: Extensive experiments on SurgRS demonstrate improvements over existing reasoning-aware baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed RA-SIS formulation and SIRA framework successfully enhance semantic-visual consistency in surgical instrument segmentation through query-conditioned reasoning, outperforming existing reasoning-aware baselines.

title: The Communication Bottleneck: A Round-Trip Study of Tree-Structured Expression Serialization in Language Models
summary: When language models reason in chain-of-thought or exchange free-text intermediates, they serialize structured information into natural language. How much tree-structured compositional content survives this bottleneck? We propose a round-trip protocol that answers this question empirically for tree-structured expressions. A generator converts a procedurally generated arithmetic expression into a word problem, a separate extractor recovers the expression from the word problem alone, and symbolic equivalence provides an exact oracle. Evaluating all pairwise combinations of sixteen models yields a communication matrix whose marginals separate generation quality from extraction quality. Three main findings emerge. First, the channel is lossy and asymmetric: swapping which model generates and which extracts shifts accuracy by up to 60.4 points, and the best pair reaches 92.9% by combining different models on each end rather than the same model on both. Second, at least 73.6% of round-trip failures originate at generation, and difficulty is driven by tree structure (operator count, depth, right-branching) rather than model family. Third, the channel is trainable: ~3600 fine-tuning examples that share the evaluation's operators and tree shapes lift every open-weight model above untrained Gemini-3.1-Pro, an upper bound under matched semantics. A disjoint-domain regime with new operators and vocabulary also raises every open-weight model, confirming the gain is not an artifact of matched semantics, though a gap to the frontier remains. Together these results identify tree-structured expression serialization as a primary limiting factor when models communicate hierarchical structure through natural language.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how well language models preserve tree-structured compositional information when converting it to natural language (word problems) and back. Using a round-trip protocol with 16 models in pairwise combinations, the study finds that the communication channel is lossy and asymmetric, with generation being the primary bottleneck (73.6% of failures). Fine-tuning with ~3600 examples can improve performance beyond even Gemini-3.1-Pro, identifying tree-structured expression serialization as a key limiting factor in hierarchical communication.
AI.motivation: The core question is: when language models reason with chain-of-thought or free-text intermediates, they serialize structured information into natural language—but how much of the original tree-structured compositional content survives this bottleneck? This is important because hierarchical reasoning is fundamental to mathematical and logical reasoning, and understanding the limitations of natural language as a serialization medium is crucial for improving model capabilities.
AI.method: The authors propose a round-trip protocol: (1) a generator converts procedurally generated arithmetic expressions into word problems, (2) a separate extractor recovers the expression from the word problem alone, and (3) symbolic equivalence provides an exact oracle for evaluation. They evaluate all 16 model pairwise combinations (256 combinations), creating a communication matrix that separates generation quality from extraction quality.
AI.result: Three main findings: (1) The channel is lossy and asymmetric—swapping which model generates vs extracts shifts accuracy by up to 60.4 points, and the best pair achieves 92.9% by combining different models rather than using the same model. (2) At least 73.6% of round-trip failures originate at generation, with difficulty driven by tree structure (operator count, depth, right-branching) rather than model family. (3) The channel is trainable—~3600 fine-tuning examples lift every open-weight model above untrained Gemini-3.1-Pro, and a disjoint-domain regime confirms the gain isn't just artifact of matched semantics.
AI.conclusion: Tree-structured expression serialization is a primary limiting factor when models communicate hierarchical structure through natural language. The asymmetry between generation and extraction suggests that different model architectures excel at different tasks, and fine-tuning can significantly improve performance, though a gap to frontier models remains.

title: Quantization-Aware Kalman Estimation for Diffusion Sampling
summary: Quantization offers a practical path to deploying diffusion models with reduced memory and computation, but aggressive compression can cause quantized outputs to deviate substantially from their full-precision counterparts. Sampling-stage correction methods seek to compensate for such deviations during sampling, but existing approaches rely primarily on local information and underexploit trajectory history, limiting their ability to correct errors that propagate across timesteps. In this work, we formulate sampling with a quantized denoiser as an online estimation problem, using the history of quantized denoiser outputs to recover the underlying full-precision outputs required by the sampler. We propose QuAKE, a Quantization-Aware Kalman Estimator that combines a smooth trajectory prior with a conditional Gaussian observation model. At each sampling step, QuAKE recursively updates the posterior over the output window in closed form and feeds its posterior mean to the sampler. QuAKE is a lightweight plug-and-play corrector that requires no modification to the quantized network and naturally supports arbitrary high-order multistep ODE samplers. Experiments across W4A4-quantized text-to-image diffusion models show that QuAKE consistently outperforms existing methods in reducing the distributional discrepancy from full-precision sampling.

AI.tldr: QuAKE addresses quality degradation in quantized diffusion models by formulating sampling as an online estimation problem, using a Kalman filter-based approach to recover full-precision outputs from quantized denoiser history. The method is lightweight, plug-and-play, and works with arbitrary high-order ODE samplers.
AI.motivation: Quantization enables practical deployment of diffusion models but causes aggressive compression leading to deviations from full-precision outputs. Existing sampling-stage correction methods rely mainly on local information and fail to exploit trajectory history, limiting their ability to correct errors that propagate across timesteps.
AI.method: QuAKE (Quantization-Aware Kalman Estimator) combines a smooth trajectory prior with a conditional Gaussian observation model. At each sampling step, it recursively updates the posterior over the output window in closed form and feeds the posterior mean to the sampler. It requires no modification to the quantized network.
AI.result: Experiments across W4A4-quantized text-to-image diffusion models show that QuAKE consistently outperforms existing methods in reducing distributional discrepancy from full-precision sampling.
AI.conclusion: QuAKE provides an effective solution for maintaining output quality in quantized diffusion models without requiring network modifications, demonstrating particular value for high-compression scenarios like W4A4 quantization.

title: Learning-to-Optimize as the Missing Architectural Layer of AI-Native Networks
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming a fundamental design principle of future AI-native communication networks, enabling autonomous resource management, adaptive control, and zero-touch network operation. While current AI-native architectures increasingly embed intelligence across network functions, they provide little guidance on how optimisation knowledge should be systematically generated, transferred, and exploited by AI models. This paper argues that the Learning-to-Optimize (L2O) represents the missing architectural layer between optimisation and AI-native intelligence. Rather than viewing optimisation merely as an online decision engine, the proposed paradigm redefines optimisation algorithms as offline knowledge generators that produce high-quality supervisory information for neural surrogate models. The resulting models inherit optimisation expertise while enabling low-latency runtime inference suitable for dynamic network environments. A generic four-stage L2O workflow is introduced, comprising optimisation, knowledge generation, surrogate learning, and runtime inference. Unlike existing Learning-to-Optimize approaches, which primarily focus on algorithm acceleration, the proposed framework establishes L2O as an architectural abstraction applicable across heterogeneous communication and computing systems. The proposed paradigm is illustrated by an NR-V2X relay-selection problem, in which optimisation-generated solutions from a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solver are used to train a Graph Neural Network that can reproduce near-optimal decisions in real time. The presented perspective positions Learning-to-Optimize as a key architectural enabler for future AI-native networks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes integrating Learning-to-Optimize (L2O) as a missing architectural layer in AI-native communication networks. L2O enables offline knowledge generation from optimization algorithms to train neural surrogate models for low-latency runtime inference, illustrated through an NR-V2X relay-selection problem using MILP and Graph Neural Networks.
AI.motivation: Current AI-native architectures lack guidance on systematically generating, transferring, and exploiting optimization knowledge by AI models. The authors identify this as a missing architectural layer between optimization and AI-native intelligence.
AI.method: A generic four-stage L2O workflow is introduced: (1) optimisation, (2) knowledge generation, (3) surrogate learning, and (4) runtime inference. The approach is demonstrated using MILP solver for optimization-generated solutions fed to a Graph Neural Network for real-time decision-making.
AI.result: The proposed framework establishes L2O as an architectural abstraction applicable across heterogeneous communication and computing systems. The NR-V2X relay-selection case demonstrates that the GNN can reproduce near-optimal decisions in real time.
AI.conclusion: Learning-to-Optimize should be positioned as a key architectural enabler for future AI-native networks, bridging optimization expertise with low-latency AI inference capabilities.

title: Reliability-Centered Evaluation of Sparse Longitudinal CT Lesion-Size Forecasting with Conformal Interval Calibration and Gompertz-Inspired Regularization
summary: Sparse longitudinal CT follow-up limits lesion-size forecasting when only a few prior observations are available. We constructed a five-visit DLT-derived same-lesion trajectory benchmark from DeepLesion and Deep Lesion Tracker (DLT), yielding 205 trajectories from 129 patients. We compared an exploratory conventional sparse-to-final analysis with a primary fixed visit-index horizon design predicting the common log change from T3 to T4 while progressively adding earlier observations, evaluating predictive accuracy, uncertainty reliability, post-hoc conformal interval calibration, subgroup performance, and Gompertz-inspired trajectory regularization. The evaluated methods showed partially overlapping point-prediction accuracy but distinct uncertainty behavior. Mean held-out RMSE across ten training seeds was 0.4726, 0.4305, 0.4499, and 0.4513 for m = 1, 2, 3, 4, indicating the lowest mean RMSE at m = 2; additional history did not improve RMSE. At m = 4, raw Cohort-Level Feature GP coverage was near the 95% nominal level, whereas MC Dropout, Deep Ensemble, and residual-scale intervals were conservative. Patient-level conformal calibration generally produced near-nominal or conservative coverage at the cost of wider intervals. Patient-grouped development cross-validation selected lambda* = 0 for the Gompertz-inspired term. A global population reference frequently opposed lesion-level change directions, and prediction difficulty varied across anatomical subgroups. Overall, additional historical observations provided limited predictive benefit once the prediction horizon was controlled, while predictive accuracy, uncertainty reliability, and trajectory consistency did not necessarily improve together, and should be evaluated jointly in sparse longitudinal imaging.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates lesion size prediction methods in sparse longitudinal CT imaging, finding that additional historical observations beyond two visits provide limited predictive benefit when the prediction horizon is controlled, with distinct trade-offs between predictive accuracy and uncertainty reliability.
AI.motivation: Sparse longitudinal CT follow-up in clinical practice limits the ability to forecast lesion size changes when only a few prior observations are available. This study addresses the need to understand how the number of prior observations affects prediction accuracy and uncertainty quantification in lesion tracking.
AI.method: The authors constructed a five-visit benchmark dataset from DeepLesion and Deep Lesion Tracker (DLT) with 205 trajectories from 129 patients. They compared conventional sparse-to-final analysis with a fixed visit-index horizon design predicting log change from T3 to T4 while progressively adding earlier observations (m = 1, 2, 3, 4). They evaluated predictive accuracy (RMSE), uncertainty reliability, post-hoc conformal interval calibration, subgroup performance, and Gompertz-inspired trajectory regularization across multiple methods including GP, MC Dropout, Deep Ensemble, and residual-scale intervals.
AI.result: Mean held-out RMSE across ten training seeds was 0.4726, 0.4305, 0.4499, and 0.4513 for m = 1, 2, 3, 4 observations respectively, with the lowest mean RMSE at m = 2; additional history did not improve RMSE. At m = 4, raw Cohort-Level Feature GP coverage was near the 95% nominal level, while MC Dropout, Deep Ensemble, and residual-scale intervals were conservative. Patient-level conformal calibration produced near-nominal or conservative coverage at the cost of wider intervals. The Gompertz-inspired regularization term was set to lambda* = 0 (no regularization). A global population reference frequently opposed lesion-level change directions, and prediction difficulty varied across anatomical subgroups.
AI.conclusion: Additional historical observations provide limited predictive benefit once the prediction horizon is controlled. Predictive accuracy, uncertainty reliability, and trajectory consistency do not necessarily improve together and should be evaluated jointly in sparse longitudinal imaging. The study highlights the importance of comprehensive evaluation frameworks that consider both point prediction and uncertainty quantification in clinical applications.

title: When Online Adaptation Hurts: Parameter-Frozen Test-Time Ensembling for Continual Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Medical image segmenters often get worse when sites, scanner vendors, or protocols change. Continual test-time adaptation (CTTA) addresses this problem without target labels, but it can be impossible to update a model on a non-stationary stream and can lead to a lot of errors. We examine a more reasonable and meaningful alternative: parameter-frozen inference enhancement(PIE). We use a source-trained segmenter that learns about anatomy-preserving scale and flip views, maps their predictions back to the native location, and averages the probabilities. We do not modify the weights of the model or the normalization statistics. On a cardiac MRI stream from M\&Ms, which is trained on vendor A and evaluated sequentially on vendors B, C, and D, PIE has 0.7786 mean Dice, compared to 0.7680 for source-only inference and 0.7388--0.7416 for five other online-adaptation baselines. The controlled ablations show that performance saturates at 28 views, and confidence weighting, class-prior correction, connected-component filtering, morphological refinement, and inter-slice smoothing have no effect or cause negative transfer. Qualitative results on cardiac MRI and fundus images are also consistent with the frozen ensemble keeping thinner and nested anatomical structures. These results provide a strong, stable baseline for medical CTTA and expose an important failure mode: adaptation and handcrafted refinement can be less reliable than carefully designed inference.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Parameter-frozen Inference Enhancement (PIE), a method that uses a pre-trained medical image segmenter with multi-view (scale and flip) ensemble averaging to improve robustness across different scanner vendors without modifying model weights. PIE achieves 0.7786 mean Dice on M&M cardiac MRI dataset, outperforming source-only inference (0.7680) and five other online adaptation baselines (0.7388-0.7416).
AI.motivation: Medical image segmenters degrade significantly when deployment conditions differ from training (different sites, scanner vendors, or protocols). Existing Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) methods have critical limitations: they require updating model parameters on non-stationary data streams, which can be computationally impossible in practice and may propagate errors. This work seeks a more reliable alternative that doesn't modify the model.
AI.method: The proposed PIE method uses a source-trained segmenter with anatomy-preserving geometric augmentations (scale and flip views). The key innovations are: (1) Learning anatomy-preserving scale and flip transformations, (2) Mapping predictions back to native location, and (3) Averaging the probabilities from multiple views. Importantly, no model weights or normalization statistics are modified. The method was evaluated on the M&M cardiac MRI dataset, trained on vendor A and tested sequentially on vendors B, C, and D.
AI.result: PIE achieves 0.7786 mean Dice, compared to 0.7680 for source-only inference and 0.7388-0.7416 for five other online adaptation baselines. Ablations show performance saturates at 28 views. Various refinement techniques (confidence weighting, class-prior correction, connected-component filtering, morphological refinement, and inter-slice smoothing) showed no improvement or caused negative transfer. Qualitative results confirm the frozen ensemble better preserves thinner and nested anatomical structures.
AI.conclusion: PIE provides a strong, stable baseline for medical CTTA, demonstrating that carefully designed inference-time augmentation can outperform complex adaptation mechanisms. The study exposes an important failure mode: adaptation and handcrafted refinement methods can be less reliable than parameter-frozen inference enhancement. This challenges the prevailing assumption that model adaptation is necessary for domain generalization in medical imaging.

title: Dual-Interest Sequential Product Recommendation With Multi-Granular SSM
summary: Sequential recommendation aims to predict the next item a user will interact with based on their historical behavior. Advances in Transformers have significantly improved sequential recommendation but are still limited by cost efficiency. Although State Space Models (SSMs) have recently enabled efficient long-range modeling, most existing methods encode each item with a single static contextual role, overlooking the phenomenon of item polysemy. In fact, the same item often plays different semantic roles depending on user context, and existing methods are limited in capturing dynamic behavior across different temporal granularities. In this work, we propose DSRec, a novel dual-interest cross-SSM model that explicitly disentangles item roles across long-term and short-term semantic context. Sequential items are encoded into long-term interest embeddings that capture stable preferences via historical aggregation, and a short-term interest branch that emphasizes local session intent modulated by inter-click time intervals. These interest embeddings are processed through distinct SSM encoders: a full-sequence Mamba for long-term modeling, and a time-modulated SSM that dynamically adjusts state evolution based on temporal gaps. To enable effective cross-granularity alignment, we adopt a residual cross-fusion mechanism that exchanges contextual information between the two branches while preserving semantic independence. Experiments on public benchmarks demonstrate that DSRec outperforms other state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: DSRec is a dual-interest cross-SSM model for sequential recommendation that disentangles item roles across long-term and short-term semantic contexts, using Mamba for long-term interest modeling and a time-modulated SSM for short-term session intent, with a residual cross-fusion mechanism for effective cross-granularity alignment.
AI.motivation: Existing sequential recommendation methods using Transformers suffer from cost efficiency issues. While State Space Models (SSMs) enable efficient long-range modeling, they encode items with single static contextual roles, overlooking item polysemy (items playing different semantic roles depending on user context) and fail to capture dynamic behavior across different temporal granularities.
AI.method: DSRec proposes a dual-interest approach with two branches: (1) Long-term interest embeddings capturing stable preferences via historical aggregation, processed by a full-sequence Mamba encoder; (2) Short-term interest branch emphasizing local session intent modulated by inter-click time intervals, processed by a time-modulated SSM that dynamically adjusts state evolution based on temporal gaps. A residual cross-fusion mechanism enables cross-granularity alignment while preserving semantic independence.
AI.result: Experiments on public benchmarks demonstrate that DSRec outperforms other state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DSRec successfully addresses item polysemy and temporal granularity challenges in sequential recommendation by explicitly disentangling item roles across long-term and short-term contexts, providing a more efficient and accurate alternative to Transformer-based methods.

title: MIRCID: Inferred Hub-miRNAs Drive Cross-Task Improvements in Drug Mechanistic Modeling
summary: Drug mechanism-of-action (MoA) modeling commonly relies on perturbational transcriptomes, but matched microRNA (miRNA) measurements are often unavailable. Inferred regulatory features offer a scalable way to reuse these data. Here, we present MIRCID, a framework comparing gene expression with inferred transcription factor (TF) activity and miRNA expression across pathway classification and similarity-based MoA retrieval. HubmiRNet infers 414 pan-cancer hub miRNAs (HubmiRs) from 977 L1000 landmark genes, achieving a Pearson correlation coefficient of 87.72\%; its 1,298-output variant also outperformed SiCmiR on the full-miRNA task (71.21\% versus 67.30\%). In the evaluated comparisons, miRNA augmentation provided more consistent gains than TF activity. Generic embedding controls showed model-dependent utility, while complementarity analyses identified a distinct, partially linearly recoverable representation that retained gene-derived structure. Illustrative rescue cases linked improved classification to biologically plausible miRNA patterns in samples with weak transcriptional signatures. These findings support inferred HubmiRs as a biologically informed recoding of transcriptomic data for perturbational drug modeling, while leaving recovery of measured perturbational miRNA responses to further validation.

AI.tldr: MIRCID is a framework that uses inferred microRNA (miRNA) and transcription factor (TF) activity features to model drug mechanism-of-action (MoA) from perturbational transcriptomes. The method infers hub miRNAs from landmark genes and shows that miRNA augmentation provides more consistent gains than TF activity for MoA classification and retrieval.
AI.motivation: Drug MoA modeling typically uses perturbational transcriptomes, but matched miRNA measurements are scarce. This work addresses the need to reuse abundant transcriptomic data by inferring regulatory features (miRNA and TF activity) to improve drug MoA classification.
AI.method: MIRCID framework compares gene expression with inferred TF activity and miRNA expression across pathway classification and similarity-based MoA retrieval. HubmiRNet infers 414 pan-cancer hub miRNAs from 977 L1000 landmark genes using a 1,298-output variant. Performance was evaluated against SiCmiR on full-miRNA task.
AI.result: HubmiRNet achieved 87.72% Pearson correlation. The 1,298-output variant outperformed SiCmiR (71.21% vs 67.30%). miRNA augmentation provided more consistent gains than TF activity. Generic embedding controls showed model-dependent utility. A distinct, partially linearly recoverable representation retaining gene-derived structure was identified. Rescue cases linked improved classification to biologically plausible miRNA patterns.
AI.conclusion: Inferred HubmiRs serve as a biologically informed recoding of transcriptomic data for perturbational drug modeling. However, recovery of measured perturbational miRNA responses requires further validation.

title: P$^3$-SAM: SAM with Perceptual Parallel Prompt for Few-Shot Strip Steel Surface Defect Segmentation
comment: Accepted by ICME 2026, 6 pages, 3 figures. Corresponding authors: Anpeng Wang and Runmin Cong
summary: Few-shot semantic segmentation (FSS) of strip steel surface defects (S$^3$D) has posed significant challenges distinct from natural scenes. Unlike natural images, S$^3$D task exhibits unique characteristics including low local contrast, uneven illumination, and complex fine-grained texture patterns. Although recent methods based on Segment Anything Model (SAM) have shown promise in FSS on natural images by leveraging SAM's powerful pre-trained representations, these unique industrial characteristics of S$^3$D images lead to performance drop when directly applying SAM to industrial defect scenarios. In this paper, we propose a novel Perceptual Parallel Prompt (P$^3$) framework that empowers SAM, creating the P$^3$-SAM model to address these challenges through two core strategies. First, we develop a Perceptual-Optimized Encoding (POE) strategy that enhances local contrast and preserves critical texture details for S$^3$D segmentation. Second, we introduce the Parallel Prompt Generator (PPG) strategy that simultaneously generates both semantic and spatial prompts, enabling comprehensive guidance for SAM's decoder across varying images. Extensive experiments on three few-shot S$^3$D benchmarks demonstrate that P$^3$-SAM achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly notable improvements of 12.00% in mIoU on Surface Defects-4i dataset.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes P³-SAM, a novel framework that adapts the Segment Anything Model (SAM) for few-shot semantic segmentation of strip steel surface defects (S³D). The method addresses unique industrial challenges like low local contrast, uneven illumination, and complex texture patterns through two core strategies: Perceptual-Optimized Encoding (POE) for enhancing local contrast and preserving texture details, and Parallel Prompt Generator (PPG) for generating both semantic and spatial prompts to guide SAM's decoder.
AI.motivation: Few-shot semantic segmentation of strip steel surface defects (S³D) faces unique challenges distinct from natural scenes, including low local contrast, uneven illumination, and complex fine-grained texture patterns. While SAM-based methods show promise in natural image FSS, direct application to industrial defect scenarios results in performance drop due to these unique industrial characteristics.
AI.method: The proposed P³-SAM framework incorporates two core strategies: (1) Perceptual-Optimized Encoding (POE) - enhances local contrast and preserves critical texture details for S³D segmentation; (2) Parallel Prompt Generator (PPG) - simultaneously generates both semantic and spatial prompts to provide comprehensive guidance for SAM's decoder across varying images.
AI.result: P³-SAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on three few-shot S³D benchmarks, with particularly notable improvements of 12.00% in mIoU on the Surface Defects-4i dataset.
AI.conclusion: The P³-SAM framework effectively adapts SAM to industrial defect segmentation by addressing the unique challenges of S³D images through perceptual optimization and parallel prompt generation, demonstrating significant performance improvements over existing methods.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Centroid-Guided Contrastive Loss for Structured Fraudulent Job Posting Detection
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to IEEE Open Journal of the Computer Society. Code: https://github.com/ali-ahmed925/CGCL_code
summary: Fraudulent job posting detection aims to identify job advertisements that are corrupted either through fake content, misleading information, or negative intent, disrupting the online eco-system of job-seekers and employers. Existing studies in this domain lack effective methods to simultaneously achieve high accuracy and meaningful structure of latent-space representations that capture subtleties among fake posts. To this end, we propose Centroid-Guided Contrastive Loss (CGCL), a loss function which unifies classification with densely formulated clustering to consistently reshape latent-space through a centroid-driven top-$k$ push-and-pull mechanism. The complementary nature of CGCL enables the model to enforce accurate decision boundaries and maintain high clustering compactness, effectively capturing both class separability and latent structure. Extensive experiments demonstrate the state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance of our method on EMSCAD, a public benchmark dataset. The code associated with this work is available at: https://github.com/ali-ahmed925/CGCL_code

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Centroid-Guided Contrastive Loss (CGCL), a novel loss function that combines classification and clustering to detect fraudulent job postings. The method uses a centroid-driven top-k push-and-pull mechanism to achieve both accurate decision boundaries and meaningful latent-space representations, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the EMSCAD benchmark dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing methods in fraudulent job posting detection fail to simultaneously achieve high accuracy and meaningful latent-space representations that capture subtleties among fake posts. There is a need for methods that can both classify accurately and maintain structured latent representations.
AI.method: The proposed CGCL unifies classification with densely formulated clustering through a centroid-driven top-k push-and-pull mechanism. This approach reshapes the latent space by enforcing class separability while maintaining clustering compactness, enabling the model to capture both accurate decision boundaries and meaningful latent structure.
AI.result: The method achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on EMSCAD, a public benchmark dataset for fraudulent job posting detection.
AI.conclusion: CGCL effectively addresses the dual challenge of high accuracy and meaningful latent-space representations in fraudulent job detection by combining classification and clustering objectives in a unified loss function.

title: Multi-Subject Pretraining Enables Short-Calibration Personalization for Closed-Corpus Surface EMG Speech Decoding
summary: Surface electromyography (sEMG)-based silent speech interfaces are limited by cross-user variability and calibration burden. We study a limited-data setting in which each of 27 speech-typical participants contributed less than 0.5 h of data (21.3 min on average) across Aloud and Mimed speech. Within a closed 50-sentence corpus, we used leave-one-subject-out evaluation, initializing from a released single-subject checkpoint, pretraining on non-held-out participants, and fine-tuning on the target participant. This pipeline achieved 21.7% character error rate (CER) and 31.9% word error rate (WER), compared with 49.3% CER without target-subject calibration and 68.0% CER for direct checkpoint fine-tuning. Multi-subject pretraining from random initialization followed by fine-tuning reached 44.9% CER and did not converge under the fixed schedule in 5 of 27 folds, indicating substantial optimization and accuracy benefits from checkpoint initialization. Macro-averaged CER declined from 74.4% with one pretraining participant to 21.7% with 26. Three minutes of target-subject calibration achieved 20.5% CER and 31.7% WER, with no statistically significant difference from the full approximately 13-min pool (21.7% CER and 31.9% WER). A subject-specific adapter provided no detectable benefit. Excluding the five evaluation sentences from all sEMG model-training data increased CER and WER to 78.6% and 99.9%. These results support short-calibration personalization in a standardized-montage, closed-corpus setting.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses cross-user variability in sEMG-based silent speech interfaces using a limited-data approach with 27 participants contributing under 0.5 hours each. The study demonstrates that checkpoint initialization combined with multi-subject pretraining and short target-subject fine-tuning achieves 21.7% CER and 31.9% WER, significantly outperforming direct fine-tuning (68.0% CER). Three minutes of calibration data achieves comparable performance to 13 minutes, supporting the feasibility of short-calibration personalization.
AI.motivation: Surface electromyography (sEMG)-based silent speech interfaces suffer from cross-user variability and calibration burden, making them impractical for real-world deployment. The study aims to reduce the data requirements and calibration time while maintaining acceptable recognition accuracy.
AI.method: The study used 27 speech-typical participants, each contributing less than 0.5 hours of data (21.3 min average) across Aloud and Mimed speech conditions. A leave-one-subject-out evaluation was conducted within a closed 50-sentence corpus. The pipeline initialized from a released single-subject checkpoint, performed multi-subject pretraining on non-held-out participants, and fine-tuned on the target participant. Various configurations were tested including different numbers of pretraining participants, calibration durations, and the use of subject-specific adapters.
AI.result: The full pipeline achieved 21.7% CER and 31.9% WER, compared to 49.3% CER without target-subject calibration and 68.0% CER for direct checkpoint fine-tuning. Multi-subject pretraining from random initialization achieved 44.9% CER but failed to converge in 5 of 27 folds. Macro-averaged CER decreased from 74.4% with one pretraining participant to 21.7% with 26 participants. Three minutes of target-subject calibration achieved 20.5% CER and 31.7% WER, with no significant difference from the full 13-min pool. Subject-specific adapters provided no detectable benefit. Excluding evaluation sentences from training data increased CER and WER to 78.6% and 99.9%.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that checkpoint initialization from a released model provides substantial optimization and accuracy benefits. Short-calibration personalization (as brief as 3 minutes) is feasible in a standardized-montage, closed-corpus setting, significantly reducing the calibration burden for sEMG-based silent speech interfaces.

title: Think Locally, Refine Globally for Memory-Efficient 3D Reconstruction
summary: We propose LoG-VGGT, a memory-efficient framework for long-sequence 3D reconstruction that balances local temporal modeling with global camera consistency. Instead of relying on full global attention, our method introduces cross-window attention at a small subset of transformer blocks, enabling effective information propagation across adjacent temporal windows while keeping memory usage bounded. To mitigate long-term pose drift, we further design a global camera consistency refinement module, where camera tokens interact with compact register tokens via cross-attention to enforce scene-level constraints across the entire sequence. This design enables joint optimization of camera representations and significantly improves long-horizon pose stability without incurring the high cost of sequence-wide attention. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LoG-VGGT achieves improved depth accuracy and robust camera pose estimation across multiple long-sequence benchmarks, while delivering competitive streaming reconstruction performance.

AI.tldr: LoG-VGGT is a memory-efficient framework for long-sequence 3D reconstruction that balances local temporal modeling with global camera consistency using cross-window attention and a global camera consistency refinement module.
AI.motivation: Long-sequence 3D reconstruction suffers from two key challenges: 1) high memory consumption when applying full global attention across long sequences, and 2) long-term pose drift that degrades camera pose estimation quality over time. Existing methods either incur prohibitive memory costs or fail to maintain scene-level constraints for stable pose estimation.
AI.method: The paper proposes two key innovations: 1) Cross-window attention at a small subset of transformer blocks to enable information propagation across adjacent temporal windows while keeping memory bounded; 2) A global camera consistency refinement module where camera tokens interact with compact register tokens via cross-attention to enforce scene-level constraints across the entire sequence without sequence-wide attention.
AI.result: LoG-VGGT achieves improved depth accuracy and robust camera pose estimation across multiple long-sequence benchmarks, while delivering competitive streaming reconstruction performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively balances local temporal modeling with global camera consistency, achieving state-of-the-art performance on long-sequence 3D reconstruction tasks with bounded memory usage and significantly improved pose stability.

title: Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education
summary: Access to academic support is a key determinant of student success, yet students experience it unequally: some readily seek help from lecturers or tutors, while others hesitate due to anxiety, fear of judgement, uncertainty about expectations, or low confidence in their understanding. This may be especially evident in computing education, where programming tasks are cumulative and cognitively demanding. Although students increasingly turn to general-purpose generative AI tools, these can produce responses that are inaccurate, insufficiently contextualised, or misaligned with module expectations. This study presents and evaluates Beacon, a course-specific Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system providing private, immediate, module-aligned academic support. Grounding responses in approved teaching materials, Beacon was designed to lower barriers to help-seeking while encouraging independent learning. Using a design-based research approach, Beacon was developed iteratively and evaluated via mixed methods, combining questionnaires and semi-structured interviews with students and staff at a Higher Education institution. Students described Beacon's responses as closely aligned with module content and more trustworthy than unrestricted generative AI tools, valuing its use of pseudocode and scaffolded explanations over direct solutions. Although participants remained cautious about trusting AI-generated responses without verification, they viewed the system as a valuable first point of support before consulting lecturers or official resources. The findings suggest that carefully designed course-specific AI systems may reduce barriers to academic support by occupying an intermediary space between independent study and formal support. Rather than replacing educators, educational AI may be most valuable when it broadens access to guidance while preserving the pedagogical role of lecturers.

AI.tldr: Beacon is a course-specific Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed to provide private, immediate, module-aligned academic support in computing education. It addresses barriers to help-seeking (anxiety, fear of judgment, uncertainty) by grounding responses in approved teaching materials. Evaluated using mixed methods (questionnaires and interviews) with students and staff, it was found to offer trustworthy, scaffolded explanations valued as a first point of support before consulting lecturers.
AI.motivation: Students experience unequal access to academic support due to anxiety, fear of judgment, and low confidence. While some turn to general-purpose generative AI, these tools often provide inaccurate or misaligned responses. There is a need for course-specific AI systems that lower help-seeking barriers while remaining aligned with module expectations.
AI.method: Design-based research approach with iterative development. Mixed methods evaluation combining questionnaires and semi-structured interviews with students and staff at a Higher Education institution.
AI.result: Students perceived Beacon's responses as closely aligned with module content and more trustworthy than unrestricted generative AI tools. They valued the use of pseudocode and scaffolded explanations over direct solutions. Participants remained cautious about trusting AI-generated responses without verification but viewed the system as a valuable first point of support before consulting lecturers or official resources.
AI.conclusion: Carefully designed course-specific AI systems may reduce barriers to academic support by occupying an intermediary space between independent study and formal support. Rather than replacing educators, educational AI may be most valuable when it broadens access to guidance while preserving the pedagogical role of lecturers.

title: FairLMs: A Turnkey Library for Fairness in Language Models
summary: Fairness research on language models involves measuring bias, applying mitigation methods, and examining the evidence on which an evaluation rests. Existing tools offer complementary functionality through different interfaces, so combining them requires reconciling model interfaces, evidence formats, access constraints, and result types before applicability can be checked or methods compared. We introduce \textbf{FairLMs}, a Python library that connects these activities through explicit declarations of model capabilities and input requirements. It provides 33 intrinsic and extrinsic metrics, 14 mitigation components spanning four intervention categories, 14 dataset and scoring-instrument diagnostics, adapters for the three Transformer architectures and supported hosted completion APIs, and benchmark loaders. Declarations are checked before execution and results carry the configuration under which they were obtained, so that compatible components can be combined, methods compared under a common protocol, and workflows extended to new models and datasets. The source code is available at: https://github.com/FairLMs/FairLMs.

AI.tldr: FairLMs is a Python library that integrates fairness research activities for language models, including bias measurement, mitigation methods, and evidence examination, through explicit declarations of model capabilities and input requirements.
AI.motivation: Existing fairness tools for language models offer complementary functionality but through different interfaces, requiring reconciliation of model interfaces, evidence formats, access constraints, and result types before combining them or comparing methods.
AI.method: The library provides explicit declarations of model capabilities and input requirements, with 33 intrinsic and extrinsic metrics, 14 mitigation components across four intervention categories, 14 dataset and scoring-instrument diagnostics, and adapters for three Transformer architectures and hosted completion APIs. Declarations are checked before execution and results carry configuration metadata.
AI.result: FairLMs enables compatible components to be combined, methods to be compared under a common protocol, and workflows to be extended to new models and datasets.
AI.conclusion: FairLMs provides a unified framework that bridges the gap between disparate fairness tools, facilitating more systematic and comparable fairness research on language models.

title: ME-Dex 1.0: Bringing Heterogeneous Tactile Sensing into World Action Modeling
summary: World Action Models bring the predictive capabilities of video models into robot action generation, providing a rich foundation for modeling future visual states. Tactile sensing complements this foundation with direct measurements of physical interaction. Some existing methods use tactile features as conditioning inputs without jointly predicting future tactile states, visual observations, and actions. Our key insight is that tactile signals, like video, provide observations of the evolving world state and should be modeled as future observations alongside video. We present ME-Dex-1.0 (MachEmbodied-Dex-1.0), a unified World Action Tactile Model for joint visual, tactile, and action learning. ME-Dex-1.0 adopts a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture comprising a Video Expert, a Tactile Expert, and an Action Expert, all trained with flow matching. We use shared attention connects the experts in intermediate layers, allowing action generation to draw on learned representations of visual and tactile dynamics during joint denoising. To support multi-source heterogeneous tactile inputs, a Canonical Hand Model and a Unified Tactile Autoencoder map tactile observations from different embodiments and sensing layouts into shared spatial and latent spaces. To address the limited availability of paired visual, tactile, and action data, we develop the Agentic Tactile Data Engine, an agent-based data production platform. It supplements RoboTwin and DexJoCo with tactile data recorded directly from force sensors during trajectory replay in simulation. Experiments on the RoboTwin, DexJoCo, and ManiFeel simulation platforms, together with real robot evaluations, demonstrate improved manipulation performance using both grippers and dexterous hands equipped with tactile sensing.

AI.tldr: ME-Dex-1.0 is a unified World Action Tactile Model that jointly predicts visual, tactile, and action futures using a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture with Video, Tactile, and Action Experts, all trained with flow matching and connected via shared attention.
AI.motivation: Existing methods use tactile features only as conditioning inputs without jointly predicting future tactile states, visual observations, and actions. The key insight is that tactile signals, like video, provide observations of the evolving world state and should be modeled as future observations alongside video.
AI.method: ME-Dex-1.0 uses a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture with three experts (Video Expert, Tactile Expert, Action Expert) trained with flow matching. Shared attention connects experts in intermediate layers for joint denoising. A Canonical Hand Model and Unified Tactile Autoencoder map heterogeneous tactile inputs into shared spaces. An Agentic Tactile Data Engine supplements limited paired visual-tactile-action data.
AI.result: Experiments on RoboTwin, DexJoCo, and ManiFeel simulation platforms, plus real robot evaluations, demonstrate improved manipulation performance using both grippers and dexterous hands equipped with tactile sensing.
AI.conclusion: ME-Dex-1.0 successfully integrates tactile sensing with visual predictions for robot action generation, showing that jointly modeling tactile futures alongside visual observations improves manipulation capabilities across different robotic embodiments.

title: Calibrating Teacher--Student Discrepancy for On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves reasoning models by learning the token-level discrepancy between a stronger teacher and an on-policy student. However, this discrepancy does not purely reflect the capability gap between the teacher and the student: it also contains deviations arising from the teacher itself, which are consequently mixed into the observed teacher--student discrepancy and indiscriminately learned by standard OPD during training. This issue is further exacerbated by privileged OPD, where privileged information induces larger teacher-side likelihood shifts, thereby encouraging the student to learn more of the teacher's own deviation. We introduce \textbf{Calibrated On-Policy Distillation (Cal-OPD)}, which estimates the teacher's self-deviation region through positive and negative privileged interventions and calibrates the original teacher--student discrepancy by retaining only the component that lies beyond this region. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that, while retaining only about 52--65\% of the original teacher--student discrepancy as the optimization signal, Cal-OPD consistently outperforms standard OPD and its variants across model scales.

AI.tldr: Cal-OPD addresses a flaw in on-policy distillation where the teacher-student discrepancy inadvertently includes the teacher's own self-deviation. By calibrating the discrepancy to retain only the component beyond the teacher's self-deviation region, the method improves reasoning models while using only 52-65% of the original optimization signal.
AI.motivation: In on-policy distillation, the discrepancy between teacher and student models contains not just the capability gap but also the teacher's own deviations from its optimal behavior. This problem is exacerbated in privileged OPD where privileged information induces larger teacher-side likelihood shifts, causing students to learn more of the teacher's own deviations rather than true capability improvements.
AI.method: Cal-OPD estimates the teacher's self-deviation region through positive and negative privileged interventions, then calibrates the original teacher-student discrepancy by retaining only the component that lies beyond this self-deviation region.
AI.result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that Cal-OPD consistently outperforms standard OPD and its variants across model scales, while retaining only about 52-65% of the original teacher-student discrepancy as the optimization signal.
AI.conclusion: Cal-OPD successfully filters out the teacher's self-deviation from the distillation signal, resulting in better student model performance. This suggests that the quality of the distillation signal matters more than quantity - using a smaller but more targeted discrepancy signal leads to superior reasoning capabilities.

title: Fast And Accurate Text Content File Type Identification
comment: To appear in The 13th IEEE International Conference on Data Science and Advanced Analytics (DSAA 2026)
summary: A common requirement across organizations is to have a tool that can identify file types based on their contents, particularly in the cybersecurity domain where magic numbers and file extensions can not be trusted. While existing tools work well in practice, there is plenty of room for improvement either in terms of computational load and time for detection in the case of model based tools like Magika or in terms of accuracy of detection in the case of file parsing tools that use programming language constructs. In this study, we propose a neural network model for identification of types of text content files, especially source code, that is more accurate and faster than other available tools. Our experiments on open-source files indicate that it is not only more accurate on average for text-content file-type identification, but also approximately four times faster than Magika, while being 28% smaller in size.

AI.tldr: A neural network model for identifying file types based on content, specifically targeting text content files and source code, that achieves higher accuracy and faster detection than existing tools like Magika.
AI.motivation: In cybersecurity, traditional file identification methods (magic numbers, file extensions) are unreliable. Existing tools have limitations: model-based tools like Magika have high computational load, while parsing tools lack accuracy. There's a need for a faster and more accurate file type identification tool.
AI.method: A neural network model designed for text content and source code file type identification.
AI.result: The model is more accurate on average for text-content file-type identification, approximately 4 times faster than Magika, and 28% smaller in size.
AI.conclusion: The proposed neural network model outperforms existing tools in both speed and accuracy for identifying text content and source code file types, making it a promising solution for cybersecurity applications requiring reliable file type detection.

title: CompAdapt: Adaptable Composite Motion Modeling for Physics-Consistent Text-to-Video Generation
comment: 23 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Project page: https://makapic.github.io/CompAdapt/
summary: While diffusion-based text-to-video (T2V) models have demonstrated impressive capability in generating realistic and temporally coherent videos, they often fail to respect fundamental physical dynamics. Although recent physics-constrained methods incorporate explicit dynamics priors to improve physical plausibility, they remain limited to simple single-type motions, depend on manually specified parameters, and struggle to generalize to unseen physical laws. In this work, we propose CompAdapt, a physics-consistent T2V framework for adaptable generation across complex real-world scenarios. It extends neural dynamics modeling beyond single-type motions to encompass composite physical behaviors, including coupled motions, multi-stage transitions, and multi-object collisions. Furthermore, CompAdapt translates natural language prompts into structured physical semantics, enabling end-to-end specification of motion types, temporal relations, and initial physical parameters. To generalize to novel physical environments, CompAdapt introduces dynamics-aware prior matching, achieving one-shot adaptation without retraining the core dynamics module. In addition, a physics-aware latent feature fusion module improves visual fidelity under fast and complex motion. Experiments on physics-focused T2V benchmarks demonstrate that CompAdapt improves physical consistency over both general T2V models and physics-constrained baselines, while preserving high visual quality and adaptability to unseen dynamics. The project page is available at https://makapic.github.io/CompAdapt/ .

AI.tldr: CompAdapt is a physics-consistent text-to-video framework that extends neural dynamics modeling to handle complex real-world scenarios including coupled motions, multi-stage transitions, and multi-object collisions. It translates natural language prompts into structured physical semantics and achieves one-shot adaptation to novel physical environments through dynamics-aware prior matching.
AI.motivation: Current diffusion-based text-to-video models fail to respect fundamental physical dynamics. Existing physics-constrained methods are limited to simple single-type motions, depend on manually specified parameters, and struggle to generalize to unseen physical laws. There is a need for a framework that can handle composite physical behaviors and adapt to novel environments without retraining.
AI.method: CompAdapt introduces three key components: (1) Extension of neural dynamics modeling to composite physical behaviors including coupled motions, multi-stage transitions, and multi-object collisions; (2) Translation of natural language prompts into structured physical semantics for end-to-end specification of motion types, temporal relations, and initial physical parameters; (3) Dynamics-aware prior matching for one-shot adaptation to novel physical environments without retraining; (4) Physics-aware latent feature fusion module to improve visual fidelity under fast and complex motion.
AI.result: CompAdapt improves physical consistency over both general T2V models and physics-constrained baselines while preserving high visual quality and adaptability to unseen dynamics, as demonstrated on physics-focused T2V benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: CompAdapt successfully addresses the limitations of existing physics-constrained T2V methods by handling complex composite physical behaviors, enabling natural language-driven physical specification, and achieving one-shot adaptation to novel physical environments. The framework balances physical consistency with visual quality and demonstrates strong generalization capabilities.

title: One Prompt Does Not Fit All: Self-Meta-Evolve for Personalized Information Extraction
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for enterprise information extraction (IE), where the same document must be reorganized differently for each user. Existing prompt optimization methods, however, rely on a single prompt optimized against a global objective, which is misaligned with the inherent user heterogeneity of real workplaces. We formulate enterprise IE as per-user prompt adaptation under interaction feedback and propose Self-Meta-Evolve, a hierarchical framework that maintains a dedicated prompt for each user and continuously refines it through a dual-loop process: an inner loop that edits structured prompts based on persona-conditioned feedback, and an outer loop that evolves the meta-prompt itself by distilling successful editing patterns. To enable scalable training and evaluation, we release a persona-driven IE benchmark of 292 simulated enterprise users, paired with a reproducible persona-generation pipeline grounded in O*NET occupational taxonomies. On this benchmark, Self-Meta-Evolve achieves a 74.58% success rate, outperforming the strongest prompt-optimization baseline by 13.56 absolute points, and reaches 52.54\% within only two iterations. A double-blind human study with twenty real professionals further confirms that prompts adapted by our framework win against static baselines in 71% of pairwise comparisons.

AI.tldr: Self-Meta-Evolve is a hierarchical prompt optimization framework that addresses user heterogeneity in enterprise information extraction by maintaining dedicated prompts for each user through a dual-loop process (inner loop for persona-conditioned prompt editing, outer loop for meta-prompt evolution), achieving 74.58% success rate and 52.54% within two iterations on a benchmark of 292 simulated users.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt optimization methods rely on a single prompt optimized against a global objective, which is misaligned with the inherent user heterogeneity in real workplaces where the same document must be reorganized differently for each user.
AI.method: Self-Meta-Evolve uses a hierarchical dual-loop framework: (1) Inner loop edits structured prompts based on persona-conditioned feedback for each user, (2) Outer loop evolves the meta-prompt by distilling successful editing patterns.
