The framework is evaluated on a persona-driven IE benchmark of 292 simulated enterprise users generated via a pipeline grounded in O*NET occupational taxonomies, plus a double-blind human study with 20 real professionals.
AI.result: Self-Meta-Evolve achieves a 74.58% success rate, outperforming the strongest prompt-optimization baseline by 13.56 absolute points, and reaches 52.54% within only two iterations. In human evaluation, adapted prompts win against static baselines in 71% of pairwise comparisons.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Self-Meta-Evolve framework effectively addresses user heterogeneity in enterprise IE through personalized prompt adaptation, significantly outperforming global prompt optimization approaches. The persona-driven benchmark and reproducible generation pipeline enable scalable training and evaluation for per-user LLM customization.

title: An Introduction to Compression-Based Machine Learning
comment: To appear in The 13th IEEE International Conference on Data Science and Advanced Analytics (DSAA 2026)
summary: Any lossless compression algorithm (like gzip) may be converted into a machine learning method, via either Normalized Compression Distance or the Minimum Description Length principle. Any auto-regressive model may be converted into a lossless compression method via entropy coding. This seemingly circular dependence has unrealized potential in modern artificial intelligence and machine learning, and we survey and formalize the various strategies that have been used to leverage compression for machine learning. We introduce and empirically validate a design framework for compression-based ML, finding compression-based methods competitive with conventional baselines and decisively stronger on malware. We find that varying these design choices yields accuracy gains of up to 0.62.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys and formalizes the connection between lossless compression algorithms and machine learning, showing that compression-based methods (using Normalized Compression Distance or Minimum Description Length) can be converted into ML methods, and vice versa. The authors introduce a design framework for compression-based ML and validate it empirically, finding these methods competitive with conventional baselines and particularly strong for malware detection, with accuracy gains up to 0.62.
AI.motivation: The authors recognize an unrealized potential in the circular dependence between compression algorithms and machine learning methods. Despite the theoretical equivalence between lossless compression (like gzip) and certain ML approaches (via NCD or MDL), and between auto-regressive models and compression (via entropy coding), this connection has not been systematically leveraged in modern AI/ML research.
AI.method: The paper surveys existing strategies for leveraging compression in machine learning and introduces a formal design framework for compression-based ML. The framework is empirically validated through experiments comparing compression-based methods against conventional ML baselines, with particular focus on malware detection tasks.
AI.result: Compression-based methods are competitive with conventional baselines and decisively stronger on malware detection. Varying the design choices within the framework yields accuracy gains of up to 0.62, demonstrating the importance of proper configuration in compression-based ML approaches.
AI.conclusion: The circular relationship between compression and machine learning provides a valuable and underexplored design space. The proposed design framework successfully formalizes this approach, and compression-based methods represent a promising alternative, especially for domains like malware detection where they outperform conventional methods.

title: PSEE: Progressive Sensor Event Expansion for Point-Supervised Temporal Action Localization
summary: Temporal action localization (TAL) in wearable sensor streams identifies action classes and temporal boundaries, enabling finer-grained activity understanding than conventional action recognition. However, training typically requires costly start--end annotations for every action instance. To reduce this burden, we study point-supervised TAL, where each instance is labeled with only one timestamp and its class. We propose Progressive Sensor Event Expansion (PSEE), which combines semantic activations, sensor-specific transition evidence, and adaptive temporal ownership to recover point-supervised pseudo segments. These segments supervise standard TAL detectors without modifying their inference procedures. Cross-subject experiments on four inertial-sensing benchmarks demonstrate improved pseudo-boundary quality over adapted point-supervised baselines, compatibility with different TAL detectors, and robustness to point sampling. Code is available at https://github.com/joeeeeyin/PSEE.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes PSEE, a point-supervised temporal action localization method for wearable sensor streams that uses semantic activations, sensor-specific transition evidence, and adaptive temporal ownership to generate pseudo segments from single timestamp labels, reducing annotation costs while maintaining detection performance.
AI.motivation: Temporal action localization in wearable sensor streams enables fine-grained activity understanding but requires costly start-end annotations for training. This work aims to reduce annotation burden by only requiring a single timestamp and class label per action instance (point supervision).
AI.method: Progressive Sensor Event Expansion (PSEE) combines three components: (1) semantic activations to identify action-related sensor patterns, (2) sensor-specific transition evidence to detect boundary changes, and (3) adaptive temporal ownership to recover pseudo segments from point labels. These pseudo segments then supervise standard TAL detectors without modifying their inference procedures.
AI.result: Cross-subject experiments on four inertial-sensing benchmarks demonstrate: (1) improved pseudo-boundary quality over adapted point-supervised baselines, (2) compatibility with different TAL detectors, and (3) robustness to point sampling variations.
AI.conclusion: PSEE effectively reduces the annotation burden for temporal action localization in wearable sensors while maintaining detection quality, showing strong cross-subject generalization and detector-agnostic compatibility.

title: Accelerating Dense LLMs via L0-regularized Mixture-of-Experts
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance but suffer from slow and costly inference. Existing acceleration methods often lead to noticeable performance degradation, while Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models require extensive computational resources. In this paper, we propose L0-MoE, a lightweight MoE approach using L0-regularization to accelerate dense LLMs nearly without performance loss. Our method introduces a cluster confusion matrix for domain-aware dataset curation and applies dynamic batching for efficient training. Experiments show that L0-MoE achieves up to 2.5x speedup over dense models while maintaining competitive performance, outperforming existing LLM acceleration baselines.

AI.tldr: L0-MoE is a lightweight Mixture-of-Experts approach that uses L0-regularization to accelerate dense LLMs with nearly no performance loss, achieving up to 2.5x speedup.
AI.motivation: Large language models achieve strong performance but suffer from slow and costly inference. Existing acceleration methods lead to performance degradation, while MoE models require extensive computational resources.
AI.method: The paper proposes L0-MoE, which uses L0-regularization to enable sparse expert activation in a lightweight MoE framework. It introduces a cluster confusion matrix for domain-aware dataset curation and applies dynamic batching for efficient training.
AI.result: L0-MoE achieves up to 2.5x speedup over dense models while maintaining competitive performance, outperforming existing LLM acceleration baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed L0-MoE approach successfully balances inference efficiency and model performance, offering a practical solution for accelerating LLMs without significant quality loss.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with Buffered Quantile Objectives
summary: Quantile-based reinforcement learning provides an interpretable approach to risk-sensitive decision-making by optimizing a prescribed quantile of the cumulative-return distribution. Despite this appeal, learning under a point quantile objective is challenging: quantiles can change abruptly under small perturbations of the return distribution, and exact quantile-sensitive planning requires computationally demanding distributional optimization. Lower-buffered quantiles alleviate the former difficulty by averaging neighboring quantiles immediately below the target level, providing a smoother surrogate while preserving the underlying point-quantile objective. Existing methods based on this principle, however, remain model-based and rely on explicit return-law planning, limiting their applicability beyond small tabular problems. We develop Deep-BQRL, a model-free distributional reinforcement-learning framework that extends buffered-quantile learning to neural function approximation. The method learns conditional return quantiles directly from sampled transitions, constructs buffered action scores from the relevant region of the learned quantile function, and uses ensemble disagreement to guide exploration. An augmented input representation allows the learned policy to respond to trajectory information without explicitly reproducing the quantile-state recursion required by exact planning. Experiments on an asset-selling optimal-stopping problem and slippery FrozenLake compare Deep-BQRL with model-based UCB-BQRL and tabular PPO and TRPO implementations. In asset selling, Deep-BQRL attains smaller mean cumulative point-quantile policy gaps than PPO and TRPO at the reported target levels, while UCB-BQRL retains the smallest gaps. The learned stopping decisions also vary with the target quantile, providing an interpretable illustration of the method's risk-sensitive behavior.

AI.tldr: Deep-BQRL is a model-free distributional RL framework that extends buffered-quantile learning to neural function approximation for risk-sensitive decision-making, achieving better performance than PPO/TRPO in asset-selling while maintaining interpretability.
AI.motivation: Point quantile objectives in reinforcement learning are challenging due to abrupt changes under small perturbations and computationally demanding distributional optimization. Lower-buffered quantiles provide a smoother surrogate but existing methods remain model-based and limited to small tabular problems.
AI.method: Deep-BQRL learns conditional return quantiles from sampled transitions, constructs buffered action scores from the learned quantile function's relevant region, uses ensemble disagreement for exploration guidance, and employs an augmented input representation to capture trajectory information without explicit quantile-state recursion.
AI.result: In asset-selling, Deep-BQRL achieves smaller mean cumulative point-quantile policy gaps than PPO and TRPO at target levels, while UCB-BQRL retains the smallest gaps. Learned stopping decisions vary with target quantile, demonstrating interpretable risk-sensitive behavior.
AI.conclusion: Deep-BQRL effectively extends buffered-quantile reinforcement learning to neural function approximation, achieving smaller mean cumulative point-quantile policy gaps than PPO and TRPO in asset selling while maintaining interpretable risk-sensitive behavior. UCB-BQRL retains the smallest gaps, suggesting a trade-off between model-based and model-free approaches.

title: SkillIR: Evolving Scene-Aware Skills for Agentic Image Restoration
summary: This paper studies agentic image restoration, in which multimodal agents coordinate specialized restoration tools to recover images affected by complex degradations. Existing restoration agents often derive complete tool-use plans from the original degraded image or retrieve previously successful trajectories, providing limited support for adapting individual actions to evolving intermediate restoration states. We find that accepted tool executions can change the residual degradation state and, consequently, the applicability of subsequent tools. To address this issue, we propose SkillIR, a skill-guided framework that represents restoration experience as degradation-centered action evidence rather than complete tool-use trajectories. SkillIR consolidates context-dependent action outcomes into scene-aware restoration skills that characterize applicable conditions, expected effects, and attributable failure cases. Instead of prescribing a complete restoration plan, the retrieved skills guide one bounded action at a time within a verified residual-state loop: each tool output is treated as a candidate, committed only after transition verification, and followed by reassessment of the active residual degradations. After each rollout, the resulting evidence is used to create, refine, or patch dynamic skills, enabling accumulated restoration experience to improve decision-making for subsequent inputs. Experiments on synthetic and real-world multi-degradation datasets demonstrate that SkillIR improves restoration quality and enables more reliable and effective tool use.

AI.tldr: SkillIR is a skill-guided framework for agentic image restoration that represents restoration experience as degradation-centered action evidence rather than complete tool-use trajectories. It uses scene-aware restoration skills to guide one bounded action at a time within a verified residual-state loop, where each tool output is validated before commitment and followed by reassessment of residual degradations.
AI.motivation: Existing restoration agents derive complete tool-use plans from degraded images or retrieve previous successful trajectories, but they provide limited support for adapting individual actions to evolving intermediate restoration states. The key insight is that accepted tool executions can change the residual degradation state, which consequently affects the applicability of subsequent tools.
AI.method: SkillIR consolidates context-dependent action outcomes into scene-aware restoration skills that characterize applicable conditions, expected effects, and attributable failure cases. Instead of prescribing a complete restoration plan, the retrieved skills guide one bounded action at a time within a verified residual-state loop: each tool output is treated as a candidate, committed only after transition verification, and followed by reassessment of active residual degradations. After each rollout, resulting evidence is used to create, refine, or patch dynamic skills.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world multi-degradation datasets demonstrate that SkillIR improves restoration quality and enables more reliable and effective tool use.
AI.conclusion: SkillIR provides a more adaptive and reliable approach to agentic image restoration by dynamically updating restoration skills based on intermediate states and accumulated experience, rather than relying on static plans or complete trajectory retrieval.

title: GUARD: Natural Forgetting in Large Reasoning Models via Guided Answer-Reasoning Distillation
summary: Recent advances in large reasoning models (LRMs) have made machine unlearning more challenging, as protected facts or unsafe rationales may surface in intermediate chain-of-thought (CoT) traces before the final answer is produced. Existing unlearning objectives typically suppress the target content or redirect internal representations, but they never specify how the post-forgetting trajectory should continue, which can lead to hallucinated substitutes, malformed boundaries, or repetitive outputs. We argue that LRM unlearning should instead learn a natural forgetting trajectory: a coherent non-disclosing CoT followed by a stable refusal-style answer that replace the original disclosure. To this end, we propose Guided Answer-Reasoning Distillation (GUARD), which converts model-generated unsafe disclosures into safe-exit trajectories, aligns a frozen LRM via guidance tokens, and distills the guided behavior into model parameters.To address the lack of metrics for replacement quality beyond leakage, we further introduce Natural Forgetting Reasoning Score (NFRS), which captures structural stability, fluency, and unsupported substitutes in forgotten outputs. Extensive experiments on R-TOFU and a STAR-1-derived harmful-intent setting show that GUARD substantially reduces unsafe and privacy disclosures across two widely adopted distilled LRMs while preserving reasoning utility. Codes are available at https://github.com/zeyu-Yan/GUARD

AI.tldr: This paper addresses machine unlearning in large reasoning models (LRMs), where unsafe content may appear in intermediate chain-of-thought traces. The authors propose GUARD, which converts unsafe disclosures into safe-exit trajectories and distills this behavior into model parameters, along with NFRS, a new metric for evaluating forgetting quality beyond just leakage.
AI.motivation: Existing machine unlearning methods for LRMs only suppress target content or redirect internal representations but fail to specify how the post-forgetting trajectory should continue. This leads to problematic outputs like hallucinated substitutes, malformed boundaries, or repetitive responses. The authors argue that unlearning should produce a natural forgetting trajectory: a coherent non-disclosing CoT followed by a stable refusal-style answer.
AI.method: The authors propose GUARD (Guided Answer-Reasoning Distillation), which has three key components: (1) converting model-generated unsafe disclosures into safe-exit trajectories, (2) aligning a frozen LRM via guidance tokens, and (3) distilling the guided behavior into model parameters. They also introduce NFRS (Natural Forgetting Reasoning Score) to measure replacement quality, capturing structural stability, fluency, and unsupported substitutes in forgotten outputs.
AI.result: Experiments on R-TOFU and a STAR-1-derived harmful-intent setting demonstrate that GUARD substantially reduces unsafe and privacy disclosures across two widely adopted distilled LRMs while preserving reasoning utility.
AI.conclusion: GUARD provides an effective approach for LRM unlearning that produces natural forgetting trajectories with stable refusal outputs. The proposed NFRS metric addresses the lack of evaluation metrics for replacement quality beyond mere leakage. The method successfully balances safety preservation with reasoning utility maintenance.

title: Routine Blood Tests Outperform CRP for Distinguishing Bacterial From Viral Infection in Children
summary: Acute infectious diseases are among the leading causes of medical consultations and hospitalizations in children worldwide. These infections are predominantly caused by viruses or bacteria, yet differentiating between the two remains a common clinical challenge. As a result, pediatricians often default to the safer option of prescribing antibiotics contributing to the growing problem of antimicrobial resistance. The objective is to assess the additional predictive value of CBC towards determining the current infection. This retrospective study used data from 906 pediatric patients aged between 2 and 14 years who were tested positive either for viral or bacterial infection between 2022 and 2026. Inclusion criteria further required availability of CBC results and CRP level measurements. These laboratory parameters as well as age were used as input features for several supervised classification models. Model performance was evaluated using AUC, sensitivity and specificity. The best performing model is XGBoost, which included all features, achieving out of-sample performance of AUC of 81.7% and sensitivity of 70.8%, specificity of 79.2%. All trained models outperform a CRP-based only decision-rule model in terms of AUC. We suggest that the decision to prescribe antibiotics should be based on a number of factors, including but not limited to CBC, some of which are not currently incorporated into routine practice.

AI.tldr: This retrospective study (906 pediatric patients, ages 2-14) demonstrates that combining Complete Blood Count (CBC) with CRP and age improves differentiation between viral and bacterial infections compared to CRP-only testing, with XGBoost achieving 81.7% AUC, 70.8% sensitivity, and 79.2% specificity.
AI.motivation: To address the clinical challenge of differentiating viral from bacterial infections in children, which leads to antibiotic overprescription and contributes to antimicrobial resistance.
AI.method: Retrospective analysis of 906 pediatric patients (2022-2026) with confirmed viral or bacterial infections. Used CBC results, CRP levels, and age as input features for supervised classification models (XGBoost, and others). Performance evaluated using AUC, sensitivity, and specificity.
AI.result: XGBoost model including all features achieved the best performance: AUC of 81.7%, sensitivity of 70.8%, and specificity of 79.2%. All trained models outperformed the CRP-only decision-rule model in terms of AUC.
AI.conclusion: The decision to prescribe antibiotics should be based on multiple factors, including CBC parameters beyond CRP alone, which are not currently incorporated into routine clinical practice.

title: MT-WAM: Reorienting the One-Pass Predictive Representation Toward Action Generation
summary: Fast-WAM shows that video-action co-training improves control without generating future video at inference, making the representation from a single video diffusion Transformer forward central to action generation. However, future-observation prediction does not explicitly prioritize the future dynamics and visual structure needed for control. We present MT-WAM, which retains the original training objectives and adds complementary supervision for future two-dimensional point trajectories and visual features. A lightweight dual-stream branch copied from the video backbone's final blocks provides target-specific processing, while a structured attention mask prevents cross-stream attention. Motion-stream tokens supply additional dynamics conditions to the action expert. Future visual-feature prediction provides supervision in a feature space that captures object and spatial structure. This supervision trains the video backbone to provide more informative visual context for action generation under changing visual conditions, without adding visual-feature-stream tokens to action conditioning. At inference, MT-WAM uses video and motion caches computed once per replan and skips future-video prediction. Without additional embodied policy pretraining, MT-WAM achieves 98.2% success on LIBERO and 73.7% on LIBERO-Plus, exceeding Fast-WAM by 23.8 percentage points on the latter. On RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Rand, Random success increases from 6.30% to 19.40%; across four real-world tasks, average success increases from 67.0% to 77.8%.

AI.tldr: MT-WAM improves video-action co-training for robot control by adding complementary supervision for future 2D point trajectories and visual features, using a dual-stream architecture with motion tokens. It achieves 98.2% on LIBERO and 73.7% on LIBERO-Plus, outperforming Fast-WAM by 23.8 percentage points on the latter, with significant gains on RoboTwin 2.0 and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Fast-WAM's video-action co-training improves control without generating future video at inference, but future-observation prediction does not explicitly prioritize the future dynamics and visual structure needed for control. MT-WAM aims to address this limitation by adding complementary supervision.
AI.method: MT-WAM retains original training objectives and adds two complementary supervisions: (1) future 2D point trajectories and (2) visual features. A lightweight dual-stream branch from the video backbone's final blocks provides target-specific processing with a structured attention mask preventing cross-stream attention. Motion-stream tokens supply additional dynamics conditions to the action expert. Future visual-feature prediction provides supervision in a feature space capturing object and spatial structure. At inference, MT-WAM uses video and motion caches computed once per replan, skipping future-video prediction.
AI.result: MT-WAM achieves 98.2% success on LIBERO and 73.7% on LIBERO-Plus, exceeding Fast-WAM by 23.8 percentage points on the latter. On RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Rand, Random success increases from 6.30% to 19.40%. Across four real-world tasks, average success increases from 67.0% to 77.8%.
AI.conclusion: MT-WAM significantly improves robot control performance through complementary supervision of future trajectories and visual features, without requiring additional embodied policy pretraining. The dual-stream architecture with motion tokens enables more informative visual context for action generation under changing visual conditions.

title: IntBMoE: Integrating Block-Level Conditioning into Expert Composition for Full-Participation Mixture-of-Experts
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) scales capacity, but existing designs cannot set three quantities independently. For a single token, participation is how many experts contribute knowledge to its output, execution is how many are actually computed (compute cost), and materialization is how many expert-sized parameter sets must be built and stored (memory cost). Sparse routing keeps execution and materialization low, but shrinks participation: for each token, only a few experts contribute. Dense output-mixing restores full participation, but its execution grows with the number of experts. Parameter-merging keeps execution at one expert, but its materialization grows with the number of routing decisions. We propose IntBMoE, a block-conditioned MoE that decouples all three by pairing dense expert composition with sparse block execution. Its blocks come from a small learned codebook, one per entry. At each internal layer, a lightweight hypernetwork merges all expert bases in that layer's pool into one composed expert. Participation is full, because every composed expert draws on the entire pool. Execution stays sparse, because a router sends each token to only a few blocks. Materialization is bounded, because the codebook, not the input, fixes how many blocks exist. Dual-Path Residual Gating (DPRG) further couples two independently composed paths through multiplicative gating. Experiments on image classification show consistent gains over representative sparse and dense MoE baselines. Additional experiments on language modeling and sequential recommendation validate its generalization beyond vision. IntBMoE is fully deployed in AMap's generative recommendation system, serving hundreds of millions of users under a 60ms latency budget, with a 2.4% relative UVCTR gain in online A/B testing. Our code is available at https://github.com/AMAP-ML/DreamX-Rec/.

AI.tldr: IntBMoE is a block-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts model that decouples three key metrics (participation, execution, materialization) by combining dense expert composition with sparse block execution, achieving state-of-the-art results in image classification, language modeling, and real-world recommendation systems.
AI.motivation: Existing MoE designs cannot independently control three critical quantities: participation (how many experts contribute to token output), execution (actual compute cost), and materialization (memory cost for storing expert parameters). Sparse routing keeps execution/materialization low but reduces participation; dense output-mixing restores full participation at the cost of execution; parameter-merging keeps execution low but increases materialization. This work aims to decouple all three metrics for better efficiency-performance tradeoffs.
AI.method: IntBMoE pairs dense expert composition with sparse block execution. Key innovations: (1) Blocks derived from a small learned codebook, one per entry; (2) Lightweight hypernetwork merges all expert bases in each layer's pool into one composed expert; (3) Dual-Path Residual Gating (DPRG) couples two independently composed paths through multiplicative gating. This achieves full participation (composed experts draw on entire pool), sparse execution (router sends tokens to few blocks), and bounded materialization (codebook fixes block count).
AI.result: Image classification shows consistent gains over representative sparse and dense MoE baselines. Additional experiments on language modeling and sequential recommendation validate generalization beyond vision. In production deployment at AMap (hundreds of millions users, 60ms latency budget), IntBMoE achieves 2.4% relative UVCTR gain in online A/B testing.
AI.conclusion: IntBMoE successfully decouples participation, execution, and materialization in MoE architectures through block-conditioned design with learned codebook and DPRG. The approach demonstrates strong empirical results across vision, language, and recommendation tasks, with proven real-world effectiveness in a large-scale production system.

title: OpenSAL360: Open-Source Crowdsourcing Platform for Omnidirectional Video Saliency Collection
summary: Omnidirectional video saliency prediction plays an important role in many immersive multimedia applications, including viewport-adaptive streaming and compression, foveated rendering, mesh simplification, perceptual quality assessment. Yet progress in this area remains constrained by the cost and complexity of collecting eye-tracking data with VR headsets, which makes large-scale dataset creation difficult to extend. We present OpenSAL360, the first open-source platform for scalable, low-cost 360° video saliency collection. Unlike conventional VR-based protocols, it requires only a standard screen, mouse, and internet connection, enabling parallel saliency data collection from common crowdsourcing assessors without specialized hardware. We validate our collection protocol against seven well-established VR eye-tracking datasets and conduct ablation studies on key interface, pre-, and post-processing parameters. To demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed methodology, we collect and publicly release a saliency dataset covering 500 omnidirectional videos annotated by 2,000+ crowdsourcing assessors, making it, to the best of our knowledge, the largest dataset in this field. We make OpenSAL360 publicly available at https://github.com/msu-video-group/OpenSAL360.

AI.tldr: OpenSAL360 is the first open-source platform for scalable, low-cost 360° video saliency data collection using standard screens and crowdsourcing, eliminating the need for expensive VR headsets. The platform was validated against 7 VR eye-tracking datasets and enabled the creation of the largest dataset in this field: 500 omnidirectional videos annotated by 2,000+ assessors.
AI.motivation: Eye-tracking data collection with VR headsets is expensive and complex, making large-scale dataset creation difficult. This constrains progress in omnidirectional video saliency prediction, which is important for applications like viewport-adaptive streaming, foveated rendering, mesh simplification, and perceptual quality assessment.
AI.method: The authors developed OpenSAL360, a crowdsourcing-based protocol requiring only a standard screen, mouse, and internet connection. They validated the collection protocol against seven well-established VR eye-tracking datasets and conducted ablation studies on interface, pre-processing, and post-processing parameters.
AI.result: The methodology enabled the collection and public release of the largest 360° video saliency dataset in the field: 500 omnidirectional videos annotated by 2,000+ crowdsourcing assessors.
AI.conclusion: OpenSAL360 provides a scalable, low-cost alternative to VR-based saliency collection, making large-scale dataset creation feasible through crowdsourcing. The platform and dataset are publicly available to advance research in omnidirectional video saliency prediction.

title: World Modeling in Transformers
summary: Behavioral failures can make a transformer appear to lack a world model even when it has learned faithful representations of its environment. We demonstrate this in TaxiGPT, a transformer trained on random walks through Manhattan whose failures have been interpreted as evidence of an incoherent internal map. Through mechanistic analysis and causal interventions, we show that the model represents intersections and streets, tracks its position, and uses a goal compass to navigate. We trace its failures to interference between superposed intersection features, which disrupts localization within the internal map. Affordance packing, which groups representations of intersections with the same legal moves, helps limit the consequences of these errors. Finally, we propose mechanistic indicators that we use to compare models and show that world-modeling capacities emerge at different stages of training. Our findings motivate a shift from asking whether a model has a world model to mechanistically studying its world modeling: the interacting capacities through which it represents its environment and uses those representations to guide behavior.

AI.tldr: Transformer models trained on navigation tasks can learn faithful world representations even when behavioral failures suggest otherwise. Through causal interventions on TaxiGPT (a navigation transformer), the authors reveal that the model actually represents intersections and streets, tracks position, and uses goal-directed navigation—failures stem from interference between superposed intersection features rather than lack of internal world modeling.
AI.motivation: Previous work interpreted behavioral failures in TaxiGPT as evidence of an incoherent internal map. This paper challenges that interpretation by investigating whether the model has learned meaningful environmental representations despite its failures.
AI.method: The authors used mechanistic analysis and causal interventions to probe TaxiGPT's internal representations. They analyzed how the model represents intersections and streets, tracks position, and uses goal-directed navigation. They also proposed mechanistic indicators to track world-modeling capacities during training.
AI.result: TaxiGPT actually represents intersections and streets faithfully, tracks its position, and uses a goal compass for navigation. Failures are caused by interference between superposed intersection features that disrupt localization within the internal map. Affordance packing (grouping intersections with the same legal moves) helps limit these errors. World-modeling capacities emerge at different stages of training.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest shifting from asking "whether" a model has a world model to mechanistically studying "how" it models the world—the interacting capacities through which it represents its environment and uses those representations to guide behavior. This represents a new paradigm for analyzing internal representations in navigation models.

title: Knowledge-Graph-Augmented Chronos-2 for HEC-RAS Surrogate Forecasting
summary: We investigate whether coupling a time-series foundation model to hydraulic project knowledge improves surrogate forecasting of HEC-RAS water-surface elevation (WSE). We present KG-Chronos-2, which combines a frozen Chronos-2 predictor with exact-state residual decoding, graph-conditioned historical retrieval, and input-aligned correction. We compare the method with persistence, a residual LSTM, project-conditioned recurrent GeoFNO, a hydraulic DCRNN-style model, and frozen Chronos-2. Task-specific fitting uses the 2008 simulation. Evaluation covers 64 fixed 24-hour windows from the 2011 and 2002 simulations at 4,675 cross sections in 71 reaches on a shared geometry. KG-Chronos-2 achieves event-balanced root-mean-square error 0.246970 in native WSE units. It reduces RMSE by 14.13% relative to frozen Chronos-2, 29.38% relative to the hydraulic DCRNN-style model, and 39.54% relative to recurrent GeoFNO. The 95% hierarchical-bootstrap interval for its event-balanced RMSE difference from frozen Chronos-2 is [-0.075177, -0.016317]. KG-Chronos-2 also achieves the lowest active-window and final-lead RMSE among the six completed systems. These results support coupling a frozen temporal predictor to project knowledge for warm-start HEC-RAS forecasting on the fixed benchmark.

title: VoxelTTO: Voxel-Aligned Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Test-Time Optimization
summary: Recent feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods typically regress pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives, often causing excessive overlap and artifacts, while inaccuracies in predicted camera poses can lead to misalignment in novel-view synthesis (NVS). We present VoxelTTO, a feed-forward framework for reconstructing geometrically accurate 3DGS scenes from an arbitrary number of images and optional camera parameters. VoxelTTO aggregates dense image features into a global voxel representation and decodes Gaussians from voxel features, breaking the pixel-to-Gaussian correspondence. To exploit known camera parameters while keeping the pretrained visual foundation model (VFM) parameters frozen, we introduce test-time optimization (TTO) that adapts lightweight LoRA modules using pose supervision. We further replace vanilla 3DGS rasterization with stochastic solid volume rendering during training and inference, improving geometric fidelity. Training updates only the voxel-aligned Gaussian reconstruction modules, requiring 80 GPU hours. Experiments on Replica, Tanks and Temples, and DTU demonstrate improved RGB-D NVS and camera-pose estimation relative to prior methods.

AI.tldr: VoxelTTO is a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that reconstructs geometrically accurate 3D scenes from multiple images. It uses a global voxel representation to decode Gaussians, breaking the pixel-to-Gaussian correspondence that causes artifacts in prior methods. The approach includes test-time optimization with LoRA modules for camera pose adaptation and stochastic volume rendering for improved geometric fidelity.
AI.motivation: Current feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting methods suffer from two key problems: (1) regressing pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives causes excessive overlap and artifacts, and (2) inaccuracies in predicted camera poses lead to misalignment in novel-view synthesis. This work aims to address both issues simultaneously.
AI.method: VoxelTTO proposes three key innovations: (1) A global voxel representation that aggregates dense image features, from which Gaussians are decoded - breaking the pixel-to-Gaussian correspondence; (2) Test-time optimization (TTO) using lightweight LoRA modules adapted with pose supervision while keeping the pretrained visual foundation model frozen; (3) Replacing vanilla 3DGS rasterization with stochastic solid volume rendering during both training and inference to improve geometric fidelity. Only voxel-aligned Gaussian reconstruction modules are trained, requiring 80 GPU hours.
AI.result: Experiments on Replica, Tanks and Temples, and DTU datasets demonstrate improved RGB-D novel-view synthesis and camera-pose estimation relative to prior methods.
AI.conclusion: VoxelTTO provides a feed-forward solution for high-quality 3DGS reconstruction with accurate geometry and pose estimation. The combination of voxel-based Gaussian decoding, LoRA-based test-time optimization, and stochastic volume rendering achieves state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: ECG Mirage: Revealing and Mitigating the Underutilisation of ECGs in Vision-Language Models for Clinical Prediction
summary: Emergency department (ED) decision-making relies on heterogeneous clinical information, including patient history, vital signs, laboratory results, and electrocardiograms (ECGs). Vision--language models (VLMs) can jointly process these modalities, but strong predictive performance does not necessarily imply meaningful use of the correct patient's ECG. We term this failure mode ECG Mirage: apparent multimodal capability without useful dependence on patient-specific ECG information. We distinguish two forms: ECG neglect, where ECGs provide little predictive benefit, and ECG confusion, where matched ECGs outperform no-image inputs but not mismatched ECGs. To evaluate these behaviours, we compare predictions obtained with matched ECGs, outcome-discordant mismatched ECGs, and no-image inputs while holding the clinical text and prediction targets fixed. Across four VLMs on MDS-ED, matched ECGs provide no consistent advantage for either ICU admission or clinical deterioration prediction. We then train four restricted visual prompts using supervised learning followed by conditional direct preference optimisation, while keeping the VLM backbone frozen. The resulting models achieve balanced accuracies of 70.6% for ICU admission and 67.5% for deterioration and increase the matched-versus-mismatched performance gap to approximately 16.5 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively. Overall, our study identifies ECG Mirage in multimodal clinical prediction and introduces visual prompt tuning as an efficient mitigation strategy.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "ECG Mirage" - a failure mode in vision-language models (VLMs) where apparent multimodal capability exists without meaningful use of patient-specific ECG information. The authors propose visual prompt tuning as an efficient mitigation strategy, achieving significant improvements in model performance and reducing this failure mode.
AI.motivation: Emergency department (ED) decision-making requires processing heterogeneous clinical information (patient history, vital signs, lab results, ECGs). While VLMs can process multiple modalities, strong predictive performance doesn't guarantee actual utilization of patient-specific ECG data. The authors aimed to identify and address this failure mode.
AI.method: 1. Evaluation: Compared predictions using matched ECGs, outcome-discordant mismatched ECGs, and no-image inputs across four VLMs on MDS-ED dataset for ICU admission and clinical deterioration prediction. 2. Mitigation: Trained restricted visual prompts using supervised learning followed by conditional direct preference optimisation (DPO), keeping VLM backbone frozen.
AI.result: 1. Original VLMs showed no consistent advantage from matched ECGs across four models. 2. After visual prompt tuning: achieved 70.6% balanced accuracy for ICU admission and 67.5% for deterioration. 3. Increased matched-versus-mismatched performance gap to ~16.5 percentage points (ICU) and ~5.5 percentage points (deterioration).
AI.conclusion: The study successfully identifies ECG Mirage as a significant problem in multimodal clinical prediction and demonstrates that visual prompt tuning is an efficient mitigation strategy that enhances VLM reliance on patient-specific ECG information without requiring full model retraining.

title: Probabilistic Forecasting of Business Process Executions with Neural Temporal Point Processes
summary: Operators of service-based systems act on forecasts of how a running execution will continue, and such a forecast is actionable only if its reliability is known. Mainstream deep-learning models for this task are discriminative and deterministic: they emit a single next activity and a single remaining-time estimate, without a distribution to reason over. We instead cast the problem as generative sequence modelling with marked temporal point processes, which define a joint density over the next mark and its inter-event time and therefore deliver predictive distributions by construction. Real event logs violate the simple-point-process assumption these models rest on, since consecutive events frequently carry identical timestamps; we handle such ties explicitly and combine a transformer encoder with a mixture decoder over inter-event times, trained by exact log-likelihood. On ten public logs, the resulting model matches discriminative baselines on point accuracy, dominates them on the calibration and sharpness of remaining-time distributions, and is the cheapest at inference, since a full predictive distribution is obtained in a single forward pass without sampling.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a generative approach to process prediction using marked temporal point processes, which provides predictive distributions instead of point estimates. The model handles timestamp ties, uses a transformer encoder with mixture decoder, and achieves better calibration and sharpness than discriminative baselines while being computationally cheaper at inference.
AI.motivation: Operators of service-based systems rely on forecasts of ongoing executions, but existing deep learning models are discriminative and deterministic—they produce single predictions (next activity, remaining time) without uncertainty quantification. This limits their actionability since reliability cannot be assessed.
AI.method: The paper reframes the prediction problem as generative sequence modeling using marked temporal point processes. This approach defines a joint density over the next mark (activity) and inter-event time, naturally providing predictive distributions. The model handles timestamp ties (common in real event logs) explicitly, combines a transformer encoder with a mixture decoder over inter-event times, and is trained via exact log-likelihood.
AI.result: On ten public event logs, the model matches discriminative baselines on point accuracy (next activity prediction), while significantly outperforming them on calibration and sharpness of remaining-time distributions. It also achieves the lowest inference cost, as a full predictive distribution is obtained in a single forward pass without sampling.
AI.conclusion: The proposed generative approach successfully delivers reliable predictive distributions for service-based system forecasting, matching point accuracy of discriminative baselines while providing valuable uncertainty information. The single forward pass architecture makes it computationally efficient for practical deployment.

title: Adaptive World Memory 3D Foundation Model for Scalable 3D Mapping, Localization, and Rendering
summary: Recent 3D foundation models enable generalizable geometric reasoning from RGB images but remain limited in persistent memory, scalability, and renderable scene modeling. We present a memory-centric 3D foundation model for scalable robotic localization, reconstruction, and Gaussian rendering. Its core is an adaptive world memory mechanism that combines transformer-based gated updates with test-time temporal-spatial regulation. Learned gates control recurrent memory propagation, while temporal state evolution and spatial observation-state consistency regulate token-wise updates and forgetting over long image sequences. To support large-scale mapping, we organize memory into local submaps and integrate progressive mapping and tracking, loop closure, and SL(4)-based global refinement to maintain local accuracy and global consistency. A Gaussian reconstruction head decodes memory-enhanced features into renderable primitives, unifying camera pose estimation, dense point-cloud reconstruction, and photorealistic rendering within a single model. Experiments on public benchmarks and self-collected datasets from diverse robotic platforms demonstrate improved trajectory accuracy, reconstruction completeness, and rendering quality over existing 3D foundation reconstruction and SLAM baselines. These results support adaptive memory as a foundation for persistent robotic world modeling. The dataset and code will be made publicly available at \href{https://github.com/dtc111111/AWM-3DFM}{https://github.com/dtc111111/AWM-3DFM}.

AI.tldr: This paper presents AWM-3DFM, a memory-centric 3D foundation model that addresses limitations in persistent memory, scalability, and renderable scene modeling of existing 3D foundation models. It uses an adaptive world memory mechanism with transformer-based gated updates and temporal-spatial regulation to enable scalable robotic localization, reconstruction, and Gaussian rendering within a single model.
AI.motivation: Current 3D foundation models enable generalizable geometric reasoning from RGB images but are limited in persistent memory, scalability, and renderable scene modeling. These limitations hinder their application in robotics for long-term, large-scale world modeling.
AI.method: The proposed method uses: (1) An adaptive world memory mechanism combining transformer-based gated updates with test-time temporal-spatial regulation; (2) Learned gates controlling recurrent memory propagation with temporal state evolution and spatial observation-state consistency; (3) Memory organized into local submaps with progressive mapping/tracking, loop closure, and SL(4)-based global refinement; (4) A Gaussian reconstruction head decoding memory-enhanced features into renderable primitives.
AI.result: Experiments on public benchmarks and self-collected datasets from diverse robotic platforms demonstrate improved trajectory accuracy, reconstruction completeness, and rendering quality over existing 3D foundation reconstruction and SLAM baselines.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive memory mechanisms can serve as a foundation for persistent robotic world modeling, unifying camera pose estimation, dense point-cloud reconstruction, and photorealistic rendering within a single model.

title: LLM-Generated Feature Pools for Time Series Anomaly Detection
summary: We study how far a simple statistical pipeline can go on univariate time series anomaly detection under a strict selection protocol. The method extracts a small pool of statistics over sliding windows, scores each window with a transductive robust (MAD) model, and selects a feature subset per domain on a held-out tuning split. On TSB-AD-U it reaches $0.529$ per-series VUS-PR, above the best neural ($0.45$) and statistical ($0.44$) entries on the public leaderboard and within $0.06$ of the strongest pretrained foundation model, several of which use more supervision than ours. Ablations locate the cause: across three selection strategies and a hindsight oracle the score moves by $0.031$, and across the aggregation grid by $0.096$, while changing the candidate pool moves it by $0.226$. The candidate pool sets the ceiling; the search over it is second-order. We therefore generate a pool per domain by prompting a multimodal LLM with in-context example windows from that domain. The generated pools match the hand-crafted one under matched selection, and the two cover different domains: selecting over their union improves on the generated pool in all twelve generator-seed pairs and lifts the pipeline to $0.588$, matching the performance of the best entry on the leaderboard.

AI.tldr: A simple statistical pipeline using sliding window statistics, MAD scoring, and feature subset selection achieves competitive performance (0.529 VUS-PR) on univariate time series anomaly detection, matching pretrained foundation models. The key insight is that the candidate pool of features is the primary performance driver, while selection strategies have secondary impact. Combining hand-crafted and LLM-generated feature pools further improves performance to 0.588.
AI.motivation: To explore how far a simple statistical pipeline can go on univariate time series anomaly detection under a strict selection protocol, and to understand what factors most significantly impact detection performance.
AI.method: The method extracts a small pool of statistics over sliding windows, scores each window with a transductive robust MAD (Median Absolute Deviation) model, and selects a feature subset per domain on a held-out tuning split. Additionally, the authors generate candidate pools per domain by prompting a multimodal LLM with in-context example windows from that domain.
AI.result: The pipeline achieves 0.529 per-series VUS-PR on TSB-AD-U, outperforming the best neural (0.45) and statistical (0.44) entries on the public leaderboard and within 0.06 of the strongest pretrained foundation model. Ablations reveal that the candidate pool has the largest impact (0.226), followed by aggregation grid (0.096), while selection strategies only move the score by 0.031. Combining generated and hand-crafted pools improves to 0.588, matching the best leaderboard entry across all twelve generator-seed pairs.
AI.conclusion: The candidate pool sets the ceiling for performance; the search over it is second-order. Simple statistical methods can match or exceed pretrained foundation models when provided with appropriate feature pools. The approach demonstrates that sophisticated neural architectures are not always necessary for competitive time series anomaly detection.

title: Tracing the Evidence Behind Zero-Shot Time-Series Forecasting: A Source-First Taxonomy and Audit Framework
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures. Accepted to ACM AI Summit 2026 (Visionary Papers)
summary: Zero-shot time-series forecasting (TSF) is often described as forecasting without target-specific parameter updates, but that training-status condition does not specify what evidence the system may use. A frozen language model prompted with serialized values, a time-series model pretrained on broad forecasting corpora, and a retrieval-augmented forecaster may all satisfy the no-update condition while drawing on different transferable evidence. This paper argues that zero-shot TSF should therefore be governed as an evidence-access claim. We propose a source-first taxonomy that separates three primary evidence sources---frozen LLM prior reuse, parametric time-series pretraining, and retrieval-augmented external memory---from the architectures that implement them. After the source is identified, four additional audit questions remain: task interface, forecast object and scoring, prediction-time context, and resource budget. The resulting agenda is to make zero-shot leaderboards auditable by reporting evidence boundaries and interface assumptions alongside scores, so that benchmark progress reflects transferable forecasting capability rather than undisclosed changes in context, memory, or budget.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that zero-shot time-series forecasting (TSF) should be defined by "evidence access" rather than just "no parameter updates." The authors propose a source-first taxonomy separating three evidence sources (frozen LLM prior reuse, parametric time-series pretraining, and retrieval-augmented external memory) from architectures. Four additional audit questions are proposed: task interface, forecast object and scoring, prediction-time context, and resource budget. The goal is to make zero-shot leaderboards auditable by reporting evidence boundaries and interface assumptions alongside scores.
AI.motivation: Current zero-shot TSF definitions only specify "no target-specific parameter updates" but fail to specify what evidence the system may use. Different methods (frozen LMs, pretrained time-series models, retrieval-augmented forecasters) all satisfy the no-update condition but draw on different transferable evidence. This lack of clarity makes benchmark progress difficult to evaluate.
AI.method: The authors propose a source-first taxonomy that separates three primary evidence sources from the architectures implementing them: (1) frozen LLM prior reuse, (2) parametric time-series pretraining, and (3) retrieval-augmented external memory. After identifying the source, four additional audit questions must be addressed: task interface, forecast object and scoring, prediction-time context, and resource budget.
AI.result: A framework for categorizing and auditing zero-shot TSF methods based on their evidence sources and interface assumptions, enabling more transparent and comparable benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Zero-shot leaderboards should report evidence boundaries and interface assumptions alongside scores so that benchmark progress reflects genuine transferable forecasting capability rather than undisclosed changes in context, memory, or budget. This will make the field more auditable and progress more measurable.

title: 2D GauSS-MI: Efficient Active Scene Reconstruction with Balanced Visual and Geometric Quality
summary: Active reconstruction requires efficient active view selection to achieve high-quality reconstruction within limited onboard computational resources. Existing methods face challenges in adequately balancing visual and geometric quality with the computational efficiency required for real-time operation. In this work, we present an active reconstruction framework based on 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS). We develop an efficient online 2DGS mapping pipeline for incremental RGB-D observations and introduce a probabilistic reliability model that characterizes the view-dependent reconstruction quality of individual 2D Gaussian splats. Building on this model, we formulate 2D Gaussian Splatting Shannon Mutual Information (2D GauSS-MI), a mutual-information-based metric that exploits the explicit surface orientation of 2DGS to evaluate the expected information gain of candidate views. The proposed metric enables active view selection to account for both visual and geometric reconstruction quality. We evaluate the proposed system against three state-of-the-art baselines on eight Replica scenes. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves a favorable balance between visual and geometric reconstruction quality with substantially lower computational cost and competitive model storage.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an active reconstruction framework based on 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) that introduces a mutual-information-based metric (2D GauSS-MI) for efficient view selection, balancing visual and geometric reconstruction quality with lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Active reconstruction requires efficient view selection to achieve high-quality 3D reconstruction within limited computational resources. Existing methods struggle to adequately balance visual quality, geometric quality, and computational efficiency needed for real-time operation.
AI.method: The framework includes: (1) An efficient online 2DGS mapping pipeline for incremental RGB-D observations, (2) A probabilistic reliability model characterizing view-dependent reconstruction quality of individual 2D Gaussian splats, (3) 2D GauSS-MI - a mutual-information-based metric that exploits explicit surface orientation of 2DGS to evaluate expected information gain of candidate views.
AI.result: The proposed method was evaluated against three state-of-the-art baselines on eight Replica scenes, demonstrating favorable balance between visual and geometric reconstruction quality with substantially lower computational cost and competitive model storage.
AI.conclusion: The 2DGS-based active reconstruction framework with 2D GauSS-MI metric achieves superior balance of quality and efficiency compared to existing methods, making it suitable for real-time robotic applications with limited computational resources.

title: MIST: Multimodal Survival Prediction with Genomic-Guided Histology Attention
comment: Accepted at the COMPAYL 2026 Workshop on Computational Pathology and Multimodal Data at MICCAI 2026. 11 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables
summary: Multimodal survival models can combine complementary prognostic information from whole-slide images and genomic profiles, but effective fusion remains challenging amid external cohort shift and computational complexity. To address these challenges, we propose MIST, multimodal survival prediction with genomic-guided histology attention. MIST represents genomic features as tokens and allows them to query compact foundation-model-derived histology context tokens before survival prediction. This design enriches molecular information with histology context rather than merging separately encoded modalities only at the final stage. Training combines discrete-time survival prediction with genomic feature masking, WSI dropout, and paired WSI-genomics contrastive alignment. Across four external evaluations in colon, renal, lung, and glioblastoma cohorts, MIST improves external C-index over standard fusion baselines in the primary comparisons. These results support genomic-guided histology attention as a compact and effective strategy for multimodal oncology outcome prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/samiyavuuz/MIST .

AI.tldr: MIST introduces genomic-guided histology attention for multimodal survival prediction, representing genomic features as tokens that query foundation-model-derived histology context tokens, achieving improved external C-index across four cancer cohorts.
AI.motivation: Multimodal survival models combining whole-slide images (WSI) and genomic profiles face challenges in effective fusion, external cohort shift, and computational complexity. Standard fusion approaches merge separately encoded modalities only at the final prediction stage, limiting their ability to deeply integrate complementary prognostic information.
AI.method: MIST represents genomic features as tokens and allows them to query compact foundation-model-derived histology context tokens before survival prediction. This architecture enriches molecular information with histology context rather than simple late fusion. Training combines discrete-time survival prediction with genomic feature masking, WSI dropout, and paired WSI-genomics contrastive alignment.
AI.result: Across four external evaluations in colon, renal, lung, and glioblastoma cohorts, MIST improves external C-index over standard fusion baselines in primary comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Genomic-guided histology attention represents a compact and effective strategy for multimodal oncology outcome prediction, successfully addressing challenges of effective fusion and external cohort shift.

title: Decision-Focused Learning for Mean-Variance Portfolio Optimization via KKT-Based Reformulation
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Accepted at PRICAI 2026 (Pacific Rim International Conference on Artificial Intelligence)
summary: Mean-variance portfolio optimization (MVO) is a central framework in data-driven asset management. A widely adopted approach is a two-stage framework that first predicts expected returns and then solves the optimization problem based on these predictions, with the predictive models trained by minimizing prediction errors. However, this objective of prediction is not aligned with the quality of the downstream portfolio decision. Decision-focused learning (DFL), which directly minimizes the downstream decision loss within the learning process, has thus emerged as a promising direction. However, existing DFL approaches to MVO rely on surrogate losses or constraint relaxations for tractability, creating a structural mismatch between predictive model training and the constrained MVO solved at evaluation. We propose a single-level optimization formulation that incorporates the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) optimality conditions of the lower-level MVO into the upper-level learning problem. This formulation explicitly preserves the budget and short-sale constraints while remaining tractable for standard nonlinear optimization solvers. Rolling-window experiments on real-world ETF (Exchange Traded Funds) data across two asset universes with different correlation structures show that our method achieved the best performance on multiple investment metrics and also demonstrated performance improvement due to the proposed regularization.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a single-level optimization formulation for decision-focused learning in mean-variance portfolio optimization, which directly incorporates the KKT optimality conditions of the constrained MVO problem into the learning process, preserving budget and short-sale constraints while remaining tractable for standard solvers.
AI.motivation: Traditional two-stage MVO frameworks (predict then optimize) train predictive models by minimizing prediction errors, which is misaligned with the downstream portfolio decision quality. Existing DFL approaches rely on surrogate losses or constraint relaxations, creating a structural mismatch between training and the actual constrained MVO solved at evaluation.
AI.method: The authors propose a single-level optimization formulation that embeds the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) optimality conditions of the lower-level MVO into the upper-level learning problem. This explicitly preserves budget and short-sale constraints while maintaining tractability for standard nonlinear optimization solvers. The method was validated via rolling-window experiments on real-world ETF data across two asset universes with different correlation structures.
AI.result: The proposed method achieved the best performance on multiple investment metrics compared to baseline approaches. The method also demonstrated performance improvement attributable to the proposed regularization.
AI.conclusion: The KKT-based single-level optimization formulation successfully bridges the gap between predictive model training and constrained portfolio optimization, providing a tractable DFL approach that directly optimizes for portfolio decision quality while respecting investment constraints.

title: VidOmni-Bench: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Video Understanding via Spatio-Temporal Event Verification across Complexity and Duration
summary: While Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) have recently demonstrated strong performance, reliably evaluating their fine-grained video understanding remains challenging. Existing benchmarks often rely on question answering or ground-truth caption matching, where models may succeed through superficial cues and incomplete annotations. To this end, we introduce VidOmni-Bench, a benchmark that requires models to verify whether each event in dense video captions is supported by the video. VidOmni-Bench consists of 500 videos spanning five complexity types and diverse durations from 4 seconds to 90 minutes. After collecting videos along these axes, we use diverse Video-LLMs to generate dense captions and obtain human-verified sentence-level labels, where sentences containing incorrect events serve as hard negatives for evaluation. Our experiments on VidOmni-Bench reveal three key findings: (i) Video-LLMs frequently generate hallucinated descriptions in dense video captioning; (ii) they also struggle as verifiers, failing to reliably detect plausible but incorrect event descriptions; and (iii) model weaknesses vary across video complexity and duration, revealing diverse, model-specific bottlenecks in current Video-LLMs.

AI.tldr: VidOmni-Bench is a new benchmark for evaluating Video-LLMs' fine-grained video understanding by requiring models to verify whether events in dense video captions are supported by the video content. The benchmark contains 500 videos of varying complexity and duration, with human-verified sentence-level labels for evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for Video-LLMs rely on question answering or ground-truth caption matching, where models can succeed through superficial cues and incomplete annotations. There is a need for a more rigorous evaluation method that truly tests fine-grained video understanding.
AI.method: The benchmark collects 500 videos spanning five complexity types and durations from 4 seconds to 90 minutes. Dense captions are generated using diverse Video-LLMs, and human-verified sentence-level labels are obtained. Sentences containing incorrect events serve as hard negatives for evaluation.
AI.result: Three key findings: (i) Video-LLMs frequently generate hallucinated descriptions in dense video captioning; (ii) they struggle as verifiers, failing to reliably detect plausible but incorrect event descriptions; (iii) model weaknesses vary across video complexity and duration, revealing diverse, model-specific bottlenecks.
AI.conclusion: VidOmni-Bench reveals significant limitations in current Video-LLMs, including hallucination problems and verification failures. The benchmark exposes diverse, model-specific weaknesses across different video types and durations, highlighting the need for improvement in fine-grained video understanding capabilities.

title: EnterpriseVal: Quantifying the Efficacy, Reliability and Value of Generative AI in the Enterprise
summary: Frontier language models now produce professional deliverables that expert graders judge to match human work on a substantial share of economically valuable tasks, yet most enterprise GenAI initiatives fail to show a measurable business effect and a large fraction of agentic projects are expected to be cancelled. We argue that this is substantially a measurement problem: public benchmarks answer "what can the model do?", whereas a deployment decision requires "is this workflow fit, reliable, safe and worth scaling - here, on our data, under our controls?". We present EnterpriseVal, a use-case-level evaluation system that closes this gap. It comprises (i) a formal specification of the use case and of the frozen socio-technical configuration under test, model, prompts, retrieval, tools, guardrails and human oversight, with an autonomy level and consequence tier that jointly set the required evaluation intensity; (ii) a metric catalogue spanning fidelity, utility, efficiency, reliability, assurance and oversight; (iii) a grading protocol that scales blinded expert judgement with calibrated LLM-as-judge scoring through prediction-powered inference; (iv) a two-tier threshold gate, stated as an executable algorithm, that maps metric vectors with confidence bounds to REJECT/CONDITIONAL/SCALE decisions; and (v) a value-and-risk model in which the reviewer catch rate is a measured parameter. We report a pilot across three workflows in a global bank. In credit-memo drafting, human-graded citation precision reached 88% and hallucination rate 1.6% for the best model against gates of 70% and 5%; in procedure transformation, analyst refinement effort fell from an estimated 27.4 to 2.9 hours per document. We separate established results, documented pilot evidence, the proposed system and open hypotheses, and specify the experiments required for full validation

AI.tldr: EnterpriseVal is a use-case-level evaluation system designed to bridge the gap between public benchmarks (which measure what models can do) and deployment decisions (which require evidence that specific workflows are fit, reliable, safe, and worth scaling). The system includes formal use-case specifications, a metric catalogue, a grading protocol using expert judgment and LLM-as-judge, a two-tier threshold gate for decision-making, and a value-and-risk model.
AI.motivation: The authors identify a fundamental measurement problem: frontier language models can produce professional-quality outputs, yet most enterprise GenAI initiatives fail to show measurable business effects and many agentic projects are cancelled. Public benchmarks answer "what can the model do?" but deployment requires "is this workflow fit, reliable, safe and worth scaling here, on our data, under our controls?"
AI.method: The paper presents EnterpriseVal comprising five components: (i) formal specification of use case and socio-technical configuration (model, prompts, retrieval, tools, guardrails, human oversight) with autonomy level and consequence tier; (ii) metric catalogue spanning fidelity, utility, efficiency, reliability, assurance, and oversight; (iii) grading protocol scaling blinded expert judgment with calibrated LLM-as-judge through prediction-powered inference; (iv) two-tier threshold gate (REJECT/CONDITIONAL/SCALE) as executable algorithm; (v) value-and-risk model with measured reviewer catch rate. Pilot testing was conducted across three workflows in a global bank.
AI.result: Pilot results from a global bank: (1) Credit-memo drafting: human-graded citation precision reached 88% and hallucination rate 1.6% for the best model against gates of 70% and 5%; (2) Procedure transformation: analyst refinement effort fell from estimated 27.4 to 2.9 hours per document. The paper separates established results, documented pilot evidence, proposed system, and open hypotheses requiring further validation.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that the enterprise AI evaluation gap is substantially a measurement problem. EnterpriseVal provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating AI at the use-case level rather than relying on public benchmarks. The pilot demonstrates feasibility but full validation requires additional experiments. The paper distinguishes between established results, documented pilot evidence, the proposed system, and open hypotheses.

title: Optimal Randomized Proper Online Learning
summary: We prove that the optimal expected mistake bound of online learning a function class $\mathcal{H}$ by a randomized proper learning algorithm is $O(\mathtt{L}(\mathcal{H}) \log T)$, where $\mathtt{L}(\mathcal{H})$ is the Littlestone dimension of $\mathcal{H}$ and $T$ is the time horizon. Our result improves upon the previously best known bound of $O(\mathtt{L}(\mathcal{H}) \log^6 T)$ given by Daskalakis and Golowich (STOC 2022), and is optimal up to a universal constant for worst-case classes.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that the optimal expected mistake bound for randomized proper online learning of a function class H is O(L(H) log T), improving upon the previous best bound of O(L(H) log^6 T). This result is optimal up to a universal constant for worst-case classes.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to tighten the bound on the optimal expected mistake bound in online learning. The previous best bound had an unnecessary polylogarithmic factor (log^6 T), and the authors sought to prove the optimal bound.
AI.method: The abstract doesn't provide explicit methodological details, but the result involves analyzing the Littlestone dimension L(H) and its relationship to the mistake bound in online learning.
AI.result: The main result is an O(L(H) log T) bound on the optimal expected mistake bound, which improves the previous O(L(H) log^6 T) bound by removing a factor of log^5 T. This is proven to be optimal up to a universal constant for worst-case classes.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion establishes the tight bound for online learning mistake bounds, showing that the dependence on both the Littlestone dimension and log T is optimal.

title: Refine Then Fusion: Training-Free 3D Point Cloud Adaptation with Priority Refinement and Multi-Modal Knowledge Fusion
summary: Recent pre-trained foundation models provide rich multi-modal priors for downstream 3D vision tasks. However, the effectiveness of these representations in few-shot scenarios is limited by two fundamental challenges: High-dimensional features often contain substantial channel redundancy and task-irrelevant noise, while the reliability of different modalities varies across samples. Consequently, direct aggregation of heterogeneous representations overlooks sample-dependent modality reliability and may obscure the discriminative cues essential. To address these limitations, we propose Refine Then Fusion(RTF), a training-free framework for few-shot 3D recognition. RTF first identifies discriminative feature channels by jointly modeling inter-class similarity and intra-class stability, thereby decoupling domain-specific knowledge refinement from the cached representations of pre-trained models. It then introduces a reliability-aware fusion mechanism that estimates sample-wise modality reliability from the distribution shifts induced by feature refinement, enabling adaptive aggregation of multi-modal representations. Furthermore, RTF constructs a memory cache that integrates instance-level support features with class-level prototypes to infer query labels. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate that RTF consistently outperforms single-modal baselines, partial-fusion variants, and existing lightweight adaptation methods, achieving state-of-the-art few-shot 3D recognition performance without gradient optimization, additional training data, auxiliary training, or parameter updates.

AI.tldr: RTF is a training-free framework for few-shot 3D recognition that addresses channel redundancy and modality reliability issues in pre-trained foundation models through discriminative channel identification and reliability-aware fusion.
AI.motivation: Two fundamental challenges in few-shot 3D recognition: 1) High-dimensional features contain channel redundancy and task-irrelevant noise, 2) Modality reliability varies across samples, making direct aggregation of heterogeneous representations suboptimal.
AI.method: RTF has three components: 1) Discriminative channel identification via joint modeling of inter-class similarity and intra-class stability to refine domain-specific knowledge; 2) Reliability-aware fusion that estimates sample-wise modality reliability from distribution shifts; 3) Memory cache integrating instance-level support features with class-level prototypes for query inference.
AI.result: RTF consistently outperforms single-modal baselines, partial-fusion variants, and existing lightweight adaptation methods on five benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art performance without gradient optimization, additional training data, auxiliary training, or parameter updates.
AI.conclusion: The proposed RTF framework effectively addresses channel redundancy and modality reliability challenges in few-shot 3D recognition through training-free adaptation, demonstrating superior performance across multiple benchmarks while requiring no model parameter updates.

title: AutoRecLab: Describe the Experiment, Get the Code!
comment: Accepted at the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys '26), Demo Track. 4 pages, 2 figures
summary: Empirical evaluation is central to recommender-systems (RecSys) research, but turning experimental designs into executable code remains a manual and error-prone task. We present AutoRecLab, a Python-based autonomous RecSys lab that automates RecSys experiments from natural-language prompts. Given a research idea, AutoRecLab derives explicit experiment requirements, builds and validates a prototype, and iteratively expands it into the requested full experiment. The workflow combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for documentation lookup, static type verification, and execution-steered tree search. In our demonstration, AutoRecLab autonomously implements an explicit-to-implicit feedback conversion study. In a baseline comparison across six algorithms and three datasets, 8 of 9 runs succeed at an average cost of approx- imately $1 per run with GPT-5.4-mini.
