title: Understanding LLM Quantization through Activation-Guided Compensation and Orthogonal Residuals
summary: Post-training weight-activation quantization reduces the memory and inference costs of large language models, but aggressive W4A4 quantization remains difficult because activation outliers degrade effective quantization resolution. Although weight optimization, channel-wise scaling, and orthogonal rotation mitigate this problem, the error components they address and their relationship remain unclear. Using an exact decomposition of local weight-activation quantization error into an activation-guided weight compensation term and an orthogonal residual, we bound the residual using persistent channel-wise outlier and regular activation quantities. This decomposition clarifies which error components can be addressed by weight compensation and which require transformation design. We then use the residual bounds to derive practical guidelines for applying randomized Hadamard rotation, sign selection, and channel scaling. In particular, the analysis explains how random signs suppress constructive interference among persistent outlier channels, how sampling multiple sign patterns can improve transformation selection, and how second-moment balancing leads to an $L_2$ scaling rule while a further relaxation recovers SmoothQuant-style $L_\infty$ scaling. We evaluate these guidelines through backpropagation-free configurations across eight Llama and Mistral models, obtaining performance competitive with gradient-trained SpinQuant.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses aggressive W4A4 quantization for LLMs by decomposing quantization error into activation-guided weight compensation and orthogonal residual components. The analysis provides practical guidelines for randomized Hadamard rotation, sign selection, and channel scaling, achieving performance competitive with gradient-trained SpinQuant without backpropagation.
AI.motivation: Post-training weight-activation quantization reduces memory and inference costs, but aggressive W4A4 quantization remains difficult due to activation outliers degrading effective quantization resolution. Prior methods (weight optimization, channel-wise scaling, orthogonal rotation) mitigate this problem but the error components they address and their relationships remain unclear.
AI.method: The paper uses an exact decomposition of local weight-activation quantization error into: (1) an activation-guided weight compensation term, and (2) an orthogonal residual. The residual is bounded using persistent channel-wise outlier and regular activation quantities. This decomposition clarifies which error components can be addressed by weight compensation versus transformation design. Practical guidelines are derived for randomized Hadamard rotation, sign selection, and channel scaling, including: random signs to suppress constructive interference among persistent outlier channels, sampling multiple sign patterns for transformation selection, and second-moment balancing leading to L2 scaling (with relaxation recovering SmoothQuant-style L∞ scaling).
AI.result: Evaluated through backpropagation-free configurations across eight Llama and Mistral models, achieving performance competitive with gradient-trained SpinQuant.
AI.conclusion: The theoretical decomposition provides clear understanding of which error components can be addressed by different techniques. The derived practical guidelines enable effective W4A4 quantization without requiring gradient-based training, making quantization more accessible while maintaining competitive performance.

title: Purification and Regulation: Comorbidity-Aware Multi-Label Few-Shot Learning for Medical Image Classification
summary: Multi-label few-shot learning (MLFSL) remains a significant challenge in medical image analysis (MIA). Current metric-based meta-learning methods face two critical limitations in MIA. First, conventional prototype generation often entangles irrelevant disease information, leading to contaminated prototypes and degraded performance. Second, prior studies typically enforce inter-class separability in embedding space, largely neglecting the inherent correlations among diseases. To overcome these challenges, we propose Prototype Purification and Regulation (PPR), a novel MLFSL framework for MIA. PPR first performs prototype purification by leveraging sample-level comorbidity scores to emphasize disease-specific features, producing purified prototypes that better characterize each disease. Building upon these purified prototypes, PPR further addresses the underexplored problem of inter-class prototype distance in MIA by incorporating disease-level comorbidity statistics to adaptively regulate inter-class similarity, forming a comorbidity-aware embedding space. Overall, PPR sequentially enables the model to capture pure disease features and inter-class relationships for reliable MLFSL in MIA. Extensive experiments across four chest X-ray benchmark datasets, including cross-domain evaluation, show that PPR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, significantly improving disease detection while demonstrating robust generalization and clinical applicability.

AI.tldr: PPR (Prototype Purification and Regulation) is a novel multi-label few-shot learning framework for medical image analysis that addresses two key limitations in existing metric-based meta-learning methods: contaminated prototypes from entangled disease information and neglect of inter-class disease correlations. The method uses sample-level comorbidity scores for prototype purification and disease-level comorbidity statistics for adaptive inter-class similarity regulation.
AI.motivation: Current metric-based meta-learning methods for MLFSL in medical imaging face two critical limitations: (1) conventional prototype generation entangles irrelevant disease information, leading to contaminated prototypes and degraded performance; (2) prior studies enforce inter-class separability while neglecting inherent correlations among diseases (comorbidities).
AI.method: PPR consists of two sequential components: (1) Prototype Purification - leverages sample-level comorbidity scores to emphasize disease-specific features, producing purified prototypes that better characterize each disease; (2) Prototype Regulation - incorporates disease-level comorbidity statistics to adaptively regulate inter-class similarity, forming a comorbidity-aware embedding space.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across four chest X-ray benchmark datasets, including cross-domain evaluation, show that PPR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, significantly improving disease detection while demonstrating robust generalization and clinical applicability.
AI.conclusion: PPR successfully enables models to capture pure disease features and inter-class relationships for reliable MLFSL in medical image analysis, with strong performance and generalization across multiple datasets.

title: What Should We Ask Next? Retrieval-Aware Question Learning under Partial Evidence
summary: Interactive retrieval under partial evidence is a sequential information-acquisition problem: an agent must decide which question will create the most useful evidence for the next retrieval update. Existing systems train this decision by imitating an offline ordering of candidate QA pairs, although question value is determined by the response it elicits and its downstream effect on retrieval. We establish that candidate discriminativeness and perceived usefulness provide weak supervision for this objective, then introduce RAVEL, a retrieval-aware online reinforcement learning framework for interactive person re-identification. RAVEL initializes from supervised question generation, observes the current Top-4 candidates directly, and optimizes the question policy with rank feedback from the full question-answer-retrieval loop. Experiments on Interactive-PEDES show that RAVEL delivers progressively stronger retrieval performance across five interaction rounds. Further analysis shows that RAVEL reallocates the questioning budget toward localized open-ended attributes, which provide more useful retrieval evidence and yield the largest gains on initially difficult queries.

AI.tldr: RAVEL is a retrieval-aware online reinforcement learning framework for interactive person re-identification that optimizes question-asking policy through rank feedback from the full QA-retrieval loop, outperforming imitation learning approaches that rely on weak supervision signals like candidate discriminativeness.
AI.motivation: Existing interactive retrieval systems train question-selection decisions by imitating offline orderings of candidate QA pairs, but this approach fails to capture the downstream effect of questions on retrieval performance since question value depends on the response elicited and its impact on retrieval quality.
AI.method: RAVEL initializes from supervised question generation, directly observes the current Top-4 candidates, and optimizes the question policy using rank feedback from the complete question-answer-retrieval loop through online reinforcement learning.
AI.result: RAVEL delivers progressively stronger retrieval performance across five interaction rounds on the Interactive-PEDES dataset. The method reallocates questioning budget toward localized open-ended attributes, which provide more useful retrieval evidence and yield the largest gains on initially difficult queries.
AI.conclusion: The full question-answer-retrieval loop feedback is crucial for training effective question policies; simply using weak supervision signals like candidate discriminativeness or perceived usefulness is insufficient. RL-based optimization enables the system to learn which questions create the most valuable evidence for retrieval.

title: Efficient Architecture Search under Leave-One-Subject-Out Evaluation
summary: Deep neural architectures are widely used for signal processing in automated pain assessment systems. However, architecture design has remained largely a manual task despite the potential efficiency benefits of Neural Architecture Search (NAS). Embedding NAS in a Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) evaluation is computationally demanding because a fully nested implementation requires $N$ independent architecture searches and, assuming approximately linear training cost, scales as $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$. We propose a block-based, leakage-controlled approach that shares NAS runs between subjects, reducing the number of searches from $N$ to $B$, where $B \ll N$, dubbed PainNAS. On the BioVid Heat Pain dataset, PainNAS yields comparable subject-level accuracy with substantially fewer parameters and FLOPs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes PainNAS, a block-based neural architecture search approach that reduces computational cost from O(N²) to O(B) for leave-one-subject-out evaluation in automated pain assessment systems, while achieving comparable accuracy with fewer parameters and FLOPs on the BioVid Heat Pain dataset.
AI.motivation: Manual design of deep neural architectures for signal processing in automated pain assessment is inefficient. Neural Architecture Search (NAS) offers potential benefits but becomes computationally prohibitive when embedded in Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) evaluation, scaling as O(N²) due to requiring N independent architecture searches.
AI.method: The authors propose a block-based, leakage-controlled approach called PainNAS that shares NAS runs between subjects. This reduces the number of required architecture searches from N to B, where B << N, dramatically reducing computational cost while maintaining evaluation integrity.
AI.result: On the BioVid Heat Pain dataset, PainNAS yields comparable subject-level accuracy while using substantially fewer parameters and FLOPs compared to traditional approaches.
AI.conclusion: PainNAS successfully addresses the computational challenge of NAS in LOSO evaluation for pain assessment, offering an efficient alternative that maintains performance accuracy with reduced model complexity.

title: From Retrieval to Recognition:How Vision--Language Models Become OCR Specialists
summary: Does a general vision--language model acquire specialized OCR ability by developing a new reading circuit or by reusing an existing mechanism? We address this question in the setting of full-sequence OCR, rather than local-answer retrieval. Using an evidence-grounded protocol with held-out causal interventions, we identify sparse and stable OCR-head sets in GLM-OCR, MinerU2.5, and PaddleOCR-VL-1.6. We then investigate the mechanistic origin of these OCR heads by comparing them with independently identified textual retrieval/copy heads in general VLMs. Across two general VLMs, visual OCR heads strongly overlap independently identified textual retrieval/copy heads, yielding untuned top-20 intersections of 73.3% and all-head Spearman correlations of 0.677-0.886. The overlap and causal interventions suggest that full-sequence OCR operates as dense sequential multimodal copy-and-paste, repeatedly retrieving visual evidence and routing it to the current output position. Finally, we examine how this shared circuit changes as a general VLM becomes an OCR specialist. Matched base-to-specialized comparisons show that OCR specialization largely preserves head identity, retaining 17-20 of the top 20 heads per task with all-head rank correlations of 0.874-0.942, while redistributing their functional and causal strengths.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether OCR capability in vision-language models emerges from new neural circuits or by reusing existing mechanisms. Using evidence-grounded protocols with causal interventions, the study finds that OCR heads strongly overlap with textual retrieval/copy heads (73.3% intersection), suggesting OCR operates as dense sequential multimodal copy-and-paste rather than developing novel reading circuits. OCR specialization largely preserves head identity while redistributing functional strength.
AI.motivation: To understand how specialized OCR abilities emerge in general vision-language models - whether they develop new dedicated neural circuits or repurpose existing mechanisms for textual retrieval and copy operations.
AI.method: Evidence-grounded protocol with held-out causal interventions to identify OCR-head sets in GLM-OCR, MinerU2.5, and PaddleOCR-VL-1.6. Compared these OCR heads with independently identified textual retrieval/copy heads in general VLMs. Analyzed overlap and correlations, then performed matched base-to-specialized model comparisons.
AI.result: Visual OCR heads strongly overlap with textual retrieval/copy heads: 73.3% untuned top-20 intersection, with all-head Spearman correlations of 0.677-0.886. OCR specialization preserves 17-20 of top 20 heads per task with all-head rank correlations of 0.874-0.942, while redistributing functional and causal strengths.
AI.conclusion: Full-sequence OCR operates as dense sequential multimodal copy-and-paste, repeatedly retrieving visual evidence and routing it to output positions. This is achieved by reusing existing textual retrieval/copy mechanisms rather than developing new reading circuits. OCR specialization primarily involves redistributing functional strength while largely preserving head identity.

title: AutoViewMem: Self-Configuring Orthogonal Views for Conversational Long-Term Memory
summary: Long-term memory is essential for large language model (LLM) agents to maintain consistency and personalization over extended interactions. Existing memory systems typically rely on fixed granularities or static schemas, but these designs struggle when heterogeneous information, such as preferences, events, constraints, and temporal updates, is embedded in a single mixed representation. The resulting semantic interference makes top-K retrieval sensitive to noise and often leaves relevant evidence poorly ranked. We present AutoViewMem, a data-driven framework that organizes long-term conversational memory into self-configuring, low-overlap semantic views before indexing. AutoViewMem discovers candidate views from interaction traces, selects a compact complementary view set, and uses these views to guide write-time structured extraction of provenance-grounded memories. This representation-first design moves semantic disentanglement from retrieval time to write time, allowing standard top-K similarity search to retrieve focused evidence without explicit routing or iterative retrieval. We further apply offline consolidation to improve memory compactness and consistency. Experiments on the LoCoMo and PersonaMem benchmarks, under both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B backbones, show that AutoViewMem improves long-horizon question answering and personalization over strong memory baselines while preserving a simple inference pipeline.

AI.tldr: AutoViewMem is a data-driven framework that organizes long-term conversational memory into self-configuring, low-overlap semantic views before indexing, improving retrieval quality by moving semantic disentanglement from retrieval time to write time.
AI.motivation: Existing memory systems for LLM agents rely on fixed granularities or static schemas, which struggle when heterogeneous information (preferences, events, constraints, temporal updates) is embedded in a single mixed representation. This causes semantic interference, making top-K retrieval sensitive to noise and leaving relevant evidence poorly ranked.
AI.method: AutoViewMem operates in three phases: (1) Discover candidate views from interaction traces; (2) Select a compact complementary view set; (3) Use these views to guide write-time structured extraction of provenance-grounded memories. This representation-first design moves semantic disentanglement from retrieval time to write time, allowing standard top-K similarity search to retrieve focused evidence without explicit routing or iterative retrieval. Offline consolidation is applied to improve memory compactness and consistency.
AI.result: Experiments on LoCoMo and PersonaMem benchmarks under Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B backbones show that AutoViewMem improves long-horizon question answering and personalization over strong memory baselines while preserving a simple inference pipeline.
AI.conclusion: AutoViewMem successfully addresses the challenge of heterogeneous information in long-term memory by using self-configuring semantic views, achieving superior retrieval quality and personalization performance without requiring complex inference-time routing mechanisms.

title: What Must Survive? Exact Task-Information--State Frontiers for Resource-Sufficient Learning
summary:
A system may be compressed before its downstream task is fully known. We ask how much retained state is then necessary and how much can be saved by limited advance task information.
  For a finite family of linear tasks, a task message is revealed before state formation and the exact task only afterwards. For an advice alphabet of size $K$, the exact frontier is \[ p^*(K)= \min_{\substack{\Pcal\text{ partition of }\U\\|\Pcal|\le K}} \max_{C\in\Pcal}\rank(T_C), \] with the $b$-bit frontier obtained by setting $K=\min(2^b,|\U|)$. Thus advance task information reduces state through partitions whose joint task operators have low rank.
  We also give an approximate singular-value frontier, a common-core lower bound and exact direct-sum law, and strong NP-hardness of finding an optimal advice partition. The hardness persists at every fixed positive approximation tolerance.
  Three examples illustrate the result. A well-conditioned softmax attention construction gives an exact $524{,}288\to1{,}024$ coordinate frontier when nine bits resolve one of $512$ continuations. A domain-decomposed digital twin yields an interface-plus-local-state law and a weighted partition problem for heterogeneous regions.
  A hierarchical multi-task model gives a two-stage frontier in which three bits reduce the required state from $3136$ to $448$ coordinates, with further task information approaching the irreducible $328$-coordinate single-task floor.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the fundamental question of how much state information must be retained when compressing a system before its downstream task is fully known. The authors derive an exact frontier formula for the minimum state size needed given an advice alphabet of size K, showing that advance task information reduces state through partitions with low-rank joint task operators. The work also establishes NP-hardness results and provides three practical examples including softmax attention, digital twins, and hierarchical multi-task models.
AI.motivation: The core motivation is understanding the tradeoff between compression and task knowledge: when a system must be compressed before the exact downstream task is known, how much retained state is necessary? Can limited advance task information help reduce state requirements? This addresses fundamental limits of compression in scenarios where task information is revealed incrementally.
AI.method: The authors use a mathematical framework involving: (1) Finite families of linear tasks with task operators; (2) Partition-based state formation where an advice alphabet of size K allows partitioning the task space; (3) Rank analysis of joint task operators T_C for each partition block; (4) The frontier is defined as p^*(K) = min over partitions P (with |P| ≤ K) of max over C∈P of rank(T_C). Additional techniques include singular-value approximations, direct-sum analysis, and hardness reduction proofs.
AI.result: The exact frontier formula is established: p^*(K) = min_{P: partition of U, |P|≤K} max_{C∈P} rank(T_C), with the b-bit frontier obtained by setting K = min(2^b, |U|). Key findings include: (1) NP-hardness of finding optimal advice partitions (hard even with any positive approximation tolerance); (2) A common-core lower bound; (3) An exact direct-sum law. Three examples demonstrate practical utility: (a) Softmax attention: 524,288→1,024 coordinates with 9 bits for 512 continuations; (b) Digital twin: interface-plus-local-state law; (c) Hierarchical model: 3 bits reduce state from 3,136 to 448, approaching 328-coordinate floor.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a complete theoretical framework for understanding state compression with partial task information. The frontier formula precisely characterizes the minimum state requirement given K advice symbols. The NP-hardness result shows the optimization problem is computationally intractable in general, though the three examples demonstrate practical relevance in attention mechanisms, digital twins, and multi-task learning. The framework bridges information theory, linear algebra, and computational complexity in a novel way.

title: Learning Cardiac Features: ECG Biometrics Across Time and~Exercise
summary: Electrocardiograms (ECGs) carry subject-specific patterns enabling reliable individual discrimination, forming the basis of ECG biometrics. Beyond authentication, this paradigm holds significant potential to secure sensitive cardiac data and to serve as a pretext task in self-supervised learning. Yet, most studies remain confined to singlesession, resting data, leaving robustness to temporal and physiological variations largely untested. We address this gap by evaluating ECG biometrics under realistic conditions involving exercise-induced stress and cross-session variability. A Siamese ResNet with late multi-lead fusion strategy is trained on a large ECG dataset extracted from cardiopulmonary exercise tests and evaluated with a exercise-and time-aware protocol, as well as on public benchmarks. This first extensive assessment of ECG biometrics under combined physiological and temporal variability achieves an intra-session rest-to-peak EER of 1.7% and stateof-the-art 3.9% on the CYBHi dataset. Findings support the presence of an intrinsic cardiac signature resilient to physiological and temporal drift.
