title: IncentRL: The Trade-Off Between Preference Guidance and Task Performance
summary: Preference-based reward shaping can guide reinforcement learning, but adding preference signals to the reward may unintentionally change the task being optimized. We address this problem with IncentRL, a framework that introduces preference guidance while explicitly characterizing its effect on external-task performance. IncentRL adds a Kullback--Leibler (KL) penalty between a specified outcome distribution and a preferred distribution. For finite discounted Markov decision processes with bounded shaping costs, we derive an external-value perturbation bound, establish a sufficient strict-action-gap condition for preserving the original optimal policy, and characterize the large-weight regime through discounted cumulative preference cost. Exact examples clarify the limits of these guarantees, including tied optima and support mismatch. We study a practical implementation using a hand-designed, distance-based outcome proxy, a fixed preference distribution, and score-weighted coefficient search. On MiniGrid DoorKey-8x8, the reported three-seed mean success rate after two million training steps reaches 98\% with coefficient 0.01, compared with 90.5\% for the reported zero-coefficient baseline, while the search progressively shifts toward smaller coefficients. Together, these results provide a principled view of the central trade-off in preference-based RL: using additional guidance to improve learning without excessively distorting the original task objective. The current experiments remain descriptive and do not yet isolate KL shaping from simpler alternatives.

AI.tldr: IncentRL is a framework that adds preference guidance to reinforcement learning while explicitly characterizing its effect on the original task performance. It uses a KL divergence penalty between specified outcome and preferred distributions to shape rewards without excessively distorting the original task objective.
AI.motivation: Preference-based reward shaping can guide RL learning, but adding preference signals to rewards may unintentionally change the task being optimized. The authors want to address this fundamental trade-off: using additional guidance to improve learning without excessively distorting the original task objective.
AI.method: IncentRL introduces a KL penalty between a specified outcome distribution and a preferred distribution. The method includes: (1) deriving an external-value perturbation bound for finite discounted MDPs with bounded shaping costs, (2) establishing a sufficient strict-action-gap condition for preserving the original optimal policy, and (3) characterizing the large-weight regime through discounted cumulative preference cost. Practical implementation uses a hand-designed, distance-based outcome proxy, fixed preference distribution, and score-weighted coefficient search.
AI.result: On MiniGrid DoorKey-8x8, the three-seed mean success rate reaches 98% with coefficient 0.01 after 2 million training steps, compared with 90.5% for the zero-coefficient baseline. The search progressively shifts toward smaller coefficients. The paper provides theoretical guarantees including external-value perturbation bounds and conditions for preserving optimal policies.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a principled view of the central trade-off in preference-based RL: using additional guidance to improve learning without excessively distorting the original task objective. The authors note limitations including: exact examples clarifying limits of guarantees (tied optima, support mismatch), and that current experiments remain descriptive and do not yet isolate KL shaping from simpler alternatives.

title: A benchmark dataset and baseline methods for four-dimensional STEM diffraction patterns
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures. Data and trained model weights: https://doi.org/10.57760/sciencedb.nbsdc.00281. Code: https://github.com/Gaiya69-rgb/4D-ImageNet
summary: Four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) records a two-dimensional diffraction pattern at each electron-probe position, yielding spatially resolved reciprocal-space information but large, heterogeneous data volumes. Here we describe 4D-ImageNet, a collection of 174,000 diffraction patterns comprising 145,000 experimental patterns selected from 29 acquisitions and 29,000 multislice simulations. The experimental data cover acquisition-level labels for Ag, Au, mixed Au-Ag, CoO, Pd and ZnO specimens across multiple fields of view, scan dimensions, camera lengths and exposure times. Each acquisition contributes 5,000 quality-ranked patterns with source scan coordinates and acquisition metadata. A set-prediction detector provides model-derived pseudo-labels for the direct-beam position and Bragg-disk centres, with a confidence score for each disk. The simulation data cover 13 crystal structures and include Euler rotations, reciprocal-space sampling and approximate low-index beam directions. A grouped mixed-domain masked-reconstruction benchmark is provided to assess leakage-resistant loading and evaluation across experimental and simulated data. The dataset is intended for representation learning, disk detection, diffraction-pattern retrieval, orientation analysis and simulation-to-experiment studies.

AI.tldr: 4D-ImageNet is a large-scale dataset of 174,000 diffraction patterns (145,000 experimental + 29,000 simulated) from 4D-STEM experiments, designed for training and benchmarking machine learning models in electron microscopy analysis.
AI.motivation: 4D-STEM generates large, heterogeneous data volumes with spatially resolved reciprocal-space information, but there lacks a comprehensive, labeled dataset for developing and evaluating computational methods for diffraction pattern analysis.
AI.method: The dataset comprises experimental patterns from 29 acquisitions across multiple materials (Ag, Au, Au-Ag, CoO, Pd, ZnO) with varying acquisition parameters, plus multislice simulations for 13 crystal structures. A set-prediction detector provides pseudo-labels for beam positions and Bragg-disk centers with confidence scores. A grouped mixed-domain masked-reconstruction benchmark is included for leakage-resistant evaluation.
AI.result: The dataset provides 5,000 quality-ranked patterns per acquisition with source coordinates, acquisition metadata, and model-derived pseudo-labels. It covers diverse experimental conditions and crystal structures with known orientation parameters.
AI.conclusion: 4D-ImageNet serves as a foundational resource for developing and benchmarking methods in representation learning, disk detection, diffraction-pattern retrieval, orientation analysis, and simulation-to-experiment transfer learning for 4D-STEM analysis.

title: A Lie Detector Test for Language Models: Reading Knowledge a Model Won't Reveal
summary: Large language models can hold knowledge they do not report. A model may sandbag on a capability evaluation, or answer against what it internally knows, and its outputs alone cannot tell whether it is hiding an answer or simply does not have one. We borrow the Concealed Information Test, a forensic method that identifies guilty knowledge by presenting a suspect with the true detail among plausible decoys and measuring a stronger response to the item they recognize. Our method, Probe of Internal Recognition (PIR), does the same inside a model. It presents a question with its candidate answers and reads, from the model's internal states, which candidate the model recognizes as correct. PIR is reference-free, needing no honest reference model and no labeled truth corpus. Across eight models from five families (Gemma, Qwen, Llama, Mistral, and Phi), PIR recovers the recognized answer at 0.70 to 0.87 balanced accuracy, well above the 0.28 to 0.40 unknown-item baseline and the 0.25 chance rate. It stays readable across every form of concealment we test, from prompted deception and trained sandbagging to external password-locked and circuit-broken checkpoints, with recognition between 0.85 and 0.93. When the model hides a known answer, recognition stays high. When unlearning removes the knowledge, recognition drops to the level of a question the model never knew. PIR therefore separates a model that will not answer from one that cannot, which supports sandbagging audits and unlearning verification. The signal is causal, adds information beyond black-box behavioral cues, and extends from multiple-choice questions to free-form generation.

AI.tldr: PIR is a reference-free method that detects whether a language model internally recognizes the correct answer to a question by probing its internal states, distinguishing between models that withhold knowledge (sandbagging) versus those that lack knowledge entirely.
AI.motivation: Large language models can hold knowledge they do not report—they may sandbag on evaluations or answer against their internal knowledge. Existing outputs cannot distinguish whether a model is hiding an answer or simply doesn't have one, creating a critical gap for safety auditing and knowledge verification.
AI.method: The method adapts the forensic Concealed Information Test to model internals. PIR presents a question with candidate answers and reads the model's internal activations to detect which candidate the model recognizes as correct—no honest reference model or labeled truth corpus required. The approach uses internal state probing to identify recognition patterns.
AI.result: Across eight models from five families (Gemma, Qwen, Llama, Mistral, Phi), PIR achieves 0.70–0.87 balanced accuracy, significantly above the 0.28–0.40 unknown-item baseline and 0.25 chance rate. It maintains 0.85–0.93 recognition across all concealment methods tested (prompted deception, trained sandbagging, password-locked checkpoints, circuit-broken checkpoints). When models hide known answers, recognition remains high; when unlearning removes knowledge, recognition drops to baseline levels.
AI.conclusion: PIR successfully separates models that will not answer from those that cannot, enabling sandbagging audits and unlearning verification. The signal is causal, provides information beyond black-box behavioral cues, and generalizes from multiple-choice questions to free-form generation, offering a powerful tool for AI safety and transparency.

title: OpenMAS-GCom. A Diagnostic Benchmark for Graph-enhanced Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Graph-enhanced multi-agent systems (G-MAS) coordinate large language model agents through communication graphs and role assignments, which determine how agents exchange information and divide responsibilities. However, final-score comparisons across systems combine differences in models, communication patterns, roles, and computation costs, making performance differences difficult to attribute to specific communication structures, role assignments, and information flows. To address this evaluation attribution problem, we introduce OpenMAS-GCom, a benchmark for diagnosing how these components affect G-MAS performance through controlled interventions. We represent systems through collaboration units, communication links, shared intermediate information, and execution rules. OpenMAS-GCom compares original systems with versions modified by changing one component while keeping tasks, models, prompts, and budget limits fixed. We rewire communication edges, remove specialist or critic agents, replace intermediate messages with incorrect content, and disable workers during execution. The benchmark evaluates 17 single-agent, ordinary multi-agent, and graph-enhanced configurations on 29 datasets across six domains. We add 400 G-MAS-Complex tasks requiring agents to combine information from multiple documents, resolve conflicting records, and return specified values with source identifiers. Experiments show larger mean losses after specialist removal than after critic removal, different performance degradation under incorrect messages and worker failures despite similar original scores, and different configurations achieving the highest accuracy and accuracy per token on G-MAS-Complex.

AI.tldr: OpenMAS-GCom is a benchmark designed to diagnose how specific components (communication structures, role assignments, information flows) affect Graph-enhanced Multi-Agent Systems (G-MAS) performance by comparing original systems with controlled modifications.
AI.motivation: Current G-MAS evaluation combines differences in models, communication patterns, roles, and computation costs, making it difficult to attribute performance differences to specific components. There was a need for controlled interventions to isolate the effect of each component.
AI.method: The benchmark represents systems through four elements: collaboration units, communication links, shared intermediate information, and execution rules. It compares original systems with versions modified by: rewiring communication edges, removing specialist/critic agents, replacing intermediate messages with incorrect content, and disabling workers during execution. Evaluates 17 configurations on 29 datasets across 6 domains, plus 400 G-MAS-Complex tasks requiring multi-document information synthesis.
AI.result: Larger mean performance losses after specialist removal than critic removal; different performance degradation patterns under incorrect messages vs worker failures despite similar original scores; different configurations achieve highest accuracy vs highest accuracy per token on G-MAS-Complex tasks.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark enables attribution of G-MAS performance differences to specific components, revealing that specialist roles, message correctness, and worker availability have distinct impacts on system performance, and that optimal configurations differ depending on whether accuracy or efficiency (accuracy per token) is the primary metric.

title: HAT: Hypothesis-Anchored Tracking for Video Monocular Spacecraft Pose Estimation
summary: Monocular 6-DoF pose estimation of non-cooperative targets is important for on-orbit servicing and debris removal. A single-image estimator can confuse near-symmetric spacecraft orientations, and tracking can preserve an incorrect pose. We present Hypothesis-Anchored Tracking (HAT), a causal framework that uses inter-frame motion to select among competing CAD-based pose hypotheses before alignment and fusion. Rather than independently choosing the highest-scoring hypothesis in each image, HAT retains competing orientation histories and selects a pose to anchor the relative trajectory estimated by monocular SLAM. Sparse anchors and pose fusion provide per-frame estimates after initialization without revising past outputs. The method requires only a calibrated RGB sequence, a metric CAD model, and target image regions, which can be supplied by detection or segmentation. The pretrained pose and SLAM networks require no target-specific training or fine-tuning. We evaluate two versions, Mega-HAT and Pico-HAT, using MegaPose and PicoPose, on SPARK-2024, SwissCube and SHIRT, with YCB-Video assessing performance outside the space domain. Using one temporal configuration per method, the arithmetic means of the four dataset-wise comparisons show 9.4% lower mean pose error and 3.76 times the sustained input FPS for Mega-HAT relative to independent MegaPose, and 23.9% lower mean pose error and 2.42 times the FPS for Pico-HAT relative to independent PicoPose. Mega-HAT ablations on SPARK and an offline reference examine component contributions and the effect of revising past estimates.

AI.tldr: HAT (Hypothesis-Anchored Tracking) is a causal framework for monocular 6-DoF pose estimation of non-cooperative space targets. It uses inter-frame motion to select among competing CAD-based pose hypotheses and anchors relative trajectories from monocular SLAM, providing per-frame estimates without revising past outputs.
AI.motivation: Single-image pose estimators can confuse near-symmetric spacecraft orientations, and tracking can preserve incorrect poses. This is critical for on-orbit servicing and debris removal applications.
AI.method: HAT retains competing orientation histories and selects poses to anchor relative trajectories estimated by monocular SLAM. Sparse anchors and pose fusion provide per-frame estimates. Requires only calibrated RGB sequence, metric CAD model, and target image regions from detection/segmentation. Pretrained pose and SLAM networks require no target-specific training.
AI.result: Mega-HAT: 9.4% lower mean pose error and 3.76x sustained FPS vs independent MegaPose. Pico-HAT: 23.9% lower mean pose error and 2.42x FPS vs independent PicoPose. Evaluated on SPARK-2024, SwissCube, SHIRT, and YCB-Video datasets.
AI.conclusion: HAT successfully addresses pose ambiguity in near-symmetric spacecraft orientations through hypothesis tracking and SLAM-based trajectory anchoring. The method achieves significant improvements in pose accuracy and inference speed without requiring target-specific training or fine-tuning.

title: CodeMidas: Scaling Agentic Coding RL Environments from Code Itself
summary: Training capable coding agents via reinforcement learning (RL) requires diverse tasks with reliable verifiers. Open-source codebases offer a rich source of such tasks, while existing methods typically rely on development artifacts such as issues and commits, limiting the range of tasks that can be extracted. To better scale RL environments, we present CodeMidas, an agentic pipeline that turns implemented functionality in existing codebases into executable RL environments using source code as its only task-specific input. CodeMidas allocates agentic compute to every stage of environment construction: agents explore implemented functionality to formulate behavioral specifications, construct tests grounded in execution of the original code, and validate and filter candidate tasks through execution checks and repeated solution rollouts. The resulting dataset has 5,545 training tasks from 3,185 open-source codebases spanning 23 programming languages and 15 technical domains. Training MiMo-V2.5 on these tasks with GRPO improves performance on all five diverse benchmarks, covering issue repair (DeepSWE + 11.7%), whole-program construction (ProgramBench +17%), and terminal work (Terminal-Bench v2.1 +8.5%). Ablations show that increasing the number of high-quality training tasks improves performance. Trajectory analysis shows the RL-trained agent demonstrates better behaviors like increasing codebase exploration and more diverse self-verification. These results establish source code as a scalable foundation for constructing RL environments that improve coding agents across diverse software tasks.

AI.tldr: CodeMidas is an agentic pipeline that automatically constructs RL training environments from source code, generating 5,545 tasks across 23 languages. Training with GRPO improves coding agent performance on issue repair (+11.7%), program construction (+17%), and terminal work (+8.5%).
AI.motivation: Existing RL training for coding agents relies on development artifacts (issues, commits), which limits the diversity and scalability of training tasks. The authors aim to use source code as the sole input to create diverse, executable RL environments at scale.
AI.method: CodeMidas uses agents to: (1) explore implemented functionality to formulate behavioral specifications, (2) construct tests grounded in original code execution, (3) validate/filter tasks through execution checks and repeated solution rollouts. The resulting dataset trains MiMo-V2.5 using GRPO.
AI.result: 5,545 training tasks from 3,185 open-source codebases across 23 languages and 15 domains. GRPO training improves DeepSWE (+11.7%), ProgramBench (+17%), and Terminal-Bench v2.1 (+8.5%). Ablations show more high-quality tasks improve performance. Trajectory analysis shows better exploration and self-verification behaviors.
AI.conclusion: Source code alone can serve as a scalable foundation for constructing RL environments that improve coding agents across diverse software tasks, demonstrating the potential for significant expansion of RL training data from existing codebases.

title: MACE: Memory-Agent Co-Evolution with Adaptive Memory Graphs for Multi-Agent Systems
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems generate collaboration traces that record how agents plan tasks, verify intermediate results, and repair failures. Reusing these procedures requires preserving an action's prerequisites and the outputs needed by subsequent agents. Our empirical studies show that grouping these dependencies into functional memory units improves their retention, while connecting units increases retrieval of the units and links jointly required by a task. The preferred combination of units also changes between instructions and checklists, even when each combination's content is fixed across formats. Updating choices from the outcomes of each combination and format pairing outperforms scoring combinations and formats separately. These findings motivate MACE, a memory-agent co-evolution framework that adapts memory organization and agent memory use through execution feedback. Its MemGoG structure represents functional units as subgraphs of related conditions, actions, and outputs, connecting them through support, conflict, and repair relations. MACE Loop selects task-relevant units and relations within a memory budget and provides each agent with instructions or checklists for its current operation. It records the selected units, presentation formats, agent outputs, and task outcomes to update unit scores and relations for retrieval and inform subsequent presentation choices. Across eight benchmarks, MACE outperforms ten baselines with an average score of 81.11%, compared with 78.97% for the strongest baseline, SAGE.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MACE, a memory-agent co-evolution framework for LLM-based multi-agent systems that organizes collaboration traces into functional memory units (MemGoG) connected through support, conflict, and repair relations. It outperforms 10 baselines across 8 benchmarks, achieving 81.11% vs SAGE's 78.97%.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems generate collaboration traces that record agent planning, verification, and failure repair. Reusing these procedures requires preserving action prerequisites and outputs needed by subsequent agents. Current approaches struggle with organizing these dependencies effectively for retrieval and reuse.
AI.method: The paper proposes (1) MemGoG structure representing functional units as subgraphs of conditions, actions, and outputs connected via support/conflict/repair relations; (2) MACE Loop that selects task-relevant units within memory budget and provides agents with instructions or checklists; (3) Outcome-based updating that combines unit scores and presentation format choices based on task outcomes.
AI.result: Empirical studies show: (1) Grouping dependencies into functional memory units improves retention; (2) Connecting units increases joint retrieval; (3) Preferred unit combinations differ between instructions and checklists; (4) Outcome-based updating outperforms separate scoring. Across 8 benchmarks, MACE achieves 81.11% vs SAGE's 78.97%.
AI.conclusion: The memory-agent co-evolution framework MACE effectively addresses the challenge of organizing and retrieving collaboration traces in multi-agent systems by using functional memory units with relational connections and outcome-based adaptation, significantly outperforming existing baselines.

title: Learned Parametric Emotion Editing: Real-Time Affective Filtering for On-Device Social Media Video
summary: Problematic internet use affects a growing share of the population, yet common interventions, e.g., time limits, blocking, forced breaks, are coercive and easily circumvented. We explore a less restrictive alternative: adapting the emotional intensity of visual content. Prior work has shown that optimization can steer an image's affective content, but its per-image optimization cost makes it impractical for real-time deployment. We instead learn a model that predicts this transformation in a single forward pass: a MobileNetV4 backbone with FiLM-based emotion conditioning outputs parameters for differentiable global transformations. This replaces prior iterative optimization (80 s per image) with a single 3.7 ms forward pass. In a user study (N = 54), the model reduced viewer-reported arousal relative to unedited images, comparably to the grayscale well-being filter, while being rated higher in perceived quality. We integrate the model into an Android app that adapts Instagram video in real time, sustaining 60 fps on a Samsung Galaxy S23.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a real-time emotion conditioning model that adapts visual content's emotional intensity to reduce problematic internet use. The model uses a MobileNetV4 backbone with FiLM-based emotion conditioning, achieving a single 3.7 ms forward pass (vs. 80s per image in prior work). In a user study (N=54), it reduced arousal comparably to grayscale filters while maintaining higher perceived quality. The system runs at 60 fps on a Samsung Galaxy S23.
AI.motivation: Problematic internet use is a growing concern, but existing interventions (time limits, blocking, forced breaks) are coercive and easily circumvented. The authors explore a less restrictive alternative by adapting the emotional intensity of visual content to reduce its arousal potential.
AI.method: The approach uses a MobileNetV4 backbone with FiLM (Feature-wise Linear Modulation)-based emotion conditioning that outputs parameters for differentiable global transformations. This learned model predicts the transformation in a single forward pass, replacing prior per-image optimization approaches.
AI.result: The model reduced viewer-reported arousal relative to unedited images, performing comparably to the grayscale well-being filter while being rated higher in perceived quality. The model achieves 3.7 ms inference time (vs. 80s for prior iterative optimization) and sustains 60 fps in an Android app on Samsung Galaxy S23.
AI.conclusion: The proposed FiLM-based emotion conditioning model offers a practical, real-time solution for reducing emotional arousal in visual content. It provides a less restrictive alternative to conventional internet well-being filters, maintaining higher quality while effectively reducing viewer arousal.

title: Designer-RSI: Evolving Procedural Memory from User Traffic for Agentic Graphic Design
summary: Professional graphic design is a long-horizon agentic task in which structured, editable artifacts emerge from many interdependent actions, yet outcomes admit no reliable programmatic oracle. We introduce a continual adaptation framework in which a frozen frontier model operates professional design software through more than 230 tools, while an external procedural memory of natural-language skills accumulates and refines reusable design procedures from experience. The memory widens by acquiring procedures for recurring uncovered subtasks and deepens by revising existing procedures against their own successful and failed executions, while a matched replay gate admits only changes that repair failures without regressing observed successes. Five rounds over 1,406 real user briefs and 1,869 automatically graded trajectories, with no weight updates and no human labels, grow the bank from 76 documentation-derived skills to 139 and raise GenEval2 execution success on Claude-Sonnet-4 from 72.7% to 99.3% (+11.99 points in generation quality), with 61.8% and 67.6% win rates against the no-skill agent across four specialized design benchmarks on Claude-Sonnet-4 and Claude-Opus-4.6. We further show the two mechanisms are effective in combination: on 200 held-out briefs from user-traffic benchmark, widening or deepening alone reaches a 49.4% / 48.6% win rate over the no-skill agent, while their combination reaches 58.5% (p = 0.025). Procedural memory offers a practical route to continual adaptation of agents under noisy, unverifiable feedback.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a continual adaptation framework for professional graphic design agents using a frozen frontier model with 230+ tools and an external procedural memory system that accumulates and refines reusable design procedures through widening and deepening mechanisms, achieving significant performance improvements without weight updates or human labels.
AI.motivation: Professional graphic design is a long-horizon agentic task where outcomes cannot be reliably verified programmatically, making it challenging to improve agent performance through traditional feedback mechanisms. The authors aim to enable continual adaptation of agents under noisy, unverifiable feedback.
AI.method: The framework uses: (1) a frozen frontier model operating professional design software through 230+ tools; (2) an external procedural memory of natural-language skills with two mechanisms - widening (acquiring procedures for recurring uncovered subtasks) and deepening (revising existing procedures against successful/failed executions); (3) a matched replay gate that admits only changes repairing failures without regressing observed successes. Five rounds of adaptation over 1,406 real user briefs and 1,869 automatically graded trajectories.
AI.result: The bank grew from 76 documentation-derived skills to 139. GenEval2 execution success on Claude-Sonnet-4 improved from 72.7% to 99.3% (+11.99 points in generation quality). Win rates of 61.8% and 67.6% against no-skill agent across four specialized design benchmarks. On 200 held-out briefs, widening alone achieved 49.4%, deepening alone 48.6%, and combination achieved 58.5% win rate (p=0.025).
AI.conclusion: Procedural memory offers a practical route to continual adaptation of agents under noisy, unverifiable feedback, achieving significant performance gains through skill accumulation and refinement without requiring weight updates or human labels.

title: OneBid: A Unified Auto-Bidding Foundation Model for Diverse oCPX Advertising Scenarios
summary: Auto-bidding is central to computational advertising, where strategies must maximize advertisers' conversion value under economic constraints. It has evolved from rule-based controllers to reinforcement learning and generative methods such as Decision Transformer (DT). Yet these methods increasingly mismatch the prevailing optimized cost-per-X (oCPX) paradigm, which spans heterogeneous scenarios (e.g., registration, purchase), each served by a separate model, leading to fragmented pipelines and underexploring cross-scenario modeling. Inspired by foundation models like LLMs, unifying these oCPX scenarios into one model raises three challenges: multi-objective control, scalable capacity under strict latency, and safe offline policy improvement. We present OneBid, a unified auto-bidding foundation model that learns a reusable backbone from heterogeneous oCPX logs and adapts it to scenario-specific deployments via offline post-training. Building on DT, OneBid extends single Return-to-Go conditioning to two atomic signals, Return-to-Go for conversion value and Cost-to-Go for cost ratio, plus value-aware regularization on next-action prediction. To absorb distributional heterogeneity, we design a sequence-level Mixture-of-Experts architecture, where shared experts encode cross-scenario knowledge and sparsely-routed experts capture scenario-specific patterns at low latency, yielding consistent scaling with model size and data. During post-training, we align the backbone with scenario preferences via Critic-guided Relative Offline Policy optimization (CROP): a learned critic scores candidate actions group-relatively, avoiding the unsafe online exploration of GRPO-style fine-tuning while constraining policy shift to reduce OOD risk. Validated via online A/B tests and fully deployed at Kuaishou, OneBid delivers an overall +2.2% ADVV gain on oCPX Ads, peaking at +13.1% in the ROAS scenario.

AI.tldr: OneBid is a unified auto-bidding foundation model that addresses the fragmentation of heterogeneous oCPX (optimized cost-per-X) scenarios in computational advertising by learning a reusable backbone from cross-scenario data and adapting it via offline post-training, achieving +2.2% ADVV gain in online A/B tests at Kuaishou.
AI.motivation: The prevailing oCPX paradigm in computational advertising spans heterogeneous scenarios (registration, purchase, etc.), each served by separate models, leading to fragmented pipelines and underexploring cross-scenario modeling. Existing methods (rule-based controllers, RL, Decision Transformer) mismatch this paradigm. The goal is to create a unified foundation model inspired by LLMs that can handle multiple objectives, scale under latency constraints, and safely improve offline.
AI.method: OneBid extends Decision Transformer with: (1) Dual atomic conditioning signals - Return-to-Go for conversion value and Cost-to-Go for cost ratio, plus value-aware regularization on next-action prediction; (2) Sequence-level Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture with shared experts for cross-scenario knowledge and sparsely-routed experts for scenario-specific patterns at low latency; (3) Critic-guided Relative Offline Policy optimization (CROP) for offline post-training that aligns backbone with scenario preferences using group-relative action scoring, avoiding unsafe online exploration while constraining policy shift to reduce OOD risk.
AI.result: Validated via online A/B tests and fully deployed at Kuaishou, OneBid delivers an overall +2.2% ADVV gain on oCPX Ads, peaking at +13.1% in the ROAS scenario. The MoE architecture achieves consistent scaling with model size and data.
AI.conclusion: OneBid successfully unifies heterogeneous oCPX scenarios into one foundation model, demonstrating that cross-scenario modeling can outperform fragmented scenario-specific approaches. The combination of dual conditioning, MoE architecture, and CROP post-training enables safe offline policy improvement with strict latency constraints, achieving significant business impact at scale.

title: Detection is solved, delineation is not: what governs tooth segmentation on panoramic radiographs
summary:
Automatic tooth segmentation and FDI numbering on panoramic radiographs underpins computer-assisted dental diagnosis, yet which factors govern performance remains unclear. We assemble a corpus of 1,422 panoramic radiographs containing 42,142 expert-delineated tooth polygons across the 32-class FDI taxonomy, annotated by 30 dental practitioners and independently reviewed by two others, and use it to isolate input resolution, architecture and anatomical priors under a single evaluation protocol.
  First, resolution dominates: across a controlled 640/1024/1280 ablation, mask mAP50-95 rises 0.656 -> 0.710 -> 0.717 while mAP50 stays flat at ~0.982. Both gains are significant under a paired bootstrap over images (p < 0.001, p = 0.024); neither mAP50 change is distinguishable from zero. Added resolution buys boundary precision, not detection. Second, architecture is nearly irrelevant in-domain: a query-based transformer with 2.1x the parameters is statistically equivalent to a one-stage detector (95% CI [-0.0064, +0.0064]), only marginally better under domain shift, 5.5x slower on CPU and not executable under standard ONNX runtimes. Third, three targeted interventions fail: a LoRA-adapted self-supervised encoder underperforms, a promptable foundation segmenter degrades masks by 39%, and globally optimal anatomical label assignment yields +0.0007 despite correcting a constraint violated in 40% of out-of-domain predictions.
  Zero-shot transfer to an independent multi-centre cohort, verified overlap-free, costs 62% of mask mAP50-95 but only 18% of mAP50, reproducing the dissociation. Decomposing masks along the tooth axis localises the residual error to the apical third. Boundary precision is therefore the binding constraint, and effort is better directed at resolution and acquisition diversity than at architectural novelty.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates factors affecting automatic tooth segmentation and FDI numbering on panoramic radiographs using a dataset of 1,422 images with 42,142 tooth annotations. The study finds that input resolution is the dominant factor affecting performance (especially boundary precision), while architecture choice has minimal impact in-domain. Three targeted interventions (LoRA-adapted encoder, promptable foundation segmenter, anatomical label assignment) all failed to improve performance. Zero-shot transfer to an independent cohort shows that boundary precision remains the primary constraint.
AI.motivation: To identify which factors (resolution, architecture, anatomical priors) govern performance in automatic tooth segmentation and FDI numbering on panoramic radiographs, as thisunderpins computer-assisted dental diagnosis.
AI.method: The authors assembled a corpus of 1,422 panoramic radiographs with 42,142 expert-delineated tooth polygons across the 32-class FDI taxonomy, annotated by 30 dental practitioners and independently reviewed by two others. They conducted controlled ablation studies varying resolution (640/1024/1280), compared architecture types (query-based transformer vs one-stage detector), and tested three interventions: LoRA-adapted self-supervised encoder, promptable foundation segmenter, and globally optimal anatomical label assignment. They also performed zero-shot transfer to an independent multi-centre cohort.
AI.result: 1) Resolution dominates: mask mAP50-95 rises 0.656 → 0.710 → 0.717 (p < 0.001) while mAP50 stays flat at ~0.982 (p = 0.024, not distinguishable from zero). Resolution improves boundary precision but not detection. 2) Architecture is nearly irrelevant in-domain: a query-based transformer with 2.1x parameters is statistically equivalent to a one-stage detector (95% CI [-0.0064, +0.0064]), only marginally better under domain shift, 5.5x slower on CPU. 3) All three targeted interventions fail: LoRA-adapted encoder underperforms, promptable foundation segmenter degrades masks by 39%, and anatomical label assignment yields only +0.0007 despite correcting 40% of out-of-domain constraint violations. 4) Zero-shot transfer costs 62% of mask mAP50-95 but only 18% of mAP50; error localizes to the apical third along the tooth axis.
AI.conclusion: Boundary precision is the binding constraint in tooth segmentation. Effort is better directed at resolution and acquisition diversity than at architectural novelty. The dissociation between mAP50-95 (sensitive to boundary quality) and mAP50 (detection-focused) metrics reveals that current methods excel at detecting teeth but struggle with precise boundary delineation, particularly in the apical third region.

title: ResNLS: An Improved Model for Stock Price Forecasting
summary: Stock prices forecasting has always been a challenging task. Although many research projects try to address the problem, few of them pay attention to the varying degrees of dependencies between stock prices. In this paper, we introduce a hybrid model that improves the prediction of stock prices by emphasizing the dependencies between adjacent stock prices. The proposed model, ResNLS, is mainly composed of two neural architectures, ResNet and LSTM. ResNet serves as a feature extractor to identify dependencies between stock prices, while LSTM analyzes the initial time series data with the combination of dependencies, which are considered as residuals. Our experiment reveals that when the closing price data for the previous 5 consecutive trading days is used as input, the performance of the model (ResNLS-5) is optimal compared to those with other inputs. Furthermore, ResNLS-5 demonstrates at least a 20% improvement over current state-of-the-art baselines. To verify whether ResNLS-5 can help clients effectively avoid risks and earn profits in the stock market, we construct a quantitative trading framework for back testing. The result shows that the trading strategy based on ResNLS-5 predictions can successfully mitigate losses during declining stock prices and generate profits in periods of rising stock prices.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ResNLS, a hybrid neural network model combining ResNet and LSTM for stock price prediction. The model uses ResNet as a feature extractor to capture dependencies between adjacent stock prices, while LSTM analyzes time series data with these dependencies as residuals. Using 5 consecutive trading days of closing price data as input, ResNLS-5 achieves at least 20% improvement over state-of-the-art baselines and demonstrates effectiveness in risk mitigation and profit generation in quantitative trading backtesting.
AI.motivation: Stock price forecasting is a challenging task, and while many research projects address this problem, few pay attention to the varying degrees of dependencies between stock prices. This research aims to improve prediction accuracy by explicitly modeling these dependencies.
AI.method: The proposed ResNLS model combines two neural architectures: ResNet serves as a feature extractor to identify dependencies between stock prices, while LSTM analyzes the initial time series data with the combination of dependencies considered as residuals. The optimal input uses closing price data for the previous 5 consecutive trading days.
AI.result: ResNLS-5 demonstrates at least a 20% improvement over current state-of-the-art baselines. In quantitative trading backtesting, the trading strategy based on ResNLS-5 predictions can successfully mitigate losses during declining stock prices and generate profits during rising stock prices.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid ResNLS model effectively captures dependencies between adjacent stock prices and significantly improves prediction accuracy. The framework shows practical value for risk mitigation and profit generation in real-world stock trading applications.

title: On Repulsive and Attractive Teachers: Separating Correctness from Behavior in Self-Distillation
summary: On-policy self-distillation provides dense, token-level supervision by conditioning a model on privileged information and distilling the resulting teacher distribution back into the model. However, privileged information can change not only what the teacher knows, but also how it behaves, entangling correctness-relevant learning signals with unintended behavioral shifts. We study this effect in reasoning tasks by contrasting attractive self-distillation, which moves the model toward a privileged teacher, with repulsive self-distillation, which moves it away from a privileged teacher. We find that both objectives can induce strong and opposing behavioral shifts: attraction suppresses exploratory reasoning and promotes shorter, more confident responses, whereas repulsion increases response length, can trigger unintended switches into a model's latent thinking mode, and ultimately becomes unstable. Motivated by these observations, we study contrastive self-distillation, which combines attraction toward a correct-solution-conditioned teacher with repulsion from an incorrect-solution-conditioned teacher. In contrast to prior work that combines such distillation signals with a GRPO objective, we isolate the self-distillation objective and study its behavior on its own. We find that the shared behavioral shifts of the two teachers largely cancel, leaving a token-level signal that more directly reflects correctness. Across non-thinking, instruct-only, and already-thinking models, this contrastive objective improves reasoning performance while maintaining stable response lengths.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates on-policy self-distillation for reasoning tasks, where a model distills its own outputs when conditioned on privileged information. It contrasts attractive (toward privileged teacher), repulsive (away from privileged teacher), and proposed contrastive self-distillation (combining both). The key finding is that attractive and repulsive objectives induce opposing behavioral shifts that largely cancel in contrastive distillation, leaving a more direct correctness signal that improves reasoning across different model types while maintaining stable response lengths.
AI.motivation: The authors observe that privileged information in self-distillation can change not just what the teacher knows, but how it behaves—entangling correctness signals with unintended behavioral shifts. They want to understand and isolate these effects to improve reasoning performance.
AI.method: The study compares three self-distillation approaches: (1) attractive self-distillation - moving the model toward a teacher conditioned on correct solutions; (2) repulsive self-distillation - moving the model away from a teacher conditioned on incorrect solutions; (3) contrastive self-distillation - combining attraction toward correct-solution-conditioned teacher with repulsion from incorrect-solution-conditioned teacher. They isolate the self-distillation objective (not combined with GRPO) and test on non-thinking, instruct-only, and already-thinking models.
AI.result: Attractive self-distillation suppresses exploratory reasoning and promotes shorter, more confident responses. Repulsion increases response length, can trigger latent thinking modes, and becomes unstable. Contrastive self-distillation causes the behavioral shifts to cancel out, providing a token-level signal that more directly reflects correctness. This improves reasoning performance across all model types while maintaining stable response lengths.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive self-distillation effectively addresses the behavioral shift problem in on-policy self-distillation by using both attraction and repulsion signals, which largely cancel out unintended behavioral changes while preserving correctness-relevant learning signals. This approach improves reasoning without the instability issues of pure repulsive distillation.

title: Extending Decoupled Attention to Dense Prediction and Masked Training for Multi-Channel Images
summary: Multi-Channel imaging (MCI) data differs fundamentally from natural images, as each channel records a semantically distinct signal rather than a colour band. To adapt vision encoders to MCI data, Multi-Channel Vision Transformers (MC-ViTs) tokenize each channel independently and concatenate the resulting tokens into one sequence, and the channel count is no longer fixed by the architecture. Self-attention is then computed across all channel-patch tokens with no restriction on which channels attend to which, which dilutes the features of individual channels. The Decoupled Vision Transformer (DC-ViT) regulates this by separating updates computed within a channel from updates computed across channels, and by forming a representation per channel before the channels are combined. Its formulation, however, pairs tokens by spatial position, and thus requires the same visible tokens in every channel. Correspondence under independent per-channel masking is recovered by solving a linear assignment between the retained patches of each channel, which allows decoupled attention to be combined with current masked multi-channel training in its standard configuration rather than a restricted one. Across three classification and three segmentation benchmarks spanning fluorescence microscopy, imaging mass cytometry and satellite imaging, including dense prediction at high channel counts, the resulting formulation outperforms the strongest MC-ViT baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an improved Decoupled Vision Transformer (DC-ViT) for Multi-Channel Imaging (MCI) data. The method addresses the feature dilution problem in standard MC-ViTs by solving a linear assignment between retained patches of each channel under independent per-channel masking, enabling decoupled attention to work with standard masked multi-channel training. The approach outperforms the strongest MC-ViT baseline across three classification and three segmentation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Multi-Channel Imaging (MCI) data differs from natural images as each channel records semantically distinct signals. Existing MC-ViTs tokenize each channel independently and compute self-attention across all channel-patch tokens without restrictions, which dilutes the features of individual channels. While DC-ViT separates within-channel and cross-channel updates, it requires the same visible tokens in every channel, limiting its applicability under independent per-channel masking.
AI.method: The proposed method recovers correspondence under independent per-channel masking by solving a linear assignment between the retained patches of each channel. This allows decoupled attention to be combined with current masked multi-channel training in its standard configuration rather than a restricted one. The approach maintains separate representations per channel before combining them.
AI.result: The resulting formulation outperforms the strongest MC-ViT baseline across three classification and three segmentation benchmarks spanning fluorescence microscopy, imaging mass cytometry, and satellite imaging, including dense prediction at high channel counts.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method successfully enables decoupled attention to work with standard masked multi-channel training configurations, achieving superior performance on various MCI tasks including classification and segmentation across different imaging modalities.

title: A Hybrid Computational Intelligence Framework for scRNA-seq Imputation: Integrating scRecover and Random Forests
summary: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables transcriptomic profiling at cellular resolution but suffers from pervasive dropout events that obscure biological signals. We present SCR-MF, a modular two-stage workflow that combines principled dropout detection using scRecover with robust non-parametric imputation via missForest. Across public and simulated datasets, SCR-MF achieves robust and interpretable performance comparable to or exceeding existing imputation methods in most cases, while preserving biological fidelity and transparency. Runtime analysis demonstrates that SCR-MF provides a competitive balance between accuracy and computational efficiency, making it suitable for mid-scale single-cell datasets.

AI.tldr: SCR-MF is a two-stage workflow for scRNA-seq data that combines scRecover for dropout detection and missForest for imputation, achieving robust performance comparable to or exceeding existing methods while preserving biological fidelity and computational efficiency for mid-scale datasets.
AI.motivation: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables transcriptomic profiling at cellular resolution but suffers from pervasive dropout events that obscure biological signals, necessitating effective imputation methods.
AI.method: A modular two-stage workflow: (1) principled dropout detection using scRecover, followed by (2) robust non-parametric imputation via missForest.
AI.result: SCR-MF achieves robust and interpretable performance comparable to or exceeding existing imputation methods in most cases, while preserving biological fidelity and transparency. Runtime analysis demonstrates competitive balance between accuracy and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: SCR-MF is suitable for mid-scale single-cell datasets, providing a good balance between accuracy and computational efficiency for dropout imputation in scRNA-seq analysis.

title: Trading Depth for Time in Recurrent Transformers
summary: Recurrent Transformers increase computational depth through temporal recurrence, feeding each token's high-level hidden state into the computation of the next. This raises a natural question: is additional computation better spent on more temporal steps or greater physical depth? We investigate this question using Latent Recurrent Transformers (LRTs), which retain one backbone forward pass per vocabulary token during decoding and provide a controlled setting for comparing these two ways of adding computation. Specifically, we insert a latent thought token between consecutive vocabulary tokens. Each thought token passes through the same $L$ layers as a vocabulary token, sharing the backbone parameters and providing an additional stage of hidden-state refinement before predicting the next token. We compare this $L$-layer LRT against a $2L$-layer LRT without thought tokens. Both execute $2L$ Transformer blocks per vocabulary token during decoding, but the thought-token model uses fewer parameters. On 16- and 20-layer mixture-of-experts NanoChat backbones, one thought token brings the shallower model within 0.006 and 0.004 bits per byte of its double-depth counterpart, recovering 67% and 81% of the improvement with approximately 48% fewer total parameters. These results suggest that temporal thinking offers a parameter-efficient alternative to increasing physical depth in recurrent Transformers.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether computation in recurrent Transformers is better spent on more temporal steps (recurrence) or greater physical depth. Using Latent Recurrent Transformers (LRTs), which insert latent thought tokens between vocabulary tokens, the study compares L-layer models with thought tokens against 2L-layer models without them.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to answer a fundamental question: in recurrent Transformers, is additional computation more effective when used for temporal recurrence (feeding hidden states into next timestep's computation) or for increasing physical depth (more layers per forward pass)? This has implications for efficient model design.
AI.method: LRTs retain one backbone forward pass per vocabulary token during decoding, with a latent thought token inserted between consecutive vocabulary tokens. Each thought token passes through the same L layers as a vocabulary token, sharing backbone parameters and providing additional hidden-state refinement. The study compares L-layer LRTs with thought tokens against 2L-layer LRTs without thought tokens—both executing 2L Transformer blocks per vocabulary token, but the thought-token model uses fewer parameters. Experiments used 16- and 20-layer mixture-of-experts NanoChat backbones.
AI.result: On 16-layer and 20-layer MoE NanoChat backbones, one thought token brings the shallower model within 0.006 and 0.004 bits per byte of its double-depth counterpart, respectively. This recovers 67% and 81% of the improvement with approximately 48% fewer total parameters.
AI.conclusion: Temporal thinking (via latent thought tokens) offers a parameter-efficient alternative to increasing physical depth in recurrent Transformers. Adding computation through temporal recurrence achieves comparable performance to doubling physical depth while using significantly fewer parameters.

title: Configurable Multi-Stage Vision Pipeline for Crop Disease and Pest Diagnosis
summary:
Farmer.Chat is Digital Green's farm advisory service for smallholder farmers. When something looks wrong with a crop, the farmer takes a photograph and sends it, and that photograph is the whole question: no symptom described, no crop named, often no text at all. The service has to determine whether the picture can be used, what crop it shows, and what is wrong with it, from images taken on cheap phones in a field, in poor light and with a moving camera. The system doing this today cannot be adjusted. It has no adjustable thresholds for photograph rejection, crops and problems cannot be added, and there is no confidence cut-off to set.
  We study about 1.16 million photographs sent to Farmer.Chat from Ethiopia, India, Kenya and Nigeria. The production quality gate rejected 46.8% of the images it judged, over a quarter of those reaching diagnosis returned no crop name, and 35.8% of the labelled problems filed under "disease" are pests, identifiable without the crop. We therefore split the work into three stages: a quality gate (M0), a crop detector (M1), and a disease or pest detector (M2). Route A fills all three with one fine-tuned vision-language model (Qwen3-VL-4B) answering in a single call. Route B fills each with a small specialist model (DaViT, YOLO26).
  We replace our production GPT-4o quality gate with a small MobileNetV3 gate at 86.9% F1 in 12 ms. On one test set scored the same way for every system, a hierarchical DaViT-Base achieves 95.41% crop accuracy against 91.46% for the production baseline. It also leads on diagnosis and never declines to answer, while every language model in the comparison leaves a large share of rows with no diagnosis. The fine-tuned model retains two capabilities the specialists do not have: one call for all three stages, and a request for a better photograph when the image cannot support an answer.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an improved image-based farm advisory system for smallholder farmers. The study analyzes 1.16 million photographs from Farmer.Chat and identifies three key problems: the production quality gate rejects 46.8% of images, over a quarter of diagnoses return no crop name, and 35.8% of problems labeled as "disease" are actually pests. The solution splits the system into three stages: quality gate (M0), crop detector (M1), and disease/pest detector (M2), comparing a single vision-language model (Qwen3-VL-4B) versus specialist models (DaViT, YOLO26).
AI.motivation: The existing Farmer.Chat system has critical limitations: it cannot be adjusted (no thresholds for rejection, cannot add crops/problems, no confidence cut-off). Additionally, the production quality gate rejects nearly half of submitted images, a significant portion of diagnoses lack crop identification, and there is substantial misclassification between diseases and pests. These issues necessitate a more flexible and accurate system architecture.
AI.method: The study analyzed approximately 1.16 million photographs from Ethiopia, India, Kenya, and Nigeria. The proposed system is split into three stages: M0 (quality gate to determine if images are usable), M1 (crop detection), and M2 (disease/pest detection). Two approaches were compared: Route A uses a single fine-tuned vision-language model (Qwen3-VL-4B) answering all three stages in one call, while Route B uses specialist models (DaViT for classification, YOLO26 for detection). The MobileNetV3 was tested as a lightweight quality gate alternative.
AI.result: The MobileNetV3 quality gate achieves 86.9% F1 score with only 12ms inference time. On the same test set, the hierarchical DaViT-Base achieves 95.41% crop accuracy compared to 91.46% for the production baseline. The specialist model approach leads in diagnosis accuracy and never declines to answer, while language model-based approaches leave many rows without diagnosis. The fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B retains two unique capabilities: answering all three stages in a single call and requesting a better photograph when image quality is insufficient.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical specialist model approach (DaViT-Base) outperforms both the production baseline and language model alternatives for crop diagnosis. While the fine-tuned vision-language model offers convenience (single call for all stages) and the ability to request better photographs, the specialist models achieve superior accuracy and reliability. The proposed three-stage architecture with specialized models provides a more flexible and accurate solution for farm advisory services.

title: Making Latent Evolution Explicit: Operator-Structured Transitions for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) augment robot policies by predicting how task-relevant scene states may evolve under interaction. Recent WAMs increasingly perform such prediction in latent representation spaces, avoiding full appearance-level generation while preserving control-relevant information. Yet latent transitions are commonly realized with Transformer-based predictors whose inductive structure is centered on token interaction rather than temporal evolution. We study transition realization as an architectural choice distinct from predictive representation and prediction-policy coupling. We introduce the Latent Evolution Operator Network (LEON), which models latent evolution in a learned observable space through context-modulated operator-based propagation and additive forcing. Grounded in the controlled Koopman generator view of evolution, LEON organizes context-dependent transition variation around a shared evolution-operator structure while retaining a complementary path for additive change. Controlled dynamical systems verify the resulting evolution-specific inductive bias and the complementary roles of operator propagation and forcing. Across two WAM formulations that integrate latent prediction into the policy differently, LEON improves closed-loop performance and robustness while remaining effective under full transition replacement. These results establish transition realization as a consequential architectural choice in latent WAMs.

AI.tldr: LEON (Latent Evolution Operator Network) introduces a novel architecture for modeling latent evolution in World Action Models (WAMs) using context-modulated operator-based propagation and additive forcing, grounded in controlled Koopman generator theory. This addresses the limitation of Transformer-based predictors that focus on token interaction rather than temporal evolution.
AI.motivation: Recent WAMs use latent representation spaces for prediction but rely on Transformer-based predictors whose inductive structure emphasizes token interaction over temporal evolution. The authors argue that transition realization is a distinct architectural choice from predictive representation and should be explicitly designed for temporal dynamics.
AI.method: LEON models latent evolution in a learned observable space through: (1) context-modulated operator-based propagation for organized transition variation around a shared evolution-operator structure, and (2) additive forcing for complementary path-independent change. This is grounded in the controlled Koopman generator view of evolution. The approach was validated on controlled dynamical systems and integrated into two different WAM formulations.
AI.result: LEON provides evolution-specific inductive bias and demonstrates complementary roles of operator propagation and forcing. Across two WAM formulations with different prediction-policy coupling, LEON improves closed-loop performance and robustness while remaining effective under full transition replacement.
AI.conclusion: Transition realization is a consequential architectural choice in latent WAMs. LEON's operator-based approach with additive forcing provides a principled way to model temporal evolution in latent spaces, outperforming Transformer-based predictors. This work establishes the importance of designing architectures specifically for temporal dynamics rather than adapting models designed for other purposes.

title: Riemannian Neural Hamiltonian Flows: Geodesic Symplectic Transport and Interpretability
summary: Hamiltonian normalizing flows are attractive generative models because their phase-space maps are invertible and volume preserving, but most neural constructions are formulated in Euclidean space. We introduce Riemannian Neural Hamiltonian Flows, which combine the fixed kinetic energy of a Riemannian manifold, a learned scalar potential, and an explicit geodesic leapfrog integrator. Our analysis explains how the learned Hamiltonian can be made interpretable. Every normalizable potential defines an implicit profile, and the position marginal initially accelerates along the relative score between that profile and the base. The matched potential is the interpretable specialization for which the implicit profile is the target. In the isotropic Gaussian case, the mechanism corresponds to a phase-space rotation. A local harmonic analysis extends this result around each mode of a general target on a manifold. The gap between the learned and the matched potential is the sum of a residual memory of the base and a bias of the model, and the two potentials agree when the position base has been transferred to the momentum. This can be achieved when the former is broader than the target. Numerical experiments on Euclidean, hyperbolic, and spherical spaces show competitive sample quality and numerical cost against a Riemannian continuous normalizing flow, and confirm the interpretability of the learned potential.

title: DRT: Dense Reasoning Trace for Efficient and Grounded Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Despite the remarkable progress in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), prevailing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) paradigms remain confined to the natural-language expression space. Consequently, they inherently incur excessive linguistic overhead, leading to information dilution and weak visual grounding. To address this challenge, we propose Dense Reasoning Trace (DRT), a paradigm that departs from natural-language-centered CoT by expressing reasoning as compact structured traces, which include concise intermediate states with symbolic connectors and disentangle visual observations from logical deductions. First, we introduce the Dense Trace Initialization to internalize the DRT reasoning mode into the model, substantially improving token efficiency while preserving visual evidence. To further enable the model to faithfully capture the logical relations within traces, we propose the Trace-Grounded Reinforcement Learning framework, which builds reference traces through a tri-perspective verification pipeline and employs Trace-Grounded GRPO with structured rewards, encouraging the model to generate concise DRT-style traces with reduced hallucination and stronger logical grounding. Extensive experiments on challenging reasoning benchmarks show that DRT achieves 5.5$\times$ token efficiency improvement while improving 1.3 accuracy points over the Qwen3-VL baseline. These findings suggest that complex multimodal reasoning may not require verbose natural-language traces, opening a more efficient path for next-generation MLLMs. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/HIT-leaderone/DRT

AI.tldr: DRT proposes a structured reasoning trace paradigm for Multimodal LLMs that replaces verbose natural-language Chain-of-Thought with compact symbolic traces, achieving 5.5× token efficiency and 1.3% accuracy improvement over Qwen3-VL baseline.
AI.motivation: Current CoT paradigms in MLLMs are confined to natural-language expression space, incurring excessive linguistic overhead that leads to information dilution and weak visual grounding. This limits the efficiency and reasoning capability of multimodal models.
AI.method: Two key innovations: (1) Dense Trace Initialization to internalize DRT reasoning mode into the model, improving token efficiency while preserving visual evidence; (2) Trace-Grounded Reinforcement Learning framework using tri-perspective verification pipeline to build reference traces and Trace-Grounded GRPO with structured rewards to encourage concise DRT-style traces with reduced hallucination and stronger logical grounding.
AI.result: 5.5× token efficiency improvement and 1.3 accuracy points improvement over Qwen3-VL baseline on challenging reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Complex multimodal reasoning may not require verbose natural-language traces, opening a more efficient path for next-generation MLLMs. DRT demonstrates that structured symbolic traces can achieve better performance with significantly reduced token usage.

title: Beyond Gaussian Worlds: Latent Geometry Matters for JEPAs
summary: Recent Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) prevent representation collapse by constraining learned representations to follow a prescribed target distribution, such as an isotropic Gaussian or the uniform distribution on a hypersphere. Klindt et al. (2026) showed that, under their Euclidean assumptions, matching a Gaussian target can recover Gaussian latent variables up to a linear transformation, and that the Gaussian is the unique distribution with this guarantee. We extend their analysis to latent variables supported on embedded Riemannian manifolds and derive conditions on the latent geometry and positive-pair dynamics under which alignment and exact distribution matching guarantee linear recovery. In particular, when the latent variables are uniformly distributed on a sphere and the representations are matched to the same spherical distribution, every optimal representation recovers the latent state up to an orthogonal transformation. This shows that Gaussian uniqueness is not a universal property of distribution-matched JEPAs: non-Euclidean latent geometries can admit other linearly recoverable distributions. We further derive an approximate-recovery bound that is strictly tighter for the spherical world than for the Gaussian world. Experiments on Gaussian, spherical, and toroidal latent spaces show that geometrically compatible targets yield better linear recovery when optimization succeeds, whereas mismatched targets distort the latent structure. This advantage persists in high-dimensional Clifford-torus worlds.

AI.tldr: This paper extends prior analysis of distribution-matched Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) from Euclidean Gaussian spaces to Riemannian manifold latent spaces. It demonstrates that spherical latent geometry with uniform distribution enables linear recovery up to orthogonal transformation, challenging the notion that Gaussian is the unique linearly recoverable distribution. The spherical case provides tighter recovery bounds than Gaussian, with experiments validating these findings across various manifold geometries.
AI.motivation: Current JEPAs prevent representation collapse by constraining learned representations to follow prescribed target distributions (Gaussian or uniform on hypersphere). While prior work established Gaussian as uniquely guaranteeing linear recovery in Euclidean spaces, the question of whether non-Euclidean latent geometries could admit other linearly recoverable distributions remained open. This work aims to generalize distribution matching theory to embedded Riemannian manifolds.
AI.method: The authors extend the Euclidean analysis framework from Klindt et al. (2026) to latent variables supported on embedded Riemannian manifolds. They analyze conditions linking latent geometry and positive-pair dynamics under which alignment and exact distribution matching guarantee linear recovery. Specifically, they examine the spherical case where latent variables are uniformly distributed on a sphere and representations are matched to the same spherical distribution, deriving approximate-recovery bounds and comparing them to Gaussian-world bounds.
AI.result: When latent variables are uniformly distributed on a sphere and representations are matched to the same spherical distribution, every optimal representation recovers the latent state up to an orthogonal transformation. This demonstrates that Gaussian uniqueness is not universal in distribution-matched JEPAs. Additionally, the derived approximate-recovery bound is strictly tighter for the spherical world than for the Gaussian world. Experiments on Gaussian, spherical, and toroidal latent spaces confirm that geometrically compatible targets yield better linear recovery, while mismatched targets distort latent structure. This advantage persists in high-dimensional Clifford-torus worlds.
AI.conclusion: Non-Euclidean latent geometries can admit distributions (like uniform on sphere) that enable linear recovery, contradicting the apparent uniqueness of Gaussian distributions. The spherical latent space offers theoretically tighter recovery bounds than Gaussian space. For practical applications, matching the target distribution to the latent geometry is crucial—geometric compatibility significantly improves linear recovery quality, while distribution mismatches distort the underlying latent structure. These findings extend the theoretical understanding of JEPAs and provide guidance for designing architecture-target pairings in self-supervised learning.

title: Diffusion-Based Tumor Inpainting for Renal Segmentation under Clinical Data Scarcity
summary: Deep learning segmentation of renal tumors requires large annotated datasets, yet clinical deployments typically offer only a handful of tumor-positive cases from the target site. We propose a diffusion-based inpainting framework that synthesizes anatomically plausible renal tumors within healthy CT scans, requiring no additional annotation, and provide the first systematic comparison of 2D, 2.5D, and full 3D (MAISI) synthesis strategies for this task. Training the diffusion model on public data (KiTS23, KIRC) and evaluating nnU-Net segmentation on a internal cohort across three low-data regimes, we find that 2.5D and 3D augmentation substantially reduce false positives (from $\sim$18--20\% to $\sim$3--6\%) while maintaining Dice, whereas 2D provides no consistent benefit. Crucially, the proposed 2.5D method matches full 3D synthesis on every metric at substantially lower computational cost, indicating that local volumetric consistency alone is sufficient for effective augmentation in data- and resource-scarce clinical settings.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a diffusion-based inpainting framework to synthesize renal tumors in healthy CT scans, addressing the data scarcity problem in clinical tumor segmentation. The study systematically compares 2D, 2.5D, and 3D synthesis strategies, finding that 2.5D and 3D approaches significantly reduce false positives (from ~18-20% to ~3-6%) while maintaining Dice scores, with 2.5D matching 3D performance at lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Deep learning segmentation of renal tumors requires large annotated datasets, but clinical deployments typically have only a handful of tumor-positive cases from the target site, creating a significant data scarcity problem that limits model performance and generalizability.
AI.method: The authors propose a diffusion-based inpainting framework that synthesizes anatomically plausible renal tumors within healthy CT scans without requiring additional annotations. They systematically compare three synthesis strategies: 2D, 2.5D, and full 3D (MAISI). The diffusion model is trained on public datasets (KiTS23, KIRC), and nnU-Net segmentation is evaluated on an internal cohort across three low-data regimes.
AI.result: 2.5D and 3D augmentation substantially reduce false positives from ~18-20% to ~3-6% while maintaining Dice scores, whereas 2D provides no consistent benefit. The proposed 2.5D method matches full 3D synthesis on every metric at substantially lower computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Local volumetric consistency alone is sufficient for effective augmentation in data- and resource-scarce clinical settings. The 2.5D approach offers an optimal balance between performance and computational efficiency, making it particularly valuable for clinical deployments with limited data and computational resources.

title: Multi-Domain Clustering via Measure Quantization
summary: Clustering is a fundamental task in data analysis, typically addressed through centroid-based methods such as K-means. In this work, we present a general framework for multi-domain clustering via measure quantization: given samples from multiple domains, we learn a shared set of cluster prototypes by minimizing a probability metric, such as the Sinkhorn divergence or the Maximum Mean Discrepancy, between each domain's probability measure and the measure of prototypes. Data points are then assigned to clusters either via nearest centroid, or via optimal transport, a collaborative strategy that couples all samples within a domain. A mini-batch optimization strategy makes both fitting and assignment scalable, reducing memory and computational cost while preserving clustering performance. Experimental results on 5 multi-domain benchmarks spanning image, audio and sensor data show that our Sinkhorn-based method consistently outperforms classical and multi-domain clustering baselines, and that this advantage persists when scaling to hundreds of thousands of samples.

AI.tldr: A general framework for multi-domain clustering using measure quantization, where shared cluster prototypes are learned by minimizing probability metrics (Sinkhorn divergence or MMD) between domain measures and prototype measures. Assignments use nearest centroid or optimal transport, with mini-batch optimization for scalability.
AI.motivation: Standard centroid-based clustering (e.g., K-means) struggles with multi-domain data where samples come from different distributions. Existing multi-domain clustering methods lack a unified framework and often fail to scale to large datasets.
AI.method: 1) Learn shared cluster prototypes by minimizing probability metrics (Sinkhorn divergence or MMD) between each domain's probability measure and the prototype measure. 2) Assign data points via nearest centroid or optimal transport coupling. 3) Use mini-batch optimization for scalable fitting and assignment.
AI.result: The Sinkhorn-based method consistently outperforms classical and multi-domain clustering baselines across 5 multi-domain benchmarks (image, audio, sensor data). The advantage persists when scaling to hundreds of thousands of samples.
AI.conclusion: The measure quantization framework provides an effective and scalable approach to multi-domain clustering, with Sinkhorn divergence showing particularly strong performance across diverse data types.

title: SignGPT: Toward LLM-Mediated Sign Language Interaction through Gloss-Free Translation and Generation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) provide limited support for sign language interaction. Unifying sign language translation (SLT) and generation (SLG) to enable sign language as both input and output can reduce switching between separate models during sign-text interaction. We present SignGPT, a unified, pose-based framework for gloss-free SLT and SLG. SignGPT integrates part-aware hierarchical representations of body, hand, and facial motion into a shared language model and employs asymmetric multi-token prediction and progressive training for bidirectional modeling. We evaluate SignGPT on How2Sign (ASL) and Phoenix-2014T (DGS) through benchmark comparisons, qualitative analyses, and component ablations. An exploratory study with 12 Deaf ASL signers assesses an LLM-mediated sign-to-sign response pipeline, highlighting the potential of unified modeling to support sign language conversation (SLC).

AI.tldr: SignGPT is a unified pose-based framework that enables bidirectional sign language translation (SLT) and generation (SLG) using a single language model, addressing the limitation of separate models in sign-text interaction.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs provide limited support for sign language interaction. Existing approaches use separate models for SLT and SLG, requiring switching between models during sign-text conversation. This paper aims to unify SLT and SLG to enable sign language as both input and output, facilitating seamless sign language conversation (SLC).
AI.method: SignGPT integrates part-aware hierarchical representations of body, hand, and facial motion into a shared language model. It employs asymmetric multi-token prediction and progressive training for bidirectional modeling. The framework is evaluated on How2Sign (American Sign Language) and Phoenix-2014T (German Sign Language) through benchmark comparisons, qualitative analyses, and component ablations.
