An exploratory user study with 12 Deaf ASL signers tests an LLM-mediated sign-to-sign response pipeline.
AI.result: SignGPT demonstrates the feasibility of unified sign language translation and generation in a single framework. The user study with 12 Deaf ASL signers highlights the potential of unified modeling to support sign language conversation.
AI.conclusion: SignGPT presents a promising approach for unified sign language interaction, enabling sign language as both input and output through a single model. The framework shows potential for supporting sign language conversation (SLC), though full effectiveness would need further validation through larger-scale studies.

title: Optimization Geometry of Equivalent Brownian RKHS Representations
summary: Equivalent finite parameterizations can represent the same functions and intrinsic norm yet induce different optimization algorithms. We study this effect in a controlled finite Brownian RKHS with nodal, increment, and spectral coordinates. Classical finite-element, RKHS-interpolation, Brownian-covariance, and mixed-boundary DCT identities make the shared hypothesis class, Brownian energy, approximation operator, and coordinate maps explicit. Our main results concern the optimization geometry of this fixed model. With mapped initialization, identical scalar steps, and identical minibatches, nodal and spectral GD/SGD have exactly the same mapped trajectories. Increment GD is an explicit Euler step for the constant Brownian/Sobolev metric, with factor $1/h$. For Brownian-regularized least squares, $κ_2(\mathbf H_{\mathrm{inc}})\le1+A/ρ$, independently of grid resolution $G$ for fixed $A$, $ρ>0$, and the stated normalization. Under the stated standard-Adam convention, the universal orthogonal equivariance group is exactly the signed permutations; the block DCT-VIII transform is not one. Float64 tests over five grids numerically verify the finite identities, mapped one-layer and recursive trajectories, conditioning predictions, and theorem-matched Adam separation. Thus coordinate effects are isolated without changing the represented functions, intrinsic regularizer, or approximation space.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how different coordinate parameterizations (nodal, increment, spectral) in a finite Brownian RKHS affect optimization algorithms while representing identical functions and intrinsic norms. Key findings show trajectory equivalence under mapping, increment GD as an explicit Euler step, grid-independent conditioning bounds, and that Adam's equivariance group is exactly signed permutations.
AI.motivation: Understanding how coordinate choice in finite parameterizations affects optimization algorithms, even when representing the same functions and using the same intrinsic regularizer.
AI.method: Using finite-element, RKHS-interpolation, Brownian-covariance, and mixed-boundary DCT identities to make coordinate maps explicit; analyzing optimization geometry with mapped initialization and identical step sizes.
AI.result: Nodal and spectral GD/SGD have identical mapped trajectories. Increment GD corresponds to explicit Euler step with factor 1/h. Condition number bound κ₂(H_inc) ≤ 1 + A/ρ independent of grid resolution. Adam equivariance group is signed permutations, not block DCT-VIII.
AI.conclusion: Coordinate effects are isolated from the represented functions, intrinsic regularizer, and approximation space—demonstrating that coordinate choice significantly impacts optimization behavior despite mathematical equivalence in the hypothesis class.

title: ZYT-World: A Real-Time Controllable World Model for Closed-Loop Autonomous-Driving Simulation
comment: Technical Report. Videos and additional results are available at zyt-aim.github.io/ZYT-World
summary: Generative world models offer controllable and repeatable closed-loop simulation for end-to-end and vision-language-action driving policies, but production deployment exposes three unresolved requirements: faithfully reproducing a mixed fisheye-pinhole rig at native resolutions; reconciling causal, per-timestep interaction with long-horizon stability and low latency; and preserving scene identity when a location is revisited. We present ZYT-World, a single architecture that natively generates four fisheye views with field of view > 180° and three pinhole views. Projection-specific Plucker adapters encode camera geometry, ego-motion adaptive layer normalization provides global motion control, and a lightweight pixel-aligned layout conditions traffic participants and signals through instance-level boxes, headings and colors. Heterogeneous training combines full-rig geometric coverage with high-resolution detail. Teacher forcing, causal consistency distillation, self-rollout distribution matching distillation, and RigCritic transform a 40-step bidirectional teacher into a one-step, per-latent streaming generator, with RigCritic evaluating the seven-view rig jointly. A 19M-parameter variational autoencoder decoder (TinyVAE), W8A8 quantization, and our inference engine reduce decoding, backbone, and incremental-execution costs, respectively. Finally, cross-trajectory pairs derived from real captures train a plug-in implicit-memory module that preserves place-specific evidence. On the internal multi-view test set, the one-step model retains more than 90% of the teacher's PSNR and SSIM, while FID, FVD, and LPIPS stay within 11% of the teacher. Under the generator-only timing in Figure 2, it is 107.7 times faster than the 40-step bidirectional teacher. TinyVAE decodes 59.8 times faster than Wan. 30s rollouts and cross-trajectory revisits show the intended long-horizon and memory behavior.

AI.tldr: ZYT-World is a generative world model for autonomous driving that produces 4 fisheye views (>180° FOV) and 3 pinhole views simultaneously. It transforms a 40-step bidirectional teacher into a one-step streaming generator through heterogeneous training and distillation techniques, achieving 107.7x speedup while retaining >90% of the teacher's PSNR/SSIM quality.
AI.motivation: Three critical requirements for production deployment of generative world models in autonomous driving: (1) faithful reproduction of mixed fisheye-pinhole camera rigs at native resolutions, (2) reconciling causal per-timestep interaction with long-horizon stability and low latency, and (3) preserving scene identity when revisiting locations.
AI.method: ZYT-World uses: (1) Projection-specific Plucker adapters for camera geometry encoding, (2) Ego-motion adaptive layer normalization for global motion control, (3) Pixel-aligned layout conditioning for traffic participants/signals via instance boxes/headings/colors. Training combines heterogeneous data with teacher forcing, causal consistency distillation, self-rollout distribution matching distillation, and RigCritic. Efficiency achieved through 19M-parameter TinyVAE decoder, W8A8 quantization, and optimized inference engine. Implicit-memory module trained on cross-trajectory pairs preserves place-specific identity.
AI.result: On internal multi-view test set: one-step model retains >90% of teacher's PSNR and SSIM; FID, FVD, and LPIPS stay within 11% of teacher. 107.7x faster than 40-step bidirectional teacher. TinyVAE decodes 59.8x faster than Wan. Demonstrates intended long-horizon stability (30s rollouts) and memory behavior (cross-trajectory revisits).
AI.conclusion: ZYT-World successfully addresses production deployment challenges for generative world models in autonomous driving, achieving a practical balance between rendering quality, computational efficiency, and temporal consistency across diverse camera configurations.

title: SpecQuant: Speculative Decoding with Multi-Parent Quantization for Adaptive LLM Inference
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. Published in the 2026 Fifth International Conference on Power, Control and Computing Technologies (ICPC2T)
summary: Running large language models (LLMs) locally continues to be limited by restrictions of compute and memory on consumer hardware. The popular acceleration technologies, such as quantization, speculative decoding, and adaptive inferencing, offer substantial speed boosts but usually necessitate retraining, per architecture tuning, or draft models. SpecQuant is a trainingfree framework, that combines speculative decoding with multiparent quantization to perform adaptive, efficient inference of LLMs. SpecQuant derives multiple quantized variants (INT4, FP8, FP16) from a shared base model, and dynamically routes queries based on predicted complexity; lightweight variants are used for simple or factual tasks, and full-precision models are used for complex reasoning tasks or long-context inputs. The shared-weight design of SpecQuant ensures sufficient token acceptance for speculative decoding without compatibility issues using separate draft parent models. We evaluate SpecQuant on Qwen2.5 based models on the MMLU, AlpacaEval, and GSM8K datasets, or benchmarks, demonstrating 35-43% speedups without degrading accuracy greater than 2%, substantial within the LLM community. SpecQuant enables practical on-device LLM deployment across diverse hardware without special infrastructure or expertise.

AI.tldr: SpecQuant is a training-free framework that combines speculative decoding with multiparant quantization to enable adaptive, efficient LLM inference on consumer hardware. It creates multiple quantized variants (INT4, FP8, FP16) from a shared base model and dynamically routes queries based on complexity - using lightweight variants for simple tasks and full-precision for complex reasoning.
AI.motivation: Running large language models locally is limited by compute and memory constraints on consumer hardware. While existing acceleration techniques (quantization, speculative decoding, adaptive inference) offer speed improvements, they typically require retraining, architecture-specific tuning, or separate draft models.
AI.method: SpecQuant combines speculative decoding with multiparent quantization in a training-free framework. It derives multiple quantized variants (INT4, FP8, FP16) from a shared base model and dynamically routes queries based on predicted complexity - lightweight variants for simple/factual tasks, full-precision models for complex reasoning or long-context inputs. The shared-weight design ensures sufficient token acceptance for speculative decoding without compatibility issues.
AI.result: Evaluated on Qwen2.5-based models across MMLU, AlpacaEval, and GSM8K benchmarks, SpecQuant achieves 35-43% speedups while maintaining accuracy within 2% of baseline.
AI.conclusion: SpecQuant enables practical on-device LLM deployment across diverse hardware without requiring special infrastructure or expertise, offering substantial speedups with minimal accuracy trade-offs.

title: Balanced Prompt Adaptation against Entropy-Induced Collapse for Test-Time Binary Segmentation
summary: Entropy minimization is a standard objective for test-time adaptation (TTA), but it can fail in imbalanced binary segmentation. Unlike image classification, dense segmentation aggregates thousands of pixel predictions, allowing the larger predicted class to dominate the update, pull minority predictions toward itself, and produce a degenerate mask as predictions saturate and their entropy gradients vanish. We theoretically establish this collapse in a shared-shift model. This analysis motivates Balanced-Anchor Prompt Adaptation (BAPA), which combines two complementary modules. The Class-Balanced Anchors (CBA) module selects high-confidence anchors separately from each predicted class and gives foreground and background equal total loss weight, preventing the larger region from dominating the update. Dynamic Prompt Adaptation (DPA) refreshes these anchors after each prediction update and optimizes only text-side prompt residuals while keeping the vision-language encoders frozen. This prompt-only update refines the foreground-background decision boundary without altering the pretrained dense visual representation. Across experiments from four domains, BAPA achieves the highest mean Dice among the evaluated methods. Factorized ablations further validate the complementary roles of CBA and DPA, supporting balanced prompt adaptation as an effective alternative to entropy minimization for test-time binary segmentation.

AI.tldr: Entropy minimization fails in imbalanced binary segmentation for test-time adaptation because dense predictions allow the larger class to dominate updates, causing prediction collapse. BAPA addresses this by combining Class-Balanced Anchors (equal loss weight for foreground/background) with Dynamic Prompt Adaptation (optimizing only text prompts while keeping vision-language encoders frozen), achieving state-of-the-art Dice scores across four domains.
AI.motivation: Entropy minimization is a standard TTA objective but fails in imbalanced binary segmentation because aggregated pixel predictions allow the larger class to dominate updates, pulling minority predictions toward itself and producing degenerate masks as predictions saturate and entropy gradients vanish.
AI.method: BAPA combines two complementary modules: (1) Class-Balanced Anchors (CBA) selects high-confidence anchors separately from each predicted class and gives foreground and background equal total loss weight, preventing larger region from dominating; (2) Dynamic Prompt Adaptation (DPA) refreshes anchors after each prediction update and optimizes only text-side prompt residuals while keeping vision-language encoders frozen.
AI.result: BAPA achieves the highest mean Dice among evaluated methods across experiments from four domains. Factorized ablations validate the complementary roles of CBA and DPA.
AI.conclusion: Balanced prompt adaptation is an effective alternative to entropy minimization for test-time binary segmentation, addressing the class imbalance collapse problem through class-balanced anchor selection and prompt-only optimization.

title: GEM-MPC: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation through Expert-Guided Planning
summary: Effective exploration in high-dimensional continuous control remains a central challenge in reinforcement learning. Planning-based methods address this by combining online planning with learned policies and value functions, but their components can become misaligned during training: learned sampling policies may diverge from planner behavior, while planning distributions stored in replay become stale as the model and value function evolve. Reanalysis can refresh these targets, but at substantial computational cost. We propose GEM-MPC, an MPPI-based reinforcement learning method that improves the interaction between planning and learning. GEM-MPC uses MPPI to combine a policy trained to clone the planner with a KL-regularized policy that explores around it, providing complementary exploitation and guided exploration within planning. We further introduce Gated Prior Distillation, which selectively learns from stored planning distributions only when they provide a better target than the current prior, reducing the impact of stale planning data without requiring full reanalysis. Across continuous-control benchmarks, GEM-MPC consistently outperforms existing planning-based baselines under lower computational budgets.

AI.tldr: GEM-MPC is an MPPI-based reinforcement learning method that combines a planner-cloning policy with a KL-regularized exploration policy for improved exploration in continuous control. It introduces Gated Prior Distillation to selectively learn from stored planning distributions, reducing the impact of stale data without costly reanalysis.
AI.motivation: Address the misalignment between planning and learning components in planning-based RL methods: learned sampling policies diverge from planner behavior, and planning distributions in replay become stale as models evolve. Reanalysis is computationally expensive, requiring a more efficient solution.
AI.method: GEM-MPC uses MPPI to combine two policy components: (1) a policy trained to clone the planner for exploitation, and (2) a KL-regularized policy that explores around the planner for guided exploration. Gated Prior Distillation selectively learns from stored planning distributions only when they provide better targets than the current prior, avoiding stale data issues without full reanalysis.
AI.result: GEM-MPC consistently outperforms existing planning-based baselines under lower computational budgets across continuous-control benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method effectively addresses the exploration challenge in high-dimensional continuous control by improving the interaction between planning and learning, providing a computationally efficient alternative to reanalysis-based approaches.

title: SFVO: Decoupled Confidence-Guided Stereo-Flow Visual Odometry with Bidirectional PnP
summary: Deep learning-based visual odometry (VO) has achieved significant progress, yet most existing methods focus on a monocular approach, which suffers from scale ambiguity. Stereo VO provides real metric by its nature, but remains less studied in deep learning VO due to its high computational cost and modeling complexity. Recent advances in stereo matching and optical flow estimation have made dense visual correspondence increasingly accurate and reliable, but their complementary geometric information has not been fully exploited for VO. In this paper, we present SFVO, a correspondence-driven stereo VO framework that directly builds upon pretrained stereo matching and optical flow models. SFVO exploits pretrained stereo matching and optical flow models to estimate stereo and temporal correspondences. Instead of learning pose directly from images, SFVO maps learned correspondences into geometric constraints and predicts which points are trustworthy. To improve the reliability of visual correspondence-based geometric constraints, we introduce decoupled confidence maps for rotation and translation. This design better aligns the characteristics of visual correspondence and 6-DoF transformations. Extensive experiments on outdoor and indoor datasets demonstrate that SFVO achieves robust and accurate pose estimation with strong generalization capability. The code will be released.

AI.tldr: SFVO is a correspondence-driven stereo visual odometry framework that leverages pretrained stereo matching and optical flow models to estimate correspondences, which are then mapped into geometric constraints with decoupled confidence maps for rotation and translation prediction, achieving robust and accurate 6-DoF pose estimation.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of monocular VO (scale ambiguity) and stereo VO (high computational cost and modeling complexity) by exploiting dense visual correspondence from pretrained stereo matching and optical flow models.
AI.method: Directly builds on pretrained stereo matching and optical flow models to estimate stereo and temporal correspondences. Maps learned correspondences into geometric constraints rather than learning pose directly from images. Introduces decoupled confidence maps for rotation and translation to improve reliability of visual correspondence-based geometric constraints.
AI.result: Achieves robust and accurate pose estimation with strong generalization capability on outdoor and indoor datasets.
AI.conclusion: The correspondence-driven approach with decoupled confidence maps effectively combines geometric information from stereo matching and optical flow for 6-DoF pose estimation, demonstrating the potential of leveraging pretrained correspondence models for visual odometry.

title: GraphSkillEvo: Evolutionary Optimization of Graph-Structured Agent Skills
summary: Skills can improve the performance of Large Language Model (LLM) agents by providing task-specific procedural guidance, while skill optimization further improves their effectiveness through iterative refinement. However, existing skill optimization methods typically represent skills as unstructured natural-language instructions, creating two key challenges: 1) Unstructured skills often lack explicit workflow-level guidance and contain substantial redundancy, making them difficult for LLMs to execute; 2) the vast search space of unconstrained natural-language skills makes skill optimization ineffective. To address these challenges, we propose representing skills as graph-structured natural-language artifacts. In graph-structured skills, each node represents an execution step together with its operational guidance, while directed edges encode context-dependent transitions between steps. Compared to unstructured skills, graph-structured skills can provide clear workflow-level guidance. Moreover, the proposed graph-structured skill can also facilitate skill optimization. Building on this structured representation, we introduce GraphSkillEvo, a population-based evolutionary optimization framework with mutation and crossover operators for graph-structured skills. By maintaining multiple candidate skills and combining effective components, GraphSkillEvo enables broader and more comprehensive exploration of the structured skill space than purely LLM-based iterative self-refinement. Extensive experiments across five agent benchmarks demonstrate that GraphSkillEvo consistently outperforms the strong skill optimization baseline SkillOpt, improving average accuracy by 4.01% on GPT-5.4-nano and 1.76% on GPT-5.4. Our code is available at https://github.com/ruisun7/GraphSkillEvo.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GraphSkillEvo, a population-based evolutionary optimization framework that represents skills as graph-structured natural-language artifacts (nodes = execution steps, edges = transitions) to improve LLM agent performance. It addresses two key challenges of unstructured skills: lack of workflow-level guidance and large search space. Experiments on five benchmarks show improvements of 4.01% on GPT-5.4-nano and 1.76% on GPT-5.4 over the SkillOpt baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing skill optimization methods represent skills as unstructured natural-language instructions, which lack explicit workflow-level guidance, contain redundancy, and result in an ineffective search space due to its vast, unconstrained nature.
AI.method: The paper introduces: (1) Graph-structured skills - nodes represent execution steps with operational guidance, edges encode context-dependent transitions between steps; (2) GraphSkillEvo - a population-based evolutionary optimization framework with mutation and crossover operators for graph-structured skills, maintaining multiple candidate skills and combining effective components.
AI.result: GraphSkillEvo consistently outperforms the strong skill optimization baseline SkillOpt across five agent benchmarks, improving average accuracy by 4.01% on GPT-5.4-nano and 1.76% on GPT-5.4.
AI.conclusion: Representing skills as graph-structured natural-language artifacts provides clearer workflow-level guidance compared to unstructured skills. The population-based evolutionary optimization enables broader and more comprehensive exploration of the structured skill space than purely LLM-based iterative self-refinement.

title: Beyond Benchmark Scores: Auditing Medical Vision-Language Models for Chest X-Ray Tuberculosis Screening
comment: 27 pages, 7 figures, and 21 tables; includes extended methods, statistical analyses, and robustness evaluations
summary: A medical model's benchmark score does not establish that the same conclusion holds under a different evaluation. This study tests whether claims about model ranking, score reliability and screening performance survive changes in cohort, prompt, negative spectrum, specified prevalence and operating threshold. We audit three medical vision-language models (BioMedCLIP, CheXficient, and MedSigLIP) and a general-domain OpenCLIP comparator on 12,200 chest radiograph records from four datasets (Montgomery, Shenzhen, TBX11K, and VinDr-CXR). Five fixed prompt families yield 244,000 model--image--prompt scores. No model leads every cohort and reliability criterion. Prompt-family changes alter AUROC in 21 of 48 multiplicity-controlled comparisons. Replacing healthy controls with sick non-tuberculosis controls reduces AUROC by 0.075--0.306 across all four models. On VinDr-CXR, the three medical models distinguish tuberculosis from no-finding controls substantially better than from pneumonia or lung tumor; their AUROC point estimates for both named diseases fall below 0.5. CheXficient has documented VinDr-CXR pretraining exposure, which limits the interpretation of its results. Thresholds chosen for 95\% sensitivity on TBX11K training retain that constraint by point estimate in only four of sixteen target evaluations. A five-seed supervised source model reaches 0.999 AUROC on TBX11K validation but 0.629 on each of two external cohorts. Conservative exclusion of perceptual-overlap candidates narrows this gap without closing it. These retrospective, single-task results show that discrimination, score reliability and threshold retention support different portability claims. Evidence for chest X-ray tuberculosis screening should identify the complete evaluation specification rather than attribute clinical portability to a checkpoint alone.

AI.tldr: This study audits medical vision-language models (BioMedCLIP, CheXficient, MedSigLIP, and OpenCLIP) on chest X-ray tuberculosis screening across multiple datasets and evaluation conditions, demonstrating that benchmark scores do not generalize across different cohorts, prompts, negative spectra, prevalence levels, or operating thresholds.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to challenge the common assumption that a model's benchmark score establishes its clinical portability. The authors argue that claims about model ranking, score reliability, and screening performance may not hold when evaluation conditions change.
AI.method: The study audited three medical vision-language models and one general-domain comparator on 12,200 chest radiograph records from four datasets (Montgomery, Shenzhen, TBX11K, VinDr-CXR). They tested five fixed prompt families yielding 244,000 model-image-prompt scores. They evaluated changes across cohort, prompt, negative spectrum, prevalence, and operating threshold. They also tested a five-seed supervised source model.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) No model leads every cohort and reliability criterion; (2) Prompt-family changes alter AUROC in 21/48 comparisons; (3) Replacing healthy controls with sick non-TB controls reduces AUROC by 0.075-0.306; (4) On VinDr-CXR, medical models distinguish TB from no-finding controls better than from pneumonia or lung tumor; (5) Thresholds for 95% sensitivity on TBX11K training retain that sensitivity in only 4/16 target evaluations; (6) A supervised model reaches 0.999 AUROC on TBX11K validation but 0.629 on external cohorts.
AI.conclusion: Discrimination, score reliability, and threshold retention support different portability claims. Evidence for chest X-ray TB screening should identify the complete evaluation specification rather than attribute clinical portability to a model checkpoint alone. Conservative exclusion of perceptual-overlap candidates narrows but does not close the external validation gap.

title: Bilevel Optimization of Topology and Hyperparameters (BOTH)
comment: Currently under submission to SMO journal
summary: Topology optimization (TO) represents a significant step towards automating the design process: given a working simulation, TO can produce a viable prototype at the press of a button by differentiating the simulation and iteratively improving the design. In practice, however, TO is riddled with ``magic numbers''---hyperparameters whose tuning significantly affects the outcome. Finding the right values typically requires not only deep problem-specific knowledge but also extensive trial-and-error. While practitioners can use surrogate-assisted hyperparameter optimization as an alternative, this approach requires strictly limiting the number of hyperparameters through careful problem formulation. Here, we propose differentiating TO itself using automatic differentiation. This yields ``hypergradients'' that allow us to tune these hyperparameters in tandem with the primary optimization. We show that evaluating just one or two steps of TO is sufficiently informative and that the method scales favorably to thousands of hyperparameters at an expense comparable to only a few standard TO runs. We demonstrate this approach on stress-constrained and compliance problems, with the latter utilizing a neural parameterization of the density field.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using automatic differentiation to compute "hypergradients" for tuning topology optimization (TO) hyperparameters, eliminating the need for manual tuning and trial-and-error. The method scales to thousands of hyperparameters with comparable computational cost to standard TO runs.
AI.motivation: Topology optimization is hampered by "magic numbers" (hyperparameters) that require extensive problem-specific knowledge and trial-and-error to tune properly. Existing surrogate-assisted hyperparameter optimization approaches require limiting the number of hyperparameters, making them impractical for many real-world applications.
AI.method: The authors propose differentiating TO itself using automatic differentiation to compute hypergradients. This allows simultaneous tuning of hyperparameters alongside the primary design optimization. The approach was tested on stress-constrained and compliance problems, with the latter using a neural parameterization of the density field.
AI.result: Evaluating just one or two steps of TO provides sufficient information for hyperparameter tuning. The method scales favorably to thousands of hyperparameters at an expense comparable to only a few standard TO runs.
AI.conclusion: Automatic differentiation of TO enables efficient hyperparameter tuning without manual intervention or strict limitations on hyperparameter count. This represents a significant step toward fully automated design processes in topology optimization.

title: XCalib Depth-Guided Geometric Optimization for Dense Thermal-Visible Video Registration
summary: Image registration is a vital preprocessing step in multimodal perception tasks, including image fusion, object detection, and semantic segmentation. In Advanced Driver- Assistance Systems (ADAS), spatial misalignment between visible (RGB) and infrared (IR) cameras -caused by non-coincident optical axes and field-of-view differences- introduces non-uniform parallax and visual ghosting. Classical keypoint-based methods are restricted to global homographies that fail under dynamic depth, while unconstrained dense flow algorithms lack structural regularization and suffer from temporal instability. In this paper, we propose XCalib, an unsupervised dense thermal-visible registration framework that bridges this gap. Rather than serving as an absolute metric calibration tool, XCalib leverages virtual pinhole camera parameterization strictly as a geometric constraint space. By optimizing effective relative pose and intrinsics alongside predicted monocular metric depth, XCalib restricts the search space of spatial displacements to physically valid projection geometries. Our key contributions are: (1) a novel registration paradigm that uses camera parameterization as an implicit regularizer for dense cross-modal warping; (2) Normalized Edges Correlation (NEC), a robust structural similarity metric tailored to cross- spectral alignment; and (3) extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations across public ADAS datasets, demonstrating superior temporal stability and alignment accuracy over unconstrained dense flow baselines.

AI.tldr: XCalib is an unsupervised framework for registering thermal and visible camera images in ADAS applications. It uses virtual pinhole camera parameterization as a geometric constraint space, optimizing relative pose and intrinsics with monocular metric depth to restrict displacement search to physically valid geometries. The method includes Normalized Edges Correlation (NEC) as a cross-spectral alignment metric.
AI.motivation: In ADAS, spatial misalignment between RGB and infrared cameras caused by non-coincident optical axes and FOV differences leads to non-uniform parallax and visual ghosting. Existing methods are limited: classical keypoint-based approaches use global homographies that fail under dynamic depth, while unconstrained dense flow algorithms lack structural regularization and suffer temporal instability.
AI.method: XCalib proposes a novel registration paradigm using camera parameterization as an implicit regularizer for dense cross-modal warping. It optimizes effective relative pose and intrinsics alongside predicted monocular metric depth, restricting the search space to physically valid projection geometries. The method introduces Normalized Edges Correlation (NEC), a robust structural similarity metric tailored for cross-spectral alignment.
AI.result: Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations on public ADAS datasets demonstrate superior temporal stability and alignment accuracy over unconstrained dense flow baselines.
AI.conclusion: XCalib successfully bridges the gap between classical keypoint-based methods and unconstrained dense flow algorithms by leveraging virtual pinhole camera parameterization as a geometric constraint space. The approach achieves robust thermal-visible registration with improved temporal stability and accuracy, representing a promising solution for multimodal perception in ADAS.

title: RegKT: Interpretable and Robust Deep Knowledge Tracing With IRT-Regularizer
summary: As deep learning models continue to advance, knowledge tracing models have achieved higher accuracy. However, these gains come at the cost of reduced interpretability, which is crucial for practitioners in educational settings to adopt new methodologies. Additionally, deep learning models are prone to overfitting, particularly when dealing with the small datasets that are common in educational applications. In this paper, we propose a novel regularization technique designed to enhance the robustness of deep-learning-based knowledge tracing models, while simultaneously improving their interpretability. Our method addresses both the interpretability and overfitting challenges, making it more feasible for real-world educational applications.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses two critical challenges in deep learning-based knowledge tracing: (1) reduced interpretability of complex models, and (2) overfitting on small educational datasets. The authors propose a novel regularization technique that simultaneously improves model robustness and interpretability for real-world educational applications.
AI.motivation: Deep learning knowledge tracing models have achieved higher accuracy but suffer from two major issues: (1) reduced interpretability, which is crucial for educational practitioners to adopt new methods, and (2) overfitting tendency, especially problematic with small datasets common in educational settings. These limitations hinder practical deployment in real-world educational applications.
AI.method: The paper proposes a novel regularization technique specifically designed for deep-learning-based knowledge tracing models. This method is intended to enhance model robustness while simultaneously improving interpretability.
AI.result: The proposed method addresses both interpretability and overfitting challenges, making deep learning knowledge tracing models more feasible for real-world educational applications.
AI.conclusion: The novel regularization technique successfully enhances robustness and interpretability of deep learning knowledge tracing models, bridging the gap between accuracy and practical applicability in educational settings.

title: PointLAM: Local Attentive Mamba for Efficient Point-based 3D Object Detection
summary: 3D object detection from LiDAR point clouds faces a fundamental dilemma: voxel-based methods achieve efficiency at the cost of geometric quantization, while point-based methods preserve fidelity but suffer from prohibitive computational bottlenecks. Specifically, point-based architectures are crippled by slow downsampling strategies (e.g., FPS) and expensive dynamic neighbor queries (e.g., k-NN) coupled with costly continuous interactions. To tackle these systemic inefficiencies, we propose PointLAM, a highly efficient and powerful point-based architecture driven by two synergistic innovations. First, to resolve the downsampling bottleneck, we develop the Laplacian Point Sampler (LPS). LPS employs an implicit discrete Laplacian high-pass filter and Doubly Sorted Sampling to achieve fast, structure-aware foreground preservation. Second, to overcome local modeling latency, we design the Local Hadamard Aggregator (LHA). LHA decouples spatial indexing from feature representation using transient grids, and replaces complex continuous interactions with a Hadamard Gating mechanism for topology-aware, attentive modulation. By coupling this local gating with Bi-Directional Mamba (BDM) layers for global sequence modeling, we formulate the Local Attentive Mamba (LAM) block. Powered by this architecture, PointLAM achieves competitive performance on nuScenes and Waymo for point-based detectors. It rivals highly optimized voxel competitors while requiring a fraction of the computational footprint, demonstrating marked superiority in detecting small instances and handling extreme sparsity. Project page: https://pointlam.github.io/.

AI.tldr: PointLAM is a novel point-based 3D object detection architecture that addresses the computational inefficiencies of traditional point-based methods while maintaining their geometric fidelity. It introduces two key innovations: Laplacian Point Sampler (LPS) for fast structure-aware downsampling and Local Hadamard Aggregator (LHA) for efficient local modeling. The architecture achieves competitive performance on nuScenes and Waymo datasets with significantly reduced computational cost compared to voxel-based competitors.
AI.motivation: The paper tackles a fundamental dilemma in LiDAR-based 3D object detection: voxel-based methods are efficient but suffer from geometric quantization loss, while point-based methods preserve geometric fidelity but are computationally prohibitive due to slow downsampling (FPS) and expensive dynamic neighbor queries (k-NN). The goal is to develop an efficient yet powerful point-based architecture.
AI.method: The proposed PointLAM incorporates two synergistic innovations: (1) Laplacian Point Sampler (LPS) uses an implicit discrete Laplacian high-pass filter and Doubly Sorted Sampling for fast, structure-aware foreground preservation during downsampling; (2) Local Hadamard Aggregator (LHA) decouples spatial indexing from feature representation using transient grids and replaces complex continuous interactions with a Hadamard Gating mechanism for topology-aware attentive modulation. These are combined with Bi-Directional Mamba (BDM) layers for global sequence modeling to form the Local Attentive Mamba (LAM) block.
AI.result: PointLAM achieves competitive performance on nuScenes and Waymo datasets for point-based detectors. It rivals highly optimized voxel-based competitors while requiring a fraction of the computational footprint, demonstrating superior capability in detecting small instances and handling extreme sparsity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PointLAM successfully addresses the efficiency bottlenecks of point-based 3D detection architectures through innovative downsampling (LPS) and local modeling (LHA) mechanisms. By achieving a favorable trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency, PointLAM establishes a new paradigm for point-based LiDAR detection, particularly excelling in challenging scenarios like small object detection and sparse point clouds.

title: Matrix AdaGrad: Row-wise and Column-wise Adaptive Subgradient Methods
summary: Adaptive optimization methods such as AdaGrad and Adam are widely used in modern neural-network training, but their adaptive scaling is primarily designed for vector-valued parameters and does not explicitly exploit matrix structure. Recent matrix-aware optimizers demonstrate the benefits of structured optimization, yet a general theoretical framework for deriving matrix-aware adaptivity comparable to that of AdaGrad remains lacking. In this work, we develop a general Online Mirror Descent framework with adaptive proximal functions for matrix-valued parameters, providing a principled approach to deriving matrix-aware adaptive optimization through online regret minimization. By introducing row-wise and column-wise matrix proximal functions and analyzing the resulting regret trade-off, we derive Row-wise Matrix AdaGrad (Row-AdaGrad) and Column-wise Matrix AdaGrad (Column-AdaGrad), with adaptive scaling determined by the accumulated row-wise or column-wise gradient norms. We establish regret guarantees and show that these matrix-aware bounds can be strictly tighter than those of entry-wise AdaGrad under structured gradients. Experiments on matrix factorization and deep neural-network training further demonstrate the benefits of aligning adaptive scaling with matrix structure, including improved optimization stability and trainability at larger learning rates and greater network depths.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a general Online Mirror Descent framework for matrix-valued parameters, deriving Row-AdaGrad and Column-AdaGrad that achieve tighter regret bounds than entry-wise AdaGrad under structured gradients, with improved stability in matrix factorization and deep neural network training.
AI.motivation: Existing adaptive optimization methods (AdaGrad, Adam) are designed for vector-valued parameters and don't explicitly exploit matrix structure. While matrix-aware optimizers exist, a general theoretical framework for deriving matrix-aware adaptivity comparable to AdaGrad was lacking.
AI.method: The authors develop an Online Mirror Descent framework with adaptive proximal functions for matrix-valued parameters. They introduce row-wise and column-wise matrix proximal functions and analyze the resulting regret trade-offs to derive Row-AdaGrad and Column-AdaGrad, with adaptive scaling determined by accumulated row-wise or column-wise gradient norms.
AI.result: The paper establishes regret guarantees showing matrix-aware bounds can be strictly tighter than entry-wise AdaGrad under structured gradients. Experiments on matrix factorization and deep neural-network training demonstrate improved optimization stability and trainability at larger learning rates and greater network depths.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a principled approach to deriving matrix-aware adaptive optimization methods. Row-AdaGrad and Column-AdaGrad successfully align adaptive scaling with matrix structure, offering both theoretical advantages (tighter regret bounds) and practical benefits (improved stability and trainability in deep networks).

title: A Principled Approach to Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
summary: Traditional unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) methods are designed to flag or localise deviations from a normative distribution, ignoring the underlying generative mechanisms of the anomalies. Yet the nature of an anomaly is often as important as its presence. We reformulate UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem, in which the objective is to infer the most probable corruption responsible for each observation. Our framework yields a probabilistic anomaly score as the energy of the inferred corruption parameters, and serves as a principled recipe for developing new UAD algorithms. We derive several existing methods as instances of the general framework, each corresponding to the same energy score under different modelling choices. Experimentally, we study the framework's components in a controlled setting, and improve object-class AUROC on the MVTec AD dataset by 2.3% by adapting the underlying corruption model. Finally, we validate the framework on a brain MRI benchmark, achieving strong detection performance while producing estimates of pathology intensity, bias, and geometry. Code is available at https://github.com/jgmyles/inverse-uad.

AI.tldr: This paper reformulates unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) as a Bayesian inverse problem, where the goal is to infer the most probable corruption that caused each observation. The framework provides a probabilistic anomaly score based on the energy of inferred corruption parameters and serves as a principled basis for developing new UAD algorithms.
AI.motivation: Traditional UAD methods only flag or localize deviations from a normative distribution but ignore the underlying generative mechanisms of anomalies. The nature of an anomaly is often as important as its presence, so the authors seek a more principled approach that can infer what type of corruption caused the anomaly.
AI.method: The authors reformulate UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem. They propose using a probabilistic anomaly score defined as the energy of inferred corruption parameters. The framework derives several existing methods as special cases under different modeling choices.
AI.result:
1. The framework improves object-class AUROC on MVTec AD dataset by 2.3% through adapting the underlying corruption model.
2. On brain MRI benchmark, the method achieves strong detection performance while producing estimates of pathology intensity, bias, and geometry.
AI.conclusion: The Bayesian inverse problem formulation provides a principled and unified framework for UAD. It not only detects anomalies but also characterizes their generative mechanisms, enabling both improved detection performance and interpretable outputs (pathology intensity, bias, geometry estimates).

title: Federated Deep Clustering Networks for High-Dimensional and Heterogeneous Data
comment: Accepted to the 4th International Conference on Federated Learning Technologies and Applications (FLTA 2026)
summary: Clustering high-dimensional data is a fundamental task in unsupervised machine learning with applications to a variety of domains. In the centralized data scenario, this task is commonly solved using deep clustering methods that utilize deep neural network architectures to learn clustering-friendly latent space representations. In Federated Learning, where data is distributed between clients and is private, deep clustering methods are less explored. In particular, recently introduced federated deep clustering methods, despite showing very promising performance, still fall short in reliably providing good performance if data across clients are non-identically-independently distributed. In this work, we introduce a generalization of Deep Clustering Networks to the federated scenario, named FedDCN, that simultaneously optimizes a reconstruction loss and a clustering loss. To ensure robustness and latent space alignment in non-identically-independently distributed data scenarios, FedDCN generates synthetic data augmentations, and its learning objective includes a geometric regularization for latent space alignment. Through experimental evaluation, the effectiveness of the approach under IID and non-IID assumptions is demonstrated, and future research directions are identified.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FedDCN, a federated deep clustering method that extends Deep Clustering Networks to the distributed learning setting. It addresses the challenge of clustering high-dimensional data across clients while handling non-IID data distributions through synthetic data augmentations and geometric regularization for latent space alignment.
AI.motivation: While deep clustering methods excel in centralized data scenarios, they are underexplored in Federated Learning where data is distributed across clients and must remain private. Existing federated deep clustering methods fail to provide reliable performance when data across clients is non-identically-independently distributed (non-IID).
AI.method: FedDCN extends Deep Clustering Networks to the federated setting by simultaneously optimizing: (1) a reconstruction loss, and (2) a clustering loss. To ensure robustness with non-IID data, the method generates synthetic data augmentations and includes a geometric regularization term for latent space alignment across clients.
AI.result: The effectiveness of FedDCN is demonstrated through experimental evaluation under both IID and non-IID data distribution assumptions.
AI.conclusion: FedDCN successfully generalizes deep clustering to the federated scenario. The approach shows effectiveness under both IID and non-IID settings, with future research directions identified for further improvement.

title: VideoReloc: Long-Term Indoor Video Relocalization against a Kilobyte-Scale Semantic Scene Graph
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://videoreloc.github.io
summary: Given a compact semantic scene graph, long-term indoor video relocalization estimates a map-frame trajectory after lighting and furniture changes. Visual methods rely on appearance and become unreliable under these changes; localizing one frame at a time from object classes and geometry instead leaves sparse, ambiguous evidence. We introduce VideoReloc, whose adaptive clips use odometry to gather spatial evidence until object and motion criteria are met, adapting query length to the observed scene. Its run-level decision rechecks conflicting placements using evidence accumulated across connected clips, stabilizing the trajectory beyond adjacent-clip tracking. Hypothesis-first registration proposes poses from object triplets and verifies each using clip-wide object centers and box surfaces. Orientation-aware refinement uses box faces, gravity and wall directions to resolve ambiguity in camera orientation and refine the full pose. This reframes sparse-map relocalization as verification of spatially extended video queries, moving discriminative support from stored appearance to temporal context and permitting a 100 kB map of class-labelled boxes. On RIO10 and ReplicaCAD, the all-frame localization success rate at 1 m/10$^\circ$ is 73.5% and 61.1% under causal evaluation, rising to 90.6% and 74.8% with clip closure. The evaluated per-frame scene coordinate regressors reach up to 47.6% and 49.8%, respectively, with maps of 12.6-42 MB. Project page: https://videoreloc.github.io

AI.tldr: VideoReloc is a long-term indoor video relocalization method that uses adaptive video clips with odometry to gather spatial evidence, combined with hypothesis-first registration and orientation-aware refinement to achieve robust localization using only 100 kB maps of class-labeled boxes.
AI.motivation: Visual appearance-based methods become unreliable under lighting and furniture changes; per-frame localization from object classes and geometry provides sparse, ambiguous evidence. The goal is to handle long-term indoor scene changes with minimal map size.
AI.method: Adaptive clips use odometry to gather spatial evidence until object and motion criteria are met. Run-level decision rechecks conflicting placements using evidence across connected clips. Hypothesis-first registration proposes poses from object triplets verified by clip-wide object centers and box surfaces. Orientation-aware refinement uses box faces, gravity, and wall directions to resolve camera orientation ambiguity.
AI.result: On RIO10: 73.5% (causal) → 90.6% (with clip closure) at 1m/10°. On ReplicaCAD: 61.1% (causal) → 74.8% (with clip closure). Per-frame scene coordinate regressors achieve 47.6% and 49.8% respectively, using maps of 12.6-42 MB, compared to VideoReloc's 100 kB maps.
AI.conclusion: Spatially extended video queries with temporal context provide more discriminative support than stored appearance or single-frame methods. The approach achieves high localization accuracy with extremely compact maps (100 kB vs 12.6-42 MB), successfully reframing sparse-map relocalization as verification of video queries.

title: The Weight Is Over - Interactive Diffusion on Consumer GPUs
summary: On-device inference is booming, but the momentum is almost all in language models. Diffusion pipelines are memory hungry, latency-sensitive, and require orchestrating an embedder, a transformer, a decoder, and often further postprocessing that is not as standardized as LLM inference loops are. We navigate the trade-off between performance, quality, and model footprint to reach as many client devices in the wild as possible. We make three contributions: an embedding translator that maps a small text encoder into a large encoder space to cut weight and latency; a reproducible sweep recipe for navigating the speed/quality/memory triangle in diffusion pipelines; and an interactive on-device image generation editor achieving sub-second TTFI on recent GPUs.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of deploying diffusion models for on-device image generation, which is complex due to high memory requirements, latency issues, and multi-component orchestration. The authors propose three key contributions: an embedding translator to reduce encoder size, a systematic evaluation method for speed/quality/memory trade-offs, and an interactive editor achieving sub-second image generation on GPUs.
AI.motivation: While on-device inference has grown rapidly for language models, diffusion-based image generation faces significant challenges in deployment due to memory intensity, latency sensitivity, and the complexity of orchestrating multiple components (embedder, transformer, decoder, postprocessing). The motivation is to make diffusion models accessible on client devices while maintaining acceptable quality and performance.
AI.method: The authors introduce: (1) An embedding translator that maps a small text encoder into a large encoder space, reducing weight and latency while preserving quality; (2) A reproducible sweep recipe—a systematic methodology for exploring the trade-off space between speed, quality, and memory in diffusion pipelines; (3) An interactive on-device image generation editor built on these optimizations.
AI.result: The proposed approach achieves sub-second TTFI (time to first image) on recent GPUs while maintaining quality. The embedding translator effectively reduces model footprint and latency by mapping small encoders into large encoder spaces, enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that diffusion models can be effectively deployed on client devices through careful architectural optimizations (embedding translation) and systematic evaluation methods. The interactive on-device editor proves the practical viability of sub-second image generation, making diffusion-based image creation accessible on consumer hardware.

title: Object Detection Benchmarks are Incomplete: The Role of Label Errors and Annotation Uncertainty
summary: While object detection has advanced through improved architectures and open-vocabulary models, we provide strong evidence that benchmark quality is limited by annotation incompleteness. Across four widely used datasets (COCO, Pascal VOC, Cityscapes, KITTI), re-annotation reveals substantial increases in annotated objects (e.g., up to +60% on KITTI and +40% on COCO), driven primarily by previously unlabeled small, occluded, or densely packed instances. While some differences arise from dataset-specific annotation conventions, we consistently find that missing annotations are the main source of label errors across all datasets. To achieve high data quality, we introduce a scalable annotation pipeline that emphasizes high recall and captures ambiguity through soft labels aggregated from at least 11 annotators per object. The resulting annotations improve coverage and align well with human calibration. We show that benchmark performance is highly sensitive to annotation quality, although model rankings remain largely stable. We introduce two large-scale benchmarks: (i) an uncertainty-aware object detection benchmark, and (ii) a label error detection benchmark grounded in real label errors. We show that current detectors are strongly depended on annotation quality and are misaligned with human perception. Current label error detection methods, which have been shown to perform well on synthetic noise, struggle to achieve high recall and precision on real label errors. Our results highlight the need for future object detection benchmarks to move beyond deterministic annotations toward high-recall, uncertainty-aware evaluation that maximizes valid instances and better reflects real-world ambiguity.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that existing object detection benchmarks (COCO, Pascal VOC, Cityscapes, KITTI) suffer from significant annotation incompleteness, with re-annotation revealing up to 60% more objects. The authors propose a scalable high-recall annotation pipeline with soft labels from 11+ annotators, creating two new benchmarks: an uncertainty-aware detection benchmark and a label error detection benchmark. They demonstrate that while benchmark performance is sensitive to annotation quality, model rankings remain stable, but current detectors are misaligned with human perception.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from the observation that while object detection models and architectures have advanced significantly, the quality of benchmarks themselves may be limiting progress. The authors provide strong evidence that annotation incompleteness - missing annotations for objects that exist in images - is a major issue across widely-used datasets, which could lead to misleading performance evaluations and misaligned model development.
AI.method: The authors conducted a comprehensive re-annotation study across four major datasets (COCO, Pascal VOC, Cityscapes, KITTI). They developed a scalable annotation pipeline emphasizing high recall, using soft labels aggregated from at least 11 annotators per object to capture ambiguity. They also created two new large-scale benchmarks: (i) an uncertainty-aware object detection benchmark with probabilistic annotations, and (ii) a label error detection benchmark based on real label errors identified during re-annotation.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) Substantial increases in annotated objects were found across all datasets - up to +60% on KITTI and +40% on COCO. (2) Missing annotations are the primary source of label errors, mainly affecting small, occluded, or densely packed instances. (3) While benchmark performance is highly sensitive to annotation quality, model rankings remain largely stable. (4) Current detectors are strongly dependent on annotation quality and are misaligned with human perception. (5) Existing label error detection methods that perform well on synthetic noise struggle with real label errors, failing to achieve high recall and precision.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that future object detection benchmarks need to move beyond deterministic annotations toward high-recall, uncertainty-aware evaluation that maximizes valid instances and better reflects real-world ambiguity. This requires new annotation approaches that capture the inherent uncertainty in object detection and provide more comprehensive coverage of objects in images.

title: Neural Cellular Automata Learn General Features in their Hidden Channels
summary: Modern deep learning models achieve impressive generalization through over-parameterization, but this paradigm often struggles with overfitting and memorization in few-shot regimes. Neural Cellular Automata (NCAs) offer a highly parameter-efficient alternative, yet research has focused primarily on their output, leaving the role of their internal hidden channels largely unexplored. In this paper, we investigate the internal dynamics of NCA hidden channels and introduce a novel transfer-learning mechanism that injects a pretrained teacher's hidden states into a student model to guide early optimization. Evaluated on few-shot and scale-variant MNIST benchmarks, NCAs outperform comparable recurrent and feed-forward architectures, demonstrating superior generalization with a minimal parameter budget (~9,800 parameters). Mechanistic analysis reveals that the hidden channels decouple feature extraction from uniform classification consensus by absorbing morphological complexity and converging to mutually orthogonal states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these hidden channels capture general, scale-invariant topological primitives rather than class-specific templates. This allows a student model to achieve strong few-shot performance on unseen classes using features transferred from a teacher trained only on a subset of digits (0-5). Our results highlight the potential of utilizing hidden-state dynamics as a robust, decentralized computational substrate for parameter-efficient transfer learning

AI.tldr: This paper investigates Neural Cellular Automata (NCAs) for few-shot learning, introducing a transfer-learning mechanism that uses pretrained teacher hidden states to guide student optimization. NCAs with ~9,800 parameters outperform recurrent and feed-forward architectures on few-shot and scale-variant MNIST benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Modern deep learning struggles with overfitting in few-shot regimes despite over-parameterization. NCAs offer parameter-efficient alternatives, but prior research focuses on outputs rather than internal hidden channels. This work explores hidden channel dynamics and their potential for transfer learning.
AI.method: 1) Investigate NCA hidden channel dynamics 2) Develop transfer-learning mechanism injecting pretrained teacher's hidden states into student model 3) Evaluate on few-shot and scale-variant MNIST benchmarks 4) Analyze mechanistic behavior of hidden channels
AI.result: NCAs outperform comparable recurrent and feed-forward architectures with minimal parameter budget (~9,800). Hidden channels decouple feature extraction from uniform classification consensus by absorbing morphological complexity and converging to mutually orthogonal states. These channels capture general, scale-invariant topological primitives rather than class-specific templates, enabling student models to achieve strong few-shot performance on unseen classes using features from teacher trained only on digits 0-5.
AI.conclusion: NCA hidden-state dynamics serve as a robust, decentralized computational substrate for parameter-efficient transfer learning, capturing generalizable topological features that transfer across classes and scales.

title: Morphology-Aware Ambiguity Learning for Wafer Defect Decision Support
summary: Wafer map defect recognition is commonly formulated as a fixed-taxonomy classification problem that assigns each wafer to a single defect class. However, some wafers exhibit morphologies near class boundaries, for which forcing a single prediction may be less informative than providing plausible diagnostic alternatives. This paper proposes a morphology-aware ambiguity learning framework that supports three diagnostic actions: automatic single-class diagnosis, assisted diagnosis with two plausible defect classes, and full review. Using the radial, angular, and geometric characteristics of training wafer maps, the framework constructs a class-level ambiguity matrix representing defect-class pairs with similar morphology and plausible diagnostic alternatives. It guides the model to learn plausible alternative classes rather than treating all incorrect classes equally. During inference, the matrix determines whether an uncertain prediction can be represented by a meaningful two-class diagnostic set or should be escalated for full review. Experiments on WM-811K show that the proposed framework outperforms conventional approaches in defect recognition and diagnostic decision support, providing meaningful two-class alternatives while reserving full review for cases with unresolved ambiguity. Illustrative cost analyses further show the potential cost advantage of the proposed routing strategy. The diagnostic behavior of the framework remains consistent across different backbone architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a morphology-aware ambiguity learning framework for wafer map defect recognition that supports three diagnostic actions: automatic single-class diagnosis, assisted diagnosis with two plausible alternatives, and full review. It uses radial, angular, and geometric characteristics to construct a class-level ambiguity matrix that guides learning of plausible alternative classes.
AI.motivation: Conventional wafer map defect recognition treats the problem as fixed-taxonomy classification assigning each wafer to a single defect class. However, wafers with morphologies near class boundaries are poorly served by single predictions, as they may have multiple plausible diagnostic alternatives. This work addresses the need for more informative diagnostic support for ambiguous cases.
AI.method: The framework uses radial, angular, and geometric characteristics of training wafer maps to construct a class-level ambiguity matrix representing defect-class pairs with similar morphology. This matrix guides the model to learn plausible alternative classes rather than treating all incorrect classes equally. During inference, the matrix determines whether an uncertain prediction can be represented by a meaningful two-class diagnostic set or should be escalated for full review.
AI.result: Experiments on WM-811K dataset show the proposed framework outperforms conventional approaches in defect recognition and diagnostic decision support. It provides meaningful two-class alternatives while reserving full review for cases with unresolved ambiguity. Cost analyses demonstrate potential cost advantages of the routing strategy. The diagnostic behavior remains consistent across different backbone architectures.
AI.conclusion: The morphology-aware ambiguity learning framework effectively addresses boundary cases in wafer map defect recognition by providing flexible diagnostic options. The approach maintains performance while offering valuable diagnostic alternatives, with consistent results across architectures and potential cost benefits.

title: Geometric Mean Pooling for Equal-Weight Multiplicative Coarse-Graining
summary: As an alternative to the additive and extremal biases of average and max pooling, we introduce Geometric Mean Pooling (GMP), a signed pooling operator that combines the product of feature signs with the geometric mean of feature magnitudes. Motivated by local-to-global composition in quantum many-body physics, GMP retains both joint sign information and a characteristic multiplicative scale without introducing learnable pooling parameters. We show that non-overlapping hierarchical GMP preserves the corresponding global multiplicative statistic and evaluate it on synthetic sequence tasks, iterative coarse-graining, image classification, and molecular lipophilicity regression. On the synthetic tasks, GMP recovers product-based signals more accurately than average and max pooling and maintains predictive performance under the tested levels of multiplicative input noise. On image and molecular data, however, its effectiveness depends on the representation, target parameterization, and placement of local and global pooling. These results position GMP as a complementary, regime-dependent inductive bias for tasks in which equal-weight multiplicative composition is plausible, rather than as a universal replacement for standard pooling operators.

AI.tldr: Geometric Mean Pooling (GMP) is introduced as an alternative pooling operator that combines feature sign products with geometric mean of magnitudes, addressing biases in average and max pooling. It preserves multiplicative scale without learnable parameters and shows promise on synthetic tasks but effectiveness varies on real-world data depending on representation and task characteristics.
AI.motivation: To address the additive bias of average pooling and extremal bias of max pooling by introducing a pooling operator motivated by local-to-global composition in quantum many-body physics, which can preserve joint sign information and multiplicative scale.
AI.method: GMP combines the product of feature signs with the geometric mean of feature magnitudes. It is a non-learnable pooling operator that preserves global multiplicative statistics in hierarchical compositions. Evaluated on synthetic sequence tasks, iterative coarse-graining, image classification, and molecular lipophilicity regression.
AI.result: On synthetic tasks, GMP recovers product-based signals more accurately than average and max pooling and maintains performance under multiplicative input noise. On image and molecular data, effectiveness depends on representation, target parameterization, and placement of local and global pooling.
AI.conclusion: GMP serves as a complementary, regime-dependent inductive bias suitable for tasks where equal-weight multiplicative composition is plausible, rather than a universal replacement for standard pooling operators.

title: Chronosphere: Space-Time Tessellation of Local Climate Experts
summary: We introduce Chronosphere, a spatio-temporal neural field that learns representations of climate. A central challenge in geographic representation learning is modeling environmental processes whose spatial and temporal complexity varies widely. Yet existing location encoders typically fix a single level of detail everywhere. Global bases such as spherical harmonics spread capacity uniformly across space and time. Localized bases resolve only predefined regions. Learned tessellations adapt, but are inefficient at representing higher frequencies. Chronosphere unifies these approaches, pairing an adaptive tessellation of learnable sites on the spacetime torus $S^2\times S^1$ with a shared bank of local basis functions. Both where capacity is placed and how much detail each region carries adapt to the data, across space and time. Trained to reconstruct climatology, Chronosphere matches or leads state-of-the-art location encoders across spatial and temporal tasks, with the largest gains under spatial and temporal transfer.

AI.tldr: Chronosphere is a spatio-temporal neural field that learns adaptive representations of climate data by combining learnable site tessellation on the spacetime torus (S² × S¹) with shared local basis functions, allowing capacity allocation to adapt across both space and time.
AI.motivation: The central challenge is that environmental processes have varying spatial and temporal complexity, but existing location encoders use fixed detail levels everywhere. Global bases like spherical harmonics spread capacity uniformly, localized bases only resolve predefined regions, and learned tessellations are inefficient for higher frequencies. There's a need for a unified approach that can adaptively allocate computational capacity based on the data.
AI.method: Chronosphere combines two components: (1) an adaptive tessellation of learnable sites on the spacetime torus S² × S¹ (representing spatial sphere S² and temporal circle S¹), and (2) a shared bank of local basis functions. Both the placement of capacity (where detail is added) and the level of detail per region adapt to the data across space and time. The model is trained to reconstruct climatology.
AI.result: Chronosphere matches or exceeds state-of-the-art location encoders across spatial and temporal tasks. The most significant improvements are observed under spatial and temporal transfer conditions, demonstrating strong generalization capability.
AI.conclusion: Chronosphere successfully unifies global, local, and learned tessellation approaches to representation learning. Its adaptive capacity allocation across spacetime enables superior performance, particularly for transfer learning scenarios where the model must generalize to new spatial regions or time periods not seen during training.

title: Detecting Pretraining Data in Large Language Models from a Free-Energy Perspective
summary: Detecting pretraining data in large language models is challenging because high likelihood can reflect either training exposure or strong generalization. In the joint space of prediction loss and predictive entropy, a likelihood-only detector uses a horizontal boundary and can mistake predictable non-members for members. Motivated by this, we introduce an inclined boundary that evaluates prediction loss relative to predictive entropy. Our analysis shows that entropy correction can preserve the expected membership signal while reducing its variance, thereby improving standardized member--non-member separation. We further extend the mean--variance analysis to the more general setting with a nonzero mean entropy gap. Interestingly, this entropy-adjusted score admits a Helmholtz free-energy interpretation, leading to Energy Transfer Detection (ETD), which views pretraining data detection from a macroscopic residual free-energy transfer perspective. Extensive experiments show that ETD achieves the best average detection performance, improving average AUROC by up to 3.5\% and TPR@5\%FPR by up to 5.1\%, while remaining robust across diverse settings.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Energy Transfer Detection (ETD), a method for detecting pretraining data in large language models by using an entropy-corrected score that evaluates prediction loss relative to predictive entropy, achieving up to 3.5% AUROC and 5.1% TPR@5%FPR improvements.
AI.motivation: Detecting pretraining data in LLMs is challenging because high likelihood can result from either training exposure or strong generalization. Existing likelihood-only detectors use horizontal boundaries in the joint space of prediction loss and predictive entropy, which can mistakenly identify predictable non-members as members.
AI.method: The authors propose an inclined boundary that evaluates prediction loss relative to predictive entropy (entropy correction). They extend mean-variance analysis to the general setting with nonzero mean entropy gap and show that the entropy-adjusted score admits a Helmholtz free-energy interpretation, leading to the Energy Transfer Detection (ETD) approach.
AI.result: ETD achieves the best average detection performance, improving average AUROC by up to 3.5% and TPR@5%FPR by up to 5.1% while remaining robust across diverse settings.
AI.conclusion: The entropy correction approach preserves the expected membership signal while reducing its variance, thereby improving standardized member-non-member separation. The Helmholtz free-energy interpretation provides a theoretical foundation for viewing pretraining data detection from a macroscopic residual free-energy transfer perspective.

title: Benchmarking the Explanatory Quality of Open-Weight Vision-Language Models in Face Recognition
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have recently been proposed as promising tools for face recognition, as they can produce natural language explanations alongside similarity scores. This capability is considered appealing for face comparisons in forensic contexts, which require decisions to be transparent and auditable. However, existing evaluations of VLMs for that use case focus mostly on recognition accuracy, while the validity of generated explanations remains unquantified. In this work, we introduce a benchmarking framework for VLM-based face recognition that treats explanation quality as a core evaluation axis. We propose two criteria that explanations should satisfy: relevance, i.e., reliance on identity-stable facial features; and faithfulness, i.e., alignment with the visible image content without hallucinated features. We jointly develop a methodology enabling the quantification of relevance and faithfulness of evaluated models, based on constraining model outputs to a structured explanation format that supports automated querying and auditing. Using this framework, we benchmark several families of open-weight VLMs, jointly evaluating face verification accuracy and explanation quality. Our results highlight remaining shortcomings of produced explanations, and emphasize the need for such explanation quality metrics to get a complete picture of model performance. The proposed benchmark and open-source evaluation harness provide a foundation for proper benchmarking and future fine-tuning of explainable face recognition systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a benchmarking framework for evaluating Vision-Language Models (VLMs) used in face recognition, with a focus on assessing the quality of natural language explanations generated alongside similarity scores. The framework evaluates two key criteria: relevance (reliance on identity-stable facial features) and faithfulness (alignment with actual image content without hallucinations).
AI.motivation: While VLMs have been proposed for forensic face recognition due to their ability to provide transparent, auditable decisions through natural language explanations, existing evaluations focus solely on recognition accuracy without quantifying the validity of generated explanations. This gap in evaluation methodology creates a critical need for proper assessment of explanation quality.
AI.method: The authors propose a benchmarking framework that constrains model outputs to a structured explanation format enabling automated querying and auditing. They develop a methodology to jointly quantify relevance (extent to which explanations rely on identity-stable features) and faithfulness (alignment with visible image content without hallucinated features). Several open-weight VLM families are benchmarked, evaluating both face verification accuracy and explanation quality.
AI.result: The results reveal significant shortcomings in the quality of explanations produced by current VLMs. The study emphasizes that explanation quality metrics are essential for obtaining a complete picture of model performance in explainable face recognition systems.
AI.conclusion: The proposed benchmark and open-source evaluation harness provide a foundation for proper benchmarking and future fine-tuning of explainable face recognition systems. The work highlights the need to move beyond accuracy-only evaluations when deploying VLMs in forensic contexts where transparency and auditability are critical requirements.

title: LLMs as Feature Engineers for Text-and-Tabular Prediction
summary: We introduce an iterative framework that automates the extraction of interpretable, schema-bound categorical features from unstructured text for tabular prediction models. To navigate the feature space, a generator LLM proposes semantic definitions, a separate extractor LLM materializes the features, and a downstream tabular model evaluates their predictive performance. We optimize this search by translating explicit model errors, such as AUC ranking inversions, into natural-language feedback, steering the LLM to resolve specific predictive failures. Evaluated across three public datasets, this error-driven loop accelerates feature discovery by up to $3\times$ compared to unguided search. Empirically, the generated features demonstrate strong multi-view complementarity, strictly outperforming any subset when combined with TF-IDF and dense embeddings. Finally, the framework guarantees instance-level interpretability: the discovered features dominate SHAP importance rankings and provide a fully transparent, semantic audit trail for every prediction.
