AI.tldr: An iterative framework that automates extraction of interpretable categorical features from unstructured text using dual LLMs (generator and extractor) with error-driven feedback loops for tabular prediction models.
AI.motivation: Automate the extraction of interpretable, schema-bound categorical features from unstructured text to improve tabular prediction models, addressing the need for both predictive performance and interpretability.
AI.method: Dual-LLM approach: (1) Generator LLM proposes semantic feature definitions, (2) Extractor LLM materializes features, (3) Downstream tabular model evaluates predictive performance. Error-driven feedback loop translates model errors (e.g., AUC ranking inversions) into natural language to guide LLM search.
AI.result: Up to 3× faster feature discovery vs unguided search; generated features show strong multi-view complementarity, strictly outperforming any subset when combined with TF-IDF and dense embeddings; dominate SHAP importance rankings.
AI.conclusion: The framework achieves both high predictive performance and full instance-level interpretability with transparent semantic audit trails for every prediction.

title: Catena: A Comprehensive Software Suite for Large-Scale Connectomics
summary: The gold standard datasets for mapping connectomes are electron microscopy volumes of densely labeled neural tissue at nanometer resolution. Yet reconstructing and proofreading neuronal arbors and annotating all synapses requires pipelining multiple software tools that are often fragmented, inconsistently maintained, or proprietary, hindering reproducibility and automation. Here, we introduce Catena, an open-source, comprehensive, developer-centric software suite for connectomics that integrates modules for 3D neuron and organelle segmentation, synapse detection, microtubule tracking, and neurotransmitter inference. Catena organizes its modules in composable, chunk-wise processing pipelines in a completely documented, extensible, and adaptable design. We further reduce compute and ground-truth data requirements with pretrained machine learning models, facilitating fine-tuning. Catena ships fully containerized modules that encapsulate evolving dependencies for consistent execution across workstations and clusters. By consolidating open components, shareable models, and containerized runtimes, Catena delivers a reproducible and scalable approach to mapping cellular connectomes from electron microscopy volumes. Code and documentation: https://github.com/Mohinta2892/catena.git

AI.tldr: Catena is an open-source, comprehensive, developer-centric software suite for connectomics that integrates multiple modules for 3D neuron and organelle segmentation, synapse detection, microtubule tracking, and neurotransmitter inference from electron microscopy volumes.
AI.motivation: The gold standard datasets for mapping connectomes are electron microscopy volumes, but reconstructing and proofreading neuronal arbors requires pipelining multiple software tools that are often fragmented, inconsistently maintained, or proprietary, hindering reproducibility and automation.
AI.method: Catena organizes its modules in composable, chunk-wise processing pipelines with a completely documented, extensible, and adaptable design. It uses pretrained machine learning models to reduce compute and ground-truth data requirements, facilitating fine-tuning. All modules are fully containerized to encapsulate evolving dependencies for consistent execution across workstations and clusters.
AI.result: Catena consolidates open components, shareable models, and containerized runtimes to deliver a reproducible and scalable approach to mapping cellular connectomes from electron microscopy volumes.
AI.conclusion: Catena provides an integrated solution for connectomics that enables reproducible and automated processing of electron microscopy data through its comprehensive, modular, and containerized design.

title: ExpBoN: Exponential-Noise Best-of-$n$ for Efficient Test-Time LLM Alignment
summary: Best-of-$n$ (BoN) sampling is a simple yet effective inference-time alignment method, but hard maximization provides only coarse control over the trade-off between reward and distribution shift. Soft Best-of-$n$ (Verdun et al. 2025) provides smoother control and converges to the optimal distribution associated with KL-regularized reward maximization. In this paper, we introduce ExpBoN, an alternative soft BoN method based on the exponential-noise report-noisy-max mechanism. It admits an exact finite-$n$ decomposition, which yields exponentially fast convergence in total variation, expected reward, and both directions of KL divergence. We provide comprehensive theoretical analyses of its convergence and regret behavior. We further integrate ExpBoN into the guided speculative inference (GSI) framework (Geuter, Mroueh, and AlvarezMelis 2025), resulting in ExpGSI, for efficient reward-guided LLM alignment. ExpGSI yields substantial reductions in computational cost while maintaining comparable accuracy. Experiments on MATH500, MMLU-STEM, and Minerva Math with the Qwen2.5-Math and Qwen3 model families show that ExpGSI reduces estimated computation by $14\%$-$39\%$ across candidate budgets for Qwen2.5-Math and by up to $45\%$ at $n=16$ for Qwen3. Overall, our results provide a theoretical and algorithmic foundation for exponential-noise BoN and efficient test-time LLM alignment.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ExpBoN, a novel soft Best-of-n (BoN) alignment method based on the exponential-noise report-noisy-max mechanism. It provides exact finite-n decomposition with exponentially fast convergence in total variation, expected reward, and KL divergence. The method is integrated into guided speculative inference (GSI) to create ExpGSI, achieving 14-45% computational reduction while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: Standard Best-of-n (BoN) sampling provides only coarse control over the trade-off between reward and distribution shift. While Soft BoN offers smoother control, this paper aims to develop a method with stronger theoretical guarantees including exact finite-n decomposition and exponentially fast convergence properties.
AI.method: ExpBoN is based on the exponential-noise report-noisy-max mechanism, which admits an exact finite-n decomposition. The method is integrated into the Guided Speculative Inference (GSI) framework to create ExpGSI for efficient reward-guided LLM alignment.
AI.result: ExpBoN achieves exponentially fast convergence in total variation, expected reward, and both directions of KL divergence. ExpGSI reduces estimated computation by 14-39% across candidate budgets for Qwen2.5-Math and by up to 45% at n=16 for Qwen3, while maintaining comparable accuracy on MATH500, MMLU-STEM, and Minerva Math.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a theoretical and algorithmic foundation for exponential-noise BoN and efficient test-time LLM alignment, demonstrating that ExpBoN offers strong theoretical guarantees (exact decomposition, exponential convergence) combined with practical efficiency gains through ExpGSI integration.

title: The Role of Radiometric Features in Cross-Site Leaf-Wood Segmentation of LiDAR Point Clouds
comment: 5 pages, 6 figures. Accepted for presentation at IGARSS 2026 (IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium)
summary: Leaf-wood segmentation of individual trees from LiDAR point clouds is essential for quantitative structure models (QSMs) used in non-destructive biomass estimation. Existing segmentation methods typically exclude radiometric features (e.g., intensity, return number) to maximize cross-sensor compatibility. We challenge this design choice by evaluating cross-site and cross-platform generalization: training on the public Heidelberg dataset (terrestrial TLS, 1550nm) and testing on a novel dataset from Ontario, Canada (RPA-LS, 905nm). Results show that geometry-only methods - including state-of-the-art deep learning models trained on high-density LiDAR datasets - fail to generalize to the sparse, top-down geometry of aerial scans, achieving F1 scores <= 0.56. Incorporating radiometric features (intensity, return number, number of returns) improves F1 to 0.61, but more critically, increases wood recall by 119% from 0.16 to 0.35. Furthermore, geometry-only approaches often result in fragmented stem and branch components. We find that leveraging radiometric features preserves greater structural connectivity, resulting in more coherent architectures that are better suited for QSM reconstruction. We demonstrate that while geometric patterns are view-dependent and prone to overfitting scan patterns, radiometric features encode physical material properties that generalize across disparate sensors and environments.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the common practice of excluding radiometric features in leaf-wood segmentation from LiDAR point clouds. The authors demonstrate that geometry-only methods fail to generalize across different sensors and scan patterns, while incorporating radiometric features (intensity, return number) significantly improves cross-platform generalization and preserves structural connectivity essential for quantitative structure models (QSMs).
AI.motivation: Existing leaf-wood segmentation methods typically exclude radiometric features to maximize cross-sensor compatibility. However, the authors argue this design choice is flawed because geometric patterns are view-dependent and prone to overfitting to specific scan patterns, limiting generalization to different sensors and environments.
AI.method: The authors evaluated cross-site and cross-platform generalization by training on the public Heidelberg dataset (terrestrial TLS, 1550nm) and testing on a novel dataset from Ontario, Canada (RPA-LS, 905nm). They compared geometry-only methods (including state-of-the-art deep learning models) against methods incorporating radiometric features (intensity, return number, number of returns).
AI.result: Geometry-only methods achieved F1 scores ≤ 0.56 on the cross-platform test, failing to generalize to sparse aerial scans. Adding radiometric features improved F1 to 0.61 and increased wood recall by 119% (from 0.16 to 0.35). Geometry-only approaches also resulted in fragmented stem and branch components, while radiometric features preserved greater structural connectivity.
AI.conclusion: Radiometric features encode physical material properties that generalize across disparate sensors and environments, unlike view-dependent geometric patterns. Incorporating radiometric features is crucial for developing robust leaf-wood segmentation methods suitable for QSM reconstruction across diverse scanning platforms.

title: Intervention Granularity Matters: Coherent Treatment Bundles in Counterfactual Simulation with Clinical World Models
summary: Counterfactual simulation with a clinical world model means fixing a patient's history, changing the treatment, and reading off the predicted response. Doing so requires deciding what counts as one intervention. In clinical settings, interventions are documented as bundles: a co-occurrence audit of 945,707 patient-hours from MIMIC-IV shows groups of components, such as every parameter of a dialysis circuit, that never appear apart, so an edit that changes one component on its own describes an hour that never occurs in the data. We hypothesize that the granularity at which an intervention is edited changes how a world model responds, and test this with Clin-JEPA, a latent world model of patient trajectories conditioned on hourly treatment text. At 1,019 documented onsets of invasive ventilation, we keep the patient's history and other treatments fixed and compare editing one ventilator setting with editing the complete configuration recorded for a real patient with the most similar recent trajectory. The complete bundle moves the predicted next state further than any single setting, consistently across all five settings, and the difference remains after accounting for how much each edit changes the model's input. Intervention granularity therefore materially affects the response of a clinical world model: single-component edits may understate treatment sensitivity, and bundle-aware editing may offer a better-supported basis for counterfactual treatment simulation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how the granularity of treatment interventions affects counterfactual simulation in clinical world models. Using Clin-JEPA on MIMIC-IV data, the study finds that editing complete intervention bundles produces larger predicted state changes than editing single components, suggesting single-component edits may underestimate treatment effects.
AI.motivation: The research addresses a fundamental question in clinical AI: how to appropriately model counterfactual treatment scenarios. The authors observed that clinical interventions are documented as bundles (groups of related components that always occur together), but it's unclear whether editing single components versus complete bundles affects model predictions differently.
AI.method: The study analyzed 945,707 patient-hours from MIMIC-IV to identify intervention bundles. They used Clin-JEPA, a latent world model conditioned on hourly treatment text. At 1,019 invasive ventilation onsets, they compared two editing approaches: (1) changing a single ventilator setting while keeping history and other treatments fixed, and (2) editing the complete configuration from the most similar real patient. They controlled for the magnitude of input changes to isolate the effect of granularity.
AI.result: The complete intervention bundle consistently moved the predicted next state further than any single setting, across all five ventilator settings tested. This difference persisted after accounting for how much each edit changed the model's input, indicating that granularity itself affects the model's response.
AI.conclusion: Intervention granularity materially affects clinical world model responses. Single-component edits may understate treatment sensitivity, while bundle-aware editing provides a more realistic basis for counterfactual treatment simulation. This has important implications for clinical decision support and treatment effect estimation.

title: Info3R: Information-Adaptive Test-Time Training for 3D Reconstruction
summary: Transformer-based models have recently achieved strong performance on 3D reconstruction from images, and recent works extend them to process video streams in an online manner for real-world deployment. However, existing methods overlook two key signals when handling long image streams: the importance of each incoming frame and the information saturation of the model's internal state. In this paper, we propose Info3R, a novel information-adaptive test-time training method for the online 3D reconstruction. We introduce an information-aware state update that modulates the state update strength based on the redundancy and informativeness of each incoming frame. To restore the state's plasticity -- its capacity to incorporate new observations -- we propose a dynamic state reset, triggered by the cumulative magnitude of state updates and the model's prediction confidence and accompanied by an anchor-to-world alignment. Our method achieves consistent improvements on camera pose estimation, video depth estimation, and 3D reconstruction, while substantially mitigating the performance degradation in the long sequence evaluation. Notably, on KITTI Odometry, our method achieves on average 1.68x lower ATE than LongStream, demonstrating its robustness on extended outdoor sequences.

AI.tldr: Info3R is an information-adaptive test-time training method for online 3D reconstruction that addresses frame importance and state saturation through dynamic state modulation and reset mechanisms, achieving 1.68x lower ATE than prior methods on KITTI Odometry.
AI.motivation: Existing transformer-based 3D reconstruction methods overlook two critical signals when processing long video streams: (1) the importance of each incoming frame, and (2) the information saturation of the model's internal state. This leads to performance degradation in extended outdoor sequences.
AI.method: Info3R introduces two key mechanisms: (1) Information-aware state update that modulates state update strength based on redundancy and informativeness of each frame, and (2) Dynamic state reset triggered by cumulative magnitude of state updates and model's prediction confidence, accompanied by anchor-to-world alignment to restore model's plasticity.
AI.result: The method achieves consistent improvements on camera pose estimation, video depth estimation, and 3D reconstruction tasks. On KITTI Odometry, it achieves 1.68x lower Average Trajectory Error (ATE) than LongStream, demonstrating robustness on extended outdoor sequences.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Info3R successfully mitigates performance degradation in long sequence evaluation by adaptively modulating state updates and dynamically resetting the model's internal state when saturation occurs, with anchor-to-world alignment ensuring consistent performance across extended video streams.

title: Beyond Kinematics: Benchmarking Simulation Fidelity for Muscle-Driven Imitation Learning
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables, submitted to ICRA 2027
summary: In this work, we conduct a systematic comparison of two state-of-the-art motion-imitation reinforcement learning (MIRL) pipelines, one built on SCONE/HyFyDy and one built on MuJoCo/MyoSim. HyFyDy emphasizes physiological realism through detailed musculotendon modeling, while MuJoCo prioritizes computational efficiency and scalable policy learning. While recent work has demonstrated that both pipelines reproduce human kinematics with high fidelity, it remains unclear if they accurately capture the underlying neuromuscular behavior that produced the movement. This limitation is particularly important for robotic assistive-device design and control, where outcome measures such as muscle activation patterns and metabolic cost are often used as optimization targets. To conduct a systematic comparison, our work compares both pipelines using a common set of human motion-capture and electromyography (EMG) measurements. The results find that while both pipelines produce similar kinematics with relative accuracy, the muscle activations from HyFyDy are more aligned with the experimental EMG, as supported by the average pooled (RMSE, r) values for muscle activations from HyFyDy and MuJoCo: (0.164, 0.4) and (0.344, 0.11), respectively. While we conclude that the more advanced physiological realism of HyFyDy currently makes it more suitable for musculoskeletal modeling, both require further development to bring physiological realism to GPU-parallelizable simulation environments and advance robotic assistive device design.

AI.tldr: This paper compares two motion-imitation RL pipelines (SCONE/HyFyDy vs MuJoCo/MyoSim) for reproducing human motion and neuromuscular behavior. While both achieve similar kinematics, HyFyDy's muscle activations better align with experimental EMG (RMSE 0.164, r=0.4 vs 0.344, r=0.11), making it more suitable for musculoskeletal modeling in assistive device design.
AI.motivation: To determine which pipeline better captures underlying neuromuscular behavior (not just kinematics), as this is critical for robotic assistive-device design where muscle activation patterns and metabolic cost are optimization targets.
AI.method: Systematic comparison using a common set of human motion-capture and electromyography (EMG) measurements, evaluating both kinematic accuracy and muscle activation alignment.
AI.result: Both pipelines produce similar high-fidelity kinematics. However, HyFyDy shows better muscle activation alignment with experimental EMG: (RMSE, r) = (0.164, 0.4) for HyFyDy vs (0.344, 0.11) for MuJoCo.
AI.conclusion: HyFyDy's advanced physiological realism makes it more suitable for musculoskeletal modeling. Both pipelines require further development to enable GPU-parallelizable simulation for advancing robotic assistive device design.

title: PRIME: Perception Feedback with Situational Memory Embeddings in VLA Models
summary: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving operate primarily through feedforward inference across the perception--reasoning--planning hierarchy. While modern architectures maintain temporal recurrence within the perceptual module, early perception remains blind to downstream reasoning and navigation goals, processing visual inputs agnostically without prioritizing cues informed by prior decisions. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces PRIME, a learned feedback mechanism that conditions the VLA perceptual queries on a novel Situational Memory. By aggregating latent representations of past perception, reasoning, navigation goals, and predicted behaviors across an L-step window via cross-attention, PRIME enables intent-driven perceptual attention at minimal computational cost, adding only a maximum of 29.7M parameters (0.41% of the 7.3B-parameter base model). Evaluated on the Bench2Drive closed-loop benchmark, PRIME achieves a state-of-the-art Driving Score of 82.47 (+4.73 over ORION) and a Success Rate of 60.00% (+5.38 percentage points), the highest reported Driving Score among published VLAs trained on Think2Drive demonstrations.

AI.tldr: PRIME is a lightweight feedback mechanism for autonomous driving VLAs that uses Situational Memory to enable intent-driven perceptual attention, aggregating past perception, reasoning, goals, and predicted behaviors via cross-attention.
AI.motivation: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use feedforward inference through perception-reasoning-planning hierarchy. The early perception stage processes visual inputs agnostically without considering downstream reasoning and navigation goals, missing important contextual cues informed by prior decisions.
AI.method: PRIME introduces a learned feedback mechanism that conditions VLA perceptual queries on a novel Situational Memory. It aggregates latent representations of past perception, reasoning, navigation goals, and predicted behaviors across an L-step window via cross-attention. This adds only max 29.7M parameters (0.41% of 7.3B-parameter base model).
AI.result: Evaluated on Bench2Drive closed-loop benchmark, PRIME achieves a state-of-the-art Driving Score of 82.47 (+4.73 over ORION) and a Success Rate of 60.00% (+5.38 percentage points), the highest reported Driving Score among published VLAs trained on Think2Drive demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: PRIME successfully bridges the gap between early perception and downstream reasoning/navigation goals by adding minimal computational overhead (0.41% of base model), achieving state-of-the-art performance on Bench2Drive benchmark with 4.73 points improvement in Driving Score over ORION.

title: Kinks vs. Smoothness: Identifiability of Real Analytic nICA for Laplace-like Sources
summary: Many machine learning systems try to explain complex data - like images or financial time series - in terms of hidden, independent factors that generated them. Recovering the true underlying factors, rather than some scrambled version of them, is the central challenge of nonlinear Independent Component Analysis (nICA). We prove identifiability (exact recovery) up to trivial ambiguities for real analytic generating functions when source probability density functions have a finite number of discontinuities in the first derivative. The Laplace distribution is the most prominent example satisfying this assumption. Our proof relies on the contrast between kinks in the source distribution and the smoothness of real analytic functions. Real analytic functions comprise a broad class of generating mechanisms, and can be approximated with Normalizing Flows or Variational Autoencoders with standard activation functions (e.g., tanh, softplus, GELU), so our result applies with minimal changes to existing training pipelines. We perform experiments on real and synthetic data with both Normalizing Flows and Variational Auto-Encoders demonstrating their identifiability properties. In experiments on CelebA data we recover several interpretable latent factors controlling unique attributes across the dataset.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses nonlinear Independent Component Analysis (nICA), proving that real analytic generating functions can be exactly recovered (up to trivial ambiguities) when source distributions have finite discontinuities in their first derivative (e.g., Laplace distribution). This result applies to Normalizing Flows and VAEs with standard activations, and experiments on synthetic and CelebA data demonstrate recovery of interpretable latent factors.
AI.motivation: The central challenge in nICA is recovering true underlying factors that generated complex data (like images or financial time series) rather than scrambled versions. Existing methods lack theoretical guarantees for exact recovery under realistic conditions.
AI.method: The proof exploits the contrast between "kinks" (discontinuities in first derivative) in source probability density functions and the smoothness of real analytic functions. The authors show that when source PDFs have a finite number of such kinks (with Laplace distribution as a prominent example), exact identifiability is achievable. This applies to Normalizing Flows and VAEs with standard activations (tanh, softplus, GELU).
AI.result: Theoretical identifiability (exact recovery up to trivial ambiguities) is proven for real analytic generating functions. Experiments on synthetic and real data (CelebA) demonstrate that the method recovers interpretable latent factors controlling unique attributes across the dataset.
AI.conclusion: This work provides theoretical foundations for nICA identifiability with practical relevance, showing that standard neural network architectures can be used for exact recovery of independent factors when source distributions have appropriate kinks. The CelebA experiments demonstrate real-world applicability in discovering interpretable latent representations.

title: Traffic Sign Recognition for Autonomous Driving Using Branched YOLOv2 and Geometric Features
summary: Traffic sign recognition (TSR) is an important perception task for autonomous driving and advanced driver-assistance systems, where a system must both localize traffic signs and determine their semantic classes efficiently. This work presents a TSR system based on YOLOv2 for simultaneous detection and classification. Two complementary modifications are studied. First, YOLOv2 is extended with intermediate prediction layers, forming a branched architecture that can terminate inference early for easy cases and reduce computation time. Both whole-image and cell-wise branching strategies are investigated. Second, geometric information is introduced to reduce classification errors between visually similar signs. An unsupervised Bayesian image-segmentation method produces binary representations that are compared with class-specific geometric templates inside YOLOv2 bounding boxes. This information is used either during inference or as an additional signal during training. A dedicated dataset is constructed by combining GTSDB and GTSRB samples using seamless cloning and controlled image transformations. Experiments cover ten traffic-sign classes, with 3,000 training and 300 test samples. The selected branched architecture reports 0.647 s runtime and 0.680 mAP, compared with 0.6607 s and 0.680 mAP for baseline YOLOv2. Geometric verification during inference increases mAP to 0.713, while the geometric-feature training variant achieves 0.697 mAP with a reported runtime of 0.6608 s.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a Traffic Sign Recognition (TSR) system based on YOLOv2 that performs simultaneous detection and classification. Two modifications are proposed: (1) a branched architecture with intermediate prediction layers for early termination to reduce computation, and (2) geometric verification using Bayesian image-segmentation combined with class-specific geometric templates to reduce classification errors between similar signs.
AI.motivation: Traffic sign recognition is crucial for autonomous driving and ADAS. The system must efficiently localize and classify signs. The motivation is to improve both accuracy and computational efficiency by addressing: (1) the computational cost of processing all image regions, and (2) the confusion between visually similar traffic signs.
AI.method: Two complementary modifications to YOLOv2: (1) Branched architecture with intermediate prediction layers - exploring both whole-image and cell-wise branching strategies for early termination on easy cases; (2) Geometric information integration - using unsupervised Bayesian image-segmentation to produce binary representations, compared with class-specific geometric templates within YOLOv2 bounding boxes. This geometric information is used either during inference or as an additional training signal. Dataset: combined GTSDB and GTSRB with seamless cloning and controlled transformations (10 classes, 3,000 training, 300 test samples).
AI.result: Baseline YOLOv2: 0.680 mAP, 0.6607s runtime. Branched architecture: 0.680 mAP, 0.647s runtime (slight speed improvement). Geometric verification during inference: 0.713 mAP (significant improvement). Geometric-feature training variant: 0.697 mAP, 0.6608s runtime.
AI.conclusion: The branched architecture provides marginal speed improvement with no accuracy loss. Geometric verification during inference significantly improves mAP from 0.680 to 0.713, demonstrating that incorporating geometric information is effective for reducing classification errors between visually similar signs. The training variant also shows improvement but is less effective than inference-time verification.

title: Joint Remaining Useful Life Prediction and Capacity Estimation of Lithium-Ion Batteries Using Partial-Charging Data
summary: Joint remaining useful life (RUL) prediction and capacity estimation require representations of both gradual degradation and recent battery behavior. This paper presents a cross-expert framework using partial-charging measurements without measured historical full-cycle capacity as an input. The RUL Expert encodes nominal 10-min segments from ten cycles sampled within a 30-cycle history using a pretrained gated recurrent unit (GRU) encoder, a two-dimensional convolutional neural network (2D-CNN), and a temporal GRU. The Capacity Expert processes statistical descriptors of nominal 40-min segments from ten consecutive cycles using a 2D-CNN and a Transformer. A feature-wise linear modulation module uses the short-term representation to condition the long-term representation for joint prediction. Training comprises supervised autoencoder pretraining, independent expert pretraining, and fusion training with frozen experts. On two public battery-aging datasets, the reference configuration achieves mean RUL root-mean-square errors of 143.69 and 161.10 cycles and capacity errors of 12.36 and 7.28mAh, respectively. On Dataset I, fusion reduces both mean errors relative to either standalone expert. The results demonstrate a trade-off between RUL and capacity accuracy: the proposed method attains the lowest reported RUL RMSE among the compared methods on both datasets, whereas several baselines yield lower capacity errors.

AI.tldr: A cross-expert framework for joint battery remaining useful life (RUL) prediction and capacity estimation using partial-charging measurements, without needing historical full-cycle capacity data. The framework combines an RUL Expert (GRU + 2D-CNN + temporal GRU) and a Capacity Expert (2D-CNN + Transformer), with feature-wise linear modulation to fuse short-term and long-term representations.
AI.motivation: Joint RUL prediction and capacity estimation require representations of both gradual degradation and recent battery behavior. Existing methods typically need measured historical full-cycle capacity, which is impractical. This work aims to enable accurate predictions using only partial-charging measurements.
AI.method: The framework uses two expert branches: (1) RUL Expert encodes nominal 10-min segments from ten cycles within a 30-cycle history using pretrained GRU encoder, 2D-CNN, and temporal GRU; (2) Capacity Expert processes statistical descriptors of nominal 40-min segments from ten consecutive cycles using 2D-CNN and Transformer. A feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) module conditions long-term representations using short-term representations. Training involves three stages: supervised autoencoder pretraining, independent expert pretraining, and fusion training with frozen experts.
AI.result: On two public battery-aging datasets, the reference configuration achieves mean RUL RMSE of 143.69 and 161.10 cycles and capacity errors of 12.36 and 7.28mAh. On Dataset I, fusion reduces both mean errors relative to either standalone expert. The method achieves the lowest reported RUL RMSE among compared methods on both datasets, though some baselines yield lower capacity errors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed cross-expert framework successfully performs joint RUL prediction and capacity estimation using only partial-charging data. It achieves state-of-the-art RUL prediction accuracy while demonstrating a trade-off between RUL and capacity accuracy. The fusion approach proves effective, particularly on Dataset I where it reduces errors for both tasks compared to standalone experts.

title: OmniVBench: A Benchmark and Large-Scale Dataset for Omni Reference-to-Video Generation
summary: Reference-to-video (R2V) generation is evolving toward increasingly general and versatile reference control, giving rise to the emerging paradigm of omni R2V generation. However, existing benchmarks fall short of these emerging capabilities: their test cases cover limited reference types and compositions, and their evaluation protocols largely assess holistic reference consistency, overlooking whether reference factors are properly preserved, disentangled, and routed. Meanwhile, the high cost of constructing omni R2V training data makes suitable training resources scarce. To address these gaps, we introduce OmniVBench and the Omni-R2V Dataset for evaluating and training omni R2V models. OmniVBench expands R2V evaluation across broader reference types, fine-grained control tasks, and richer reference compositions, covering 7 task families and 18 fine-grained tasks spanning content, motion, style, structure, narrative, and multi-reference settings. We introduce factor-grounded evaluation with 12,172 case-specific checklist items, assessing whether intended reference factors are faithfully preserved, correctly disentangled and bound to their targets, and properly realized according to the instruction. We further introduce the Omni-R2V Dataset, bringing industrial-grade training resources for diverse R2V tasks to the broader research community. Drawing primarily on a large-scale corpus of professional video footage, it comprises 340K processed training samples spanning diverse reference types and multi-reference compositions. We develop task-specific pipelines for reference-target pair construction, offering a practical and scalable recipe for omni R2V data construction. Extensive evaluation of advanced open- and closed-source R2V models reveals clear performance gaps across task families and evaluation dimensions on OmniVBench, highlighting remaining limitations of current R2V models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OmniVBench (evaluation benchmark) and Omni-R2V Dataset (340K training samples) for omni Reference-to-Video generation, addressing gaps in existing benchmarks that lack comprehensive reference type coverage and factor-level evaluation. The benchmark covers 7 task families, 18 fine-grained tasks, and uses factor-grounded evaluation with 12,172 checklist items to assess reference factor preservation, disentanglement, and routing.
AI.motivation: Existing R2V benchmarks are inadequate for emerging omni R2V capabilities: they cover limited reference types and compositions, and evaluate only holistic reference consistency rather than assessing whether reference factors are properly preserved, disentangled, and routed. Additionally, high costs make suitable training data scarce for omni R2V models.
AI.method: The paper develops task-specific pipelines for reference-target pair construction from professional video footage. OmniVBench implements factor-grounded evaluation with 12,172 case-specific checklist items assessing reference factor preservation, disentanglement, and proper routing according to instructions.
AI.result: Evaluation of advanced open- and closed-source R2V models reveals clear performance gaps across task families and evaluation dimensions on OmniVBench, highlighting remaining limitations of current R2V models in handling diverse reference types, fine-grained control, and multi-reference compositions.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces OmniVBench and the Omni-R2V Dataset to address critical gaps in R2V evaluation and training. OmniVBench provides comprehensive evaluation across 7 task families and 18 fine-grained tasks with 12,172 checklist items for factor-grounded evaluation. The Omni-R2V Dataset provides 340K training samples from professional video footage. Extensive testing reveals significant performance gaps in current R2V models, highlighting the need for improved reference preservation, disentanglement, and routing capabilities.

title: Learning to Move Cities: Deep Meta-Models and Reinforcement Policies for Calibration and Control in Urban Networks
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE 29th International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC), Naples, Italy. (c) 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted; permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses
summary: Urban transportation networks present complex optimization challenges spanning calibration of high-fidelity simulators and real-time operational control. This paper presents a shared latent-space framework that connects simulator calibration and reinforcement learning control through a common learned representation of urban traffic dynamics. First, we develop a combinatorial MLP-autoencoder architecture that learns low-dimensional manifolds linking simulator inputs (origin-destination demand, network parameters) to outputs (travel times, congestion patterns), enabling efficient Bayesian optimization for calibration. This approach demonstrates superior sample efficiency compared to traditional dimension reduction methods, achieving better fit to observational data within fixed computational budgets. Second, we implement a deep Q-learning agent with experience replay and target networks to optimize dynamic traffic assignment through scheduling and routing adjustments. In empirical evaluations on benchmark networks, our approach reduces system-wide travel times by up to 51% compared to baseline operations. The learned latent representation is not only used to reduce the dimensionality of Bayesian calibration, but is also incorporated into the reinforcement learning state representation, allowing the control policy to operate on compressed and calibrated traffic dynamics. This shared latent-space formulation provides a unified pathway from simulator calibration to adaptive operational control within intelligent transportation systems. Our results highlight the transformative potential of deep learning methods in urban mobility planning and management, particularly for large-scale networks where traditional optimization approaches face computational bottlenecks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a shared latent-space framework that connects urban traffic simulator calibration with reinforcement learning control through a common learned representation. The approach uses a combinatorial MLP-autoencoder for efficient Bayesian optimization calibration, and a deep Q-learning agent for dynamic traffic optimization, achieving up to 51% reduction in travel times.
AI.motivation: Urban transportation networks face complex optimization challenges in both calibrating high-fidelity simulators and achieving real-time operational control. Traditional approaches suffer from computational bottlenecks, especially for large-scale networks, and treat calibration and control as separate problems without synergy.
AI.method: The paper presents two main components: (1) A combinatorial MLP-autoencoder architecture that learns low-dimensional manifolds linking simulator inputs (origin-destination demand, network parameters) to outputs (travel times, congestion patterns), enabling efficient Bayesian optimization for calibration; (2) A deep Q-learning agent with experience replay and target networks to optimize dynamic traffic assignment through scheduling and routing adjustments. The learned latent representation is shared between both components.
AI.result: The calibration approach demonstrates superior sample efficiency compared to traditional dimension reduction methods, achieving better fit to observational data within fixed computational budgets. The control approach reduces system-wide travel times by up to 51% compared to baseline operations on benchmark networks.
AI.conclusion: The shared latent-space formulation provides a unified pathway from simulator calibration to adaptive operational control within intelligent transportation systems. Deep learning methods, particularly the proposed framework, have transformative potential in urban mobility planning and management, especially for large-scale networks where traditional optimization approaches face computational bottlenecks.

title: MintAct: A Unified Visual Agent for Digital Environments
summary: We present MintAct, a family of vision-language models that unifies UI grounding, multi-step navigation across mobile, desktop, and web, and visual tool use, trained at 2B, 4B, and 8B scales. Through careful design of our environments, data, and training recipes, MintAct models match the performance of per-domain specialists across all of these capabilities. To enable this, we develop a scalable environment and reinforcement learning (RL) infrastructure. On the environment side, we host hundreds of concurrent instances across heterogeneous per-domain backends, serving both trajectory data collection and online RL. To enable efficient and scalable RL training, an asynchronous framework keeps explicit control over the cross-domain training distribution and remains stable under noisy environment feedback and off-policy drift. Experimental results show that MintAct achieves state-of-the-art performance (48.9 on OSWorld-Verified) across a wide range of benchmarks at comparable model sizes.

AI.tldr: MintAct is a family of vision-language models (2B, 4B, 8B scales) that unifies UI grounding, multi-step navigation across mobile/desktop/web, and visual tool use, achieving state-of-the-art performance (48.9 on OSWorld-Verified) by matching per-domain specialists through carefully designed environments, data, and training recipes with scalable RL infrastructure.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to unify multiple UI-related capabilities (grounding, navigation, tool use) across different platforms (mobile, desktop, web) into a single model family, rather than having separate specialist models for each domain.
AI.method: The method involves developing scalable environment and RL infrastructure with hundreds of concurrent instances across heterogeneous per-domain backends, using an asynchronous framework with explicit control over cross-domain training distribution to handle noisy environment feedback and off-policy drift.
AI.result: MintAct achieves state-of-the-art performance at 48.9 on OSWorld-Verified across a wide range of benchmarks at comparable model sizes, matching the performance of per-domain specialists across all capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MintAct family demonstrates that unified vision-language models can match or exceed domain-specific specialists across UI grounding, multi-step navigation, and visual tool use tasks through careful environment design, data curation, and stable asynchronous RL training.

title: RACER: Role-Aligned Competence Estimation for Human-AI Routing
summary: Learning to defer asks a predictive system when to act autonomously and when to defer to a human expert. Population-adaptive deferral extends this problem to unseen experts using a small context set of expert behavior. Neural context encoders such as L2D-Pop can be query-dependent, but may learn routing shortcuts tied to absolute class coordinates. Identity-Free Deferral (IFD) removes such shortcuts through role-indexed classwise competence profiles, but its estimates are constant within each class and cannot capture instance-level expert specialization. We propose RACER---Role-Aligned Competence Estimation for Routing---a role-relative framework for estimating an unseen expert's competence from context. RACER estimates the posterior-predictive probability that the expert is correct on a query under each candidate class role, then combines these estimates with the model posterior to obtain the Bayes-relevant expert-correctness probability. Nonparametric and neural kernel-pooling estimators use candidate-role relations, shared aggregation, and symmetric summaries, excluding absolute class-identity channels. We prove coherent class-relabelling invariance, derive a Bayes-aligned deferral surrogate, and give a plug-in regret bound relating routing regret to classifier and competence-estimation error. On controlled synthetic benchmarks, including a PathMNIST histopathology context-scaling study with simulated experts, RACER benefits from additional context under hidden subtype dependence and gives the strongest aggregate performance on a separately sampled unseen-expert split in the CIFAR-100 synthetic experiments. On the radiologist and human--AI chest-radiography benchmarks (VinDr-CXR and CheXpert), the RACER family is competitive or best in budget-swept deferral, with calibration results varying across metrics and datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes RACER, a role-relative framework for estimating unseen experts' competence in learning-to-defer settings. It addresses limitations of prior work (L2D-Pop and IFD) by using candidate-role relations and symmetric summaries while excluding absolute class-identity channels, with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical performance on medical imaging benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current neural context encoders for population-adaptive deferral may learn routing shortcuts tied to absolute class coordinates. Identity-Free Deferral (IFD) removes these shortcuts but provides constant competence estimates within each class, failing to capture instance-level expert specialization. There is a need for a framework that can estimate an unseen expert's competence from context while maintaining class-relabelling invariance and capturing instance-level nuances.
AI.method: RACER estimates the posterior-predictive probability that the expert is correct on a query under each candidate class role, then combines these estimates with the model posterior to obtain the Bayes-relevant expert-correctness probability. It uses nonparametric and neural kernel-pooling estimators with candidate-role relations, shared aggregation, and symmetric summaries, excluding absolute class-identity channels. The approach provides: (1) coherent class-relabelling invariance, (2) a Bayes-aligned deferral surrogate, and (3) a plug-in regret bound relating routing regret to classifier and competence-estimation error.
AI.result: On controlled synthetic benchmarks including PathMNIST histopathology context-scaling study with simulated experts, RACER benefits from additional context under hidden subtype dependence and achieves the strongest aggregate performance on a separately sampled unseen-expert split in CIFAR-100 synthetic experiments. On real-world radiologist and human-AI chest-radiography benchmarks (VinDr-CXR and CheXpert), the RACER family is competitive or best in budget-swept deferral, with calibration results varying across metrics and datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed RACER framework successfully addresses the challenge of estimating unseen expert competence in learning-to-defer systems. By using role-relative representations instead of absolute class identities, it achieves class-relabelling invariance and captures instance-level specialization. The method demonstrates strong empirical performance across synthetic and real-world medical imaging benchmarks, making it a promising approach for practical human-AI collaboration in healthcare settings.

title: Time series generation with spectrally aligned latent flow matching
summary: Latent flow models have proven to be a reliable and cost-effective method for time series generation. However, the latent compression induces unwanted artefacts, such as a spectral mismatch with respect to the underlying dataset, thus hindering their use as training surrogates. In this article, we propose a spectrally-aligned latent-flow time series generator, where the latent space for flow matching is trained to preserve dynamical properties that are relevant for the suitability of synthetic samples. We find that incorporating fine-tuning losses based on canonical signal representations such as the Fourier, wavelet and signature transforms helps overcome these issues. The interpretability of these transformations allows us to ensure that the synthetic signals are aligned with the true ones in terms of relevant features, such as smoothness or targeted spectral content, as opposed to relying on pointwise reconstruction losses only. We compare the proposed aligned models against a base latent-flow model and the state of the art over real-world long-range univariate and multivariate benchmark datasets. Our quantitative results validate the superiority of the proposed method in terms of its performance on metrics reflecting signal realness and computational efficiency, while being aligned to the training set with respect to its local structure.

AI.tldr: A spectrally-aligned latent-flow time series generator that addresses spectral mismatch artefacts by incorporating fine-tuning losses based on Fourier, wavelet, and signature transforms to preserve dynamical properties relevant for synthetic sample quality.
AI.motivation: Latent flow models are cost-effective for time series generation but suffer from spectral mismatch artefacts due to latent compression, limiting their use as training surrogates.
AI.method: Proposes spectrally-aligned latent-flow model trained to preserve dynamical properties using fine-tuning losses based on canonical signal representations (Fourier, wavelet, and signature transforms) to ensure synthetic signals align with true ones in terms of smoothness and spectral content.
AI.result: Superior performance over base latent-flow model and state-of-the-art methods on real-world long-range univariate and multivariate benchmark datasets, demonstrating improved signal realness, computational efficiency, and alignment with training set's local structure.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating interpretable signal representation losses (Fourier, wavelet, signature) effectively overcomes spectral mismatch issues in latent flow models, providing a more reliable method for time series generation.

title: Assessment of Machine Learning-Based Critical Heat Flux Models in the CTF Subchannel Code for Square Rod Bundle Prediction
summary:
The prediction of critical heat flux (CHF), a key safety-related quantity in nuclear thermal hydraulics, remains an important challenge due to its direct relationship with fuel performance and reactor safety. Recent studies have demonstrated that relative to traditional empirical correlations and lookup tables (LUTs), machine learning (ML) methods can substantially improve CHF prediction accuracy. Most ML-based CHF models, however, have been developed and evaluated using tube databases, leaving their applicability to reactor-relevant rod bundle geometries largely unexplored.
  This study evaluates ML-based CHF models deployed within the CTF subchannel code using the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) rod bundle CHF database. Both pure and hybrid residual correction models are considered in local and semilocal formulations. The tube-trained ML CHF models generally transferred favorably to rod bundle applications and outperformed traditional CHF methods across most geometries and operating conditions. The local hybrid LUT model produced the strongest overall performance, and the semilocal pure ML model remained highly competitive. Comparison against the Bowring correlation, W-3 correlation, and 2006 Groeneveld LUT demonstrated that substantial improvements in rod bundle CHF prediction are possible even when models are trained exclusively on tube data. These findings provide one of the first large-scale assessments of ML-based CHF models in square rod bundles within a production-level subchannel analysis environment and support their broader application in reactor thermal hydraulic analysis.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates machine learning-based critical heat flux (CHF) models trained on tube data but applied to rod bundle geometries using the CTF subchannel code and EPRI rod bundle database. The local hybrid LUT model achieved the best performance, outperforming traditional correlations like Bowring, W-3, and the 2006 Groeneveld lookup table.
AI.motivation: Traditional CHF prediction methods (empirical correlations and lookup tables) have limitations in accuracy. While ML methods have shown promise for tube geometries, their applicability to reactor-relevant rod bundle geometries remained largely unexplored. This study addresses this gap by evaluating how tube-trained ML models transfer to rod bundle applications.
AI.method: The study deployed ML-based CHF models within the CTF subchannel code and evaluated them using the EPRI rod bundle CHF database. Both pure and hybrid residual correction models were tested in local and semilocal formulations. Performance was compared against traditional CHF methods including the Bowring correlation, W-3 correlation, and 2006 Groeneveld lookup table.
AI.result: Tube-trained ML CHF models transferred favorably to rod bundle applications and outperformed traditional CHF methods across most geometries and operating conditions. The local hybrid LUT model produced the strongest overall performance, while the semilocal pure ML model remained highly competitive. Substantial improvements in rod bundle CHF prediction were achieved even when models were trained exclusively on tube data.
AI.conclusion: ML-based CHF models trained on tube data can successfully transfer to rod bundle geometries and provide improved prediction accuracy compared to traditional methods. This represents one of the first large-scale assessments of ML-based CHF models in square rod bundles within a production-level subchannel analysis environment, supporting their broader application in reactor thermal hydraulic analysis.

title: Abstention and Noise Filtering: Two Missing Primitives of Softmax Attention
comment: 21 pages (8 pages main text plus appendices), 5 figures, 12 tables
summary: Gating the value pathway of attention reportedly improves language model pretraining, and prior studies disagree on why. We argue and provide experimental evidence that such gates supply two different things that softmax attention lacks: abstention and noise filtering. The first is abstention, which allows an attention head to output nothing, bypassing the requirement that attention weights must sum to one. The second is noise filtering, which allows the value pathway of an attention head to suppress interference from superposed features in the residual stream. In our experiments in matched models from 10M to 350M parameters, we supply abstention through a learned per-head sink logit in the softmax and noise filtering through a gate on each value. We report three empirical findings. First, the benefit of abstention, measured as the reduction in validation loss relative to a matched baseline, declines as models grow, whereas the benefit of noise filtering increases with scale. In particular, abstention accounts for nearly all of the gain from gating at 10M and filtering for most of it at 350M. Second, the best model at every scale is the one with both primitives built in. Third, injecting controlled interference into the values a head reads confirms that the gate removes such interference, and reveals that each of the two gate forms we study has a characteristic blind spot. Supplying both primitives adds negligible parameters and remains compatible with the key-value cache.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why gating mechanisms improve language model pretraining, arguing that gates provide two capabilities absent in standard softmax attention: abstention (bypassing attention weight normalization) and noise filtering (suppressing interference in the value pathway). Experiments across models from 10M to 350M parameters reveal that abstention benefits diminish with scale while noise filtering benefits increase, with the best performance at every scale achieved by combining both primitives.
AI.motivation: Prior studies disagree on why gating the value pathway of attention improves language model pretraining. This paper aims to resolve this disagreement by proposing that gates serve two distinct functions: abstention and noise filtering.
AI.method: The authors conducted experiments using matched models ranging from 10M to 350M parameters. They implemented abstention via a learned per-head sink logit in the softmax and noise filtering via a gate on each value. They also injected controlled interference into values to verify the gate's interference suppression capability.
AI.result: Three empirical findings: (1) Abstention's benefit declines with model scale while noise filtering's benefit increases—at 10M parameters, abstention accounts for nearly all gain, while at 350M, filtering accounts for most; (2) The best model at every scale combines both primitives; (3) Each gate form has a characteristic blind spot, but both together add negligible parameters and remain compatible with key-value cache.
AI.conclusion: Gating improves attention through two distinct mechanisms that scale differently: abstention provides early-stage benefits while noise filtering becomes more important at larger scales. Combining both primitives yields optimal performance at all scales, with minimal parameter overhead.

title: COMPLEX: A Closed-Form Certified Embedding of Multiparameter Persistence Modules
summary: Every multiparameter persistence vectorization we know of carries a one-sided Lipschitz upper bound and nothing below it: without a lower gauge there is no sense in which the features are faithful, and no per-prediction guarantee can be built on them. This paper supplies the missing side. COMPLEX is a closed-form, training-free embedding of multiparameter modules -- slice the module along a fixed near-diagonal net, embed each slice barcode by the certified PLACE/PALACE landmark map, concatenate. Under a checkable witnessing-slice coherence condition, holding on 100% of audited pairs on Orbit5k, a single slice carries a closed-form lower gauge: separated modules stay separated in the embedding. With the standard upper bound this gives, to our knowledge, the first two-sided distortion bound for a multiparameter feature map, making faithfulness measurable. Measuring it, we find the floor tight within a small factor of realized distances yet operationally local: an RBF-SVM reaches 91% where 1-NN reaches 78% on the same features. Local per-prediction certification therefore fails for a structural reason common to every landmark embedding whose lower gauge is witnessed by one coordinate. With no learned embedding and no held-out calibration -- only a cross-validated SVM head -- COMPLEX sets the state of the art on both Orbit benchmarks (91.95% on Orbit5k, 92.98% on Orbit100k), level with or above Euler-characteristic surfaces and above transformers and graphcode. On graphs it exceeds GRIL on all four shared molecular benchmarks with one fixed configuration, including the only multiparameter method to clear COX2's majority baseline by more than three points. Closed-form selection -- of the landmark radius, the kernel (certificate-preserving), and the bifiltration set -- buys further accuracy; gradient-shaped adaptation buys none.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a fundamental gap in multiparameter persistence vectorization: the lack of lower bounds (lower gauge) in existing methods. The authors propose COMPLEX, a closed-form training-free embedding that achieves the first two-sided distortion bound for multiparameter features by combining slice barcodes with certified PLACE/PALADE landmark maps under a witnessing-slice coherence condition.
AI.motivation: Every multiparameter persistence vectorization lacks a lower gauge, meaning there's no guarantee that separated modules remain separated in the embedding. This prevents per-prediction guarantees and makes features unfaithful. The paper aims to supply the missing lower bound to enable measurable faithfulness.
AI.method: COMPLEX works by: (1) slicing the multiparameter module along a fixed near-diagonal net; (2) embedding each slice barcode using the certified PLACE/PALACE landmark map; (3) concatenating the results. Under a checkable witnessing-slice coherence condition (holding on 100% of audited Orbit5k pairs), a single slice carries a closed-form lower gauge. No learned embedding or held-out calibration is used.
AI.result: COMPLEX achieves state-of-the-art results: 91.95% on Orbit5k and 92.98% on Orbit100k. It exceeds GRIL on all four shared molecular benchmarks, being the only multiparameter method to clear COX2's majority baseline by >3 points. The lower bound is verified to be floor-tight within a small factor of realized distances. However, local per-prediction certification fails due to a structural reason common to landmark embeddings with one-coordinate lower gauge.
AI.conclusion: COMPLEX provides the first two-sided distortion bound for multiparameter feature maps, making faithfulness measurable. The structural limitation of local per-prediction certification is inherent to landmark embeddings with single-coordinate lower bounds. The method outperforms transformers, graphcode, and Euler-characteristic surfaces using only cross-validated SVM without learned embeddings.

title: $λ$-Controlled GRPO: Turning Flow-Matching Ratio Instability into a Budgeted Resource
summary: Reinforcement learning is increasingly used to align image generators with reward signals, and Flow-GRPO recently extended this paradigm to flow-matching models by treating the denoising sampler as a stochastic policy that can be optimized from reward feedback. Training in this setting is unstable in a way specific to multi-step denoising: the policy update changes systematically across denoising steps, with importance ratios drifting below one, becoming increasingly dispersed, clipping at different rates, and leaving fewer usable samples late in training. Prior work treats these effects as separate failure modes and addresses each with a hand-tuned stabilizer. We show instead that they arise from a single per-step quantity, which we call path variance. This quantity is determined exactly by the sampler's Gaussian transition kernel and can be estimated cheaply during training. This reframes instability as a resource that can be measured and budgeted rather than a collection of symptoms to repair. Our method, $λ$-Controlled GRPO, calibrates importance-ratio behavior from this predicted law rather than from noisy empirical statistics, and allocates gradient effort across denoising steps according to their predicted cost. The two scales governing the update are fixed by standard policy choices rather than introduced as free tuning parameters. On a text-to-image model under two reward settings, rendering difficult target text scored by optical character recognition and matching human preferences scored by a preference model, $λ$-Controlled GRPO improves both text accuracy and preference reward over the strongest empirical stabilizer. It also keeps late-step path variance within its intended budget, precisely where the baseline systematically overshoots. The result is a Flow-GRPO update calibrated by its own transition law rather than stabilized after instability appears.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses training instability in Flow-GRPO (reinforcement learning for flow-matching image generators) by identifying "path variance" as the root cause of multiple instability symptoms across denoising steps. The proposed λ-Controlled GRPO method calibrates importance ratios using predicted transition laws rather than empirical statistics, improving text-to-image generation quality on OCR and preference-based reward tasks.
AI.motivation: Multi-step denoising in Flow-GRPO suffers from training instability manifested through drifting importance ratios, dispersion, uneven clipping, and sample attrition. Prior work treats these as separate issues requiring individual stabilizers. This paper seeks to unify these symptoms under a single explanatory quantity.
AI.method: The authors identify "path variance" as the single per-step quantity determining all instability symptoms. This quantity is derived from the sampler's Gaussian transition kernel and can be estimated cheaply during training. λ-Controlled GRPO calibrates importance-ratio behavior according to this predicted law rather than noisy empirical statistics, and allocates gradient effort across denoising steps based on predicted cost. The two governing scales are fixed by standard policy choices.
AI.result: On a text-to-image model under two reward settings (OCR-based text accuracy and preference model scoring), λ-Controlled GRPO improves both text accuracy and preference reward over the strongest empirical stabilizer. It maintains late-step path variance within its intended budget, where the baseline systematically overshoots.
AI.conclusion: The work reframes instability as a measurable and budgetable resource rather than a collection of symptoms. By calibrating the Flow-GRPO update using its own transition law rather than post-hoc stabilization, the method achieves better performance on text rendering and human preference alignment tasks.

title: Available Guardrails: Certifying Selective Prediction across ML Systems
summary: A selective predictor acts as a safety gate: it returns an output only when the prediction appears sufficiently trustworthy. Deployments increasingly require this reliability to be certified at a target precision for every reporting unit of interest, such as a tool, policy label, or patient subgroup. The main difficulty is often not whether a granted certificate is valid, but whether finite calibration data can produce one at all. As the gate becomes safer or more fine-grained, some units may receive too little evidence to certify. We make this notion of availability computable through classical exact-binomial inversion and formulate reporting-partition selection, under a fixed group order, as a dynamic program that exposes the trade-off among safety, granularity, and served traffic. The resulting frontier reveals a large population opportunity that finite-sample estimation nearly erases: a truth-informed planner gains $0.157$ mean coverage over support balancing, whereas a naive estimator recovers only $0.005$, making recovery from finite data the central challenge. Constructing candidate partitions on one planning split and selecting among them on another recovers part of this gap, improving mean coverage over support balancing by $0.060$, with the direction reproduced in $59$ of $60$ model effects across three intent-routing datasets and two architectures. A complementary validity-preserving lever, reallocating the familywise error budget across reporting units, recovers additional coverage both with population quantities and noisy estimates. The same frontier recurs, with predictor-specific ceilings, across LLM tool-calling, content moderation, lesion classification, and recommendation. Certified availability is therefore a plannable deployment resource that determines when a safety gate can be certified, at what granularity, and over how much traffic.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "certified availability" as a plannable deployment resource for selective predictors (safety gates). The authors use exact-binomial inversion to determine when a safety gate can be certified, at what granularity, and over how much traffic. The key challenge is that finite calibration data may be insufficient to certify reliability, especially for safer or more fine-grained partitions.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that deployments increasingly require certified reliability at target precision for every reporting unit of interest (tools, policy labels, patient subgroups). While validity of certificates is manageable, the fundamental difficulty is whether finite calibration data can produce certificates at all - as safety gates become stricter or more granular, some units receive insufficient evidence to certify.
AI.method: The authors formulate reporting-partition selection under fixed group order as a dynamic program using classical exact-binomial inversion. They explore two complementary approaches: (1) constructing candidate partitions on one planning split and selecting among them on another; (2) reallocating the familywise error budget across reporting units to preserve validity while improving coverage.
AI.result: A truth-informed planner gains 0.157 mean coverage over support balancing, while a naive estimator recovers only 0.005. Partition selection on held-out data improves mean coverage by 0.060, with direction reproduced in 59 of 60 model effects across three intent-routing datasets and two architectures. Reallocating familywise error budget provides additional coverage gains. The frontier recurs across LLM tool-calling, content moderation, lesion classification, and recommendation with predictor-specific ceilings.
AI.conclusion: Certified availability is a plannable deployment resource that determines: (1) when a safety gate can be certified, (2) at what granularity, and (3) over how much traffic. Recovery from finite data is the central challenge - the gap between oracle and naive estimators is large (0.157 vs 0.005), and practical methods can partially close this gap through intelligent partition selection and error budget reallocation.

title: Particle Competition and Cooperation for Robust Graph Convolutional Network Learning Under Label Noise
comment: Submitted to Neurocomputing. Code and experimental results are publicly available at https://github.com/fbreve/PCC-GCN and https://github.com/fbreve/NoisyGL
summary: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are highly sensitive to label noise, since corrupted supervision can propagate through the graph and degrade learned node representations. This work proposes PCC+GCN, a hybrid framework that uses Particle Competition and Cooperation (PCC) as a graph-based label-refinement stage before GCN training. PCC identifies suspicious labeled nodes through particle domination dynamics and determines whether their labels should be preserved, removed, or reassigned before GCN training. The framework also allows the graph used by PCC to be augmented with feature-based $k$-nearest-neighbor edges, while the GCN itself is trained on the original graph structure and node features. The proposed method was evaluated on ten graph datasets from the NoisyGL benchmark under conventional Uniform, Pair, and Random label noise, as well as under instance-dependent label noise. A detailed hyperparameter analysis was also conducted on Cora, CiteSeer, and PubMed. Under conventional noise, PCC+GCN achieved the highest overall average accuracy and the best average rank among the evaluated methods, with an average gain of $1.67$ percentage points over the baseline GCN across the clean setting and all noisy scenarios. Under instance-dependent noise, PCC+GCN remained competitive with the best-performing robust methods while requiring substantially lower execution time, being the fastest robust method on eight of the ten datasets. The results indicate that PCC-based label refinement provides an effective and computationally efficient preprocessing strategy for improving GCN robustness under noisy supervision.

AI.tldr: PCC+GCN is a hybrid framework that uses Particle Competition and Cooperation (PCC) as a label-refinement stage before GCN training to improve robustness against label noise. It identifies and handles suspicious labeled nodes before training, and can augment the graph with feature-based k-nearest-neighbor edges.
AI.motivation: Graph Convolutional Networks are highly sensitive to label noise because corrupted supervision can propagate through the graph and degrade learned node representations. There was a need for a method to clean or refine noisy labels before GCN training.
AI.method: The proposed PCC+GCN framework uses PCC (Particle Competition and Cooperation) as a graph-based label-refinement stage before GCN training. PCC identifies suspicious labeled nodes through particle domination dynamics and determines whether their labels should be preserved, removed, or reassigned. The framework allows the graph used by PCC to be augmented with feature-based k-nearest-neighbor edges, while the GCN is trained on the original graph structure and node features.
AI.result: Under conventional noise (Uniform, Pair, and Random), PCC+GCN achieved the highest overall average accuracy and best average rank, with an average gain of 1.67 percentage points over baseline GCN. Under instance-dependent noise, PCC+GCN remained competitive while being the fastest robust method on 8 of 10 datasets.
AI.conclusion: PCC-based label refinement provides an effective and computationally efficient preprocessing strategy for improving GCN robustness under noisy supervision.

title: Benchmarking World Models for Continual Learning on Compositional Tasks
summary: A desirable property of a world model is the ability to learn continually across tasks, adapting to new environments without forgetting what the agent has already learnt. In particular, the ability to retain and reuse knowledge obtained from prior experiences underpins an agent's ability to efficiently adapt to novel environments, as the dynamics of the physical world can often be described in recurring mechanisms. However, the world model's measure of adaptation entangles two abilities: the speed and capacity to learn unseen tasks, and the reuse of knowledge already acquired, since incoming tasks carry novel content alongside what recurs. In order to isolate knowledge reuse from prior experiences, we propose a compositional continual learning benchmark for world models in robot manipulation. Specifically, we design each task curriculum with compositional tasks that combine aspects of the tasks seen in the sequence. We further factorise this composition along the axes of action and perception to better understand how different input modalities bottleneck knowledge reuse. We evaluate state-of-the-art world models under canonical continual learning methods, alongside a modular world model whose dynamics backbone contains explicitly reusable components. Results show that modularity balances reuse against forgetting better than conventional methods, but none solve the problem fully, leaving clear room for continual world models built to reuse without forgetting. More details are available on our project website: https://object814.github.io/Compositional-Continual-Learning/.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a compositional continual learning benchmark for world models in robot manipulation that factors task composition along action and perception axes to isolate knowledge reuse from prior experiences. The study evaluates state-of-the-art world models under canonical continual learning methods alongside a modular world model with explicitly reusable components.
AI.motivation: Current world models measure adaptation by entangling two distinct abilities: learning speed/capacity for unseen tasks and reuse of previously acquired knowledge. This entanglement makes it difficult to understand how well agents actually reuse prior knowledge. The authors aim to create a benchmark that can isolate knowledge reuse from prior experiences in robot manipulation tasks.
AI.method: The authors design a compositional continual learning benchmark where each task curriculum contains compositional tasks that combine aspects of previously seen tasks. They factorize the composition along two axes: action and perception, to understand how different input modalities bottleneck knowledge reuse. They evaluate state-of-the-art world models using canonical continual learning methods, and also test a modular world model with explicitly reusable components in its dynamics backbone.
AI.result: Modularity balances reuse against forgetting better than conventional continual learning methods, but none of the approaches fully solve the problem. There remains clear room for improvement in continual world models that can reuse knowledge without forgetting.
AI.conclusion: The proposed compositional benchmark successfully isolates knowledge reuse from prior experiences. While modular approaches show promise in balancing reuse and forgetting, the problem remains unsolved, indicating a need for future work on continual world models specifically designed to reuse knowledge without experiencing catastrophic forgetting.

title: BrainWideBench: Benchmarking large-scale pretraining and across-animal transfer in multi-region neural recordings
summary: Advances in large-scale neural recording have made it possible to collect data across many animals and distributed brain regions, raising the question of whether this scale can be exploited to learn general-purpose neural representations transferable across diverse downstream tasks. Yet, progress toward this goal has been limited by fragmented evaluation protocols and a narrow focus on individual task domains. Here, we present BrainWideBench, a benchmark for evaluating across-animal transfer on multi-region neural recordings, built on the International Brain Laboratory Brainwide Map dataset of neural and behavioral recordings spanning 276 brain regions from 139 mice performing a sensory-guided decision-making task. The benchmark is organized around three complementary task suites that evaluate whether learned representations support downstream decoding of behavior, can predict masked or future neural activity, and can recover biologically meaningful anatomical organization. With this benchmark, we systematically evaluate pretraining methods across transfer settings, including finetuning on downstream objectives and zero-shot generalization to unseen animals. Our results confirm pretraining improves performance over matched single-session baselines, but we show current methods exhibit heterogeneity in transfer capabilities: gains depend strongly on the alignment between pretraining objectives and downstream tasks.
