No single approach performs uniformly well across all three suites, and most methods are designed to only address a subset of them. Together, these findings suggest that learning representations that jointly generalize across behavior, dynamics, and anatomy remains an open challenge. By providing a unified and reproducible evaluation suite, BrainWideBench establishes a framework for measuring progress toward general-purpose models of the mouse brain.

AI.tldr: BrainWideBench is a benchmark for evaluating general-purpose neural representations across animals and brain regions, using the IBL Brainwide Map dataset (276 regions, 139 mice). The benchmark comprises three task suites evaluating behavior decoding, neural activity prediction, and anatomical organization recovery. Results show pretraining helps but no single method excels across all tasks, highlighting that learning jointly generalizable representations remains an open challenge.
AI.motivation: Advances in large-scale neural recording enable multi-animal, multi-region data collection, but progress toward general-purpose neural representations has been hampered by fragmented evaluation protocols and narrow task focus. A unified benchmark is needed to systematically evaluate transfer learning across diverse downstream tasks.
AI.method: The authors built BrainWideBench on the IBL Brainwide Map dataset (276 brain regions, 139 mice, sensory-guided decision-making task). They designed three complementary task suites: (1) behavioral decoding, (2) masked/future neural activity prediction, and (3) anatomical organization recovery. They evaluated various pretraining methods under transfer settings including finetuning and zero-shot generalization to unseen animals.
AI.result: Pretraining improves performance over matched single-session baselines. However, current methods exhibit heterogeneous transfer capabilities: gains strongly depend on alignment between pretraining objectives and downstream tasks. No single approach performs uniformly well across all three task suites, and most methods are designed to address only a subset of them.
AI.conclusion: Learning representations that jointly generalize across behavior, dynamics, and anatomy remains an open challenge. BrainWideBench provides a unified, reproducible evaluation framework for measuring progress toward general-purpose models of the mouse brain.

title: Training-Adaptive Convolutional Sparse Coding via Information Bottleneck for Robust Visual Representation
summary: Visual signals require compact yet sufficient representations for robust downstream prediction. Convolutional sparse coding (CSC) provides an explicit mechanism for suppressing redundant components while preserving signal content, but its sparsity coefficient is typically fixed and manually selected. We propose a training-adaptive convolutional sparse coding framework for robust visual signal representation. Specifically, we unfold the CSC optimization with the Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm (FISTA) and treat the sparsity coefficient as a differentiable variable jointly learned with the network parameters. From the information bottleneck perspective, this coefficient controls the trade-off between information retention and compression: the sparsity term promotes compact representations, while the reconstruction term together with task loss preserves task-relevant signal content. We further introduce a label-free post-training strategy that adjusts the compression strength for corrupted inputs with the main network parameters fixed. Experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet demonstrate competitive clean-data recognition and greatly improved robustness under different input perturbations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a training-adaptive convolutional sparse coding framework that learns the sparsity coefficient as a differentiable variable jointly with network parameters. It also introduces a label-free post-training strategy to enhance robustness for corrupted inputs. The method achieves competitive performance on clean data while significantly improving robustness under various input perturbations.
AI.motivation: Traditional convolutional sparse coding (CSC) uses fixed, manually selected sparsity coefficients, which cannot adapt to different data distributions or training objectives. Visual signals require compact yet sufficient representations for robust downstream prediction, but there's a trade-off between information retention and compression that current methods don't address adaptively.
AI.method:
1) Unfold the CSC optimization using the Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm (FISTA) to make it differentiable
2) Treat the sparsity coefficient as a learnable parameter jointly optimized with network parameters during training
3) Apply information bottleneck perspective - the coefficient controls the trade-off between reconstruction quality and sparsity
4) Introduce a label-free post-training strategy that adjusts compression strength for corrupted inputs while keeping main network parameters fixed
AI.result: Experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet demonstrate: (1) competitive clean-data recognition accuracy, and (2) greatly improved robustness under different input perturbations (corrupted/noisy inputs).
AI.conclusion: The proposed training-adaptive CSC framework successfully learns optimal sparsity coefficients during training, providing an effective mechanism to balance information retention and compression. The additional post-training strategy further enhances robustness for corrupted inputs without requiring labels. This work bridges traditional sparse coding with modern deep learning, offering a principled approach to robust visual representation learning.
